This is a beautiful and very immersive game. While the main goal is obviously hunting, there's also a big focus on exploration, and there's even a basic RPG-style character leveling system. If you enjoy games like The Long Dark or "walking simulators", you'll definitely enjoy this game.
The game doesn't strive for total realism, but makes some concessions in order to be enjoyable and playable. I think this is a good thing, as total realism would make it too frustrating for most players. It still requires quite a bit of patience and skill as it is. The AI can be exploited for easy kills, but you'd only spoil the fun for yourself. It's more of a sandbox game where you have to make up the story as you go.
My only concern would be the DLC's, and especially the first one (the tents), which was overpriced and should have been in the game from the start. If the developer wants to win over more positive reviews, they will have to release more content for free to make up the buggy state of the game at launch.

Bad pacing, terrible checkpoint placement, a story that at first glance looks deep but isn't. Buy it on sale if you really want, but $30 can be better spent on other games.
The game has so many issues, but at half the price of a full shooter it gets that as a plus.
The story would probably hold up much better if the immersion and pacing wasn't broken so horribly on chapter 6 with a nigh-impassable section on hard or insane difficulties. If you play on normal or easy, the game might hold your attention, but the combat doesn't really get hard enough for a decent FPS player until 3 chapters after this game breaking "Freebird" scene.
The settings menu is... barely adequate. Options such as borderless windowed are not available, despite the game crashing if you attempt to alt-tab out when in fullscreen.
Gunplay is above average, but the cover system is more of a hindrance than help in most situations.
Major plot decisions are obvious in their existence, but often have not obvious way of how to trigger them until you read online. Additionally, despite nonlethal grenades and melee attacks existing, you cannot subdue enemies without killing them.
The game tries to be more than it is, and in a high-school literature level analysis it works. If you don't look into the game at all, it seems like a terrible shooter, if you look into the meaning slightly it feels like a work of art, if you look into it really deeply (or play on hard mode and lose the immersion thanks to a certain helicopter) it all falls apart.

The story - which to be said, doesn't make pretty much any sense until you reach the end - was quite intense and brutal in it's way to show the darker side of the war. It occasionally gave you the feeling of choice, but they were mostly between bad or worse. I found that it affected me psychologically a little bit and that's a good thing when it comes to videogames.
Graphics vere really good and the attention to details was in some parts quite astonishing. Game mechanics worked really well aside occasional mishaps with getting into cover for example, but I didn't feel frustrated at any point. But you'd might want to change default key mappings before starting. At least I found the default one to be a bit overly complicated.
I haven't tried the multiplayer or co-op mode so I have no opinion there, but I think the campaign alone is worth the money (not big money but still). All in all I had a very enjoyable experience with this game and I would recommend it for anyone who is into story driven shooters.

This game is awesome. Not in that "so-bad-it's-good" way or even "I'm a fan of the franchise so I'll say I like it's good even though it's eats schlanger" way. No. It is actually awesome.
It's set in the rebooted Mad Max: Fury Road universe but is far from a licensed movie title. No bad thing. The plot it is tight and compelling and the presentation is beautiful at best and brutal at worst. The titular character gives one of old Immortan Joe's sons a chansaw lobotomy within minutes of hitting the start button. Beyond that you are free to roam and cause mayhem with story missions rewarding completion with juicy car upgrades and new environments to explore.
Visually it's very impressive. Doing away with the muted colours of other post armageddon titles (I'm looking at you here Fallout 4) and instead mimicking the saturated pallet used in Fury Road. Again, no bad thing. While set in a desert wasteland you will find yourself pausing (or taking advantage of the smoothly implemented capture mode) to marvel at masterfully crafted settings at sunset and sunrise, the way shadows are cast at high noon or just how terrifying the storms can be. On my 8350 / 290X setup it has never once dipped below 60fps either.
Gamplay is Dinki Di as well. Developed by Avalanche Studios of Just Cause fame, the driving may not be 100% realistic, but it's fun and the game gives you a load of cool weapons to play with while charging around in your V8 deathmobile.
Out of the car, combat is very similar to Arkham or Sleeping Dogs. Smash the punch button and ocassionally tap the counter button to keep the increasingly bloody violence flowing. Gun play takes a little getting used to but works perfectly once you do.
When you're not smashing faces or blowing the balls of War Boys with your trusty shotgun, there are plenty of rock-scrambling exploration sections which channel Uncharted or recent Tomb Raider games which reaveal the true brutality of life in the wasteland, all aptly punctuated with Max tossing in his 2 cents about how humanity lost everything and it all went to hell in a hand basket.
If you are a fan of the franchise or feel let down by recent open wolrd titles then this is a no-brainer. Just buy it.

Rogue Legacy is a Roguelike, hack 'n slash platformer which showcases the best of what the genre has to offer.
You play as the descendant of a hero, who must enter the castle, collect treasure, and kill bosses. When you die, it's game over for your hero. Done. Gone. No coming back from the dead.
But that's where this game bends the rules of the Roguelike genre. You hero dies, but his descendants live on, and the next in line inherits their ancestor's fortune. A fortune which can be used to train skills, purchase ruins and equipment aforementioned ancestor was kind enough to unlock, and finally enter the castle again. Don't even think about hoarding coins, though, as the toll to enter the castle is whatever you didn't spend before entering it.
I like to think of it as a generational Roguelike. A Roguelike which was never intended to be won without dying. It can be done, but if you don't die, you won't be able to train your skills or use the new equipment you've unlocked - unless you somehow manage to beat the base game with no upgrades or equipment. But most players could never do that. So you'll probably be in the boat with the rest of us who isn't too sad about dying because you've had a nice run, and you can't wait to spend your treasure.
Forget about making that new character, though. Characters are randomly generated with a few different attributes: class (Barbarian, Ninja, Paladin, Wizard, etc - all with VERY different playstyles), spell (fireballs, axes, throwing knives, etc.), gender (doesn't really affect much), and a random trait.
Traits run the gamut from baldness, dysylxia, near-blindness, and irritable bowel syndrome. Some of these traits are benign. If your character is gay or bald, nothing really changes* (minus a small story element, but I won't spoil anything, no matter how insignificant). Others are slightly annoying such as irritable bowel syndrome which makes your character have flatulence when they jump. Still, others are a death sentence. Being nearly blind makes it incredibly difficult to see enemies.
The enemies and locations follow the standard forumula more closely. There are four areas in the castle. Each means new enemies, and often upgraded versions of older enemies. For example: The first version of the eyeball spits one projectile at you every few seconds. The second spits two or three. The third spits nearly a dozen. The fourth unleashes a volley of projectiles in a fairly complex (but predictable) pattern.
Thankfully, this is the kind of game that's actually quite fair to the players. Each death is an opportunity to learn about the enemies. After you die enough, you will learn to predict their movements. Even the bosses will become easier as you beat them enough times. You'll also have weapons, armor, and runes to augment your skills.
And then the difficulty will ramp up, and you need to adapt once more.

TLDR: A difficult Castlevania/Metriod style game with various random elements and RPG features thrown in to keep the game fairly fresh, and make it seemingly last longer.
-----
The game plays as smooth as butter, the controls are tight and responsive similar to games like Super Meat Boy. What you input is what you get. If you have a pad, I'd use that, but keyboard works just as well, it's all a matter of preference.
The game is hard, and that is how it's designed to be, so there are no faults there and you can expect to die... Alot. But it's to be expected and is not a bad thing, there's an achievement for it too. One slight issue I find with the controls is the down air attack. It's like using the pogostick on DuckTales, which makes you bounce off enemies and certain platforms which open when you hit them with it. The problem is? You can't hold it, so it will only keep the sword down for a slight second. This can be hellish when in a room with walls coated in spikes, enemies are flying everywhere and shooting projectiles at you, while you're trying to platform your way through the room with only the platforms I mentioned before. Miss a platform? Playing as a ninja or class with low health? You may aswell give up.
Every time you die, your child will take over in your quest. The neat part is that they all have their own traits and characteristics. You could end up playing as a gay barbarian king with tourettes, or you could be a female paladin with irritable bowel syndrome from the matrix. I'm not kidding. After playing a while though, you'll start seeing similar traits showing up, this will bother some people, but there are a fair few. Some are particularly fun to use (Using a ADHD Hokage is a LOT of fun I personally find).
Any gold your parent earns can be used to build a castle and better your child's chance of survival. so their adventure lasts longer and they earn more gold for THEIR child to progress deeper into the castle; which is also randomly generated by the way every time you enter. If you like a castle's layout, or want to revisit the "Fairy challenges" scattered around to get better items and runes, you can lock it for a small fee when you unlock a certain helper.
When you start the game there is a short introduction, and then you will find numerous diaries around the castle to keep you up to speed with the nigh-on non-existent story, infact most of them are tips... But that's not what the game is about. It just pushes you in the direction you're supposed to go and that's it, and that's all it needs. Don't expect Final Fantasy.
Your goal is to kill 4 bosses scattered in the 4 different area of the castle, followed by a final boss. This may not sound much, but given how the game plays it could take forever. This is another complaint some people may have; progress can seem painfully slow. I agreed with this until a certain point, where I started to figure out what I was good with and how to play in given situations. I suddenly got a lot stronger alot faster and felt rewarded by it. I struggled on the first boss for a while until I figured out one spell is insanely good against it... Beat it next try.
As for how the game looks... Can't fault it. It does what it's meant to do, and some of the traits you have with change it. For example for the trait where characters are colourblind, the screen will be monochrome/black and white. Can't see 3D? All characters will flip like a sheet of paper like on Paper Mario. Are you "The One" from the Matrix? The castle will transform into a funky, Tron-like state will a mix of black and neon colours. Are you short sighted? Everything that's not close to you will be blurred out. I'm sure you get the idea, and it's cool. How long for depends on how much you enjoy this kind of quirky thing.
I can't comment on sound, as I haven't played with it on, sorry. :c
The humour is pretty good, and has made me and other people I've shown chuckle a fair number of times.
Anyway, this game is aimed around people who enjoy retro, platforming adventure games like Castlevania or Metroid. But the random aspects thrown in are enough to allow anyone to have a good time on it.  It's not gonna harm you to give it a shot if you're interested.

Rogue legacy is a VERY challenging 2D platformer/scroller. This game is along the lines of the so-called Metrovania scrollers. You play as a hero who's job is to rescue the king in a mansion. Unfortunately the mansion locks behind you. And you only have one life to make it through. If you die, one of your heirs can spend any gold you've earned to buy new abilies/skills, etc.
Each time you die, three of your heirs step up to the plate. And you ahve to pick which one carries on the family Legacy. Problem is, each of your heirs comes with a host of genetic traits. One of them might be balding, another might be extra strong, another might be terrified of food. Once you've picked the heir you prefer, you can send them by the shops, and buy some new equipment. Once you've finished shopping it's time to enter the mansion again. The guard demands all of your remaining gold to allow you to enter, so spend what you got, while you got it.
Once you enter in, you'll notice very quickly that the entire mansion has changed its layout. It seems that each time you enter, the entire mansion shifts it's walls and traps, giving you a different playthrough, for every different heir. The map is basically procedurarly generated for each playthrough. You'll learn each rooms traps over time, but it still makes the replay value pretty good.
The game is clearly designed to be played with a controller, over mouse and keyboard. Even then, the controls can feel rather muddy at times. There are several times will your game will feel a little grindy while you try to earn just enough money to get one additional skill to try and earn a little more gold. This can get annoying really easily, but once you succeed it feels pretty good.
So much replayability. Love the fact it's randomly generated. Love the skill tree and the design. A must play! Makes you rage a lot

I purchased this game after reading reviews about how it deviated from the standard CoD-style 'black ops' shooter in terms of plot originality. Unofortunately, I found the story (especially the 'twist') rather contrived and predictable. The campaign was excruciatingly long and at times quite tedious, falling well short of being able to justify 15 'chapters' of gameplay.
While I applaud the creator's ambitions in creating an original story (especially one that tackles relevant issues like PTSD, American military excess, and Middle Eastern interventionism, I think the end result could have been better. As an attempt at social and industry commentary Spec Ops is solid, unfortunately as a game it is not.

The most important feature of this game is the story.
It's a really dramatic representation of the horrors of war: the line between good and evil is thin and every action lead to a consequence. It's well written and a few moment can really hit you.
The story alone is worth the price.
The ambientation is an amazing contrast between the modern Dubai architecture and the desert sand that is claiming back the town. Graphic does a good job, but don't expect nothing special.
The 7/8 hour long single player campaign is very entertaining, especially after you get hooked up by the story. Gameplay is a little repetitive but you won't notice too much.
The multiplayer is almost dead and nothing special, but you should see it only as something added as a bonus.
If you're looking for innovative gameplay and you just want some good FPS action without a story you may not like it.
But if the first thing that matter in a game is the plot you wont be disappointed.
If you're unsure simply wait for a sale and give it a try, you may find a hidden gem

There are some bugs, which I would expect, but so far they have been minor and not game-breaking. In some places the UI could do with some polishing - particular with more tooltips to indicate the function of objects, and more clarity in the 'research' system, but this information is available on the wiki if needed.
The graphics, while simple, are very attractive and work well with the game mechanics. The gameplay is quite addictive, I find myself losing track of time watchig the in-game hours fly past! The progression from a basic prison to a more advanced community is fulfilling, the missions help drive you progress well, and there seems to be a depth of gameplay t uncover as you go along without being too complex for a new player.
I would however suggest more of a tutorial. The current tutorial, while well made, doesn't do much to guide you on the first few steps of where to start a new prison and I found myself playing around for a while until I got a hold of the basics.
All in all, a great game so far!

So,
What do you get when you combine an apocalyptic wasteland with great characters, spectacular gameplay, the chaos of vehicular combat and a great levelling system?
Answer: Mad Max.
And so begins my review.
Graphics:
Stellar, with mild system requirements. Any mid-range rig (~2014) should be able to handle this title at high settings with playable framerates. At the present, there are no glitches, stutters or crashes observed while playing this title. Well optimized.
Gameplay: Engaging. Nothing here comes free, not even upgrades. Prepare to maraud and survive in this titular wasteland as you sCAVENGE for scrap, come to blows with Scrabrous' minions, destroy oil rigs, disarm mine fields and upgrade your vehicle.
Story: This is damn good. Characters are well portrayed, and the Mad max themes from the genre are easily carried over as a homage to the series. We see unrequited love, betrayal, greed, malice and survivalism. The Hope and Glory's arch moved me deeply; well developed characters who met an untimely end out of Max's choices and Chumbucket's betrayal at the end. However, the linearitty of it all lowers it a notch; the player has no real choice to make.
Overall rating: 9/10 for the fine work, attention to detail, stellar graphics and customizability, the epic photo mode and an epic and engaging playthrough. One of the severerlyunderrated epics of 2015.
You will not regret playing this. Promise.
All in all, comes highly recommended.

Well it was really fun and refreshing at first. Gameplay is good and fun, and even if you got 1 bad player on your team, no game is lost. Also the Presentation is cool and even playing Defence is rewarding.
I was fed up with NBA2k15s streetball mode, because it was lagging so hard it was unplayable. This game felt very direct and no lags at all. That part was really well done.
But that said ... what ruins my experience after over 24h ingame is the Pay2Win which is absolutely over the top.
If you play with the normal characters vs. normal characters, it is all fun and fair. I also don't mind paying for faster leveling or extra gear, not even for some additional skillslots and other minor advantages.
What absolutely kills the game are the special purchaseable characters. While there are some that only grant a minor advantage like a small stats boost in a certain stat, there are some that just can't be beaten with the free chars, unless the other player is a total noob.
As an example, playing as Center, it is impossible to get rebounds vs. some pay-centers, even with the perfect timing.  If you walk into them they just push you away automatically and you stumble backwards, for example. So no chance of even getting close to the hoop.
Also there are chars that grant you a +40 stats boost that you can assign as you wish. And that is A LOT!
So if you level up, you get +2 stats per level. so These speciial chars have a 20 level advantage over you statswise. This just can not be beaten. It is like playing a level 1 vs. level 20 char ... or 10 vs. 30 and so on.
This is just very very frustrating and unfair.
I really like the game, but I do not see a point in spending 10 bucks on chars I don't want to play because the P2W system forces me to. And then ... I don't think it is entertaining pounding normal chars with my pay chars, because they have no chance. There is no challenge in that and it would be unrewarding and boring. At least for me.
So one good thing is, the game offers a newby channel. There is a normalchannel for levels 1-11 and a newby channel 1-11. You can only get into the newby channel if you did not level a char past level 11.
While I was in there, it was the most fun and the best times. Why, because almost noone had those imba chars there.
once you move to the normal channel or past level 12 ... you encounter a pay char in what feels like 2/3 of the games. If you are "lucky" you get that guy/gal on your team ... easy mode. If you are even unluckyer, it is your direct opponent. If you quit the game, you do not get the rewards ... so you just get pounded for another 5 minutes. I always try to compete ... which in the end just makes it more frustrating. And now brings me to the point where I uninstall the game and move on.

I am a Paladin. I am a guardian of the realm. I am the sixth of my order. I am death.
I have irritable bowel syndrome. My father was color blind. My father's father was, ahem, small in stature...okay, he was a midget, but golly could he find hidden treasure.
Rogue Legacy was a sale purchase...one of those games you spend five bucks on and say to yourself, "Well, if I play for an hour I've gotten my money back." I'm about 6 hours in and this game is the epitome of "...just one more level..."
My son and I have played this game side by side for a good part of the evening and will likely do more angry exploring in the coming days. Expect to die. A lot. But the beauty is not in the death, but in that death is not permanent. Your lineage will continue...your sons, daughters, grandsons, granddaughters, great-grandsons, great-granddaughters, ad nauseum...will continue your quest long after your demise.
Get it while it's on sale. It is a simple game, but addictive and fun.

+ Great core gameplay, tight controls.
+ Fun and rewarding challenges.
+ Quite addicting.
+ Good music.
- Not being able to choose your class gets pretty annoying, and some traits make the game nearly unplayable.
- Everything you do, except killing bosses, only serves to buff your next generation. It never helps you on your current run. Basically, you are rewarded for your efforts only when you die, which isn't very satisfying.
- The grind gets very noticeable once you have to farm the same content repeatedly if you want to stand a chance against the final boss' second form.
It's a good game, but it would actually be better if it was completely randomized like Binding of Isaac (you'd automatically equip what you find in chests and restart with nothing when you die), OR if it was like a normal RPG where you'd select a class at the beginning and have the usual progression system with EXP, an inventory, loot, stats, etc.
I realize it would be a different game and the Legacy mechanic wouldn't work, so they would have to change the story, but I still think it would make the game more enjoyable, and the core gameplay would remain the same.

I was always a trucking fan. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is basically an upgraded version of Euro Truck Simulator. As more game updates were released, all the trucks have real names. My favourite truck is the Volvo FH16, which comes with analog and digital km/h or mp/h display. The game features a huge Europe map. Some countries, like Spain and Portugal are currently not available in the game. I hope it will be included later as a DLC. The trucks are looking really nice. You are able to customize it with many features. For example I can set a Cabin adjustment to the truck. Music can be added manually, and online radio stations can be added as well, which requires live internet connection. GPS is a very helpful gauge in the game. It always shows the speed limit on the road you are travelling. So if you are a trucking fan, I definitely recommend the game. Can't wait from SCS Software to release American Truck Simulator. It will be a must have game for me. ^^

Because of age and health issues I was stopped from driving unless I drove a hand adapted vehicle, which I declined. This game puts me again behind the wheel of a vehicle and I have spent in excess of 230 hours playing this simulator, I love this game and hope further expansion DLCs are soon forthcoming, the mods take this game even further, I have included American trucks, military mods and more paint jobs than I thought possible, immersed in the game you actually do feel as though you are on the road, the detail in trucks cities and countryside, and yes the A'holes that should never be allowed a license to drive are in the game, I let the AI know that if you do things to me I will do unto you, and I did, costing me £100s of pounds in repair bills and fines, but the satisfaction you get when you shove that car or truck into a river if one is close by is to much to resist, this game is for all ages, and I think it teaches all how to drive correctly, the young once familiar with driving a simulator like this will have no trouble obtaining a license, and keeping it clean, take your frustrations out on the traffic AI and drive squeaky clean in the real world, I highly recommend this game.

Rogue Legacy is an interesting take on the 2D hack'n slash and some of the core aspects of roguelikes (even though RL is not an actual roguelike)
Every death is an opportunity to upgrade your stats and start again. At first i was worried that this would lead to just a pure grind, where i would farm gold until i had enough upgrades to beat the bosses. But Rogue Legacy is more clever than that, and manages to make every run satisfying for itself, a good platform/hack'n slash gameplay that reward good players with more loot. That way, you enjoy each run, but progressively you get ready for the boss encounters, which are the main steps of progression.
On the whole, the progression is really enjoyable. The game is very good at teaching you how to be better, by introducing new ennemies regularly. It's interesting to see that, at the beginning, the most dangerous areas of the dungeon seems full of unbeatable monsters, whereas once you've got some experience, you understand they are just evolutions of the enemies you've encountering before.
A negative point though: the upgrade system is not as flexible as would like it to be, or as it seemed at the beginning. By the mid-game it was becoming clear that i have to build/upgrade in a specific way if you want to be the most efficient. And that means many of the classes tend to be very weak, which is a bit sad when the game is advertised as you having to play with the random characters. In practice, you will understand that some classes are better than the others and favor theses ones.
The game will take about 20h to finish, and doesn't overstay its welcome. It was getting a bit repetitive in the end, and I'm glad it wasn't longer.
For people who really enjoy it and want more, the game offers unlimited replayability, in the form of infinite "New Game +" mode, where each new game plus increases monster difficulty and rewards. However, the game will not offer you new stuff, just the same monsters with increased stats, so it will just be a game of grinding stats for your character.

Spec Ops is one of those under the radar hits, it probably has something to do with promotion, but this game didn't reach the public as it should've, and this is completely undeserved. First looks might pit it with any other generic modern warfare game like we've been bombarded with, but it is totally undeserved.
Were other games in this genre don't even try to innovate other than some new weapens or multiplayer perks or features, *cough* yeah we all know which ones I mean.
This game focusses on putting up a decent single player and just adds the multiplayer component under pressure of the publisher, this results in an impressive game and unimpressive multiplayer. And frankly I wouldn't have it any other way, I prefer a good story experience late night in the couch, multiplayer is not my first interest and depends largely on the community.
In-depth review follows:
The background isn't your typical modern warfare setting, but still faces you with the depraved reality of an actual conflict-zone. This is however amplified with the fact that everyone is stuck in one place with limited resources and a harsh surrounding setting. At first it is unclear what has happend in the city, wilst you're already forced to make decisions, these decisions aren't like your regular precedented choices. Like e.g. 'Press A' for choice 1 and 'Press B' for option B, I can understand why this might create some confusion for general players. Instead you can shoot a specific
character or try to bypass the situation. These stealth pathways aren't always obvious and the squad does urge you to make your decision fast which will result in most players just shooting their way out of the problem and in retrospect ask themselves were the choices in the game are made. In my opinion this is exactly what the game is trying to portray, are you a 'no-brain gunner' or do you use your hits to figure the problem out another way.
I have to say, these situation aren't that abundant as far as my first playthrough, but I might find other instances my second time. Even though the developers do try hard to create variety in the gameplay, by inserting sections with street chases, helicopter chases and by splitting you up from your squad forcing you to play for yourself or to cover your squad from a separate path. However I wouldn't have minded a few more of these stealth sections, because I do have to confess that sometimes the firefights get repetitive.
The AI including your squad is very good though, so you will be presented with a challenge. You can issue some attack commands to your squad, but it is limited. They do a pretty good job on their own and I have only been faced with them dying in the field by doing something stupid a very limited time in my whole playthrough.
The game looks very good, it is build in an Unreal 3 engine, and thus doesn't offer anything supprisingly new. But it does a very good job in painting a colorful and varied surrounding considering it is a desert setting. And believe it or not it isn't all brown and yellow sand locales you will see. You're guided through the Dubai desert, streets and even the Bubai aquarium. Theres even a very blue broadcast tower you'll be going into which reminesces of Mirror's Edge colour palette.
Most levels have been destroyed by the sandstorms an gives you some destructable aspects with very nice gameplay and visual effects. Speaking of effects, the lighting effects in the game are amazing. Obviously the sun plays a very important infuance in the levels and I believe the designers have added new lighting features not seen in the engine before. Don't quote me on the technical aspect, but it does look amazing.
In the end I must admit I have stopped numorous times to enjoy the panorama and vistas or visceral setttings.
Like I have told before the game has stealth aspects and I might have liked some more of them, but on the other hand when the action starts you are engaged with some very good music. The nice post-apocalyptic wind effects only reminiscing to Fallout are muffled away for eighties and nineties rock music. I didn't check the artist list, but it sounds good and amplifies the military setting very well, and is just upsweeping enough to keep gunning.
But he just plays good music as well, so it's all good.
Like I said before this game is worth a try if you enjoy a good story-driven game with a very twisted and realistic setting. The game including gameplay, engine, graphics and sound are build very well which cannot be said of the other generic triple A titles out there. Some of the firefights might get a little repetitive sometimes, but it is swiftly diversified by the story or environment and gameplay twists.
I didn't really play multiplayer, but it follows your basic recipe:
Cover-based gunning + Lot's of weapons + Game modes + Progressive unlocks =

Life is Strange was, for me, the second time dipping into this sort of format. I'd recently played Everybody's Gone to the Rapture and found myself thoroughly enjoying a slower pace of game where I don't need to worry about my skill level (or lack thereof), but rather just enjoy a compelling story. Life is Strange came up as a recommendation, and I'm so, so glad I brought it.
Naturally, I was keen to get the prequel game Before the Storm.
I think something that's worth pointing out is, as of Episode Two of BtS (can't comment on Episode Three yet as it isn't out), I don't think anything is spoiled for newcomers to the series. If you didn't play LiS and are wondering whether you should play that first I personally don't think it matters. The way around you play them will provide different gaming experiences depending upon whether you're armed with foresight or hindsight, but I think both of them could be equally powerful.
And it is just that, powerful. BtS has none of the vague science fiction elements of LiS. Instead, we get a purely character-driven narrative that is still engrossing. The story focuses on the relationship between Chloe and Rachel. Both girls have their own individual struggles, particularly related to their respective father figures, and bond as they support each other as a deeper plot begins to unravel around them.
Chloe was a fairly divisive character in LiS - plenty of players disliked her personality and attitude, while others loved her. BtS humanises her more. Getting inside her head helps us to better understand where her attitude comes from, and why she's frequently so defensive. Max - the protagonist of LiS - doesn't feature here, but Chloe, like Max, keeps a journal, and Max often comes up as a topic. Max effectively abandoned Chloe shortly after Chloe lost her father, despite the two of them being best friends, and it's something that continues to hurt Chloe. She writes about it frequently - drafting letters that never get sent because she knows Max won't bother replying. It sours the character of Max, but I don't think that's a bad thing. Max could feel like a bit of a Mary Sue, and BtS shows that she isn't.
The two narratives feel naturally linked, and there are plenty of homages between the games.
The gameplay is largely the same, sans the time-travel feature. It's now been replaced by the backtalk feature, which sort of works, but it feels a bit tagged on. It's a way of arguing your way to information (or access to illegal raves), but it's not especially compelling.
The dialogue itself is good, with amazing voice acting from all characters. Chloe has a new actress. To be honest, I don't think I'd have noticed if I hadn't read about it before. There is a difference if you listen side by side, but the new voice actress does a great job. The famous (infamous?) pseudo-teenspeak makes a return, and it's hella charming as it was before. It's less clunky and more natural. I did have a problem with the dialogue options sometimes. Typically you're given one or two words for each option, and often you'll have no idea what Chloe will actually say if you select them. I thnk this could be clearer.
The score and music is fantastic. The licensed songs in BtS haven't captured me in quite the same way as they did in LiS, but they suit the mood just fine. Chloe's music taste is different to Max's, and it shows. There's more rock and punk influences here, and the songs fit the narrative.
I love the animation and art style. If you liked it in LiS then you'll like it here too. A criticism would have to be that Rachel feels strangely plastic. Her eyes, in particular, remain the same irrespective of her emotion, and I actually found it a little disconcerting. Rachel just didn't seem to move naturally either. This may just be me, but I found it rather conspicuous as the animation is otherwise great.
Overall, I recommend the game wholeheartedly, to both new players and veterans of LiS. The writing and storyline is absorbing and it's fun to explore the world. It isn't as long as LiS with just three episodes, but tonally they are similar (though with completely different storylines.
(Side note, there is a bonus episode if you get the delux version. I did buy this because I wanted the extra episode, but a personal request to the developers if they happen to read this is to avoid the modern business models of microtransactions and gimmicks like buying extra outfits for Chloe, which the delux edition also includes, but I don't care about. This feels like a step in this direction. Don't go any further.)

is a standout title in the roguelike crowd that deserves attention due to its satisfying platforming elements and unique randomization premise, though its system does inhibit replayability due to difficulty issues.
This game's trademark is its dual-randomization aspect, in which both the character the player uses and the layout of the castle that the game takes place in are randomized each playthrough. The backstory under which these factors are justified is equally intriguing: for every character that dies during their journey, one of three of their descendants will be the next to journey into the castle, which is apparently renovated in between each excursion. The usage of the lineage system to limit character choices keeps the game fresh by not allowing the player to avoid bad traits or unpreferred classes when they appear. However, this method does have issues due to the limited quantity of bad traits and the fact that they often are either "not impactful to gameplay" or "downright game-destroying"; some more meaningful downgrades that players would not necessarily spell defeat for players would have benefitted the game.
Further deviation from the normal roguelike setup comes from the fact that
contains an RPG-like permanent upgrade system. Money earned in the game during a run carries over beyond death to an skill tree which grows to include unlockable classes and buffs, alongside general stat increases, over time. The game also features a basic armor system, with blueprints to be found in-game that unlock different pieces for purchase. Due to a lack of customization options for the attributes attached to the armors, however, by the end of the game there will only be around two different sets of armor that are feasible to use, since all the others would generally leave you too weak. Unlockable improvements to the armor to make the lesser sets more valuable would have made the armor system much more deep. To make up for this lack of customization, though, comes the final perk system, which allows the player to attach up to five perks before a run. These perks can acclimate to various playstyles and balances out the luck effect of the roguelike factors with the skill of the player in their preferred method of playing.
Other aspects of this game are on-point. The gameplay as a platformer is responsive and adjusts accordingly to traits and perks, helping players concisely feel the effects that they're playing under. Combat is sometimes too floaty, as many flying enemies recoil too far from attacks for the player to prepare for/respond to naturally. Largely, though, the game feels fair in how enemies and rooms are designed in order to give players a fighting chance. Bosses vary widely and require strategizing from players, especially underleveled ones, in order to be defeated. The game's aesthetics are aided in part by its catchy chiptune soundtrack and the creators' humor, which is incorporated throughout the game in unexpected places. The game's lore is even decent, as diaries laid out by a previous denizen of the castle detail prior occurrences and tease some endgame events. The castle format smartly balances randomization and predetermination by allocating certain extremities of the castle to be certain areas (and thus certain degrees of difficulty), meaning that players that wish to face challenges above or below their own level can travel in certain directions - a useful mechanism that both rewards learning the attributes of different areas and surprises new players with unexpected challenges.
There are some downfalls that occur due to
's mixing of genre elements. One significant issue involves the game's difficulty in later playthroughs. The game's balancing system levels out permanent upgrades in the skill tree with huge improvements to the enemies after the player beats the game. This system works for a number of victories through the game. However, at a certain point during games, the skill tree will eventually max out. At that point, further progress becomes largely impossible past whichever current playthrough that player is on. This issue can be exploited much earlier in a playthrough with abuse of the aforementioned perk system. With overuse of the "enemy weakening" perk, players could potentially inadvertently ruin their saves by beating the game so many times with reduced rewards (a downside of the perk) that the game may be unable to beat even with the perks, impossible to get past the first room without any of the perks and the player won't have enough resources to improve themselves. Such an exploit should have been either worked around or patched out altogether in order to protect the integrity of players' runs.
The RPG implementations cause unforeseen issues with the levelling system and prevent this roguelike from possessing the endless replayability that the genre is known for. However, as a venture into uncharted territory, this game provides an admirable experience that is driven by strong fundamentals and a memorable randomization system that fittingly gives this title a "legacy" of its own.

I don't think a video game has ever truly affected me like this one has, it's a game that just absolutely makes me hate myself. The game is basically Apocalypse Now, disguised as Call of Duty. From just looking at it, it looks like every other modern military shooter out there, you would go into it expecting to find another game of gung ho pro-America machismo bull♥♥♥♥♥♥ but you come out of it looking inwardly, thinking about the concequenses of your own actions.
The character you play as starts out as just a white bred all-American stereotype, but by the end of the game you don't even know who you are anymore, the character keeps making decisions and you have to follow along, the game willingly tells you to do things, and then when you see what it is you've actually done it just drives the point home and makes you know what you've done. You feel a disconnect between yourself and the character because the character thinks all he's doing is right, and all he's doing is just. When in reality it doesn't seem that way, you don't want to do these things but the game tells you to.
The gameplay is nothing really to write home about but it uses genre cliches to get it's message across, it doesn't try to really make the shooting fun for you, it wants you to look at what you're doing, it wants you to see the horrors you are perpetuating. It just wants to make you feel like hell.
And it's the little things that really make it hit home, the characters slowly falling apart as the game goes on, both mentally and physically, the loading screens just hitting home and blatantly telling you what is happening and what it is your doing just to show you that you are being a horrible human being.
If you aren't squeamish and want a game that doesn't conform to storytelling standards you see in most video games, buy this game as soon as you can, it's amazing how much it really affects you.

I would have never found out about this if it weren't for the multiple posts on Reddit claiming this to be one brilliant game. Do you want a game that leaves you satisfied, happy or fulfilled? Then don't buy this. Spec Ops: The Line will force you into the harsh truth of war.
You play as Cpt. Martin Walker, a soldier sent to investigate a distress call alongside Sgt. Lugo and Lt. Adams, only to find out something more terrifying than what any of them expected.
The story is set in a fictional Dubai where it is undergoing a state of emergency and destruction. Unlike other war games, the story has a really powerful impact on one's emotional and psychological health. There was honestly one point where I had to stop because it was all too much to handle..... It's one of the best war stories ever told in a videogame.
Visuals look amazing, plus I haven't experienced any crashes or bugs and it plays really smooth. It's set in Dubai so expect lots and lots of sand, and repetetive locations. There some areas where the music feels satirical and I love it :) The ambience plays a huge role in story, so I'd say they did a pretty good job in making this game the way they intended it to be.
Gameplay is probably their weakest point, it's awkward and sometimes will get you in trouble. Some buttons do multiple commands, depending on where you are and what you do and it makes the gameplay confusing at times. It's definitely not enough to ruin the experience though ^_^ I recommend using a mouse and keyboard primarily because of the aiming. I'd say the game can become brutal at certain points :( I played through this on normal and was killed several times to the point where I almost rage-quitted.
Overall Experience: This game was very hard for me to finish because I don't want to keep playing it, not because it's bad but because it forces you to commit atrocities and actually shows you the devastating truth. I don't feel like a hero, I feel like a monster and this game shames you for the acts you've done..... I love this game and I hope I never play it again. I highly recommend that you experience this game at least once (I'm sorry) because it's horribly amazing.

Spec Ops: The Line was a downer for a reason I find hard to explain. After getting past its mediocre cover shooter gameplay, I am left with a story that supposedly left people feeling the guilt punch of the ending. I however took issue with this.
The game seems to be at odds with itself. While it is understandable to assume the main character spends his time in the wrong with its elaborate (and pretty obvious) twist, the game seems to try to put you in the spotlight with its occasional "choices", which end up not effecting the game except for the final one. I give it credit, it makes me feel as confused as the main character but for all the wrong reasons. I question the game while the character questions his surroundings and by its ending I get to associate his emotion of "I really should have stopped 6 hours ago" with the game not my actions.
Maybe I am overthinking this or am just not getting the idea, but I felt cheated out of my time and money. Its far from the worst game I ever played and the game is competently made for the most part, but I cannot seem to understand the love for its way of storytelling. Not to mention I really didn't find the story that well done anyway.

Have you ever wanted to throw you best friend off a building? I know I have. Gang Beast is a multiplayer game where the aim of the game is to throw your opponent off the map. Gang Beast is a local multiplayer game where you can have one to eight players if you're all in the same room. The developers are working on a non local multiplayer but it's currently in beta. The developers for this game are from Double Fine Production and Boneloaf Games. This game has three different game modes called waves, versus and rooftop. I will be telling you about my experience playing gang beast, the highlights and the lowlights, what they can do to make this game better, The different game modes and finally the conclusion.
When I played this game I only experienced a couple of bugs, which is good considering it's in early access ( early access is when you can get a game but it's not fully released). I enjoyed playing this game with my friends but some of the scenarios can be a bit repetitive. There is a good variety of maps in the game and each one has its own unique feature, such as there's is a map called trucks and you battle on trucks and there is even a map with a giant fan and it blows you up and down the map. The only thing I didn't enjoy was playing by myself it's is boring so I recommend it to play it with friends. So I believe this game is ridiculously funny and is very enjoyable for a long time.
The highlights of this game are, the is a very minimum amount of bugs and only occurs sometimes. There is a wide character and map selection. Not only do the maps have unique features so do the different characters for example, the bear can cut ropes faster with its claw and the chicken can headbutt harder and is more effective. The lowlights of this game are, the game crashes and sometimes bring you back to the home screen, you have to have a decent computer to be able to run it max graphics. The sounds are strange when the character mumbles.
The things they can do to improve the game would be, add  online multiplayer so you don't have to be in the same room. Cut down the amount of times it randomly crashes on some computers. Make a lower set of graphics so the not so Beefy computers can run it thirty frames per seconds as well. Also having a easy interface to navigate because it is hard to chose Different game modes. The last thing they need to improve is that there's better NPC so you don't need friends to play this game.
The game modes in this game are all unique. The three game modes are versus, waves and rooftop. Versus is the main game mode you play with friends because it's the game mode when you fight your friends and try to throw them off the edge. Waves is when you or your friends fight NPC and try to battle them in waves gradually getting harder. Rooftop is one  of the hardest game modes, it drops heaps of characters on to the rooftop and you have to throw them off the roof.
To conclude my review on this absolutely beautiful game, I believe this game is one of the best party games to play with friends or family. I believe this because this review shows my three reason why this game is awesome, firstly my experience was Really good considering it's in early access, secondly I believe this is the best game because the highlights of the game were some of the best highlights in any game  and my last reason I believe this game is the best is because there isn't much to improve in this absolutely wonderful game. So in conclusion I believe this is one of the best games to play with friends.

Somewhere along the line, something went seriously wrong with the direction of this game. While the original Borderlands was nothing groundbreaking, it was greater than the sum of its parts; a cohesive, run-and-gun action RPG that pulled the quest for better loot out of high fantasy dungeons and into the post-apocalyptic wasteland. Borderlands 2 on the other hand feels like it was originally supposed to be a console MMO (that was then canned when Gearbox got the message that MMOs don't make money anymore) and instead repurposed it into whatever this mess is.
Let's start with the most glaring gameplay issue: weapon proficiencies have been removed, resulting in everyone being mediocre with every weapon type. Throughout my playthrough of the campaign, the majority of my weapons felt like they were spraying wildly; even rockets from launchers would come out at random angles, often missing a target ten feet away from me. Instead you get Badass points, a system designed to reward you with stat upgrades for doing arduous tasks such as breathing or shooting bad guys. Sure it might sound cool to have more options, but when you're made of paper and all your weapons spray like you're trying to shoot with a jackhammer it feels more like you are disabling handicaps instead of improving your character. The worst part is these stat increases have diminishing returns and you are forced to spread them; less chosen stat increases appear more often when you rank up, preventing you from rapidly increasing in any one stat. Your Badass rank is account-wide, meaning all characters will gain their buffs. If you're somehow addicted to this game, that's great for your alts, but I was obvious dead weight for my veteran allies online.
Loot options feel much more constrained in BL2. Gearbox can brag about the millions of guns but when the only worthwhile weapons are at the top rarities, who cares about all the blues and greens? Weapon effectiveness seems to dropoff a lot faster in BL2 (probably because of no proficencies), with the only weapons worth using more than 5 levels being uniques and legendaries. Of course these weapons should be the best and last for a long time... but why should I be expected to pull serial codes from internet social media to get a guaranteed "worthwhile" weapon? I saw a single legendary weapon drop during the 25 or so hours I spent playing through the campaign and even that was a mediocre rifle that was unusable after a few hours. The majority of the game I was using quest rewards because they were the best weapons I could find. Again, who cares about the millions of guns when I'm using generic handouts from NPCs anyway?
Of course all of this is just the surface of the problems with this game. After years of patches there are still tons of bugs (mouse cursor doesn't appear with a controller plugged in, getting stuck in surfaces, mouse movement breaking, various broken textures), the writing is terrible with all the characters being turned into unlikeable jerks, the story is way too long and padded with checkpoints for fetch quests, map edges are poorly defined resulting in seemingly random death pits, character classes are blander, weaker, and more boring than the original... the list goes on. I honestly hated this game and I just wanted to finish it because my brothers did. I would not recommend this miserable experience to anyone.

First before anything else: This game is pay to win.
You cant see it, when you begin to play, which makes it very seductive: You get hooked to the game and after a few hours you realize that certain things can only be obtained with real money.
Special Characters: Those start with 40 skillpoints extra! That means a headstart to lvl20 for the beginning and a 40 bonus at max lvl. You could get 1(!) by grinding matches in April which I did: Well, playing lvl 1-11 (There is a rookie channel you have to play in until you reach a higher level....even the special characters with their headstarts :D) when you are starting with lvl 20 (just attributes no skills, but thats more than enough)...I won all of my FIRST 15 matches mostly as MVP. Getting other special chars in your team of 3 increases the advantage at the end of the game...opposing teams forfeit at the start of the game if they see only special characters at the loading screen (which I can totally understand)
Special clothes:
You can get trousers, shirt and shoes and apply an attribute to them. The limit for ingame-money is 5 points per item which nets 15 additional attribute points.
Special clothes can only have an attribute added with real money. But the attribute points you get are higher/doubled: shoes give 10 points, shirt and trousers give 12 and 6 points, which sums up to 28.
28 points for real money against 15 points with ingame money.
My highest character is 24 but I dont think I will play much longer after i figured about pay to win.
The Game is pretty good otherwise, very much to do and see, good mechanics etc. I had a fun time, until I figured why I cant win vs. certain characters and teams.

Spec Ops: The Line is a great game that is unfortunately held back by so many glaring technical issues. The most obvious one being where the audio completely cuts out randomly during certain cut-scenes, completely destroying the immersion. I'm now forced to load up a YouTube video in order to understand whatever plot point I'm missing. The second biggest issue is the squad mates' artificial intelligence; there will be times where they just stand around and do nothing or run straight into enemy fire and immediately die, leaving you to revive both of them. This becomes quite frustrating on higher difficulties.
On the upside, my favourite feature about this game is its attention to detail. For instance, I'm playing a level inside what appears to be a museum. Enemies have met us in a firefight and there's a large skeletal Tyrannosaurus Rex over in the corner. I direct my squad mates to target an enemy and, to my surprise, my character yells out something extremely specific like, "Enemy by the T-Rex!" where I'd mostly expect a very generic and vague response. This continues throughout the entire game and is quite a nice change from most other team-based shooters, showing just how the developer really put a lot of thought into their game.

Other highlights of the game:
-Great graphics, especially for the trucks.
-Realistic truck parking physics. Feel the rush of backing a truck & trailer into a loading bay while you try not to jackknife.
-Driving complexity can be adjusted to suit your needs. Want to simulate gear shifting? You can. Just want to mash a button and have the truck speed up? You can do that, too.
-Wide variety of trucks available. You can customize any truck to truly make it your own.
-Large world map full of scenic views.
Downsides:
-Awkward to control with keyboard+mouse on anything but the most simplistic simulation settings.
-The cities tend to be minimalistic. A couple distributors, services for your truck, and that's about it. It works alright in smaller cities, but it comes across as odd in bigger cities.
-The AI for enemy drivers can be erratic. My biggest complaint is that they come to a screeching halt if you so much as tap them, which generally requires more law-breaking to get around.
Other:
-There's no in-game guide to european road rules. If you're not from europe, you're going to have a lot of trial and error to figure out what the signs mean & you can get away with. (Example: Turning right on red will get you a fine)

Well, what can i say about this game. im gonna start with how well my pc runs it.
I run an i5 devils canyon cpu OC to 4.8ghz, GTX 770 card and 16gb corsair vengeance RAM.
I can't run this game on max settings, my card is too old lol. But i have been a little unhappy with the graphics on this game, i.e when moving, they graphics are VERY grainy. when motionless its awesome. ive also seen a lot of people complain about this too. A solution to this is to use a 3rd party program which ive heard helps. I didnt want to do this as i feel i shouldnt need to. I messed about for ages with the settings trying to find another solution....i found one. I play on a 42" sony bravia tv (1080p) no amount of graphics changing got rid of the problem, until i changed my TV settings and lowered the sharpness. problem pretty much solved.
Anyway, back to the game. well not to put too finer point on it its bloody amazing. The immersion, the gameplay are all totally unreal! I hunt in real life and this is what im comparing it to.
There are missions and also side missions to complete for extra XP and creds. they start off pretty easy but they do get really hard. e.g shoot a red fox with a bow....sounds easy right? not when you cant see the bleeding things in the first place coz they like dense foliage! not to mention the fact that the range of the bow is shorter than jimmy cranky! another 2 spring to mind. harvest a white tail deer at over 150m...again sounds east....not when there is a whole amazon rain forest in you way!. the last one is take a photo (and there are a few "take a photo mission") of two bears, hard when you only ever see one on their own. But, these are "challenges" for a reason! and they give the game some longevity along with the massive XP needes at over level 15 to level up or aquire perk points.
I would like to point out that to people new to hunting... of any kind... that this is not a game you can play just for half an hour! it takes time.....and a lot of it! ive played now for about 55 hours and im still no where near opening up even one reserve! I think a lot of people that dont know how to hunt or are new to it are gonna find this game very frustrating. for e.g...there is a lot of dense forest and foliage. hunting like this is hard, but as i discovered there are a lot of open fields and lakes to find and this is where to hunt.
the bad points...
Like any game there are bugs, and im sorry to say there are quite a few of them in this one. But the game is relatively new and the Devs are releasing patches all the time. here is what ive found...
sometimes you hit an animal and it leaves no blood trail or any tracks (new to me as of the last patch)
sometimes you hit an animal and despite the vital wound and huge blood loss rate it never dies
sometimes you will hear an animal call and there will be no direction indicator.
sometimes your weapons will vanish from your hands and cant get them back (fix...go into inventory and swap your weapon to a new slot and back again....problem solved)
The user interface isnt too friendly, it takes a while to learn how to equip rounds and scopes etc i cant understand why bullets that are bought are not automatically added.
I also dont like the map. most of the time when you pull the map up its zoomed in on the out edges of the map....why cant it automatically be centered on your position?
there are prolly other things i cant think of off the top of my head as i write this.
There are a variety of weapons in the game from hand guns, rifles, shotguns and bows. There are also 2 different rounds for each rifle (not sure about the shotguns as i dont use them that often) but in reality there are sooo many more varieties of rounds and i wish they would put this in the game too. As you start the game you are given a .243 which in all honesty is all you will ever need...until you start coming across bison and bears. the .243 will kill them but you are going to be tracking your animal for quite a while until it bleeds out. the next rifle is the .270 which will put down pretty much most things. im currently using the 7mm and its good enough for anything, i see other people on youtube using the .338 rangemaster buts its very expensive and when looking at the stats it isnt that much better than the 7mm. actually when i think about it? there isnt a big enough gulf between the rifles to warrant spending huge amounts of in game moneyto buy anything above the 7mm...even the .270 is good enough.
so my conclusion....the game needs work but as it stands it is very very good. It needs more rifles and bullet variations and the in game graphics (grainy stuff) needs eliminating. the perks and skill tree also needs work, some of the perks you will never need. e.g the bullets tend not to be affected by wind (from what i can see) etc but there is a perk that shows you wind direction and speed (not for you own scent, this is built in already on the compass)  there is another one for weather too...again i see no real reason to have this because the games in built weather isnt severe enough to warrant having this skill at all. There are other things i might mention but id be nit-picking.
so if i had not bought this yet, would i buy? hell yes. despite the few niggles overall its a fantastic game and a must have for any hunter enthusiast. I really hope they add more reserves to hunt and more weapons and bullet variations.

Spec Ops: The Line is a great game that is unfortunately held back by so many glaring technical issues. The most obvious one being where the audio completely cuts out randomly during certain cut-scenes, completely destroying the immersion. I'm now forced to load up a YouTube video in order to understand whatever plot point I'm missing. The second biggest issue is the squad mates' artificial intelligence; there will be times where they just stand around and do nothing or run straight into enemy fire and immediately die, leaving you to revive both of them. This becomes quite frustrating on higher difficulties.
On the upside, my favourite feature about this game is its attention to detail. For instance, I'm playing a level inside what appears to be a museum. Enemies have met us in a firefight and there's a large skeletal Tyrannosaurus Rex over in the corner. I direct my squad mates to target an enemy and, to my surprise, my character yells out something extremely specific like, "Enemy by the T-Rex!" where I'd mostly expect a very generic and vague response. This continues throughout the entire game and is quite a nice change from most other team-based shooters, showing just how the developer really put a lot of thought into their game.
Worth a modest price.  It's a 3rd person shooter trying to tell a moral story.  Visuals are entertaining and combat is moderately entertaining.  Worth a run through to see the story.

This is the first time I've really considered keeping an original review entirely for reference. My opinions on Rogue Legacy have shifted substantially since my first review. I still recommend the game, but with some caveats.
After some time away from the game, I found the combat to be clunkier and shallow. Armed with short range and a delayed swing, combat can feel sloppy. Once the enemies gain speed and more attacks, your sole weapon feels underwhelming. Enemies are primarily ranged, and you'll eventually wish for more mobility and a smaller hitbox. By my third playthrough,some rooms became true bullet-hells, except randomly constructed instead of the tightly crafted affairs in other games. Later rooms can be more hectic than any of the bossfights, and some rooms will have unavoidable damage with the number of enemies filling the screen with projectiles.
I do feel like the game is very fair in the first two completions, even into the third with Difficulty decreasing runes. Beyond that, the game starts to suffer from an abundance of enemy projectiles without the means to avoid them. The health system is a bandaid fix, with each room slowly wittling your health down unless you get random food drops, or abuse life drain on slimes. By 30 hours, I'd seen (almost) everything, and I don't enjoy the game nearly as much. Unfortunately, even with all my complete runs and dozens of partials, I have yet to see the plant miniboss. Until the RNG decides to bless me, I have to do partial runs just to search for this miniboss. It's the only thing keeping me from 100%, and it's ridiculous. I've killed other minibosses over 5 times, and never seen just one.
I loved Rogue Legacy. It is a great value. But the way it is designed, it ends up running into a wall. This is a rougelite that can (and should) wrap up nicely in 30 hours of play. Rogue purists may dislike that the replayability runs dry. It's a great game to start in the genre, and can be as easy or hard as you want by New Game +1. Just be careful running that +1 much higher, or you may grow weary.
I'm incredibly hooked on Rogue Legacy since I picked it up. Spelunky was pushing me to improve my skills after I bought that recently, but little issues bothered me. Rogue Legacy hits some of the same points (looting, combat, random areas) but improves on what I want. Runs never feel like a waste, as gold can aid your progression. Combat feels crisp for being mostly melee, and the enemies are appealing. The style is humorous and compelling. It feels great to improve as a player along with stronger character stats. The design pushes random luck down in the equation, since loot is progressive. There is no single game-breaking item that makes winning a run easy.
I don't yet have the words to express why I love the game so much. It's hooked me hard.  A rogue-like with strong combat and a "Just 1 more time" appeal, it's hard to find major issues. The game could get too easy or pointless once you unlock and complete everything, but most games do the same.

Feels most of the time authentic prequel to original Life is Strange. The game lets you explore Arcadia Bay and it's people on slightly different theme than time altering powers and mystery solving. Episodes offer few interesting twists and laughs that players can try to manipulate a little bit with teenage anarchy, such as sharp-tongued backtalk or graffiti messages. Chloe Price herself has been portrayed to struggle between more subtle internal emotions/confusion such as loss of her father and evolving friendship with a popular kid in school's society.
Personally I find the options between friendship and romance kinda dull since it doesn't deliver the moral weight of the story in the same way necessarily, but to some people options like these are the juice of the game. It could be something they understand better, but as a normal guy I find it more awkward or even parodic side of the game *thinking about Commander Shephard's: We'll bang okay?*
But at the end of the day the game's philosophical and emotional thoughts are made with high quality care. Musical choices have been selected almost perfectly to bring the "soul" into the scenes and moments. I am pretty sure anyone who enjoyed the original Life is Strange can genuinely enjoy this one also, and find something to reflect into their own life aswell.

Great successor to the first Life is Strange.  Some of the dialog timings could have been better, but the story immerses you enough that you just tune out the oddities.  As long as they keep up the great story telling, Life is Strange will be a series I continue to subscribe to.  Emotionally charging, well directed, atmospheric, and cliffhangers at the end of each episode makes you beg for the next.

With the release of the second episodes, Life Is Strange: Before The Storm continues to impress me. It definitely is a faithful adaptation to Dontnod's original creation, Deck Nine definitely put as much care into this game as Dontnod did to theirs. The soundtrack, the art, the voice acting, and the writing are just as strong. Before The Storm, despite having a huge number of callbacks (or call-forwards?) to Season 1 of Life Is Strange, still manages to keep itself independent. I can definitely say for sure that BTS is an amazing game in its own right. You don't need to have played Life Is Strange to love it. You can love it as it is and that's what makes an exceptional prequel.

I'm re-writing my review to go more in depth as to why this is not a hunting sim and more of a hunting arcade game. I will also list some reasons why the game is "broken" and not getting good reviews at this time. This game fails at being a simulator for many reasons and I'm sure I will not list all of them but I will do my best to point out the biggest issues my friends and I had.
Animals & AI- There are just too many animals honestly for this to be a simulator. They are EVERYWHERE! A hunting simulator should require a bit of patience and planning on the hunters behalf ,however, in this game you can just sprint around and wait until you hear a "warning call" from an animal then go into stealth mode and call it in or stalk it. The worst thing about the AI I feel is that you can shoot at an animal and the other animals around it and yourself only run away a short distance and can be called right back after a very short time. By very short I'm talking less than 10 seconds in some instances. The game needs a longer "spook" timer and range. Animals should run further away and be gone for 10-30 minutes. There are also cases of animals running in circles right in front of you.
Weapon system/ballistics and shot placement- Something that gets me personally is that the ballistics in this game are completely made up and garbage, let me explain. Animals in the game have an integrity bonus which is there to stop you from using larger more powerful weapons on smaller animals which is fine but the weapons they have that can cause you to get that 0% bonus are very off. For example using a .270 on deer will give you 0% integrity bonus. This seems very silly to me as many people hunt deer with a .270 and many even use a 30-06 these are both extreamely common deer hunting rifles. Yet at the same time you can take that .270 and shoot an elk in the head and have it bleed at a "very low" rate and have to track it for 10 minutes. This should obviously be a critical wound. Another big issue I have with this is that if you shoot an animal in the legs or any bone used in walking and it doesn't stop the animal from running. I have shot a deer with that .270 which they claim is just so overpowered for deer and gives you a 0% integrity bonus in 3 different legs and the pelvis bone and it was able to RUN from me. Now for shot place-ment. The game is overly picky about where you shoot an animal. Taking that same overpowered .270 that just ruins your deer to the point you get a 0% integrity bonus and shooting near the heart should drop the deer dead in it's tracks if it were so damaging but it doesn't and the deer will still run off and force you to track it. You must shoot a direct shot into the heart to get that instant kill.  In theory you should be able to take one of the biggest guns either the 7mm or the .338 and shoot a deer in the neck and drop it on the spot but you can't you will still have to track it. Finally shooting doesn't place bullet holes on animals. It just doesn't make sense to me and it seems like they took everything they learned while making The Hunter Classic and tossed it out the window on this game.
Night Hunting- Night hunting should not be in the game. It is illegal in most places as well as hunting with artificial light. They could fix this by not allowing you to shoot before/after certain hours in game while still allowing you to travel or track an already shot animal. They could allow you to shoot an animal at night if you are attacked by it while traveling or tracking.
Bugs- The game has a lot of bugs currently. Some of them are minor and some are in my opinion game breaking. A few bugs I can think of are a small window pop up that is blank and says Press F1 for more info. The box blocks some of your view and is more of an annoyance than anything. Weapons, callers, and such will disappear from your hands randomly. This is really bad when you're changing from a caller to your rifle to kill that animal you just spent 20 minutes calling in only to find out your rifle is randomly missing. Sometimes you will crouch to sneak around and just randomly die. You might shoot an animal only to have it freeze in place this sounds silly but really breaks immersion. You might kill an animal only to have it disappear in front of you. You might shoot an animal to have it stop bleeding in the middle of tracking it. At times you will buy something from the shop and it won't be in your storage or inventory, I feel this one sucks because things in the game are pretty expensive to begin with. Your flashlight has no effect on animals. Panning while looking in binoculars if very slow whiled zoomed out. There are areas on the map which are bugged and will cause large mixed herds of animals to spawn at times there may be a mix of 50 animals in one area again this one breaks immersion. In multiplayer only the host can interact with landmarks, claim outposts, and build stands. Entering a stand while another player is in it will kill you. Desync issues where people who join your game can't see animals and at times can see and shoot them but when they collect the animal they recieve no xp or money. This is by no means a full list of bugs but it's long enough and I pointed out some of the more crucial ones that I am aware of.
Now for the most heated and debated topic yet. Microtransactions/DLC. This company said back in the beggining they would not have "microtransactions". Which was great as The Hunter Classic had a ton and really turned people off. They said this game would be a one time pay game. So what happens shortly after launching the game? They put out "DLC" instead. You get people who say that microtransactions and DLC are two different things. Myself and others will agree that they are the same thing under a different name when it comes down to it. Paying for additional content. Some say that microtransactions are typically small and/or temporary and are usually cheap and may give an advantage during gameplay and DLC is usually a fair amount of content like a new map or missions and once you pay for them they are permanent and can be pricey. Now from my personal experience I have seen things from one category fall into the other countless times. Skins, cosmetics, teleport stones, pets, and access to new areas in a game all permanent and being sold as microtransactions. I have seen DLC sold anywhere from a large new map full of creatures and content (Ark: Scorched Earth for example) to a few weapons or skins in a pack. So what do we have for "DLC" in The Hunter: Call of the Wild? Tents and blinds for $3.99 which basically breaks down to $1.99 each. I would hardly call it a "large" amount of content, it does give players an advantage to quickly be in an area, and also change the time of day so they can be in spawn zones when they spawn without much downtime. This leads to my conclusion that if it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck, then it's a duck. The issue here is that either one can be called the other. I am quite sure the company knew they would be releasing DLC and should have said so. You may call it what you like. You may buy it if you like. Many others will not.
Long story short I suggest people stay away from this one for another 6 months or a year and check back to see if this company has got itself together. Hopefully that is long enough as they have been very slow at bug fixes and seem to have no troubles getting out "DLC". We would all like to see this game succeed but it's currently in a questionable state.
