Honestly, for a recent (as far as 2015 goes) open world game, this one's not bad for about the first 10-15 hours. I'll break this down into categories, 'cause that's what the kids like nowadays. I'll also keep this spoiler free just so nobody gets butthurt and include a summary of my thoughts in the final paragraph so scroll down to that for a tl;dr.
It's rather rare that setting a game's graphics to low can still give you the visuals this one provides. I ran this game on low, not out of necessity, but simply because I didn't have to run it on high or ultra settings to get a really, really nice looking experience. If you've got a high end rig and decide to pick this game up, give your rig a quick breather and pop this game on medium. You really don't need much more than that unless you seriously need that x16 tessalation anti-aliasing nonsense. It doesn't make a huge difference because the game is gorgeous. This wasteland is a beautiful and varied landscape and it looks absolutely marvelous on every graphic setting.
- Fighting is slow, brutal, and feels kinda rewarding when you suplex a warboy off a cliff for the first handful of hours, but after a while you start to notice that, much like every car in the wasteland, it lacks polish. When you throw a punch, you're making a commitment. Interrupting your punches to counter someone is not an option, and you will get punished for this. A lot. If you were expecting the same fluidity of combat as the Batman Arkham games, don't. You won't find it here. The structure is similar, but the execution is different. That doesn't mean combat is all that bad though. Once you really understand it, it's kinda fun and does genuinely feel slightly different and a little more weighty.
- I find myself sad that exploration in a modern open-world title basically boils down to go to x, utilize y thing at x to make all things on this section of the map uncovered. But that's the way things are now so I can only complain so much until someone innovates this tidbit again or removes it completely to let us discover things by stumbling on them like the Elder Scrolls and Fallout games.
- Driving and vehicular combat is, thankfully, very satisfying. As is customizing your car--until you realize that all the car parts and paintjobs are locked to specific arbitrary tasks and missions that need to be completed. Peeling out in the desert sand feels good and slamming your car through a convoy just feels good. Once you get upgrades for your car, going back to a stock car hardly seems like an option. Each upgrade makes everything just a touch easier in different ways, but not in a cheaty kind of way like...
- Upgrades via Griffa tokens break the game. There, I said it. Not sure if anyone else was going into this game thinking "Oh sweet, finally a game where surviving in a post-apocalyptic wasteland means collecting water is going to be a necessity and gasoline is going to be this precious commodity that is going to be so scarce and it's going to be fun as♥♥♥♥♥♥trying to survive out here!", but uh... Disappointing doesn't even begin to describe how getting some actual character development automatically forces you to spend every last token you've gathered to that point to make this game much easier than it should have been. Which through regular play, gathering tokens is inevitable. I could seriously ramble about this for at least three more paragraphs, but for the sake of the length of this review, I'll leave it at that. This entire bullet point is just my opinion and I, for one, didn't want to mosey through this game as what essentially becomes God of the Wastes Simulator 2015. I could have appreciated this game a lot more if the entire token system was removed and Griffa was just this sage that Max visited sparingly to torture himself through his broken and fragile psyche to hopefully get a better grip of himself.
- Customizing your Max is actually kinda cool. Getting a bunch of different hair styles, beards, and clothing options to switch between was a feature I didn't know I wanted and am glad it's there. I'm also kind of okay with some of them being tied to stats. Even in the end-game, I still chose to use the most basic of clothing options just so that fights would be slightly challenging and longer, even at the expense of not wearing the trademark jacket. Like I mentioned earlier, customizing your car is actually fun and mildly rewarding. Of course, choosing to be an impenetrable tank of a car is going to make your car slow, but you'll be much sturdier and hit much harder if you actually manage to catch up to your target. On the opposite side of the scale, choosing to be a lightweight speed-demon will cause you to hit with less force and make fatal injuries more likely, but that's only if your enemies can catch you. Like previously mentioned, the only thing that really sucks about your options is that they're all locked to missions or specific points in the story. The ability to switch out any part of your car on the fly makes it both incredibly easy to experiment and slightly game breaking, due to the very nature of not needing to be at a garage to switch out parts. But again, balance doesn't really seem to be WB's concern with this game...
- Can I also just say how disappointed I was with the storm system? The storms themselves are actually a really cool mechanic and I love the entire atmosphere of them. How easy it is to get your♥♥♥♥♥♥wrecked and how rewarding the salvage is was such a great tradeoff. So what's so disappointing about them you may ask? Well, suffice it to say, in the almost 30 hours I've logged into this game I can say I've only ran into 5 storms. That's right. 5. I'm serious. This hyped up, really cool feature that looks and feels so cool is about as scarce as water and gasoline should have been in this game. And also the length of the storms. Too short. Should have been longer and more menacing. Also, entering a stronghold clears the storm immediately, even if it just started, making them completely ignorable and removing all tension they bring. Mediocre...
The story feels like it's got someplace to go and goes there fast but then peters out once you hit your first stronghold. Seriously, the game forces you to stop progressing the story and do/collect some things as what appears to be some form of padding. But really, the story after meeting the first settlement leader, Jeet, was just poorly written and everything Max does after that point doesn't make sense in regard to his character. The story seems to set up all these neat characters and it literally does nothing with them. All the leaders don't do♥♥♥♥♥♥ At all. It kinda sucks.
Back to the point though, doing anything after getting to the first stronghold really just felt like checking off a list of chores. You don't realize it at first but once you've done a couple side missions, you've done 'em all. Only metaphorically speaking though. There's a lot of side missions. Like.... Clear your schedule for the next week amounts of side missions. And they're all just one of about 6 or 7 different missions so get used to that if you plan on playing for the long haul. I went into this game knowing that and still tried to trudge through it all, but after two or three weeks, I just couldn't do it anymore. And unfortunately, due to the story's meandering and halting nature, I felt no need to replay it.
So in my opinion, Mad Max is dumb fun and does a good job of making you feel like a survivor in the Mad Max universe until you spend your first Griffa token and try to progress the story past Jeet's stronghold. Then it's just imbalanced and dull and gets old fast.
tl;dr - Buy it on sale and enjoy the scenery and fun of blowing up convoys and warboys with your custom Max and car and doing donuts in the dust for a solid 15+ hours.

Undertale is quite an interesting game
(BIAS DISCLAIMER: I like rpgs and story driven games.. A lot.. Like, quite a bit. If you dont, this game might not be for you)
A lot of people say that it's overhyped and boring because everyone talks about it, which is a fair point
That being said, if you go into it, not expecting much, you will come out of it thinking that it was one of your best gaming experiences, and let me tell you why:
*This game has interesting characters, they have so much personality and are always so much fun to talk to
*It's quite different than other rpgs as you can play it without ever killing anything, or you can litterally, kill everything, which will change the game quite a bit
*Your actions matter and have an impact
*You will feel like a child again when playing through it
*The graphics, though simple, holds quite a charm, I can't help but find some parts of the game beautiful despite it being quite a simple style
*The music is amazing
Now, you may be thinking "Wowsers, that sounds pretty good!" and yes, it does. But you've been on the internet for quite a while I asume, you know of the game but haven't played it yourself. You know the characters because of all the art and viral videos
Meeting these guys without knowing them for the first time plays a big role, so if you already know them that will lessen the experience
Here is my recommendation for picking up the game:
If you've never seen the characters and haven't seen a playthrough on youtube/twitch, get it, you will love it.
If you've already seen the characters, know the story, know stuff about the world. Wait. The game will be on steam forever, give it a couple of years until you no longer really remember much about the game, and then go into it as close as 'blind' as possible, that will truly make the game a lot better for you
I suggest picking this up at the summersale, and then playing it when you've forgotten enough about the game

This is probably the greatest game I have ever played. I really wouldn't know where to start with it. The story is unbelievably good, it is INFINITELY replayable (given the random chances of things happening each time, plus multiple endings), and you will get seriously and probably unhealthily emotionally attached to the characters. This game accidentally became my LIFE. I couldn't imagine not having played it. I constantly reference it in every day life.

This game is diffinately a must play. This is deffinately one of my favorite games and i had an absolute blast playing it, replaying it, and so on and so forth. The game took me around 7 hours to complete the firat time due to me stopping to inspect every single thing just so i could get all of the possible story i could as well as to see if i could find any secrets.
Gameplay:
Undertale is a turnbased, Bullethell, story rich, rpg that really nailed itwith how fun such a simple system can be. Infact there are only two ways to make it better: have more of it in game (especially bosses), and to maybe have the ability to fight the bosses without going back through the game. And im not saying there arent enough fights or that i have a problem going back through the game infact for me both those points are perfect.  I just think it could add jus a tad but more fun into an already incredable game. Coming from games like Battlefield, Counterstrike, and other FPS titles i can say that the simple combat system is ot only more satisfying but somehow feels more epic and chaotic then the all out warfare of the aformentioned games. And they were never frustrating just a blast but still highly challenging!!
Story:
Without getting into any spoilers the story although subtle until you do alittle digging is still one that will keep you fixated through multiple playthroughs. You play as a human that has fallen down into an underground world of monsters and you must must make your way out by any means of your choosing. You can show mercy and make alot of amazing friends, or kill everything in your path making your foes tremble before you. If i am to be honest i havnt killed a single soul in Undertale. Toby Fox did too good a job makeing me love each and every character in the game (except for one but that is to be expected with any antagonist) infact i nearly cried after doing a small amount of damage the game's first boss and ended up resetting my save so i could take it back. And if you work hard to get the true pacifist ending its deffinately incredable.. It's just one of the many tear jerking moments of this incredable game. But all of its endings are deffinately worth checking out. In this game every decision truly counts.
Soundtrack:
Toby Fox's score for this game is absolutly incredable. It adds so much personality to every location, encounter, and boss in this game. I recommend purchasing the soudtrack as well. I Hve not since i am already stretched thin on funds.
Summary:
To put it bluntly this is one of the best games i have ever played and i full heartedly recomend it to every single person who owns a computer. Its easy to run as well, infact i have it on my smart phone as a few members of the community have managed to unofficially port it to Android. But i give Undertale a 100/10 and will continue to not only remember but to play the game for many years to come.

Very good plateformer. It's rogue like in the sense that every time you die you start at the begening of a randomly generated level. At the begening of a run you can use the money you earned during your last run to buy equipements and upgrades. Then, when you enter the level, you loose what's left and start a fresh new run. This is where it gets addictive :
You did a bad run and didn't get enough money to buy stuff. I'll try a new run quick.
You did a good run and buy a lot of stuff. I'll do one last run to try it out.
Now go to step one or two until you're two hours past your bed time.
This game is hard and very precise. You'll die really quick in your first run. But that's ok, you'll get better and you'll get upgrades and equipements to help you.
The game is hard, but at the same time, you can go at your own pace and still beat it. You feel an area or boss is too hard ? No problem, just grind a few run, get better equipements and upgrades and try again.

Not gonna lie, bought this game mainly for the graphics. They are absolutely stunning. Enjoyed the landscapes, shot a doe or two. Switched to the American park. And then fun happened.
Spotted a marv deer. Took a shot, missed the lung, drats. Oh well, gonna follow the blood trail right? So I went. And I went and I went. It's been two days and 10 miles, was the deer real? Am I real? I could have sworn the superdeer used two medkits by now.  Every time I started doubting I noticed the deer on the horizon and tried to take a shot. Bugger kept running. I kept walking, cause, hell. With the surroundings so beautiful that everything looks so real I could not complain and I was entertained and stimulated visually for hours.
I decided the deer lost about 145 liters of blood judging by the splatters he left behind. When I started losing hope, a giant buck ran towards me. With pounding heart i grabbed my gun and aimed at the chest. I missed the lung. I looked at two splatters on the grass, sighed and followed the new bloody trail. It's been 20miles. Send help.
All jokes aside, this game is amazing. I get to chill and admire what technology dedicated to environment achieved so far, so that a "simple" hunting game like this makes me just turn on the game and sit back only to admire the sound and sights as I take breaks at work. And since I am an artist and I work at home, I also consider this a great inspiration for my art.
Pros:
- Everything. Sun rays, reflection of wet foliage under my feet, crunching rocks, waves of grass glazed by the wind, birds rustling in reeds in a misty lake, insects gently swirling in hot air, ever changing weather with droplets that softly graze the wet mud.
- Very fun hunting mechanics with useful tracking tips for a visual addict like me who gets lost in sightseeing and forgets where the tracks were
- Sound ambience that makes me immersed like no other game
- Observed a coyote stop and look around every time I made a noise. Such natural animations and behaviour. Love the fur variations.
- I had a feeling of being rewarded with a beautiful hunt despite never finding a deer corpse that I shot. How? These devs are witches.
- Maps. Those current two I can explore are ENORMOUS and beautifly done in every detail.
Cons:
- Maybe I am biased but could a shot deer die a bit faster? No? ok
10/10
What I'd love to see:
- Tons of more maps! Current amazing maps make me crave for more biomes like Asian forests with musk deer or barbary deer in Africa. I'd spend any $ to get more maps and never stop staring at beautiful landscapes.
You guys got me hooked on your stuff and you got a customer for life. Hopefully.

Spec Ops: The Line is incredibly bleak, emotionally and morally difficult to stomach, border-line psychologically damaging, and an excellent game.
It doesn't range too far from other third-person shooters in terms of mechanics, and it's multiplayer component seems terrible; but the story will affect you in a way few games do.
That being said, SO:TL is also a very short game, (roughly 6-7 hours) and lacking the aforementioned multiplayer, the price should be right if you're looking to pick it up.
SO:TL throws you into a place where the most base of all instincts thrive; a strange mix of the opulence of a ruined Dubai and the savagery of man. At the end of it all, it's difficult to even know how to feel, but there's no doubt you'll be haunted by the moral decisions you "had" to make long after the credits roll.

Prison Architect is still in alpha - but you really wouldn't know it.  The game is as feature-rich as a complete product (moreso, if anything) and there are no game-breaking bugs.
Prison Architect is a nod back to the micro-management games of old (I'm avoiding the word 'tycoon' because that has become a hackneyed term to mean simplified 'make lots of money' cartoon game).  It's
so don't let the first 'mission' put you off.  It did me (I didn't find it interesting) and didn't then play the game for a year or more, but that first mission is pure tutorial just to show you how the very simple tools work.  You are then left on your own with a blank canvas and all the tools you'll need for designing your own prison.
It's not at all - but it can be if you want it to be.  It's genius in design for that.  You can be in the game and designing your own prison very quickly indeed without needing to be bogged down in all the minutiae of prisoner and roster management, but the beauty of the game is that, if you WANT that level of micro-management, you can.  You can set individual punishments and such for prisoners, but you don't have to.  You can schedule different daily timetables for each level of security prisoner so there are no clashes and inevitable riots, but you don't have to.  You can individually manage reform program scheduling, but you don't have to.  You get the idea.  The game automates all these things by default, but allows you to override them if/when you want to.
Of course, getting a prison off the ground AND making money is that usual tycoon balancing act.  You have to start building foundations, but you can't go too large too soon otherwise you will be bankrupt overnight (and game over).  You can't expand one area too quickly (e.g. cells) unless you have the infrastructure in place to support them (bigger canteens, showers, and more utilities).  And not everything is available to you right away: you unlock  specialist staff and services as you go, providing a feeling of achievement on top of the creative aspect of the game.  The fun is in finding that balance and making your very own Alcatraz (or Reform Centre if you feel like being a benevolent architect).  The game scores you on the overall effectiveness of your prison (determined by how many riots and escapes you've had versus reformed and released prisoners unlikely to reoffend).
Oh, but it is!  If you like designing and tweaking 'something', then this is your game.  Maybe you played Rollercoaster Tycoon, or Transport Tycoon, or even Simcity or Theme Hospital.  Bear in mind that it's pure sandbox (right now at least; I vaguely recall reading that missions might be added later but don't take my word for it).  You have a planning tool that will allow you to freeform-design your layout without committing any money, then build on top of your design after.  The fun is in creating a layout you want, and balancing it to make it work well (no good sticking a dining hall at the other end of the map if prisoners cannot reach it in their allotted mealtime slot).
Yeah, it's not even beta, but don't be fooled.  This is in a better state than any other beta game I've tried.  There are elements still to be finished (the execution chamber does nothing I believe, despite its appearance in the tutorial mission, and some things don't seem to have much effect on environment yet), but Introversion have been updating the game very regularly over two years.  I joined the alpha at its earliest stage and still the updates come.  Even if they didn't,
, and I have close to 160 hours recorded in the Steam version alone.
The game has an incredibly open mod support scheme and there are plenty of popular mods in the Steam Workshop right now.  I've tried the Women's Prison mod and it is easy to activate or deactivate each mod in the game.  An excellent design.  Of course, with the game changing periodically there is no guarantee that mods will continue to work for each iteration, but their easy removal means no worries.
Prison Architect is a game that most certainly doesn't feel like an alpha (or even beta).  Get past the somewhat awkward-feeling introductory mission and you have all the tools needed to design your own prison.  It's a micro-management sandbox simulator that's easy to get into, fun, and will inevitably sink far too many hours of your time!  Highly recommended, and a great example of crowd-funding at its absolute best.

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

I'll be damned. You look at something like this and shake your head, thinking "How is this even a game? This just looks like Youtube fodder for people to do stupid stuff in and record it for their channel. However, when you play it, you discover that it's an engaging game involving driving your truck from point to point, picking up loads and dropping them off. You drive really long distances and can speed, but traffic lights, lane directions, speed cameras, and clipping/hitting other vehicles can result in fines and damages you have to pay to repair on your own vehicle. You start out really poor, using other companies' trucks, but the better you get and more successful you are, you can eventually buy your own truck, which incurs costs for fuel and such, but you make more money as well.
Then comes a bit of business-building, because you can buy even more trucks and then hire drivers and start paying them wages. They'll make you money while you're driving.  It's sort of a perpetual experience of getting more and more trucks. It can kinda go on forever and is a satisfying and peaceful experience since you can even play your own songs using the in-game radio, or listen to various real European radio stations. Once you get to the point where you're hiring several drivers and buying several trucks, you've basically done everything you'll ever do, but can keep on playing and doing this. I'm a bit too scatter-brained to stick to it past that point since other games beg for my attention, but this is a surprisingly good game. It's not a joke at all and a lot of hard work and care went into it.

First of all this game is incredibly relaxing. Pick the right radio station or play your own playlists and just drive around - you will start feeling better about yourself in no time.
As a simulator you'd expect difficult controls, stressful need for accuracy and high price for mistakes - but its not there. Its not arcadish in common sense either though - it balances in between. Kinda hard to explain, but if you start playing you'll feel it immediately. The game rewards you with feeling of accomplishment as much as any hard simulator does. But at the same time it will punish you for mistakes as little as arcades do, so you wouldn't get demoralised as much. And yet it feels realistic.
All that should be enough to at least check the game out but there is much much more. Active developers, lots of free stuff comes with patches, fairly priced addons with huge amounts of content, free player-made mods, good traffic AI, great visuals, sounds, optimisation etc.. Overall its a must-have for anyone who enjoys well-done games in any genre and a must-try for pretty much anyone else. Demo is free after all.

This game. THIS GAME.
If you have somehow not heard of this game from its constant exposure on the Internet or by word-of-mouth, STOP RIGHT THERE. Do yourself a favor and buy this game first -- but after this review ;). Undertale is, by genre-sorting, a turn-based RPG with bullet hell dodging mechanics. This is the most basic way to describe this game, simply because there is SO MUCH MORE.
Story:
I can't really say that much about the story, as this game is best experienced blind without a doubt.
Characters:
Again, not much to say for spoileriffic reasons, but every main character is deep and well-fleshed out. Expect the expected here however ;).
Music:
I don't even need to--wait, I do? Seriously? Ok then. Undertale's soundtrack ranges from simple 8-bit tunes (e.g. the first song, Once Upon a Time) to crisp, clear, performed instruments (e.g. Ruins, the fifth song you'll hear, most likely), and ALL OF IT IS PHENOMENAL. All the music was composed by the main content creator for the game, Toby Fox, and he did wonderfully. All of the music conveys excellent emotion and tone.
Gameplay:
This is one of the major (actually well-founded) complaints that many lodge against Undertale. As with many RPGs, the game consists of walking around, talking to people, and getting caught up in random encounters (and there are quite a few). When you enter a FIGHT (actually capitalized in-game), you have several options, but I'll let you figure that one out yourself. When it's the enemy's turn, well... trust what the first person you meet says. He won't steer you wrong. As for the overarching story, depending on what actions you take, you will fight different bosses, and some characters might like you more or less.
The biggest story plot took me ~6 hours to complete, so you won't get lost in a huge story.
Warnings: This game contains gay/bisexual characters and mentions of kidnapping, child murder, and suicide. Infrequent language throughout. Most of it can be avoided through certain actions in the game, however.
TL;DR Undertale is an astounding game that was one of the first games that I would recommend in a heartbeat. If you haven't played it, go fix that right now. Trust me, it's worth the ten bucks.

Spec Ops: The Line is incredibly bleak, emotionally and morally difficult to stomach, border-line psychologically damaging, and an excellent game.
It doesn't range too far from other third-person shooters in terms of mechanics, and it's multiplayer component seems terrible; but the story will affect you in a way few games do.
That being said, SO:TL is also a very short game, (roughly 6-7 hours) and lacking the aforementioned multiplayer, the price should be right if you're looking to pick it up.
SO:TL throws you into a place where the most base of all instincts thrive; a strange mix of the opulence of a ruined Dubai and the savagery of man. At the end of it all, it's difficult to even know how to feel, but there's no doubt you'll be haunted by the moral decisions you "had" to make long after the credits roll.

The ultimate hiking simulator (with guns)

When the wind blows over the lakes, you shiver behind your keyboard, when the sun breaks through on that perfect Indian summer day, you feel the warmth on your skin. The ambient sounds of the forest match real life one to one. Hiking through the reserves is a deeply relaxing experience. The animal animations are nice and the particle system is very pleasing. The actual hunt is inexplicably exciting. I caught myself jerking the mouse as one would overexcited jerk the trigger and miss the target because of it.... The developers have made a huge open world immersive experience and for that, they have my respect. The game is a “must have” if you enjoy beautiful landscapes and killing fury animals. About bugs: Yes, the game has bugs. After each patch there are noticeably less of them. I'm particularly impressed by the performance improvement of the particle system. That must have been a hard one. Did the bugs take the joy out of the game? Absolutely not. Still great. I'm confident they'll also fix the remaining bugs. About the price: I played the game over 150 hours and I'm still enjoying it. So, is 30 euro a fair price? Totally. Don't forget that the average AAA game costs over 50 euro and contains less then 30 hours of game play, for example the Half Life series, South Park: the stick of truth and the Portal series. I'd buy all those games again, even with those unfavourable play time to cost ratios. The Hunter COTW is a niche game. Killing digital deer is an acquired taste (at best). It will never sell like GTA or HALO. It takes a lot of balls for a game studio to reach for AAA quality in such a small market. So at 20 cents per hour, instead of 2 euro per hour, it's the best damn deal I've made on Steam to date. About paid DLC: They'd have to. It costs millions to make a game like COTW and at 30 euro per game, in the afore mentioned small market, it'd be very hard to break even. It certainly would be impossible to add new content like reserves or game play assets like Tents & Blinds. I applaud this little Swedish game studio and their brave endeavour to bring us a beautiful world for all beings without fur!

Then there are the cliques, the cool kids, the jocks, the nerds, it’s a social minefield of awkwardness.
As if being trapped there all day isn’t enough, they even give you work they expect you to do at home!
School was a pressure filled, judgemental nightmare and one which I was glad to survive.
Work, sure you’ve survived the “best days of your life” and now you’re out in the real world.
People are treating you like a grown up (not that you feel any older or wiser than you did at school).
Statistically you’ve probably found yourself in a “ground-hog day” of 9-5 soul destroying office mediocrity, you’ve got a boss you don’t like and a desk you can never leave.
Sure you’re being paid now, but the “bank of mom and dad” has closed.
You don’t think you’re being paid enough for what you do anyway and there’s always a relentless pile of bills demanding your hard earned money.
If you are lucky enough to have a little money left to buy a game or two at the end of the month, you almost certainly won’t have the free time to actually play them.
You know I miss school; they were the best days of my life....
I often sit at work, questioning my poor decision making skills which have bought me to my particular running lane in the rat race.
There must be plenty of jobs out there which don’t chain you to a desk all day whilst “the metaphorical man” breathes down your neck.
Surely there are people who aren’t trapped in the same “Yes sir, no sir, three bags full sir” tedium in which I’ve somehow managed to imprison myself.
But I have managed to find a port in the storm that is my existence, a bubble of calm escapism which grants a little respite to my jaded soul.
This soul medicine comes in the form of what I like to call the “Zen Simulator”.
You know the sort of game where you can do something repetitive, something that doesn’t require too much thought but still rewards you for your efforts.
Farming Simulator 2015 is a great example of a “Zen Simulator”, you trundle around in a tractor ploughing your fields, planting your crops and generally reaping what you sow.
The “reward hook” is the money you get from selling your produce to buy better tractors to trundle around in and more fields to tend.
It’s a million miles away from the adrenalin fuelled FPS titles I find myself playing at the weekends,
The Zen simulator is the perfect genre to escape into after a hard day of work or school and now I’ve discovered that driving a truck can be just as therapeutic as chugging around the countryside in a tractor.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is another perfect example of a “Zen Sim”.
You start the game running delivery contracts for other people.
You can peruse a list jobs requesting cargo to be picked from and delivered to various locations around Europe.
You pick a job from the list, (your choice might not only be based on the payout of a job, I’ve found myself picking contracts just because I like the idea of driving to particular delivery destination. ) then you find yourself sitting in the rig provided by your employer, trailer all hooked up and ready to go. They’ve even already set the sat nav. for you!
The core of Euro Truck Simulator 2 is spent driving along the highways and byways of Europe.
This is a driving simulator, not a racing game; you’ll want to take care of whatever Big-Rig you find yourself in.
Damage it and the repair costs will come out of your fee.
You’ll also want to drive responsibly; running red lights will cost you, as will getting caught by speed cameras.
Why would you want to rush anyway when you’ve got some beautiful European scenery to drink in as you drive?
The scenery is where Euro Truck Simulator 2 shines, this is a game that understands it’s the journey that’s important, your destination is just another way point to pause at.
As you put your “pedal to the metal” and open your rig up on the motorways of Europe you’ll be treated to a lush and changing landscape racing passed your windscreen.
Don’t get too distracted looking at the pretty fields of sunflowers though or you might miss your exit (or worse hit another vehicle and damage your truck!)
There are 69 European cities present in the vanilla game spread across a dozen countries.
(You can add more via DLC too!)
Each city has its own unique real world land marks or iconic buildings present, you can often see them looming over other city buildings as you wind your way through the suburbs.
It’s a really nice touch to be able to recognise which city you’re approaching from the skyline without having to check the sat nav. or map.
Don’t go into this thinking it’s an exact recreation of Europe though or you’ll be disappointed.
Euro Truck Simulator 2 adopts the same stance to mapping the European Continent as “The Crew” does to mapping North America.
What you have here is a condensed version of Europe, which is probably just as well, I think driving from Southern Italy to Northern England in real time might take a little while longer than the normal hour or two I have spare in the evenings.
It’s not just about driving around making money either (well it is, but there are extra game mechanics to keep things interesting).
There’s an experience based progression system here too.
As you drive around, completing deliveries, you’ll earn points which you can spend to unlock new capabilities.
You can invest points several different areas,  for example, you could focus your experience points in haulage distant which will make longer distance contracts available to you or you could invest points in licences for various types of hazardous cargo if you like the idea of trucking some dangerous chemicals around Europe.
When you’ve amassed enough wealth from “working for the man” you can invest in your own truck (there are plenty of models and varieties to choose from) and start your own haulage company.
This not only gives you more freedom with regards to delivery contracts, but also gives you the chance to invest future earnings in upgrading your rig, whether that is an engine upgrade or go faster stripes, that’s up to you.
There are plenty of stylish paint jobs you can pick as DLC too, should you like a more personalised look to your truck of choice.
Being your own boss isn’t all parts and paint jobs either, it comes with an extra layer of responsibility too.
It’ll be up to you to pull in at the services and fill up the gas tank from time to time now; running out of gas whilst on a long haul is not a good idea.
It’s also not a good idea to keep driving without a rest too, everyone needs sleep and you’re no exception so remember to keep an eye on your fatigue levels and pull in for a nap when you need one!
You’re also going to have to pay for maintenance on your truck now, so it’s even more important ... <...snip...>

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is that rare thing, a strong sim tethered to a strong game. Where other vehicle-obsessed devs seem to take player motivation for granted, Czech studio SCS understand that a pleasingly modelled steed needs a pleasingly modelled environment to shine.
On this occasion that environment is a swathe of Europe stretching from Plymouth in the west to Wroclaw in the east, from Aberdeen in the north to Milan in the South. The tangle of motorways and major roads is stylised and condensed, but feels massive. After a splendid week of non-stop trucking the stats screen tells me I've still only seen 50% of it.
There's satisfaction in exploring new routes, seeing new golden been-there-done-that squiggles appearing on the in-game map, but it tends to be the promise of cold, hard cash that gets you out of bed in the morning. Like Farming Simulator, ETS2 has a simple yet resonant economic sandbox at its centre.
You start as a low-skilled, truckless lorry jockey, forced to take work from established haulage companies. Slowly (or rapidly if you go to a bank) you amass the funds to buy your first rig and rent your first yard. Then the fun really begins. Contract perusing, truck pimping, skill upgrading, driver hiring... this is Eddie Stobart: The Game in all but name.
Spending 90 minutes ferrying a tank of propane from Sheffield to Prague could (should?) be tedious. The fact that it isn't is largely down to good-if-not-quite-OMSI-standard physics, and varied road layouts and scenery. Periods of smooth, almost soporific motorway motoring nestle between passages of edgier wheelwork. One minute you're cruising along contemplating the sunset over the central reservation, the next you're on a rain-lashed country road at night, waiting for the right moment to pass a painfully slow pantechnicon. Tiredness can't kill in ETS2, but it can leave you jack-knifed in a ditch, feeling awful with a substantial repair bill to pay.
The only time when the game itself loses concentration is when attempting to evoke certain regions and sounds. The further you get from central Europe the less convincing the landscapes become. No one seems to have told SCS's countryside crafters that rural Britain features long green things called hedges. Cities are often depicted with the shortest of visual shorthand – a few warehouses, the odd landmark if you're lucky. Don't expect to see a favourite local roundabout, slip-road, or speed camera in this highly-recommended HGV-driver RPG.
Unexpectedly engrossing. Heed the mockers and you’ll miss one of the PC’s finest and freshest driving games.

Now, first let me say that I am not voting this negatively because I think that it is a particularly bad game.  But, I do believe that you can get a better game for a similar price point.  As well, I think that while this game is difficult, in can be ocassionally unfair to the player, which I dislike in a Roguelike/light game.  For example, I dislike the genealogy system.  Quite often you get three options, and you dislike all of them for different reasons, and then you're doomed to fail from the start.  Then, you can either just give up, or you can try anyways only to inevitably fail with less money than you need to unlock anything.  It's really quite unfair, and I don't think it's a system that should be in any game, let alone a crazy-difficult roguelight.  As well, I am quite often put off by the controls.  The way you attack can get quite annoying, as once you have begun swinging, there is no way to cancel it or reverse the direction.  Based on how slow you swing and how fast-paced the game is, it can be very frustrating.  For example, if I run up to an enemy to place a well-timed attack, but I suddenly have to dodge a projectile that is coming from somewhere else in the room, I can end up swinging at the air in front of them, and then taking quite a lot of unecessary damage.  I know that situations such as these are more my fault than anything, but I prefer a more intuitive control system.  As well, I dislike that you have to press down to activate the temporary platforms.  As I am attempting to control my character to place them directly above these platforms, I find it difficult to get the timing right, and end up falling into spikes or what have you.  I would have preferred a button press (Or the ability to rebind this ability without changing the down button as well), if I were given the option.
Mostly good game, but I would not reccomend when there are so many better options out there.  Could have been better. 6/10

-After a great first game, It is difficult not to be disappointed with something so hideously bad. Straight out of a B-movie-bad.

-One of what is supposed to be the game's greatest plot-twists regarding Rachel's family can be seen coming from miles away (Episode 1).

I can understand teenagers getting engrossed by characters, and maybe even the story. But unlike the first Life Is Strange game, it is beyond me how any grown adult would be slightly even moved by the ludicrousness of all this.
It's hard to know who (writers) or what (studio) is at fault. The difference in quality between DONTNOD's LIS and Deck Nine's Before The Storm is GIGANTIC. And although listing every possible matter at hand would be too much time-consuming, it does seem that trading DONTNOD's involvement for Deck Nine's in this prequel was a huge mistake and has already put a dent in the reputation of what the Life Is Strange franchise could, and was supposed to be.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 is a relaxing (most of the time) driving game which involves you delivering cargo to different companies located all across Europe
The game includes the six main truck brands in Europe: Volvo, Iveco, MAN, Scania, Renault, and Mercedes-Benz. The developers also add new trucks from these companies into the game every few months or so
You start off the game by doing what are known as quick jobs (company loans you a truck to deliver their cargo and pays for things like toll booth, ferry, and gas fees) until you have enough money or able to take out a loan to buy your own truck. After that, you are able to use this truck to make deliveries (however, you are still able to take quick jobs if you don't feel like using your truck).
As you progress in levels, you also unlock new parts and accessories you can apply to your truck like a more powerful engine, or some lights to go on top of your truck. These upgrades can be applied in repair stations where you can also (obviously) repair your truck from any damage/wear and tear you might have sustained during your deliveries or exploration of Europe.
As well as being a truck sim, ETS2 also is a company management sim, as you are able to hire drivers to come work for you. To cope with this influx of new drivers, you'll need to buy more trucks and expand your garage all the way up from a one truck garage to a five truck one and once that's full, you can start buying more garages all over Europe.
Although ETS2 is manageable on a keyboard or a controller, a racing wheel is highly recommended (I personally use a Logitech G27).
I would recommend buying the Going East, Scandinavia, and Vive le France map expansions, as they allow for longer deliveries. I would also recommend buying the High Power Cargo DLC and/or the Heavy Cargo Pack DLC as well, because these two purchases allow for more variation in the cargo that you haul. The other DLC are mainly cosmetic

An amazing roguelike/metroidvania/action/platformer/thing! You travel throughout the castle, defeating the boss in each of the 'zones', which unlocks the path to the final boss. Things are persistent though. In between runs, you have a Castle to upgrade. Upgrading it, using Gold found in the previous run, will increase your base health, damage, mana, health restored from pickups, and will unlock classes and an upgrade to classes as well. You can also use your Gold to buy weapon and armor upgrades from the Blacksmith, and Passive/Active Runes from the Enchantress. These Runes/Weapons/Armors, once bought, are permanent until you decide to start an entirely new profile, though you can reset it yourself or make another profile in the menu if you wish.
It's not so easy to hoard Gold though. When you first start up the game and press start, you're immediately thrust into the game in what serves as both the tutorial, and a set up for the story to follow, along with the reason you're continually going through the castle. You see, the first character went in search of a cure, but died in the process. When you start a new game, you choose from 1 of 3-ish "Heirs" to take on the castle next. These Heirs have random traits, such as blurry vision at long or close range, or maybe farts every few seconds and when he jumps(not joking), and also have a Class as well, such as Paladin, Mage, Berserker, etc., though you only start out with one class. You'd think being an Heir would entitle you to some gold from your family, but nope. Right before you enter the castle, the gatekeeper Charon demands 90% of your Gold to enter, an there's no choice in this. So earn as much gold as you can through your run, and spend every last coin on upgrading your castle or buying items at the Blacksmith and Enchantress(using blueprints found in your run), because you need to pay that 90%. There is however an upgrade in the Castle that lowers the price. It's been a while, but I think fully upgraded you will only be charged 70% percent to enter. It's been a while, but I think one of the numbers is 30%; whether that's paid or kept I can't remember.
Anyway, I definitely recommend this to any metroidvania or action/platformer fans.

Rogue Legacy is an overall awesome game. Although the game starts slow, the more you play the better the game gets. Lots of enemies, rewarding battles and a ton of unlockables throughout. The character choices, traits and abilities definitely are expansive. The controls are tight and feel great, and the options for mobility upgrades are very cool. The difficulty of the game overall I'd say is harder, but well worth the effort. This is the kind of game where playing it longer means better rewards; you can get hooked easily. That being said, you'll need as much practice as you can get if you choose to try and 100% complete the game.
Rogue Legacy is just flat out fun. If you like action and platformers, then you'll have a great time. I recommend this game to anybody; it is well worth the money.

This is a really fun game.  The mechanics are tuned amazingly well.  It doesn't suffer from the problem that many roguelike games do of being overly repetitive, because it allows you to 'lock' any given dungeon and return to where you died relatively easily.  Although I initially avoided this game because the genealogical selling point of the trailer didn't really appeal to me, the gimmick of having randomly generated 'heirs' is not really what the game is all about.  It does add a little variety and challenge (and a slight bit of annoyance at times), but the main selling point is how each time you play the game you get a little bit better.  It isn't just that your stats or items get pumped up a little (as with most rpg games), but that you actually improve your reactions and tactics each time you play.  At times the game seems almost impossibly difficult, but with practice you will find yourself sailing through those challenges.  It is quite satisfying to see how much you can achieve.  This game may have the best game mechanics of any game I have ever played.

This game was easy to learn and super fun and addicting to play.  The more you play, the more you better your character and unlock other character types to play with.  The game is difficult at first, but with practice you get the hang of it. I definitely recommend.

Spec Ops: The Line is a good third-person shooter with a great story. Although the game mechanics aren't the best, the refreshing and amazingly disturbing story is a extremely good experience and makes the game woth playing.

If you want a great single player experience, this really is a great game for that.
Spec Ops The Line may look like your standard 3rd person shooter. In many ways, it is. However, this is somewhat deliberate due to the context of the game being a gritty, dark game in a unique setting that makes you question everything about shooters such as these.
This is a game that reminds you the reality of war compared to war in video games. In many games, you gun through loads of enemies because thee game told you to without thinking why. This game makes you think why.  In many games, you're a hero that saves the  day. This game makes you think what makes you that hero. The game beats you up for doing tthings that it common practice in shooters, and really makes you think differently about modern day shooters we see all so much of. This is helped by some great voice acting and script work along with both subtle and shocking story devices that make this game feel unique. The story has some shocking moments that you'll want to experience for yourself.
Those looking for a rich gameplay experience or a multiplayer masterpiece or even a game that makes you feel good for being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that kills more people than he saves may want to go elsewhere. Those looking for a unique story and setting with developed characters and good enough gameplay that questions everything in the shooter genre to date, this game is for you.

Gameplay makes Call of Duty look deep.  Yes the story is really well done, but the gameplay detracts so horribly it almost doesn't matter.
Save the money - watch a let's play on Youtube.  You'll get all the story with none of the fantastically awful gameplay.

Very few games had me engaged while the game itself isn't fun. With Spec Ops: The Line in particular, the gameplay itself isn't all that engaging but how it is executed made it so. How you might ask? Its how the gameplay itself connects with the tone of the game and story. The story? Depressing, mind-blowing, creative, and thought-provoking for something in the modern military genre, also even subtly throws a message at the player about the tropes and expectations towards this genre.
Go into this game expecting absolutly nothing, and you're in for quite a treat.
Go into this game expecting your typical modern military shooter with mocho and tough military soldiers however, and you're going to get knocked in the heart with what this game has to offer.

I have thoroughly enjoyed my time spent in the hunter cotw so far. But I do believe the route they are taking this game on is a disastrous one.
They currently released tents as a 4.99 dlc pack that lets you buy tents in the game, place them, and allow you fast travel and outpost options. I have no problem supporting game companies but you can see how this is going to go down in the future... you want a new gun? How about 6 dollars. How about new bullets that are better than the polymer and soft tip combined... 8$.  It leaves the developers an insane amount of freedom to charge ludicrous prices for things that don't take much work, and moves this into a micro transactions based game. If I wanted that I would go play candy crush, boom beach, or some other iOS/android game.
I understand the company needs to make money but they are going about it the wrong way. They need to focus on larger content releases that are bundled together. Make a new hunting reserve with 10 new animals, 6 guns, tent features, etc and then charge $20 for this. That is content people are wanting and would pay for and you might see your reviews go up because you are asking people to pay for a reasonable amount of content.
Just imagine if sky rim followed this model. You start off the game with 10 enemy types, iron/steel class weapons and armour, and 2 major cities. If you want glass, dwarven, daedric armours you purchase the bundle for $5 each separately. You want to fight 8 different enemies.. how does a $10 dlc pack sound. Oh you want access to the other 4 major cities and their quests.. $20 each, fast travel$5, horse riding$5, it can go on and on. However you include that in the base game and you get great reviews and more game purchases.
I wish the developers the best, but until they follow a less sketchy business model they do not have my positive vote for the game. I will change my vote if they change their business model and hold true to a game not based on microtansactions.

Day 1. I woke up in an island. This is strange. Hey look, a mine. Let's explore it..
Day 2. Nothing to see here. Gotta find my way out.
Day 3. Found the exit. Home sweet home here I come.
Day 4. Air doesn't seem so fresh anymore. Probably because Rocky and Torchy are my only companions on this journey.
Day 5. Some creepy cops came along and asked for my ID. I bashed their heads in with Rocky.
Day 6. Creepy guy asks if I want a slave and gear. I steer clear from him.
Day 7. I bash his head in whi;st he sleeps. He should get more creative. Why make your lock code 0000?
Day 8. Built a campsite and a sleeping bag. I'll need to fortify around it so I can live here.
Day 9. Built first foundations of my house. Will finish with stone walls and a roof soon.
Day 10. As I walk out into the wilderness, I find a relative of Rocky. He calls himself Guru Rockith. He's a wise and floating rock. I must learn the ways of Rock jitsu from him. It's the only way I'll survive.
Day 11. First trial of Rock Jitsu is to climb this mountain via this way, that is, the sheer drop way.
Day 12. Creepy guy up there. Seems friendly though, so I won't go on him with Rocky and Torchy and bash his skull in.
Day 13. I am reminded of Newton's laws. What comes up, must come down. Rock Jitsu is harder than i thought. Rock hard.
Day 14. The creepy guy came back. Today I scaled Rock mountain. I have finished the first trial. Come at me, Rock Jitsu.
Day 15. I must go down without hurting myself at all. Trial 2 here I come.
Day 16. I fell. I'm going to die here. Goodbye, Rocky, Torchy. I hope you have a good life without me.
And so ends the chronicles of Charry, the survivor of a plane crash. He met many people on the way. Nearly all seem to have fallen to their knees from Rocky's incessant bashing of their occipitals. Karma seems to have finally caught up with him.
Rocky Survived, as did Torchy

Rocky became a supreme Rock Jitsu master.
and Torchy became the King's Army Commander for the Torch Rebellion against the Rocks. Torchy and Rocky eventually wed after the war, as they had defected both their sides to finish it. Spec Ops The Line Review
Introduction
When I finished Spec Ops: The Line, I sat through the credits thinking of all the terrible things I had just done.  The newest iteration in the Spec Ops series was developed by Yager and Darkside game studios, and was published by 2K games.  It was released on June 26th, 2012 on Xbox 360, PS3, and PC.  It is an intriguing third person shooter and goes into some very dark places.  With a great setup as well as good gunplay Spec Ops has the potential to be great, but the multiplayer is lame and uninspired.
Presentation
Story is the focus in Spec Ops.  It takes place in post catastrophe Dubai and a series of the worst sandstorms in history have swept through the city, and it has become deserted wasteland.  You play as Captain Martin Walker, who is sent into Dubai with Lt. Adams and Staff Sergeant Lugo, to perform reconnaissance on the location of John Konrad, a missing in action war hero who volunteered to have his battalion help the locals evacuate the city.  Resources are scarce, and the survival of the people of dubai depended on the evacuations success.  Walker has a special connection with Konrad, which is the driving force through the length of the campaign.
However, things are not as they seem, and a simple reconnaissance mission turns into something much more personal and emotionally straining.  Walker, Adams, and Lugo transform as characters and end the story as much different people.  This is affected by the choices you make throughout the story.  Many times you will be forced to make a decision that you hate, but you have to anyway either to advance the story or because they other option is more repulsing.  This game is an experience, and at its core, explores what war will do to the soldiers that fight them.  It's the video game adaption of Apocalypse Now and Heart of Darkness.
My one gripe with the story is its length.  On normal difficulty, it took me 5 hours to complete.  Aside from playing spec ops again for trophy or achievement hunting, the only other real reason for a second play through are the multiple endings available.  I couldn't go on without mentioning the sound.  The voice acting in this game is top notch.  All the voice actors give stellar performances.  The music in spec ops is also good, and there are many set pieces throughout the game set rock music that fit very well.
Gameplay
Spec Ops' gameplay is good but nothing special.  It's the standard third person shooter affair.  There are a variety of assault rifles, sub machine guns, shotguns and sniper rifles at your disposal.  They are fun to shoot, but nothing special.  A cover system is also in place from which you can dip in and out of cover to shoot enemies and blind fire from.  You can also issue commands or rather one command to your squad.  You can highlight a target for Adams or Lugo to take out, but that is it.
The most interesting thing spec ops does in terms of gameplay is the environment effects.  Many times you can take advantage of a sandstorm for cover, or shoot out glass beneath beneath the feet of your enemies.
Where Spec Ops goes wrong is in its multiplayer.  Developed by Darkside, whereas the single player was developed by Yager, it is bland and uninspired.  Taking none of the elements that made the single player special, it fails to do anything interesting.  It's the standard Call of Duty esque leveling system and modes you would expect from a shooter.  Don't pick this up for the multiplayer.
Conclusion
If you ignore the multiplayer, Spec Ops is one hell of a game.  It prevails in creating an interesting environment and set up, and telling a dark tale.  The character development, story, and voice acting are all top notch, and the ending will leave you thinking about Captain Walker’s actions for a long time.  Yager has created an amazing story, one that should be the story on which all other military shooters should be judged by.  It's just too bad the second half of the package couldn't be more polished.
Final Score: 80/100

This game has so much potential, but Avalanche chose to reuse their "if you can't dazzle them with gameplay, bore them with tedium" formula which made Just Cause 1 & 2 lackluster.
I imagine the dev conversation went something like this...
RAD = Radical Avalanche Developer
SAD = Standard Avalanche Developer
RAD - Let's have him hijack vehicles to collect them, drive back to his shop to get upgrades off them and scrap for parts, and he'd have several frames to upgrade and use. Because in real life car thieves steal cars and take them to chop shops for parts and scrap.
SAD - Nah, let's bore the player by making them wander around for hours collecting paltry bits of garbage we hide everywhere which is used to to upgrade one single vehicle, there by removing the entertainment of hunting down vehicles.
RAD - Let's make them configure their car at a garage, so they have to strategically choose how to load it out, since they'll be stuck with it like that until they get back to base.
SAD - Nah, let's just let them insta-alter their vehicle on-the-fly, even in the middle of the desert while doing 80mph. People like convenience, so let's let them rip all the weight off their car instantly to make it go faster, then load it all back on to protect themselves right before they hit an enemy.
RAD - So you're gonna bore people to death by making them collect tons of garbage to upgrade the vehicle, but they can insta-swap parts while drifving... on the one extreme it's super inconvenient, and on the other it's illogically over-convenient.
SAD - Yeah, we like to throw logic out the door here.... whatever we can do to annoy players by either frustrating them with tedium or trashing all logic ... that's what we do.
RAD - Let's give Max a dog and mechanic companion, and he can have both ride with him in any vehicle he takes.
SAD - Nah, the mechanic can only ride along in the main car and repair it, so it's pointless driving any other car.
RAD - Well, let's make the dog cool by having to jump out of the car and go along with you to attack people when you're on foot.
SAD - Nah, let's just make him utterly pointless by having him only go along in one vehicle, and then only used for one very specific, boring task by driving around forever looking for mine fields then tediously clearing them out one at a time.
RAD - Let's add some stealth to the game to let Max sneak up on enemies out taking a leak and steal their cars!
SAD - Let's not. Let's have every enemy in the game instantly know where he is instead.
RAD - Let's have Max take over bases, supply lines and other things to help out friendly factions. The more area he controls, the easier time he'll have finding gas, water, etc, the more friendly patrols will roam around, etc.
SAD - Let's have him destroy everything, because that makes no sense to do so in a world that's already struggling to get by.
RAD - Let's have different enemy factions get into road battles instead of Max being the only one engaging. Those buzzards scavenge from anyone!
SAD - Let's have all enemy factions be friends with each other, and only attack Max.
RAD - Let's make road battles cool by letting Max get onto his car while someone else drives, and jump to other cars to get into fights and take them over!
SAD - Let's not.
RAD - Let's make there be lots of high-speed vehicle fights, and let Max drive in and wreck bases in his car!
SAD - Let's only have a few vehicle battles, all others are just random cars driving around that have nothing to do with anything and give paltry amounts of reward for defeating them, and make Max get out of his car for half the game to wander around getting into fist-fights and waste hours looking for hidden boxes of garbage.
RAD - If he's going to collect so much stuff, let's give him bonuses for collecting stuff.
SAD - Nah, let's just pad the game out with historical crap and cars to collect, but it's all pointless. We're just padding the game out with stuff that's easy to code.
RAD - Let's at least make it where if Max takes over a base he auto-collects all other scrap and memorabilia from that location.
SAD - What?! Wandering around collecting junk is half the fun! When he defeats a base, he can still spend hours enjoying the thrill of looking for junk that we hid in annoying locations.
RAD - Let's make one really awesome area with great scripted events and story and unique things to do! It'll be a shorter game, but it'll be a great experience.
SAD - Let's make several HUGE areas with the same repetitive tasks going on over and over that take hours upon hours to do, and once you clear an area it's just the same thing in the next area for hours on end, and clearing areas has no impact on the game whatsoever. That'll be boring and repetitive, but we can brag on the box about "100 hours of game play"
RAD - Let's give Max a sniper rifle!
SAD - ... that he can only use in his car, even though all the enemy snipers are carrying them on foot.
RAD - Let's have the mechanic auto-fuel up the car if there's a jerry can in the back.
SAD - Let's not. He'll auto-repair the car, and he'll auto-swap parts for you while driving 80mph down the road, but let's not get carried away with convenience here.
RAD - Let's have challenges that are difficult, but can be overcome if the player just grinds and upgrades a bit more.
SAD - Let's make a really hard race that downgrades your vehicle weapon regardless of how good it is, and put all kinds of twists and slopes on it that make the horrible driving mechanics really shine, and force the player to overcome that if they want to progress the story. That way 1/5th of the players rage quit the game and get a refund.
RAD - Let's have artillery at bases work for friendlies after Max takes over a base. This incentivizes him to sneak in and try to keep things intact.
SAD - Let's not, and just leave them standing there as pointless reminders that friends in bases don't do anything for Max.
RAD - Let's have a steady rate of progress that is either story-driven or xp driven, thus the player will gradually get better over time one way or the other.
SAD - Nah, let's be bipolar and make some upgrades unlock by clearing areas, and others unlock by following the story. So, players that ignore the story to clear areas are punished when story upgrades are kept locked until the last 10% of the game, and players that rush through are punished by having other critical upgrades locked away for not clearing areas. We want to make sure all players get punished for whatever play style they choose.
RAD - Let's make Max an understandable anti-hero that becomes more respectable over time.
SAD - Let's make him an unlikeable scumbag that treats people helping him like garbage and causes problems he later has to clear up because he's too weak-willed to take on his own personal issues.
RAD - Let's make the mechanic a likeable, quirky side-kick that Max slowly comes to trust and confide in over time.
SAD - Nah, let's have Max treat him like absolute garbage the whole time, even though he's the only person that sticks with him through thick and thin and has unwavering confidence in him and is trying to help him find his way.
RAD - Let's have Max auto-collect goodies from enemies when he defeats them.
SAD - That ruins the fun of trudging over to manually pick it up, though!
RAD - Let's have ti when the player hits a button, Max does the action.
SAD - Let's make the player hold down a button to do the action for no reason.
RAD - Why don't we really do something unique and awesome!?
SAD - Because, we're Avalanche. We used the same formula for Just Cause and Just Cause 2, and that was mediocre enough to make a profit. So, we're not going to change the formula.
RAD - I quit.
SAD - Good... we don't need people like you with creative, interesting ideas screwing up our mediocre games!

On paper, I really should love this game. I love roguelikes, I'm a fan of platformers, the humor is pretty good, and the "story" that the journals tell had me intrigued.
That said, I just can't stand playing this game for more than a few minutes at a time. The first hour alone almost made me quit. It wasn't the difficulty, necessarily. It was the controls, the lack of options, and the enemies themselves. They don't care where you are or where you're moving, touching any one of them or their projectiles will fling you and carve off a chunk of your health. It's damn near impossible to predict where an enemy is going to move, which makes a difficult game full of challenging enemies nigh impossible.  Even so, the unpredictable enemy movements might be workable if there were any way to dodge, block, avoid them. Most levels are so cramped and irregular that there's just nowhere to *go*. Most enemies can and will phase through walls in an attempt to rush up and touch you, giving you no option to hit them until they emerge through the floor (and by then, they've already hit and stunned you). Some of the mimic-type enemies will be placed in such a way that it is literally impossible to progress without hitting them, such as when they spawn and cover up a tiny ledge over spikes, with that ledge being the only way forward. Even if you hit it as you jump onto the platform, it won't move out of the way fast enough for you to avoid getting hit, sending you down onto the spikes. I can't even tell you how many times the "ghosts" flew through the floor all the way up to me, only reaching the top few pixels through the floor to touch me when it was too late for me to attack. The warlocks became the bane of my existence, because they will fly erratic patterns just outside your melee reach, causing you to touch them every single time you go to hit them, and hovering just out of reach to cast their attacks. Said attacks are undodgeable in certain hallways, they'll instantly block passageways and fly right at you, causing you to either touch them or touch their fireballs. They only need to land one hit on you, no significant amount of food or life-steal will ever bring you back to the health you had at the start.
You have to *buy* the dashes, double jumps, one class' ability to block, everything.  That means you're going to play a good chunk of the game *without* the ability to do any of those things. It was painful, frustrating, and gave no indication that any of those things even existed. Classes, items, NPCs, upgrades, entire game mechanics go completely undetected for a variable amount of time. Maybe you never use magic, and see no reason to spend your hard-earned gold on the first point to upgrade it. There may be an entire branch of the upgrade tree that you never see, including classes, stat upgrades, and Quality of Life upgrades! It's insane, and it always presents the worst possible version of the game for you to play. Large sections of each randomly-generated castle will be virtually impossible for you to complete, either because you haven't unlocked certain things or because the RNG doesn't care if the section is possible or not. Difficulty is all over the place, the only sense of consistent progression is in the "areas" of the castle.
This isn't a game you can jump into and succeed based on your skill or by learning. You'll blindly feel your way through this game by dying over and over again to frustrating mechanics, iffy controls, and absolute impossibility. If you're *lucky*, you'll gain enough gold to take another baby step toward playing the "real" game. If not, have fun plateauing partway through. If your next upgrade costs 1001 coins, and you earned 1000, have fun starting over from scratch on your next character.
Truly, this is a game that I want to like. There's a lot to love here. I really see what people enjoy about this game. That said, I will not recommend it. To me, it's like having teeth pulled by the world's most beautiful dentist. I can see why people would enjoy coming to this dentist but I'm not having any fun getting my teeth pulled.

Rogue Legacy is a GREAT game. It's just challenging and hard enough to make you try again, again and again - few games manages to stay on that thin, thin line but Rogue Legacy manages to stay there the whole game and still make you come back for 1, 2 or even 3 more playthroughs.
But then comes the added content, with the added bosses.
I love the class system in this game, it's super fun to play around with the different classes and all the different traits you can have. Even though you have to choose between 3 (or 6) kids you can still pick the one that matches your play style the best. But in the added boss fights, you're forced into a super weak character, with pre-made skills and class. This forces you to not only maybe use a class you've hardly used before but also in a super weak state against super strong bosses in hardly fair environments. It takes it's perfect balance and throws it right out the window and it really saddens me to see this, because I've REALLY enjoyed the game up to that point.
I DO still recommend this game, because it takes a couple of hours to reach that point and it's still very fun and challenging up to that point but you can only thoroughly enjoy this game if you love to fight unfair bosses over and over and over and over+∞ until you somehow manage to beat the boss thanks to luck.

I'd really love to like this game, believe me. It's filled with things that I really adore in video games, like addictive and cool customization and a real feeling of progress. It feels great to upgrade your car from a lousy rustbucket in to a real wasteland warmachine. The combat in car and on foot is also very meaty and physical, and Is a lot of fun. There is however a single very major thing that basically ruins the game for me, and that's the difficulty.
I've actually played the game on consoles for quite a while before testing it out on pc, and the problem still stands. Max is stupidly powerful even before any upgrades, and even though the on foot combat is fun and flashy, it's basically a carbon copy of the Arkham games combat system with only 2 buttons, and it gets extremely boring after you realise that the only way you can lose on foot is to ♥♥♥♥ around and try to do certain moves. The game tells you exactly when to parry, and when parrying is literally 50% of the games combat mechanics, it really makes the combat feel like a long QTE.
Max also has a plethora of things you can upgrade, including armor, weapons and perks. These make the combat even more braindead, and you can mow down a huge group of enemies with basically no effort.
The car combat starts out a bit more balanced, but has the same problem that on foot combat has: the upgrades.
You build scarp (the currency for upgrades) wayy too fast and before you've hit the mid game point you notice that not a single car patrol is actually a threat. They cant harm your armored car and you deal ridiculous damage to them.
TL;DR: Mad Max had awesome potential, but the coolness of the upgrades is negated by the incredibly easy and repetitive structure of the game.

I have been waiting for a Mad Max video game every since Fallout 3, since it had references to this series which the leather armor, Mel, Dogmeat etc. I decided to watch the movies, thought they were awesome, but was disappointed when there was no video game. Thankfully Avalanche Studios answered my prayers.
Pros
+VERY well opitimized, I don't even meet the recommended cpu or gpu specs, but I'm still able to play on high settings with 80-100fps keep in mind this might not be the case for you, but who knows.
+Graphics are superb
+Car combat is amazing, you can almost feel the impacts of crashes and the slow mo is really cool
+Voice acting is top notch
+Combat is fun, I imagine a lot of people would say it justs copying the Batman Arkham series, but how can you honestly do better then it, it fits the action adventure genre very nicely
+Story is amazing and gets especially good toward the end
+You get a dog
+Collectible finding is always nice
+Car customization is awesome
+Setting is cool, I know some might say its boring since its basically a giant desert, but that is where the movies took place, plus there are intresting locations.
+Music/sound design is amazing.
Cons
-Quests can get a little bit stale, not crazy amounts of variety, doesnt really bother me though since im diehard Mad Max fan
-To my knowlege there is no new game plus mode, which sucks because I would want this game to have as much replay value as possible
-Game is a little too easy, not the car combat, but the CQC , and I couldn't find a difficulty setting, luckily health is restored by a canteen that you have to refill or by food which is somewhat uncommon and you cant just hoard infinite amounts of it, (don't worry there is no hunger or thirst survival feature,), so at least your hp doesnt restore after every fight like the Arkham series. You can handicap yourself though by equipping the starter jacket/gloves etc.
Final Score- 9/10. Would take this game to Vahalla with me.
