It seems nice up until the point where you realize that the experience is desperately lacking a few things, and those things stand out big and bold as stuff that no self-respecting game tester would have let slide. Easiest example of this is the complete lack of transportation. Early on you're given a mission that's a significant distance away. You could fast travel... but only between outposts, and only after you've discovered them, and that only occurs after you've jogged 30-45 minutes, or more across a map, wheezing away the whole time. There are roads everywhere, sure. But no transportation? No ATVs, no bikes even? That wasn't a miss, that was a conscious decision. The inclusion of tents as the first DLC feels very much like that as well.
And let's not pretend that this is a misstep on the part of the publisher. Don't forget that the first iteration of this game required a subscription, or very expensive DLC, to permit you to hunt anything beyond exactly one type of deer. Frankly, many of the mechanics in this edition feel like they were prepared to be DLC-enabled anyway: equipment that you need to progress (sort of, it's much more difficult without it) is level locked ealy on, and requires in-game money to buy. You can sense that there were "XP and Credit Boost" microtransactions ready for this before they decided to pull it.
To be clear, I'm not anti-DLC. It can be fantastic for many cases. If this had been a complete game I'd probably be more interested in DLC that added in new regions, for instance, or added other not-basic game mechanics.
As lovely as the game seems to be on the surface, the business model here seems to be predicated on frustrating the player in very basic, obvious ways,  to ensure future DLC payouts. This is the second most cynical, ridiculous way to squeeze more money out of dissatisfied players... and this game's predecessor made use of the first most.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

When this game was announced, as a huge LiS fan I was firmly in the "this doesn't seem like a story that needs to be told" category. I continued to feel that way after seeing the first gameplay footage and hearing Ashly Burch wouldn't be reprising her role as Chloe.
Turns out, this game is actually phenomenal and in many ways surpasses the original LiS IMO.
For starters, the graphics are outstanding. The lighting, shadows, and details like character eyes look much sharper and realistic than LiS. The animation is still not great, but at least the lip sync animation have been upgraded from the slow-mo-sock-puppet look LiS: S1's characters had.
The writing is a step up from the original LiS. The characters, world building, and overall plot were what made the original LiS so great to play despite the often laughably bad dialogue. BtS has significantly better dialogue which only feels slightly weird when the player ocassionally chooses dialogue options which don't make sense. Arguably, the writers should have accounted for this, but it happens so infrequently I don't mind and IMO it adds to the charm of the game.
The designers stripped out everything that made LiS Max-specific like time travel, photography, etc. and replaced it with fun Chloe based mechanics - I found myself being extra confrontational because it's more fun to verbally spar with characters than pick a single response.
Overall I love this just as much as the original LiS, if not slightly more. The story being told here is not only good on its own, but adds significantly what the player learned/experienced in the first LiS.

This game is a good game for its time! I have heard that people liked some improvements this game made over its predecesor but I never played Borderlands 1. Something I should bring up is that if you are a liberal, aproach this game with caution! This game possibly has to be the second most unpolitically correct ever made (the first one being Postal 2). Yeah, this is a game I don't talk about in public considering there are enemies in the game called Midgets and Psychos. Okay so what about this game is good? Well everyone who has even heard little bits about Borderlands would know that it has a lot of adult and crude humor behind it. that is very true! Initially when I staarted playing, the humor didn't feel right for me at first because the humor felt better suited to an adult cartoon on Adult Swim. But as the game progressed on, I started to enjoy the humor a bit more. Something to look forward to is the fact that there is an abundance of firearms that you can find. Plus every gun has a specific manufacture and every manufacurerer has their little gimmick that comes with every firearm. The Teidore has to be my favorite company because their guns have the best reload mechanic out there. Instead of a long and tedious reload animation like in your standard Call of Duty Teidore firearms explode when reloaded, so you can throw your shotgun at a bullymong charging in at high speed and what will happen is that the shotgun you just threw exploded and caused harm to the very beast that tried to eat you. In this game, you are going to have a favorite manufacture even though you won't have a favoirte gun. Plus the game is a multiplayer and the mulitplayer was actually handedled better than I though. It's decent but it works. So the multiplayer is an online co-op where someone hosts the game and everyone can decide on their own class. So whenever you create a charcter for multiplayer, you can always use that same charatcer for another mulitplayer or single player if you want to so you can essentailly have a roster of charcters for whatever game you want to play. In my honest opinion, single-player is more fun, because it adds more tension in gameplay than in multiplayer where you knwo when someone has your back. Plus there is the shield items. Shields in this game are a must-have for your charcter. What the shields do is they absorb all of the damage for you, but the shield has a limited amount of punishment it can take before it becomes disabled. The sheild will regenerate the energy over time when you haven't taken any damage but when the sheild goes down, you will not only be vunerable, you will feel vunerable as well so you will spend time trying to find cover to wait for you sheild to go back online. Plus the four classes presented in the game lack varitety but that all have their own special power, the comando has a deployable Sentry that will automatically target enemies for a limited ammount of time, the gunzerker can temporarly dualweild any weapon at his disposal, the siren has this supernatrual ability to crush enemies in this gravitational sphere, and the assassin has the abilitty to create a false-image of himself to disoreint the eneimes. Overall I recomend this game but I recomend you have your own oppionion on this game than simply taking my word for it. The reason why is because this game is good in my oppinion and even though I have never seen anyone not like this game, I can understand why someone wouldn't like this game especially since trying to make a game funny is a lot more dificult than trying to write an episode of South Park. Comedy is the second hardest genere to write and even though this game is funny, the fact that it's a game outs it at a disadvantage. Overall the best advice I can give you about this game is to take a gander at this game over a period of about a week, not a couple days, not a couple hours, you need to give this game at least a week.

From playing just under two hours this game gives a good impression and appears to be a more realistic and more serious game than the Cabella's games, without hiding everything behind a pay wall. This is what theHunter should have been.
Graphically this game is beautiful. The way the light and the shadows look just make it so impressive and almost gives the impression of actually being there, and it makes you want to wander around. And the desire to explore is something you want in a hunting game right?
The game play is different enough from theHunter to make it truely feel like its own game. It has a "Quest" system in the game which reward the player with currency. I got over 5000 within the time I played, which seems decent. They also reward the player with equipment, for example one of the missions gave me a Predator "Jackrabbit" call, which attracts Foxes and other animals who prey one rabbits. The only drawback is that everything in the store seems to be really expensive, but it rewards those who are better hunters.
They introduced a new system which makes animals clear out of a area where there was a gunshot recently. This helps avoid the broken AI that is sometimes seen in theHunter Classic. They also made a system where the animals have a need they must fufill during certain parts of the day. This is extremely helpfun and would allow a great hunter to kill multiple animals at a time.
They also added a skill system which is a massive improvement from the base game. This affects many aspects of the game, from weather to tracking to lures.This improves the game massively and makes hunting faster, funner, and eaiser.
All in all, I have to say this is a excellent game and its very fun, however I do not feel that it jusifies a $30 dollar price tag. This would be something to pick up on sale or on a rainy day.

Spec Ops: The Line might be dismissed at first glance for being just another modern military shooter. That assumption couldn’t be more wrong though.
Based loosely on Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, Spec Ops provides one of the strongest and mature narratives in recent memory.
The story revolves around Captain Walker and his two wingmen, Lugo and Adams. Their latest mission sends them to a post-catastrophic Dubai to find Colonel Konrad who was in charge of evacuating the civilian population. Captain Walker is often forced to make difficult decisions and any pretense of him being some badass hero is quickly removed as it's clear that sometimes there's no correct decision to make. The character progression is strong and the voice acting is phenomenal.
The art direction is spectacular as Dubai provides almost a surreal experience. When you’re not avoiding sandstorms, you'll travel through luxury hotels and buildings that have all been submerged in sand. The game also gives you a taste of PTSD as you’re sometimes left wondering whether or not certain things are real.
The combat plays out similarly to other third person shooters. It will have you taking cover, blind firing and issuing commands to your squad mates. The AI is well done, making Lugo and Adams feel very capable while the enemy AI on the other hand could use a bit of work. The combat is solid but it makes no attempt to do anything new or innovative.
The soundtrack is fantastic, including a lot of real songs along with ambient guitar pieces that match the mood perfectly. The inclusion of Jimi Hendrix and other classics really give the game an ‘Apocalypse Now’ type of feel which was another Heart of Darkness adaptation.
Unfortunately, Spec Ops is fairly short (around 5 hours) but the different endings offer some incentive to replay the game. There’s a multiplayer mode that offers a few different game types, weapons, and stages but it feels a bit tacked on. It’s fairly clear that Spec Ops was designed to be experienced as a single player game primarily and it’s one I strongly recommend.
For a more detailed review, here’s a video by my friend and fellow reviewer, Trent:
Pros
+	Amazing Narrative
+	Fantastic Soundtrack
+	Beautiful Art Direction & Environments
+	Great Characters & Voice Acting
Cons
-	Short length & Linear
-	Generic Combat
-	Multiplayer isn’t very exciting

It would be easy to look at Spec Ops, groan and promptly write it off as another addition to the bloated cabal of modern military shooters, but to do so would be a mistake. What, on the outside, looks like a game about three hardened delta force commandos shooting up brown people in another sandy Middle Eastern hell hole defies outward appearances and proves to be a bit more clever and surprising. Given the fact that the earlier entries in the Spec Ops franchise preoccupied themselves with cut and dry tactical military action you would be forgiven for making such an assertion.

The game opens with a bombastic set piece that seems to have been ripped out of Call Of Duty. It looks like a deleted scene from True Lies, with your character manning a mini gun, shredding lesser enemy helicopters between the sky scrappers of Dubai. You shoot through large glass walls at choppers on the opposite sides of buildings, one unfortunate bird smashes into a crane as things are constantly going boom. It's what we have come to expect from this kind of game. The sequence ends and you flash back to the beginning of the sequence of events that led to that point. No surprises so far. You play as Walker, a Delta Force operative (voiced by Nolan North of Uncharted fame) and are accompanied by Adams and Lugo, your trusty wing men, on a mission to rescue the people of Dubai and locate Colonel John Konrad. The narrative is loosely based on Joesph Conrad's Heart of Darkness and it takes a lot of cues from Frances Ford Coppola's Apocalypse Now, which is also based on Conrad's novella.

The not-so-unusual set up is followed up with some not-so-unusual third person cover based shooting as the game introduces you to Dubai and your squad mates. The shooting mechanics work well enough. You take cover, blind fire, pop out of cover to take precise shots, order squad mates to throw flash bangs and attack. Left to their own devices, Lugo and Adams prove themselves to be competent. They will kill enemies and they generally stay out of your way and make an effort to preserve themselves. It's very refreshing to have AI squad mates that do more than shout, “Reloading!” and “Stay frosty!” every five seconds. In short order, the first wrinkle to otherwise not-so-unusual formula is introduced—environment based attacks. You will find the sandstorm has left mounds of sand heaped behind fragile barriers that can be destroyed in an effort to bury your foes. These environmental advantages are sprinkled throughout the campaign and really brings the setting to life. Engulfing enemies in sand isn't enough to warrant playing any game, but from here Spec Ops only gets more interesting. The second major deviation this game makes is placing you in the middle of moral dilemmas. These sections don't have any lasting effects on the game's narrative but act as a means of reinforcing the game's themes. These are not about playing a “good” soldier or a “bad” soldier but rather having to make a choice you may not want to make. Making these choices strips any pretense of being a bad♥♥♥♥♥hero, they remind you that you can't save the the day all of the time and sometimes you might not be able to save anything at all...

One of the most uninspiring and unappealing aspects of modern military shooters is the art direction. I can only wade through so many brown mud huts, gray warehouses made out of tin and steel, and dilapidated villages before I want to gouge my eyes out. In spite of all of the sand, Spec Ops offsets the sandy, sun baked sections with vibrant, colorful interiors. You wade through seas of abandoned cars on highways, blast your way through luxury hotels, crawl out of the apocalyptic center of the city, and bounce across glass filled rooftops. Dubai, as depicted in Spec Ops, is a surreal place. The art style lends itself to the narrative—more specifically the character's mental states. What you see may or may not be real. The characters themselves are detailed and they become more haggard and war torn as the game progresses, animations are altered a bit to reflect the change in characters. There are some visual metaphors sprinkled about if you pay attention (and you should) to the detailed and engaging setting. It's not the technical marvel that the more recent Battlefield games are but the art direction makes this infinitely more interesting to behold.

Also the soundtrack deserves special attention. Dubai has also been rigged with speakers and a DJ, known as The Radioman, is broadcasting throughout the city. He sounds like an aging hippie and the music he plays kind of reflects this. Did you ever think you would have a shoot out in a modern military game while Deep Purple's Hush plays in the background? What about Martha and the Vandellas Nowhere to Run? It's fantastic. The juxtaposition of these tunes with the violence of the gun play creates and truly unsettling tone. It seems really obvious that Apocalypse Now was a huge influence on this aspect of the game. There are also some noteworthy ambient, largely guitar-based compositions that sew together the sections of the game that don't have licensed tunes playing in a cohesive manner. The voice acting is also commendable and the writing is very self aware of genre tropes and plays off of them. The whole game centers around critiquing and in some ways defying what you have come to expect from other games in this genre. You won't play anything like it.

What sets Spec Ops back, and is likely to turn off most gamers, is its short length. It is completable in a single sitting and most players will clock in about five to eight hours depending on skill level. The moral dilemmas are not designed to alter the game but rather to set the tone for your play through and experiencing their different outcomes really doesn't extend the game play experience in any meaningful way. Spec Ops was clearly designed as a single player experience and the multiplayer is best ignored altogether. Playing the game in co-op will only further shorten the experience. It's a shame that completing the main single player experience doesn't unlock bite sized missions or episodes from your squad's past. Given that PTSD and war induced stress are huge themes it would have been an appropriate way to add to the game's content without artificially extending the main campaign.

Spec Ops is one of the most mature and interesting games of the year. It is an experience. One unlike any other in terms of the way the game mechanics reinforce the themes and concepts put forth by the narrative. It should be on your radar but don't expect to put dozens of hours into it. In terms of gameplay it's competent rather than exceptional, but where it excels is where other games in its genre need to take a hard look at what they are doing. Games like Spec Ops and Bioshock will be important examples in video game history for integrating gameplay mechanics with narrative themes. This alone makes it worth playing and possibly revisiting in a few years time.

When this game was announced, as a huge LiS fan I was firmly in the "this doesn't seem like a story that needs to be told" category. I continued to feel that way after seeing the first gameplay footage and hearing Ashly Burch wouldn't be reprising her role as Chloe.
Turns out, this game is actually phenomenal and in many ways surpasses the original LiS IMO.
For starters, the graphics are outstanding. The lighting, shadows, and details like character eyes look much sharper and realistic than LiS. The animation is still not great, but at least the lip sync animation have been upgraded from the slow-mo-sock-puppet look LiS: S1's characters had.
The writing is a step up from the original LiS. The characters, world building, and overall plot were what made the original LiS so great to play despite the often laughably bad dialogue. BtS has significantly better dialogue which only feels slightly weird when the player ocassionally chooses dialogue options which don't make sense. Arguably, the writers should have accounted for this, but it happens so infrequently I don't mind and IMO it adds to the charm of the game.
The designers stripped out everything that made LiS Max-specific like time travel, photography, etc. and replaced it with fun Chloe based mechanics - I found myself being extra confrontational because it's more fun to verbally spar with characters than pick a single response.
Overall I love this just as much as the original LiS, if not slightly more. The story being told here is not only good on its own, but adds significantly what the player learned/experienced in the first LiS.

I'd really love to like this game, believe me. It's filled with things that I really adore in video games, like addictive and cool customization and a real feeling of progress. It feels great to upgrade your car from a lousy rustbucket in to a real wasteland warmachine. The combat in car and on foot is also very meaty and physical, and Is a lot of fun. There is however a single very major thing that basically ruins the game for me, and that's the difficulty.
I've actually played the game on consoles for quite a while before testing it out on pc, and the problem still stands. Max is stupidly powerful even before any upgrades, and even though the on foot combat is fun and flashy, it's basically a carbon copy of the Arkham games combat system with only 2 buttons, and it gets extremely boring after you realise that the only way you can lose on foot is to ♥♥♥♥ around and try to do certain moves. The game tells you exactly when to parry, and when parrying is literally 50% of the games combat mechanics, it really makes the combat feel like a long QTE.
Max also has a plethora of things you can upgrade, including armor, weapons and perks. These make the combat even more braindead, and you can mow down a huge group of enemies with basically no effort.
The car combat starts out a bit more balanced, but has the same problem that on foot combat has: the upgrades.
You build scarp (the currency for upgrades) wayy too fast and before you've hit the mid game point you notice that not a single car patrol is actually a threat. They cant harm your armored car and you deal ridiculous damage to them.
TL;DR: Mad Max had awesome potential, but the coolness of the upgrades is negated by the incredibly easy and repetitive structure of the game.

Cons

This is a nostalgic side-scroller in the tradition of Castlevania with RPG elements.  You are tasked with going through a castle and killing demons, monsters, ghosts, and evil knights while traversing platforms and navigating boobytraps.  The RPG Elements allow you to upgrade your knight's abilities, weapons, and armor.
Your knights have specific abilities and weaknesses that make this game interesting.  An example of an ability is enhanced strength while a weakness may be that he suffers from a vision disorder.  As such, the screen is blurry or dark, or may only be black and white.  Playing through the castle you are given the ability to find treasure that may correct his vision problems such as glasses.
Another unique element is that if you are killed, the next knight is the offspring of a previous knight, though the abilities and weaknesses may be different.
The objective of the game is to clear out as many of the bad guys as you can.  Your rewards are gold, special armor blueprints, spells, and items to counteract your weaknesses.  You can also upgrade your character's health, mana, strength, and armor while unlocking characters who can aid in wearpons, armor, and abilities.
I would stongly suggest playing this game with a gamepad as keyboard controls make it a little difficult at times.  Its quite a bit of fun for a mindless button mashing game with an endless supply of offspring to keep the game going for hours.  Multiplayer, especially coop would be a welcomed addition to this game.

Rust is one of my all time favorite games.  You'll laugh.  You'll cry. You'll live.  You'll die.  And that last part - you'll do lots of that.  The game is brutal - more or less so depending on which server you play on.  But the game hits the right notes in so many areas.  PvP is a blast, even if the gun mechanics can be frustrating at times.  The building system is one of the best in the survival genre.  It allows a lot of creativity (even though that sometimes gets limited by other mechanics).  Procedurally generated maps and regular wipes help keep the game fresh.  The "monuments" provide interesting places to explore with some built in challenges of their own in the form of jumping puzzles to get to the best loot.
Rust is still in ealry access and the lead Developer recently said that it was "only about half done".  The game is updated weekly and detailed in one of the best dev blogs in gaming.  The first update of the month usually incorporates any major changes with smaller (but still significant) updates in between.
I hope to see more PvE content in the future.  Many concepts for NPCs have been shown over the multi year development cycle and it looks like they are close to being able to add some of those.

Rust is an incredibly addictive game and will eat up your time.

The fact that the reccomended amount of ram is 16 gigabites is a big ♥♥♥♥ you from the developers.  Granted,  I only have 6 gigabytes of ram personally, so I cannot ♥♥♥♥♥ about it.  But, the developers have been trying to improve the performance recently.  I have many problems with my amount of ram, constant lag spikes, and whenever the game has to render a new container or weapon, I get an incredible lag spike, and this degrades the immersion completly.  Currently standing, the game has horrible optimization.  Granted, this is an early access game (that has been in said early access for 4 years)
Overall, this is a great buy and it is definetly worth the price (that is, if you have at least 8 gigabytes of ram)  but if you do not have the recommended amount of ram, feel free to go spend $150 dollars on 16 gigabytes.  It is definetly worth it if you have the money.

If hunting were running through the woods with no caution at all, shooting everything without fear of it running away, then this would be a true to life experience.  But since that is not the case, it falls horrendously short.

I imagine that when I tell people the walking speed in this game is too slow, they will think 'Ok, annoyingly slow, but surely not game breaking right?'
So I'll put it this way intead: Would you rather go out into the mountains and hunt as an 80 year old or as a 90 year old?   Because you will be walking around FOREVER at your grandfathers walking speed.   And if you crouch and try to 'stalk' something...forget it.  If you asked your roommate to hand you the remote and he moved at that speed you'd punch him in the face.
Further to that analogy - when aiming your rifle, you have the steady hands and arm strength of...you guessed it, an 80 year old.   While you can (basically have to)  hold your breath briefly to steady things, you don't have much time and afterwards you will be shaking and having what I can only guess is a mild heart attack.
This all amounts to a perfect storm of frustration - slow walking makes it extremely difficult if not impossible to stalk something (on more than one occasion, I have stalked bears for 2 hours straight, can see his footprints, can hear him, can even see his steaming piles of poop but never laid eyes on him) - partly because everything 'Trots' while you're stuck trudging along at a zombies pace.

Due to shakey arm syndrom you'll likely not hit it in the heart, maybe you'll bounce a round off her head (not kidding) - anything other than a heart shot will send the animal off running and it's not uncommon for them to run for MILES.  So grab your gear and your walker grandpa, your afternoon is booked following that cow all over place.
The graphics and sound are great.  The selection of guns/accessories is not good, the game calls, seem rarely to work.   Overall, the makings of what could be a good game, if they adjusted the walking speed - not just of the hunter, but of the animals - are they really supposed to trot for 2 hours straight?  And flesh out the shop.  Would not recommend buying until you hear those are fixed.

So I've played for something like 170 hours hours now... I think it's safe to say that the game is good value for money for anybody that likes hunting games. So yes, it's definitely worth the £30. It's a difficult review because I think the game represents good value, but the way in which the developers have managed development among other issues leaves me unable to leave a positive review. My main issue with call of the wild is that it doesn't come close to reaching it's potential.
Before I actually get started, it’s worth pointing out that I’m not going to discuss any of the well-documented issues concerning the despicable state that the game was launched in, the sorry state it is in now, the countless bugs, or the pricing of DLC. Of course, these are all important issues but they have been discussed to death, and if you don’t know what it is I’m talking about, you don’t need to look too far to find out.
Call of the wild is, simply put; unrealistic, repetitive, and offers little to no challenge. The only reason I've managed to play the game for as long as I have is on the graphics and genre alone. If you want a hunting simulator, do not buy cotw. It's not a sim... it's a hunting game. Here's some reasons why...
Animal populations are stupidly high
There's so many animals that you can easily take 20+ animals in an hour. It takes away all of the satisfaction of actually shooting an animal. Players don't need to be killing dozens of animals in a single sitting to be entertained. In this case, less is more. A lot less.... 20% of the current animal population/frequency would be more appropriate. Of course, level/xp requirements would need to be adjusted to fit any population change.
Let’s not forget that in cotw, there are herds of sometimes 30+ red deer/bison/elk. When you take these into consideration, they really kick the population issues into overdrive. Realistic herds and groups are a great addition to the game, but previously exagerrated global animal populations need to be adjusted to account for this. There is also the extended view/shooting distance to take into consideration. This makes it far easier to find animals. The map contains many wide-open spaces which allows for easy spotting of animals and sniping. Again, extended view distance is another great addition, but the limited view distance in thehunter classic was one of the reasons animal populations needed to be exagerrated in the first place. With the view distance increased, there's no need for so many animals.
Animals warn you if they're about to flee
Flat out unrealistic. If you take an animal by surprise, it will flee or attack. There may be some specific circumstances under which an animal may grunt or growl at you as a warning, but it will likely be followed by it either turning and running or attacking... So yes, warning calls do happen. Just not nearly as often as this game would like you to think. It's easily exploited and kills a lot of the need for realistic hunting tactics. Many of you that have already played the game have probably fallen into the habit of sprinting from location to location until you hear a warning call, hitting the dirt > blasting your caller over and over for 30 seconds > shooting whatever it happened to be this time. This brings me onto my next point....
Callers / animal behaviour
Callers are fine on their own. Okay the callers system is pretty bare-bones, but my issues is mainly with the animals' response to callers. If you're hunting in real life, you call the deer in and take your shot and miss... that deer isn't coming back any time soon. There are anecdotes of deer that have been stupid enough to come back moments after being shot at, only to meet their demise upon their return... but these stories are significant because that kind of behaviour is so unusual. But not in call of the wild! In cotw, animals will always come back withing mere minutes of fleeing. All you need to do is blast your caller a few times and hey presto, it's a miracle. You get another chance to shoot that big buck you just missed! but don't worry if you miss again... this is an equal opportunities game after all! You get as many tries as you need, and without having to do any of that tedious tracking! why on earth would anybody want to track animals in a hunting game?
Fleeing distance
The reason you are able to call animals back in this way (other than the fact that the AI is dumb enough to fall for this trick) is because the animals only flee 70-100m. When shooting into a wide open field, you can literally spook a deer 2-3 times before it even disappears from line of sight. Again I feel I have to spout this disclaimer of 'I know this can happen in real life' because people will always use "but that happened to me one or two times, in 20 years of hunting... and thus this is the most realistic game ever made". In cotw, animals will never flee for more than 150m (and that's being generous), unless they are spooked twice. Just for comparative purposes, in real life a deer can flee for miles. A good case scenario would be 500m - 1km assuming the animal wasn’t wounded. You'll either have to track the animal down or wait for the next. THAT'S HUNTING. By failing to accurately portray animal fleeing realistically, EW have removed a huge aspect of the hunting experience. Of course, none of it would matter if they increase animal flee distance on its own, because why would anyone bother tracking an animal for 20 minutes if the populations are so high that they can find and shoot 3 more in that space of time. The only instance in which somebody might make that time investment is if it's a very high scoring buck... but who cares about high scorers. cotw is all about quantity, and not quality.
These are some of the main issues concerning realism and difficulty. There are many more issues than this, but they are mostly minor and more forgivable. I think the game was made in this way in order to attract new players to cotw and classic. EW have tried to tone down some of the sim aspects of classic so the game is more accessible to players with no real hunting experience or less time to play the game. This is, in my opinion, probably the most fatal misjudgment made by EW. Thehunter classic was not inaccessible in terms of difficulty… I, myself have introduced many people to classic and not one of them had any problem picking up the mechanics, even when I was not there to show them the ropes. Call of the wild did not need to be less challenging or realistic. In fact, there was quite a lot of room for cotw to become more challenging and realistic. There will always be an audience that has no patience for walking long distances, or waiting for 30 minutes just to see an animal, or having to spend a good deal of time tracking down an animal after they missed or messed up their shot. Truth be told, even call of the wild isn’t ‘casual’ enough for these people. All EW have achieved with their strategy is alienating players that want realism and challenge, and falling short of pleasing players that don’t want these things.
Probably the worst part of all of this is that lots of us have seen this coming since beta, just hoping that EW had the sense and willpower to turn it around. Maybe they will in the future, but I can’t see that day coming any time soon. Call of the wild is a fantastic game, but it will soon be forgotten. Thehunter stood the test of time, even with the burden of an extremely unpopular payment model, outdate graphics and hoards of negative reviews. Unfortunately I think call of the wild is nothing more than a half-baked sim that doesn’t know what it wants to be. It’s exceeded expectations in terms of graphics, but has fallen far short in terms of gameplay. Ultimately, I don’t feel it lives up to its predecessor, regardless of the many issues classic suffered from.

I can't honestly recommend this game. It looks great, but it is seriously lacking in decent content. This is some major rinse-repeat stuff and not once do you need to use your brain nor make any kind of decision.
The game focuses on the Big Chief, yet by the point of getting it I'd completed almost everything else so never really got to benefit from what was pretty much the whole point of the story. And by that point I had scrap spilling out of every orifice with nothing to spend it on.
I never once came close to running out of fuel, and there is minimal consequence to running out of water. Running out of ammo happened far more often, and was far more annoying.
Every fight is the same (spam 'X', roll around using 'B', wait for a 'Y' counter, end it with an 'A' finisher). All boss fights (except the very last one, which took me two hits and I was never in any danger) are EXACTLY the same: avoid their attack, mash your own attack and then shiv. Do this until they are dead.
Driving is a huge element of the game, yet I never really felt totally in control of a car that always felt 'swimmy'. It made driving a chore especially when trying to accurately dart in and out and around obstacles, and ESPECIALLY those rocks scattered around that either stop you dead or spin you round 180 degrees and completely ruin any sense of 'flow' and exhilaration.
The Crow Dazzle races are boring, frustrating, or both. It's infuriating being barged away from checkpoints by an AI car that DOES NOT have to pass through them, so you have to turn around, pass though the barrels, then catch back up with the pack again.
And yes, Chum, I know that if I want to win the favour of the Gods I can take part in a death run. Yes, Chum, I know Crow Dazzle is nearby. YES, CHUM, BECAUSE I'VE LITERALLY *JUST* COMPLETED HIS RACES YOU ANNOYING MORON SHUT UP SHUT UP PLEEEASE  :-(
Camps are labourious, dull, and repetitive. Scope out the clear on-screen markers, shoot their defences from afar, take the main gate down (or 'sneak' in through a hidden entrance - as if sneak or the element of surprise has any consequence), fight everyone using the techniques detailed earlier, and collect a set number of things.
The game hand holds by showing exactly where you can climb or interact with the environment, and exactly how many collectibles there are scattered around with each having a little icon above them. Yet after clearing a few camps searching for a hidden piece is just not fun.
And the whole game can be summed up using those three words: just not fun.

This is my first review on Steam and the fact that I'm writing it about a Life is Strange game is already a praise in itself. The original game was the most impactful experience I ever had in my life and this fact alone says so much about the depth of that game.
However, as I am playing this prequel, Before the Storm, after the second episide I realized I like this one just as much as the original, just in a slightly different, somewhat even better way. When I recommend the original to anyone I always say this is the most touching story you will experience from a video-game that has such real and loveable characters that you will never forget them and their story.
Now I think this prequel does even better keeping reality and believeability at the maximum, for a total immersive feeling. The original game because of the time-travel, supernatural element sometimes blows your mind and you question too much about existence and life itself, which is great, but I sometimes felt like that crushing sadness the ending of that game gives you is because you cannot wrap your brain around time travel and destinies being altered. It is a more heart-breaking game because eventually you cannot do anything because your power ♥♥♥♥ed up everything.
What I am trying to point out is that this prequel is actually telling me the story of a girl with whom I can tottaly identify with, without the twisting effect of a supernatural force. And by this it gives me an even more immersive, human and real journey with just as much beautiful sadness as its predecessor. The story of Chloe Price has to be one of the most relateable and touching of all the genuine fictional characters, especially because it's so grounded in reality that you feel like her life could well as be your own, or someone else's you know next door. And damn the struggles she has to go through are just purely sad. Don't be afraid of her sadness or yours though, her yourney is what will shape your thinking about life and if you integrate the massage of these games in yourself, I am sure you will be changed for the better.
As a finishing though I would like to recommend Life is Strange to everyone who speaks excellent english, because man these games are the hope and future of video-games.
Believe me, if a medium that can reach down and communicate with the innermost layers of your soul, making you feel things you never knew exsisted, it becomes such a universal cultural language that can truly help to make a change in our ♥♥♥♥ed-up way of treating each other, like this game discusses those issues.

A game you will love or hate, absolutely. As a military shooter, it's a generic but functional game with a useless tacked-on multiplayer mode that the developers have openly disowned. As a story-based singleplayer experience, it's notable for taking what starts as the most generic story imaginable and turning it into a meta-narrative that questions the the nature of video games while the protagonist questions his own heroism. While not perfect in its storytelling, it tries something that flies in the face of current trends and is essentially a giant middle-finger to Call of Duty and its imitators. Either you'll be on board with the idea and enjoy its ambiguous storyline, or you'll find it a pretentious attempt at an art game built on the back of a mediocre shooter. If you're curious, it's worth the time and money simply because it exists.

This game is probably in one of my top ten games that I've ever played...and it's not even because of the gameplay.
Ironically enough, I rag on games like Bioshock for having great stories but are a pain to actually play, but I can't stop raving about Spec Ops: The Line.
It is in my honest opinion that this game is the bar for storytelling in non-RPG games (hell, it even bests some RPGs too!). Sometimes is sad for me to say that there are games who we judge of how they look at first instance, or how they sound by the tittle. Or hell even of just what they show on the trailer (which will make the most sense). Sometimes if you don’t do a lot of research you may come across one of those cases on which you expect sometime in a game and turns out to be sometime completely different. In most cases is a game that looked good but it turn out to be bad, but in the case of Spec Ops the Line is just some 3rd person shooter type of call of duty that in reality turns out to be a very much enhancing and twisted adventure that “plays with the player”, speaking of the traumas of war in a gory and dark way.
It all comes down with the story and the pace that this brings to the game, the type of emotions that you may feel as you lead your squad who is looking for survivors in a post-apocalyptic Dubai after a massive sandstorm (in resume). That’s how you started the game, in an instance you may think that it is not too much in depth as I point out before, same may be said for the characters, there just your standard soldiers following orders (there is even a funny one). But it is as soon as all plans start to hit south when the game gets to shine, and it shines in a really messy pattern.
Without getting to many spoilers, in the middle of your researching you encounter dead soldiers from the previous team that were trying to rescue the survivors of the recent apocalypse, followed by angry locals that you sadly will have to gun down. You quickly start to think that the rebels had gone crazy and are confronting the USA soldiers that came to help and that the story will move on a monotonous military style way, well not on this case since later on those same comrade soldiers will be trying to wipe you down for “invading and threating their mission” (wait what?) so you are forced to defend yourself and nail down basically everybody, looking who brainwashed this soldiers, but are they really? Here is when you begin to question the game itself of whether or not you’re making the right decisions, asking if you are the bad guy or the good guy, who is the hero? Because the enemy may have a point of their actions that could only be or may not be known until the end of the game, your squad is also asking themselves the same thing, Is this the reality of the situation or is it just an illusion caused by war traumas?
I wanted to make a lot of emphasis to that because you as the player may also be in doubt every time you take a headshot, don’t get me wrong the game is scripted for the most part with merely some decision that really doesn’t affect the game’s outcome. These heavy story points and the fact that you are unsure of the protagonist’s actions is what really will make you feel the pain that the soldiers are having, as if you were there as well. That is a unique interactivity that is hard to get in other games of the same genre, especially military base shooter, it also helps that there is not a lot of cut scenes more than the necessary to tell the story, is a game that lets you play without killing the pace, maybe it was intentional or not, either way it works.
As for the rest of the aspects, it plays as you may think a third person shooter is. You carry up to 2 weapons, each with different characteristics, you can crouch, take cover, give minimal orders to your teammates and even sneak on approach if you desire. It’s all very simple and solid, but sometimes the cover and sprinting system can be frustrating, doing things that you may not wanted that leads to a painful dead and then to repeat several minutes due to not so great checkpoints. There is of course the obvious turret and “scripted you have got to be kidding” parts of the game that you could expect by this style of shooter, which can actually be delightful (maybe because of the fact that are not a lot and very far between), but other than that there is not a lot of anything else than shooting until you go through the 6 to 7 hours of the campaign. So gameplay wise it’s not revolutionary and it doesn’t merge much with the storytelling, just kind of there in another room, working for the most part.
There is also multiplayer, which is probably death by now so why bother, that can also be consider as an extra. Basically is the single player  gameplay in objectives of team death matches and so on, with unbalanced progression system and coop options, not really a lot to look at there and I really didn’t play it too much to know about it.
Other things that have to be say here are the graphic and sound option, and the PC port itself. Game use unreal 3 engine with several light adjustments that make it look just beautiful, followed by nice post-apocalyptic worlds and the amazing sand storms that happen time to time, affecting even gameplay. Merge that with compelling and fairly accurate tracks on the background, as well as ambience sounds and themes) you will have a good taste of a Dubai filled with sand (interesting setting may have to tell). The port is also great, taking advantage of my pc as much as it could without lagging, even if I max it out, and you may argue that there is not a lot of graphic option or pc features, but in the end is still a console focused game, at least it doesn’t run poorly.
Spec Ops the Line is like a kid in high cool trying to be one of the cool mainstream guys, hiding his characteristic that makes him great and innovative with layers of monotony and explosions. There is more than that on this game, like I explained extendedly, there is that emotional aspect that makes you feel a doubt of who is really the bad guy here or what is really happening, the plot or even the game is playing with you and that’s something not a lot of military shooters really have. Solid gameplay for the most part and good visual made this grim tale something to remember and also something that really deserved more attention back in 2012.

I would say this 'game' is first- nicely produced, second- only a fair simulator of truck driving, third- has a large amount of places that are not accurate representations, and fourth- a large collection of customizations for your truck (like paint jobs).
One of the main reasons that prevented me from enjoying this game was the steering:
Steering the truck does not have a realistic feel to it. The steering is not smooth (even when trying and making many different adjustments via the options screen). Steering required constant tweaking back and forth to keep the truck in the lanes and in no way did I ever feel like I was steering a real vehicle. Driving a real vehicle I don’t have to constantly keep ‘on top’ of my steering wheel like you do in this ‘game’. I never felt like I could ever relax like I do when driving on a real road trip.
Other factors for giving this game a thumbs down:
There was not a wide variety of roads; after a while the road design repeated types of roads I had already driven in other locations.
Even though there is a large amount of locations, the locations were not even close to true representations and the location design started repeating just like the roads.
For me, there are way more fun and enjoyable games out there than to waste time on this one.
Also, I wonder if a large portion of the favorable reviews for this game are fabricated in order to drive up profits; note the metacritic reviews average a good amount lower than the steam reviews.

So I've played for something like 170 hours hours now... I think it's safe to say that the game is good value for money for anybody that likes hunting games. So yes, it's definitely worth the £30. It's a difficult review because I think the game represents good value, but the way in which the developers have managed development among other issues leaves me unable to leave a positive review. My main issue with call of the wild is that it doesn't come close to reaching it's potential.
Before I actually get started, it’s worth pointing out that I’m not going to discuss any of the well-documented issues concerning the despicable state that the game was launched in, the sorry state it is in now, the countless bugs, or the pricing of DLC. Of course, these are all important issues but they have been discussed to death, and if you don’t know what it is I’m talking about, you don’t need to look too far to find out.
Call of the wild is, simply put; unrealistic, repetitive, and offers little to no challenge. The only reason I've managed to play the game for as long as I have is on the graphics and genre alone. If you want a hunting simulator, do not buy cotw. It's not a sim... it's a hunting game. Here's some reasons why...
Animal populations are stupidly high
There's so many animals that you can easily take 20+ animals in an hour. It takes away all of the satisfaction of actually shooting an animal. Players don't need to be killing dozens of animals in a single sitting to be entertained. In this case, less is more. A lot less.... 20% of the current animal population/frequency would be more appropriate. Of course, level/xp requirements would need to be adjusted to fit any population change.
Let’s not forget that in cotw, there are herds of sometimes 30+ red deer/bison/elk. When you take these into consideration, they really kick the population issues into overdrive. Realistic herds and groups are a great addition to the game, but previously exagerrated global animal populations need to be adjusted to account for this. There is also the extended view/shooting distance to take into consideration. This makes it far easier to find animals. The map contains many wide-open spaces which allows for easy spotting of animals and sniping. Again, extended view distance is another great addition, but the limited view distance in thehunter classic was one of the reasons animal populations needed to be exagerrated in the first place. With the view distance increased, there's no need for so many animals.
Animals warn you if they're about to flee
Flat out unrealistic. If you take an animal by surprise, it will flee or attack. There may be some specific circumstances under which an animal may grunt or growl at you as a warning, but it will likely be followed by it either turning and running or attacking... So yes, warning calls do happen. Just not nearly as often as this game would like you to think. It's easily exploited and kills a lot of the need for realistic hunting tactics. Many of you that have already played the game have probably fallen into the habit of sprinting from location to location until you hear a warning call, hitting the dirt > blasting your caller over and over for 30 seconds > shooting whatever it happened to be this time. This brings me onto my next point....
Callers / animal behaviour
Callers are fine on their own. Okay the callers system is pretty bare-bones, but my issues is mainly with the animals' response to callers. If you're hunting in real life, you call the deer in and take your shot and miss... that deer isn't coming back any time soon. There are anecdotes of deer that have been stupid enough to come back moments after being shot at, only to meet their demise upon their return... but these stories are significant because that kind of behaviour is so unusual. But not in call of the wild! In cotw, animals will always come back withing mere minutes of fleeing. All you need to do is blast your caller a few times and hey presto, it's a miracle. You get another chance to shoot that big buck you just missed! but don't worry if you miss again... this is an equal opportunities game after all! You get as many tries as you need, and without having to do any of that tedious tracking! why on earth would anybody want to track animals in a hunting game?
Fleeing distance
The reason you are able to call animals back in this way (other than the fact that the AI is dumb enough to fall for this trick) is because the animals only flee 70-100m. When shooting into a wide open field, you can literally spook a deer 2-3 times before it even disappears from line of sight. Again I feel I have to spout this disclaimer of 'I know this can happen in real life' because people will always use "but that happened to me one or two times, in 20 years of hunting... and thus this is the most realistic game ever made". In cotw, animals will never flee for more than 150m (and that's being generous), unless they are spooked twice. Just for comparative purposes, in real life a deer can flee for miles. A good case scenario would be 500m - 1km assuming the animal wasn’t wounded. You'll either have to track the animal down or wait for the next. THAT'S HUNTING. By failing to accurately portray animal fleeing realistically, EW have removed a huge aspect of the hunting experience. Of course, none of it would matter if they increase animal flee distance on its own, because why would anyone bother tracking an animal for 20 minutes if the populations are so high that they can find and shoot 3 more in that space of time. The only instance in which somebody might make that time investment is if it's a very high scoring buck... but who cares about high scorers. cotw is all about quantity, and not quality.
These are some of the main issues concerning realism and difficulty. There are many more issues than this, but they are mostly minor and more forgivable. I think the game was made in this way in order to attract new players to cotw and classic. EW have tried to tone down some of the sim aspects of classic so the game is more accessible to players with no real hunting experience or less time to play the game. This is, in my opinion, probably the most fatal misjudgment made by EW. Thehunter classic was not inaccessible in terms of difficulty… I, myself have introduced many people to classic and not one of them had any problem picking up the mechanics, even when I was not there to show them the ropes. Call of the wild did not need to be less challenging or realistic. In fact, there was quite a lot of room for cotw to become more challenging and realistic. There will always be an audience that has no patience for walking long distances, or waiting for 30 minutes just to see an animal, or having to spend a good deal of time tracking down an animal after they missed or messed up their shot. Truth be told, even call of the wild isn’t ‘casual’ enough for these people. All EW have achieved with their strategy is alienating players that want realism and challenge, and falling short of pleasing players that don’t want these things.
Probably the worst part of all of this is that lots of us have seen this coming since beta, just hoping that EW had the sense and willpower to turn it around. Maybe they will in the future, but I can’t see that day coming any time soon. Call of the wild is a fantastic game, but it will soon be forgotten. Thehunter stood the test of time, even with the burden of an extremely unpopular payment model, outdate graphics and hoards of negative reviews. Unfortunately I think call of the wild is nothing more than a half-baked sim that doesn’t know what it wants to be. It’s exceeded expectations in terms of graphics, but has fallen far short in terms of gameplay. Ultimately, I don’t feel it lives up to its predecessor, regardless of the many issues classic suffered from.

I'm writing this review not because I enjoy this game immensely (though I do) but instead I am writing this review in an attempt to lean you toward the game after reading the previous reviews that are frankly just immature. You will note that a lot of the reviews say they like the game but will give it a negative review for the first paid DLC.
The first paid DLC for this game is called Tents and Blinds, it enables the user to construct their own tents which function as an all in one outpost anywhere on the map or for them to create blinds which are simple hunting structures however unlike in the base game these blinds can be constructed anywhere. You may notice the DLCs price it is extremely cheap which is fair as it doesn't offer a lot and this leads me on to the immature reviews mentioned previously, these reviews say that these hunting structures and tents "Should be in the base game!" now that is up for debate as it depends on what you expect from theHunter however there was one review which stated "This was in theHunter so it should be here for free!" to which I respond if you want this for free play theHunter then? (For those unaware theHunter is a free to play version of this game that is subscription based and blocked by huge microtransaction walls)
Having played the majority of my time before this DLC I feel I can say without a doubt that this DLC is non-essential, it is helpful but again it is not necessary to have a fun time with the game. Instead I found the fact that ingame outposts may be kilometres away from your main hunting spot was good, it gave you a reason to walk and enjoy the beautiful game environments and make no mistake these tents are high level gear. You must pay a large amount of money (ingame currency) to buy one and they take up a large amount of weight in your characters inventory.
All being said and done, the DLC that is causing people to give this great game a bad review is childish and just a bunch of people who forget that games are a business and companies need to make money. Now the game does have problems, the multiplayer is quite buggy and the human models don't have great animation. The cause of this is probably that multiplayer was a secondary focus seeing as the animal models and animations are beautiful and make me want to actually visit these reserves. My biggest critique of the game would be the lack of animal species, there are 12 animals 6 on each reserve of which there are two Layton Lake District and Hirschfeltden (I have definitely mispelt that)
As a student who has a part time job spending 23.4 hours in two weeks on a game which is slow paced and offers little in terms of big progression (There are skills and perks which are great) that is a huge time investment and I can say if you didn't like theHunter you will probably enjoy theHunter Call of the Wild as I did. In a form of conclusion I find this to be a great game well worth the money and find those who are angry at a £3 DLC are ridiculous.

I can't honestly recommend this game. It looks great, but it is seriously lacking in decent content. This is some major rinse-repeat stuff and not once do you need to use your brain nor make any kind of decision.
The game focuses on the Big Chief, yet by the point of getting it I'd completed almost everything else so never really got to benefit from what was pretty much the whole point of the story. And by that point I had scrap spilling out of every orifice with nothing to spend it on.
I never once came close to running out of fuel, and there is minimal consequence to running out of water. Running out of ammo happened far more often, and was far more annoying.
Every fight is the same (spam 'X', roll around using 'B', wait for a 'Y' counter, end it with an 'A' finisher). All boss fights (except the very last one, which took me two hits and I was never in any danger) are EXACTLY the same: avoid their attack, mash your own attack and then shiv. Do this until they are dead.
Driving is a huge element of the game, yet I never really felt totally in control of a car that always felt 'swimmy'. It made driving a chore especially when trying to accurately dart in and out and around obstacles, and ESPECIALLY those rocks scattered around that either stop you dead or spin you round 180 degrees and completely ruin any sense of 'flow' and exhilaration.
The Crow Dazzle races are boring, frustrating, or both. It's infuriating being barged away from checkpoints by an AI car that DOES NOT have to pass through them, so you have to turn around, pass though the barrels, then catch back up with the pack again.
And yes, Chum, I know that if I want to win the favour of the Gods I can take part in a death run. Yes, Chum, I know Crow Dazzle is nearby. YES, CHUM, BECAUSE I'VE LITERALLY *JUST* COMPLETED HIS RACES YOU ANNOYING MORON SHUT UP SHUT UP PLEEEASE  :-(
Camps are labourious, dull, and repetitive. Scope out the clear on-screen markers, shoot their defences from afar, take the main gate down (or 'sneak' in through a hidden entrance - as if sneak or the element of surprise has any consequence), fight everyone using the techniques detailed earlier, and collect a set number of things.
The game hand holds by showing exactly where you can climb or interact with the environment, and exactly how many collectibles there are scattered around with each having a little icon above them. Yet after clearing a few camps searching for a hidden piece is just not fun.
And the whole game can be summed up using those three words: just not fun.

You know what, for all intents and purposes this should be a dull game. Mechanically it's Ubisoft's lame open world formula mixed with Rocksteady's ultra-lame Batman melee combat.
But alas, I'm having so much fun, which is probably due to two things: the driving and the fact that this game looks and feels very, very smooth and polished. The _car_ combat is fast and frenetic and more than makes up for the melee turd. It's total carnage with lots of beautiful explosions and flying car parts :P
There are some additional flaws, like sometimes very strange physics glitches while driving (resulting in crazy jumps or spins, rare) or getting stuck so you can't even "rocket-jump" (nitro) out (even more rare). The combat system does not take the (wonky) camera into account, so your combo can be messed up by some NPC that is completely off screen. My only logic bug (a gate not opening at some point in a fight at a camp) was fixable by quick traveling away and back, resetting the encounter correctly.
Yes, the amount of repetition is horrible. The amount of collectible crap (the bane of good game design) is horrible, although you're not really forced to gather up so much, since the game isn't too hard, and you get sufficient stuff from doing the main and wasteland missions. Those missions are well done. I especially loved the atmosphere on the two missions taking you to "the Underdunes". Not many games can take it that far!
And driving through this enormous (and amazingly beautiful - really, although it's mostly desert :-) landscape, wreaking havoc or just speeding along is simply fun. And whether you're just following the story or turning up every nook and cranny, you'll be treated with a surprising variety of interestingly designed places. (Part of the map was below sea level before everything turned crisp, so there's lots of whale skeletons, coral reefs and stuff :)
I also love the little touches just about everywhere. This is a game that has been crafted with an eye for the detail. The sound design is also quite awesome.
Too bad the ground combat is such a letdown. I will never understand how someone can conceive a thing like this. It's not remotely fun. It's simply an endless QTE where you wrestle the camera to see your button prompts. There's only one trick, and that is: TAKE. IT. SLOW. Don't press buttons more often than once a second, and you'll win everything - because you can react on the counters/dodges. Once you start to mash buttons, it's pain time. If you're anything like me, this will test your patience to the max.
Last thing, the races. They can be frustrating at first, but once you get then hang of them, they can be pretty fun. Almost all of them are optional (they unlock cars you can drive), but I'd recommend spending some time with them before you hit the mandatory race near the end - if you're not used to racing, you might be in for some frustration.
All in all I was more than surprised with this game. I never really intended to get it since I hate "the" open world formula - making me do the same boring little thing a hundred times over - but as it was on sale and I had a little time, I went for an impulse buy. Quite happy I did :)

I would recommend this to anyone with a love for any telltale game or visual novels. 11/10 it hits where it really hurts.
In general though if i were to be a little more specific than that I've gone through hell and back in both high school and in middle school. This resonated with me due to the sheer connection it was meant to have with those of us who have seen the horrors of kids and what they do to make themselves 'cool' or happy with their lives for once. This was an intense time for all of us considering we were so young still as well. If you or anyone you know has gone through any of this I would take a bet to say they will like or at least understand this game enough to be enjoyable.

This game is half truck building empire and half jam session, as there are many great radio streams to choose from in multiple languages. I can highly recommend this game as it's very engrossing and can take up hours of your time as you slowly but surely build up your business into a money making machine. Here are two short lists of things I enjoyed and some of the annoying aspects of the game:
PROS
- Open world that is beautifully designed and has realistic day/night cycles
- Excellent radio music variety
- Many different truck companies to buy from (Man, DAF, Scania, Majestic, etc.) with a vast array of truck models
- A huge pool of potential truck driving applicants with unique profiles to expand your company's labor force
- A great array of companies to accept jobs from and a good variety of different cargo to carry
- Challenging and engaging, not only in the business aspect of growing your company, but also in requiring driving skill to deliver cargo from point A to B without damaging your cargo

Ok, so I have played around 80 hours of this game. While currently everybody is mad as can be about the new paid dlc, I have no problem dropping $4 for it. "But it is going to be just like the old hunter, micro transactions and all" you say. Maybe, Maybe not. I personally never could get into the old hunter classic and it was for that reason. It would be sad if this game went that way, but I don't think it will. Here is why I think that. This latest dlc, while not much, didn't cost much either and it is a one time pay deal. The hunter classic was microtransactions that in some sense expired...frankly, when I pay for something, I want to keep it around for longer than just the next three months of my "membership". The new content also doesn't make the game necessarily more playable. Sure, it adds some ease to a few things (that I greatly appreciate), but it doesn't open a whole new world of possibilities like paid for content in the hunter classic. Would I have rather had this newest content for free? Absolutely, but as someone who has done coding and the like as part of my education and work, I have an appreciation that creating a game takes a ton of work and somebody has to pay for it. While I do wish that some content that should come standard in the base game, especially content like tents, should be free, I also don't think that paying a total of $34 for the game and its current dlc is crazy, especially when many games half as good as this game are going for the same if not more. Granted, it does have plenty of bugs and more paid dlc will add up, but the devs are actively fixing those bugs and adding features that people are asking for. It isn't as much or as often as people want, but I have respect for what it takes and understand you can't do everything all at once or make everyone happy. Simply put, this game has its issues but is currently in a very playable state that is very enjoyable. As someone who has spent plenty of time actually hunting in real life, this game is as close as it comes to feeling like you are actually out hunting. It's a relaxing experience and visually stunning. So complain about the bugs, complain about the dlc, but recognize that even the current paid dlc is nothing like the hunter classics business model and has no way of becoming the money sucking machine that game is. Still, the devs have families to feed and bills to pay too, so if paying for a little dlc content for a game that has so much potential as this is what it takes to do that, count me in. If you don't want to do that, nobody will make you pay. The base game is still there and very enjoyable regardless of any of the dlc. And no, nobody paid me to write this review.

I typically hate any and all rogue-like or rogue-lite games. This is really the latter, because each time you die, you can spend the gold you got on your last attempt at the game before going back in again, thus upgrading all future characters that you try to beat the game with. Granted, any money you didn't spend goes away when you go back in, so you do need to do better each time you try if you want any progress, but all of the unlockable bonuses and your own experience of playing will make you stronger and more knowledgeable about your next attempt. It's an uphill battle, but if you love tons of upgrades and the satisfaction of overcoming a challenging game, you'll like this game. More importantly, the hardcore types can forego getting a bunch of the upgrades if they really want to have a challenge and prove how awesome they are, while the total wimps like me are given enough progress through unlockable gear you get to keep and stat upgrades you get to keep that you'll eventually have the power and your own personal skill to win. I actually like this game. This, Crypt of the Necrodancer, and FTL are the only games in the "Rogue" vein that don't give me epic rage, so that's really saying something. Fun game. =D

A very linear and repetitive feeling shooter overall, though very unique visually and in the storyline.
You are one of three delta force soldiers sent into Dubai which has broken out in a confusing war with it's own population, the 33rd Infantry Division (ID) and defectors of the 33rd ID. Small twists and odd characters make the game confusing at first, but the confusion seems to make sense as the games reaches its climax.
Your comrads watch as you and them a mutilated by war, both physically and mentally, in ways that don't disappear, but rather increases for a sort of Apocalypse Now ending. In addition, and interesting prologue lets you decide what comes of the main character's fate in view of all he has suffered and done.

Care is taken to ensure you feel something, maybe even responsibility, for the horrible acts that are so light-heartedly committed in most shooters.

I absolutely do not understand the hate in recent reviews. This game is SO much better than it was even a year ago, let alone 3 years ago. So much progress has been made in the least year I cannot believe anyone could say this game's development hasn't moved at all.
THEY ARE MOVING THE GAME TO AN ENTIRELY NEW ENGINE. THIS TAKES TIME. THEY WILL NOT DESIGN NEW ANIMATIONS/THINGS TO INTERACT WITH BECAUSE .63 WILL IMPLEMENT THE NEW PLAYER CONTROLLER WHICH WILL COMPLETELY OVERHAUL THE FEEL OF THE GAME AND HOW YOUR CHARACTER INTERACTS WITH THE WORLD.
I feel like it's pretty simple to understand, working on an engine from scratch and porting an entire game over to that engine takes time. There are WEEKLY status reports highlighting what the team is working on. I have not encountered a zombie that ran through a wall in over 8 months. I have not fallen off 1 flight of stairs and broken my leg in 6+ months. My fps has tripled+ since the new renderer was implemented.
Need more convincing? .63 is the beta update, and not only does the new player controller get implemented, but base building will be added as well, or at least the simplest versions of building/locking bases. Also, MODDING will begin to be implemented in the beta update.
Still need more convincing? Go watch some .63 videos on YouTube. This shows an early build of .63 from Gamescon. Again, an EARLY build.
Any negative review about the progress of DayZ either has not played the game since before the new renderer was implemented, or has absolutely no understanding of how game development works, especially in a brand new engine.
Overall, this game does need some work, but the progress is there. What more can you want than weekly status updates from multiple members of the dev team? We get twitter updates and teaser pics/videos/gifs weekly if not more often. Just because the game hasnt been updated in a couple months does not mean the game was abandoned. Expect to see progress really speed up after the release of .63 when the dev teams can actually design new objects/items/cars/guns etc. to interact with. I would rather have a delayed GREAT update than a buggy af rushed update.
Believe me, or believe the subreddit, or believe the recent .63 videos, or believe the status updates from the devs. But, mark my words this will be the greatest hardcore survival simulator released in its time.

(9/10) Most military shooters jump from one explosion to the next, and the focus is to shoot as many people as you can while triggering sequences that are fantastic to the eye, but unreal in every scenario. Spec Ops: The Line plays with the player's psyche while progressing you through a short (6 hour) campaign. The ending will make you want to experience the game all over again. This game reminds me of Gears of War because of the third person point-of-view and cover system - both games run on the Unreal Engine. Achievements are easily obtainable through two playthroughs.
You start off thinking its a generic brown shooter, but it turns into something else entirely. Finally was a game where I didn't predict the ending. Amazingness :D

I can say, its definitely a game I really recommend to play, yet the game I don't want people to play. The Line really let oneself immersed into its deep and very much engaging story (too engaging, perhaps) while gives a realistic feedback on every action we choose.
The story, perhaps, the greatest element in the game. The way its unravel, while keeping the Heart of Darkness inspiration, really push it. It really makes me think twice on the options I chosen. Its, too great to say it.
In the end, it makes one wonder oneself on our own very morality. After all, sometimes in life, we have a clear line that we shouldn't cross. Yet, when under immense pressure, the line is blurred and we forces to choose our own path
