I've held off from writing a review for this game until most of the bugs have been fixed, there are still a few bugs but none are gamebreaking in my opinion.
The game is really beautiful, the areas are rendered wonderfully well. It also runs great, even on minimum spec systems, with plenty of options to be tweaked in the graphic settings.
If you own a decent spec system (my system is a haswell i5 @ 3.8ghz and a gtx 1080) you can maximise the graphics and even run in enhanced resolution (dsr). I run this game at 1600p and it's stunning and maintains between 45 and 55 fps :)
The hunting is fun and rewarding. You start off with a basic .243 rifle and basic ammo. As you harvest animals you get a monetary reward, xp and a score towards your weapon class.
As you level your weapon class this enables new ammunition and weapon types to be unlocked, which are paid for by your in game cash.
Xp goes towards levelling your character. For each level, up to about level 36, you get either a skill point, or perk point to spend.
Skill points are spent towards things like tracking and spotting, using scents etc.
Perk points are spent in your weapon trees, to improve things like breath control.
All these "upgrades" to your character make perfect sense, after all the more you use a rifle the better you'll get with the weapon.
There are four trees for your perk points, a tree for each weapon type.
Rifles, Bows, Handguns and Shotguns.
This enables you to customise your spec to whatever you get the most enjoyment from using. For me it's bows!
The actual hunting is great fun, the tracking system works really well and is better (imho) than in classic hunter.
There are two areas to hunt in this game and they are huge with more areas promised as dlc.
This game is well worth buying and is gradually getting better, as bugs are ironed out.
UPDATE.
I'm updating my review to include recently released dlc.
Two dlc's have been released, dlc 1 is tents and ground blinds dlc.
This DLC cost £3.99 and for that you get 5 tents and 5 Ground blinds, plus further tents and blinds can be bought for in game cash after purchase of the dlc.
My opinion of this is it offers terrific value for money and opens up new areas of the map that were previously rarely hunted, especially when combined with DLC 2.
DLC 2 is ATV's and the cost is £1.87
The atv is great fun to drive and makes accessing far flung areas a breeze.
You can drive then drop a tent enabling you to spawn in at that area for future hunts.
Both of these DLC's are not vital to enjoy the game, but they add a trememndous amount to it and are a no brainer for me!
A poll is currently in process to find out what the users of the game would like in future updates, with extra animals, weapons and new reserves on the list.
As more and more bugs are ironed out and with the devs commitment to this title, this game is going from strength to strength :)
9/10 for me :)

This is the most beautiful game I have played in some time. I would say that the game is quite modestly priced for what it provides, but it is clearly a hunting experience more than a hunting game - so it's not going to be a game for everyone.
Most of the negative reviews I see claim "bugs" for what is actually how ballistics work in the real world. Example: lower calibre headshots will often not kill an animal. Many of the animals use their heads for fighting for goodness sake! I have (in real life) shot goats in the head and have the animal up and leave. The skull on many animals is very thick and therefore you're aiming for the heart/lungs.
- The Skill/Perk/XP/Points system is insane. Obviously, this is a leftover from the game having P2W/F2P mechanics which I am glad they dropped. But it's left us with a pretty terrible and confusing system that is incredibly convoluted. It doesn't rise to the point of a negative reivew, but it's close for me.
- Multiplayer is a little buggy at times. Not overly so, and it's been acknowledged by the devs and they're clearlying targeting patches to this. It's still very playable and enjoyable.
- The range of weapons available is pretty low.
- The amount of equipment available to upgrade you weapons was much lower than I was expecting. While some of this would be quite "game-y", I was expecting being able to customize your weapons and equipment more according to how you wanted to play.
+ The game is the most beautiful game I have played a in a long time, hands down. They're using dynamic color grading, volumetric lights, dynamic shadows... I mean just everything and the results are superb!
+ The map(s) are staggering in their scale and attention to detail. They're hand made and they are huge. Much bigger than ArmA.
+ The performance of the game on a high-end PC is excellent. Don't expect to run at ULTRA on current gen hardware, and don't be mad about that! The game is made in such a way that it's going to grow with hardware and that's great.
+ The pacing of the game is really superb. It strikes an excellent balance between requiring patience and keeping something happening to the player.
+ Post kill review screen. You see the pose, entry, and damage modelling for what you killed. Absolutely amazing and makes your kill "story" fantastic.
+ Tracking is exciting and the classic "easy to do hard to master". This is a well designed mechanic that leads to excellent pacing.
If you are looking for an arcade game, this is not for you. But if you are looking for a hunting game this is a fantastic find. Even better with friends! It's modest price is worth is alone for how beautiful the terrain is to explore.

Many a gaming site gave poor old Mad Max a bit of a tanning when it came out, calling it repetitive, boring and derivative.  As such, I wasn’t really excited for it, and only picked it up on sale because I have been a huge fan of the films for many years and couldn’t get over how awesome Fury Road was.  However, I was really glad to find out that the critics got this one wrong.
First off, if this is boring, repetitive and derivative, its no more so than Shadows of More Door or any of the Arkham or recent Asscreed games.  Also, unlike Arkham Knight, this actually runs at more than 5fps.
Mad Max the game is a bit of a contrast to Mad Max the movies.  Game Max is a sort of wastleand Captain America who goes around helping people, giving water to thirsty drifters and brawling like a part-time UFC fighter, nothing like the tormented and twisted survivor of the films.  You also spend alot of time DESTROYING oil pumps, the most valuable thing in the wastleland.  But put that aside, and you'll find a brilliant, open worldy game that is most fun when you make you're own fun.
Story missions are just glorified excuses to obtain upgrades for your car.  Mad Max is at its best and most immersive when you go off rails and just explore.  Avalanche have given us one of the most beautiful game worlds (perfectly optimized for pc) i can think of in their stunning rendition of the wastleland, from the burnt-out buildings and sweeping dunes to the ramshackle monstrosities of the settlements.  You spend most of the game in your customizeable car, and its a real joy to both drive around and see whats cookin' or to engage in the exhilirating car combat, which does actually nail the feel of the movies dead on and gives you a lot of fun toys to play with.  Taking on convoys is the highlight of the game for me, without doubt.  There's also some interesting underground sections too, which are a nice change of pace.
When not in the car, you raid settlements, sabotage oil pumps, and generally have a jolly time biffing people in the face.  While many said the combat was awful, I loved ever minute I was ramming fists into mouths.  Mad Max's fisticuffs is heavily based on the very familiar Arkham system, but it work by giving you so much more control over what you are doing, with light and heavy attacks, combo finishers, weapons (THUNDERSTICKS!!!) and ability to get Max's shotgun into the mix.  Even sometimes Max loses his rag and starts drop kicking and suplexing mofos.  Seriously, once you've unlocked enough moves combat is just as good as the Batman games and definitely better than Asscreed.  Like I mentioned before, the fighting doesn't fit in well with the Max of the movies, but when you're ramming a thunderstick (grenade on a spear) into someones gut amd kicking him into a mob of bald gimps just before he explodes, do you really care that much?
What I enjopy most about Mad Max is just how immersive it is.  The world is so graphically captivating that it was just a real pleasure to exist there.  Sometimes I'm on the hunt for convoys, sometimes I'm lookin for a spot of fisticuffs, sometimes i'm doing insane jumps off ramps, sometimes i'm taking part in death races,  sometimes I'm just driving around to see what there is.  And with some many things to do and most of the gameworld unlocked after the tutorials section. you're free to explore at you're leisure and jus do whatever the hell you want.  If only this had multiplayer...
It’s not a perfect game by any means. The controls mess you up occasionally, you can only climb objects painted yellow, and there's a fair bit of grinding to do to upgrade your car.  The thing that really got my goat was when the game sends random enemies/storms at you at the worst moments.  Maybe I'm waiting to ambush a convoy and a lightning storm comes along and zaps me to cinders, or maybe I've just wrecked that convoy, no armour left, and a random bunch of war boys appear right behind me and smah me into oblivion.  Or how about the fact that all the bosses look and fight EXACTLY the same?
But all its faults are negligible in my opinion, as the experience of Mad Max as a whole was very enjoyable and immersing. Don’t like these big AAA console games?  Max ain’t gonna change your mind, sweetheart, but if you do like the Arkham/Mordor/Asscreed thing and fancy a wee bit of insane car combat in the mix, Mad Max is worth a try.

At first, this game is very entertainting. The combat is fast-paced, you can upgrade your character however you want, and the character descendants are often humorous.
But after a few hours, it gets *extremely* repetetive. The game's hook is that you will die, and you WILL indeed die A LOT. I thought games had evolved past the 3-decade old idiocy of being "touched" by anything hurts you, but apparently this game didn't get the memo. Often you are surrounded by half a dozen monsters, which means dozens of projectiles flying at you and even more chances to get "touched" by monsters. Ranged attacks would help greatly but mana is so limited for even the most basic of ranged attacks that you can't rely on it. So you're forced to melee most of the time against projectiles flying all over the screen. It makes for a very frustrating experience. So you die. And then die some more.
Dying often could be forgiveable if you're progressing. However, in this game, you are literally playing the same level over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over. It gets old fast. The only way to progress is to grind the same level repeatedly for gold, while memorizing enemies. But with limited HP and each hit taking so much HP away, not to mention the annoyance of accidental "touches" as described previously, you'll die often no matter what you do.
The upgrade system seemed really great at first, but every time you upgrade your character the price of all other upgrades increases. Essentially the carrot in front of your nose is being moved farther and farther every time.
Not only that, but every time you die, you have to give up all your gold before restarting the level. So you have 1000 gold and spend 500 on an upgrade, with the next cheapest upgrade at 510? Too bad, you have to completely waste the rest. Idiotic beyond belief. After a while, all the upgrades become so expensive that if you don't farm thousands of gold before an accidental death, you have to give it all up and you just made 0 progress. After a few hours, the game expects you to play perfectly, or you won't progress at all.
I was indeed getting really good at the end of my play time and really memorizing all the enemies and how they moved. But then I took a step back and realized that I wasn't having fun any more. Because of the extreme repetition in this game and the frustrating nature of combat, I would certainly give this game a DO NOT BUY. I bought this on sale for $2.99 and wish I could get my money back.
Money well spent.

Sandwiched in tone somewhere between Hot Shots: Part Deux and Full Metal Jacket, Spec Ops: The Line presents an engrossing, grueling and antagonistic third person shooter gameplay experience meant to uproot and tremble notions of morality and challenge the ever prominent and trifly-questioned societal intake of violent media. Spec ops plays in a third person POV. You move from cover to cover to work your way through the levels. The cover system is far from the best but it serves its purpose. You find your self stuck in cover or popping out of cover at in opportune times. Changing cover is also a little clunky. The shooting is very satisfying and feels like you actually connect when you hit a target.
The destructible elements added to cover make you have to be quick thinking, and allow you to access enemies by blowing their cover away. They intentionally wanted the combat to feel repetitive, relentless and fatiguing- not innovative and engaging- because having say bioshock style gamplay would severely interfere with the tone and emotional impact of the game. At first, you think you are above the game, disappointed with its dated gameplay- but you come to realise that was all part of the ruse, a vehicle to drive you into the narrative. I was never excited to run into a new batch of enemies- only fatigued, accepting like it was one more job i had to complete- and that's the idea. This is one of the first games ever to truly meld narrative and game play completely into one coherent piece of fiction
Spec ops is beautiful. The vast open view of Dubai from the third person perspective of your character really gives you an idea of the scale of the situation. The detail put into the level from cover elements, to scenery in the backdrop, all comes to life when you are engaging in a fire fight. The destructible elements added to cover blow up into pieces making feel like you are actually leaving your mark on the level. Reflections and Shadows are top notch. There is one mission when you are looking into a computer screen and if you look closely you can see yourself in the reflection of the screen.
One of the best stories that I have ever played. Without going into detail, their is a feeling you get about shooting at your enemies. You experience guilt and remorse like I have never felt before playing a video game. You are given choices in the game that really lay on your morals. These choices never really effect the game endings but you still feel like you should do the "right" thing in these situations. But the beauty of spec ops is that is makes you question what the "right" thing actually is. After playing through all that you reach the ending. Where you are able to make some choices that actually matter and you are shown some stuff that makes you feel some crazy emotions.
This game is definitely worth the playthrough. It is not short of some flaws in the gameplay but the story is so strong that it definitely overcomes its weaknesses. The story is short, around 5-6 hours depending on difficulty, but I feel I would rather have a strong story that is short over a weak story that is drawn out to make it longer.

While it plays like your everyday generic third-person-shooter, the story behind this game makes it so much more. The ending will really blow you away, especially anyone that thinks games like CoD and Battlefield represent "war."

First time I felt the need to write a review.  This game is truly satisfying if you're a competition junky. You don't even have to like sport games to enjoy this game.  The gameplay and game mechanics all work well, untill that point where you hit level 24. As a beginner, I started out playing against other noobs and various pro players that had their smurf accounts in the rookie/major league. I had some epic losses, epic victories, various intense close point games that went into second overtime.
Eventually, I managed to get to level 25 with a 76% win percentage overall, I felt like a solid player that played his role ( PF ) well. In good matches, I'd block about every shot, bad matches I'd let a few slide.   All the fun in the game stopped though when I entered the  Pro League.
Match after match, you get to play against level 50 characters that not only have the most ridiculous skills that you could think, they also have so much experience that not in another 1000 matches could you hope to destroy them. They also have, in almost EVERY case, dropped over 200-300 euros on cash shop roulette style items that grant bonus stats, cards and card upgrades that grant..bonus stats, extra skill slots, etc.  You name it.
So in quick summary. You might love the game in the beginning, you might think you're a genius rookie player destroying the alt characters of pros. But once you actually get to the pro league, prepare to bend over and take it, over and over again untill you yourself are level 44-50 and have unlocked all the skills + slots. Surely by that time, you would also have dropped atleast 60 euros on the game.

Rogue Legacy is a necessary evolution of the rogue-like genre. In most rogue-likes, the goal is to survive as long as you can and progress as much as you can. Upon death, all progression is lost. Rogue Legacy may seem to at first follow the familiar formula, but its formula is more familial than familiar. The ability to pass down your upgrades and items to your next life allows for a unique progression, in which each life can serve a unique purpose, instead of being a randomly reiterated version of the past life. Every death, while it restarts your dungeon-crawl, enables you to explore further in your next life. This formula is much more engaging to me than your typical rogue-like.

80s-style action at its finest. You've got big, burly dudes, juvenile homoeroticism, women getting brutally murdered for being sexually attracted to men, and big, sweaty, muscular villain named Scrotus (yeah, more like Scrotum), who's sporting a studded leather outfit and a gigantic, sharp codpiece on his crotch. I should also mention that Scrotus gives head to a big chainsaw within first five minutes of the game. Coincidence? I don't think so. We all know that big knives and chainsaws in 80s action movies were essentialy metaphors for cöcks. Then of course there's the creepy hunchback minion mechanic, who's hinted on multiple occasions to be sexually attracted to the vehicle you're driving throughout the whole game, even going as far as "spending some quality time with the Angel" (gross) when you're off to punch naked men.
Indeed, gayness is rampant throughout this game, but this is actually good, because it's very faithful to the original material, much like the whole rest of the game. You could complain that the best parts of the story don't come around until much later in the campaign, but essentialy this is as close to a perfect Mad Max video game as you can get. Living off the corpse of the dead world is what it's all about and it does this perfectly. While closely following all the themes that characterised the movies and focusing on their most iconic elements - most importantly the cool and weird vehicles - it lets you loose into a wasteland that is just as bleak, desolate and savage, as it is beautiful and haunting.
Within the whole WB Games sandbox library, I would rate this game somewhere between Shadow of Mordor and Batman: Arkham Origins, which means it's pretty good. The official reviews are bull.

I don't normally review video games, but Spec Ops: The Line just blew me away.
We've all played games like Call of Duty for it's sheer violent fun, games like Gears of War for it's amazing visuals, and games like Jak for it's deep story. Well go ahead and forget your favorite video game and replace it with The Line. This game is both amazing and terrible. You're probably wondering why those words are in the same sentence, so I'll explain why I stated it.
You play as Captain Walker, a Delta Force operative, who is leading a three man squad and has more experience than any soldier should (even special forces) of war. Your squad mates are Lieutenant Adams, a serious man that sticks to the mission at hand, and Sergeant Lugo, a young man that has a level of common sense that makes up for his comedic side. Your objective is to enter Dubai, which has been become a giant ruin from a civil war, and rescue any survivors from civilians to the US Army's 33rd Infantry. At least that is what your objective is at the start. Dubai has been marked as no man's land, so this is designated under top secret. This means Walker's squad "does not exist" here. Everything seems empty until your squad discovers that there are armed insurgents of the survivors of the city, that try to kill you. The game proceeds as your usual shooter game for a while: kill some bad guys, travel visual environments, go through a story. But everything changes at the halfway point of the game. These are changes that will test your morality.
***SPOILERS BEGIN***
The game begins to leave you with decisions. The normal person would believe that these would be good or bad decisions. The Line is different in it's choices. There is no good or bad here, only bad or worse. These choices do not majorly alter the storyline, but just test Captain Walker's moral compass (or yours in this case) while following a linear "losing everything" type of storyline. At one point of the game, an entire platoon of rogue US American soldiers are in the way of you and exploring more of what's going on in this city. You and your squad are given the option to use White Phosphorus (one of the deadliest chemical WMDs) to make killing the platoon a lot easier in order to get by. After using the White Phosphorus option, you and your squad walk through the epiphany of the men that are slaughtered (some still alive begging for you to shoot them and end the torture) by the chemical. But all of a sudden you reach the gate and everything changes. Among the men you killed, you also murdered women and children. "Did I just do that?" "Was there another option I could've chose?" The dead civilian prisoners are vividly detailed by the game developers and designed. Most games would simply flash the scene of what happened. The Line focuses the camera on what you have done and imprints it into your conscious to force you to realize the consequence of your actions. You observe a burned woman with her child in her arms that was holding on for dear life while Lugo shouts that you have turned the squad into serial killers. You can tell that the designers took their time to model this scene to be hated. Usually M rated video games are played by all kinds of young children. The Line is one game that literally means mature audiences only because the choices only become more and more graphic from this point on. The experience not only becomes deeply cinematic, but also becomes self-defining with your moral compass. No matter what choices you make from this point, everything becomes all your fault even more with the level of realism that the consequences make you feel. Do you shoot a man that stole water (a capital offense in Dubai), shoot the soldier that killed the man's entire family, or defy killing either one by letting them both die? Do you end the misery of someone who used you in his plans or let him rot to death? No matter what you do, everthing will fall apart in front of you.
10/10

Spec Ops: The Line is extremely linear, cinematic at the expense of gameplay (in order to tell a very specific story with controversial plot points), yet on a completely different level than most linear shooters. I've thought for a while that videogames with growing characters (exp, new abilities, etc.) were all kind of broken. Meaning either you quickly outgrow the game's balance (e.g. the Elder Scrolls games) and thus earn your way into being bored, or the game's balance keeps pace and therefore you accomplish nothing. So the only reason growth exists is to trick the player into being interested.
And roguelikes in general, while I admire many of them, have quickly diminishing returns, at least for me. I just play them a few times, feel like I get the point, and don't understand why I would keep playng.
But Rogue Legacy might've struck upon the formula that fixes everything. I'm not talking about the genealogy gimmick. It's cute, but it doesn't affect the game that much.
What I'm talking about is the way the game lets your accomplishments from one trip into the randomized dungeon carry over into the next trip into the randomized dungeon. It's simple, but it's executed wonderfully. Each time you go in, you can earn not only cash to purchase upgrades, but blueprints for equipment, spells, hard-wired stat improvements, etc. And after a death you can choose to revisit the same dungeon, with a penalty on cash-earning ability.
A problem with this system WOULD be the notion that it rewards you whether you play well or not, but it has a punitive growth system that fixes that by taking all the money you can't use on purchases before each trip in. This pushes you to TRY to execute properly and build your game skills during those grind-y stretches when you need better stats, rather than just rushing in, playing like a jerk, getting whatever money you can until you die, and then repeating.

Was really excited for this game, and as you can see from my play time I believed in it for a while. The platforming actually is rather good (with a tendency to use too many spikes for my taste) as is the funny genealogical system. But the major sticking point is the permanent STATS progression. At first it sounded great, you get the blood rush of permadeath with something to carry over! Unfortunately it means that initially you can't get very far without being completely destroyed, and that later on the early parts of the dungeons will likely be no-challenge pieces of cake (can't tell if they put mechanics in place to prevent this, didn't get that far with the unlocks).
Also, unless you're the absolute god of platformers you'll sooner or later hit a progression slowdown where you just can't get a run that's profitable enough to unlock anything.
I think the lesson from this, and I'm gonna repeat it in every rogue-lite review I do, is that permanently unlocking new alternate classes and new stuff that gets fed to the random generator for a run is great, but permanent stat progression just doesn't work in a roguelike, it makes it GRINDY.

This game is a Trojan horse, a game made and hyped to look like your typical second-rate Call of Duty knock-off.  It asks you to understand that mindset and be ready to be the absurd, invincible action hero.  It creates the smoke and mirrors of a world of brutal warfare where manly men pose atop the carcasses of their enemies and give nary a thought to the dozens of friends they have lost in just the last five minutes.
Then, when you have lost yourself in that fantasy of false machismo, Spec Ops: the Line brutally pulls the wool off your eyes.
This game is more of a horror game than a military shooter.  This game by design brings all of your posturing over your virtual heroism up to the fore just to take it away.  The narrative is downright brilliant with a crisp and clean delivery, without delays or lengthy exposition.  Spec Ops respects your intelligence - it expects you to see the horror of what happens and understand what it means beyond the game.
The level of attention to detail is striking.  A full discussion of just how much thought the dev team put into making the player experience what has happened would take far too long, but I have to bring up one of my favorite touches.  First, the comments made by the protagonist change as does his mindset.  In the beginning of the game, he is composed and professional, sounding like a typical military shooter character.  "Tango down."  "Agh, I'm hit."  "Target the grenedier on top of the billboard."  As the events unravel, the voice stabs change - "TANGO ♥♥♥♥ING DOWN!"  "HE'S DONE!"  "I WANT HIM ♥♥♥♥ING DEAD!"  The enemy voice stabs do the reverse, at first disorderly and pained, but later robotic, flat, and full of jargon.  Dehumanized.  It's a chilling effect for those who open their ears.
The gameplay is a fairly standard third person shooter with decent artificial intelligence on the part of both the NPCs and the enemy.  Movement is slowed to a realistic speed, enemies do occasionally seem to come out of semi-obvious spawn points, and your command over the NPC squad is limited to calling targets.  As the game takes place in Dubai after an apocalyptic sandstorm, sand is sometimes used creatively for environmental kills and often used for harrowing firefights in the middle of a storm.  There are the obligatory turret sections expected from this kind of game and they are the same turret sections you have blazed through since the early 2000's.  Don't expect any of the big set-pieces you've seen before.  Mechanically, they aren't there, and narratively, they do not make sense.  Graphically, the setting is beautiful, mixing the evocative luxury of wasted Dubai with the stunning, more human, more personal suffering of a city on the brink.  This is not the cartoony wasteland of Fallout, or the over-dark of a STALKER, but rather a level of anguish torn straight from images of real refugee camps.
But do not play Spec Ops for its average gun combat.  Play it because it's a game that confronts the player like no other.  This is not a heroic war fantasy to make you feel powerful.  This is gaming's Heart of Darkness or Apocalypse now, trying to make you think about your wish to be a virtual hero.

The combat is a tad generic, but the drive to find out what happenes next and the great story easily overcomes any flaws in the gameplay.
Overall a good game. Not perfect, certainly not highly replayable, but has one of the best stories I've ever seen in a war game, dark, thoughful and brutal.

This game is absolutely amazing and has one of the best storyline I have ever came across in any video games. Make sure you pay attention to the dialogues as the game progresses, as not fully understanding the backstory or one event in a chain may drastically hamper the feelings of what the story is trying to push onto you. In my opinion, it's far more important than the gameplay at times in order to get the most of this game because of so. The plot development is very well thought out and unpredictable, and the chain of events plus the sudden twist near the end will really make you think deeply once the game concludes. A lot of the cutscenes in the game are not like typical ones you'd find in modern shooters, as they were made to emphesize the emotions felt by the characters as well as passing it to you. A movie should be made based on the plot of this game, as there hasn't been much military movies made with plot that will make you feel emotional about what the mental torments the soldiers have to go through.
A great game in all aspects. Interesting storyline, interesting characters, this game has it all.

It's already been in early access for more than two years (Alpha 27 at this writing) so if you're expecting it to be a gold release in a few months you need to wait. However, if you can get past the "when will it ever be fully released?" issue it's a really fun game. There are some half-implemented features (for instance, the contraband system looks big at first, but actually has very little effect on gameplay) that can be frustrating, but the majority of features are well-done and really fun. The developers are very consistent at updating monthly, as well as hotfixing any errors introduced in their monthly releases.
It's a fun building/resource management game with a lot of interesting twists. You have plenty of options, you can run a strict prison which deals violently with any dissenters, or a casual free-spirited prison with reform and care as top priorities. Or anything in between.
Will this game ever be done? Will they ever fully implement things like contraband, reform, gangs, and so forth? Who knows. Is it worth $30 in the current state? I think so. It's absolutely worth grabbing it on a good sale, as long as you're willing to accept that it may not ever be "complete" in the traditional sense.

This game is an examplary way of how early access should be run. Constant communication with the player base, routine quality updates, excellent discussion of new features and tutorials with every new feature. I cannot give higher praise to the team that is developing this game.
Now onto the meat. The game itself has gotten better and better with every single patch. We're not talking small increments either, almost every patch introduces new and exciting features as well fixing any isues that may've cropped up with features from the previous versions.
If you like the "sim" genre, you're going to like this game.

Player death is an important part of most videogames and has been for a long time. Every monster wants to kill you, and then you have to start again from scratch. A lot of games hold your hand, dust you down and sit you right back where you left off, as if nothing ever happened. Not so in Rogue Legacy, death is the most important thing. Death may start your game from scratch, but it also allows you to move on, to grow your dynasty and make them stronger. It’s also about killing things and trashing furniture for spare change, but that sounds far less impressive.
Rogue Legacy is a ‘Metroidvania’ game, a platformer where your character navigates a location, backtracking where necessary and trying to solve puzzles while on your way to a final boss. As you find out pretty quickly, Rogue Legacy is not as forgiving as those games were. Your first character runs, jumps, hacks monsters, loots gold and dies. You get to see images of everything you killed and are told to press A to move on.
And move on, you must. Instead of starting from scratch, you pick one of three children, but now there are different classes, traits and spells. The opening classes are all fairly limited and the spells are pretty basic. What really stands out are their traits, and I’ll get on to those shortly.
Once you’ve picked your character, you spend your dead parent’s gold on improving your home, then pay the rest to a grim gatekeeper to enter the monsters’ castle and start again. The interior of the castle will change each time, presenting procedurally-generated rooms filled with monsters and traps. You traverse the castle trying not to die and lasting as long as possible, delving deeper into the castle.
It sounds simple, and it pretty much is. The progression and the randomly-made characters make all the difference in each playthrough. Your home helps improve your chances with each successive generation. You can upgrade classes, add new ones, get stat bumps and even buy new equipment which will inevitably be passed on to your next of kin, and oh what glorious children you’ve had.
I said before that you have three children to choose from, but sometimes it’s less a choice of how you want to play your next life, more like having to pick which dysfunctional mess of a child won’t hinder you the most. Your first kid looks to be the most powerful, gigantism doubling his sprite size and his class is barbarian king, but he has vertigo and while you play as him the screen’s flipped upside down. Your next choice is skinny and easily knocked back, but he’s a mage with OCD and will gain mana for each piece of furniture he cleans away (destroys). The third is the weak knave, but his dyslexia jumbles any words you read as him around, and his nostalgia simply puts a sepia tone on the game until he’s dead. Do you play it safe with the knave or pick the mage and hope to hang back from any monsters? It’s a difficult choice.
Each trait could potentially add something minor, although bald or gay characters have no difference to play style. You might be blessed with no feeling in your feet and not set off pressure traps. You might be totally immune to pain though, and that means you can’t see your health bar. Gigantism makes your sprite tougher and taller while characters with dwarfism are able to slip through secret passages. Each combination of traits puts the game in a new light, along with the different layout and the incremental improvements.
The improvements is one of the ways they hook you. After dying, you ‘move on’ and you can only spend your rewards after starting a new life. Then you earn more money, die and want to upgrade again, so you press A and pick a new character.
The game adopts a fairly standard ‘retro’ look, with a simple enough style to the castle, better than the original Castlevania but worse than most outings. It’s cute, but the main feature is the way each character looks slightly different depending on their traits and gear. Even though this is a PC game, it feels best on a controller, just like the Metroidvania games of old.
Roguelike games have become increasingly popular of late and it’s great to see one which rewards you for all the time spent by allowing a form of character progression. It’s mitigated to a point by having you lose all your money before entering a castle and each purchased bonus makes all the others more expensive. As much as I have enjoyed the Binding of Isaac and FTL, Rogue Legacy is a game which cares about constant progression even in a roguelike game and lets you invest in dozens of generations of knights all on their doomed quest to conquer the castle.

This is an incredible game. It is so much fun it may very well go down as one of the best games of all time. It uses a model similar to Batman Arkham City and if you play this title you will know what I mean. I want to get into it's finer points, but first I'd like to point out that Mad Max does better at capturing the Post Apocalyptic theme than does Fallout 3 & 4.
- Open World.
Similar to Arkham City in that you have free open world, but it's bigger and you have a vehicle to rampage through it in. The Open world feel is perfect. Some games try to do this but can't get it right. There are some amazingly creative contructed spots to explore. The desolation fits and makes you feel a sense of
-Customization.
The vehicle customization is unhinged and is one of the most fun aspects. To some it might be strange to center the main plot around building the perfect car, but I swear if any developer could have done it right it was these guys. If customizing your car isn't enough then customize Max Rockantowsky. Still not enough there are a bunch of different bases that have some needed customizations or upgrades too.
-Sound or music.
I work in film and I know how important this is to making a good movie. I didn't realize how well it enhanced my experience in this game as well. Whoever did sound really did nicely even down to whatever value they set for hearing a person talk from at a distance to the roar of the car engines to explosions to hearing the voices in open areas to caves. I can tell a lot of work went into this and it deserves honorable mention.
-Characters and Voice acting.
The sound crew really did well at capturing these fine actors voices. I believe it is some of the finer acting I've seen in gaming and I can be very critical as an actor myself. Character wise, oh my gosh, Chum is the best NPC I have ever seen done in a video game. The character Chum who is your mechanic is fanatastic! He is creepy, his comic relief isn't forced, and if you play this you wil see he is the most useful. When I first started playing I didn't trust him. Once he started proving himself I wastalking to my computer screen telling him to shut up. By the time we were smoking the best V6 engines I loved him, he was my pal and made me feel an array of opinions about him which I believe is the halmark of a truly well done character. Seriously, great job Warner Brothers and great job to Jason Spisak in this role.
All in all, I don't really need to go into the finer points just look at the screen shots. Look, if you have the system to run this game then you should really just reward yourself and let this game rock your world. Honestly, I'm worried that Mad Max (2015) may have ruined Fallout 4 for me; in a good way.

This game is a Trojan horse, a game made and hyped to look like your typical second-rate Call of Duty knock-off.  It asks you to understand that mindset and be ready to be the absurd, invincible action hero.  It creates the smoke and mirrors of a world of brutal warfare where manly men pose atop the carcasses of their enemies and give nary a thought to the dozens of friends they have lost in just the last five minutes.
Then, when you have lost yourself in that fantasy of false machismo, Spec Ops: the Line brutally pulls the wool off your eyes.
This game is more of a horror game than a military shooter.  This game by design brings all of your posturing over your virtual heroism up to the fore just to take it away.  The narrative is downright brilliant with a crisp and clean delivery, without delays or lengthy exposition.  Spec Ops respects your intelligence - it expects you to see the horror of what happens and understand what it means beyond the game.
The level of attention to detail is striking.  A full discussion of just how much thought the dev team put into making the player experience what has happened would take far too long, but I have to bring up one of my favorite touches.  First, the comments made by the protagonist change as does his mindset.  In the beginning of the game, he is composed and professional, sounding like a typical military shooter character.  "Tango down."  "Agh, I'm hit."  "Target the grenedier on top of the billboard."  As the events unravel, the voice stabs change - "TANGO ♥♥♥♥ING DOWN!"  "HE'S DONE!"  "I WANT HIM ♥♥♥♥ING DEAD!"  The enemy voice stabs do the reverse, at first disorderly and pained, but later robotic, flat, and full of jargon.  Dehumanized.  It's a chilling effect for those who open their ears.
The gameplay is a fairly standard third person shooter with decent artificial intelligence on the part of both the NPCs and the enemy.  Movement is slowed to a realistic speed, enemies do occasionally seem to come out of semi-obvious spawn points, and your command over the NPC squad is limited to calling targets.  As the game takes place in Dubai after an apocalyptic sandstorm, sand is sometimes used creatively for environmental kills and often used for harrowing firefights in the middle of a storm.  There are the obligatory turret sections expected from this kind of game and they are the same turret sections you have blazed through since the early 2000's.  Don't expect any of the big set-pieces you've seen before.  Mechanically, they aren't there, and narratively, they do not make sense.  Graphically, the setting is beautiful, mixing the evocative luxury of wasted Dubai with the stunning, more human, more personal suffering of a city on the brink.  This is not the cartoony wasteland of Fallout, or the over-dark of a STALKER, but rather a level of anguish torn straight from images of real refugee camps.
But do not play Spec Ops for its average gun combat.  Play it because it's a game that confronts the player like no other.  This is not a heroic war fantasy to make you feel powerful.  This is gaming's Heart of Darkness or Apocalypse now, trying to make you think about your wish to be a virtual hero.

Few games nail it, this one does.  It is 5 stars good!  I wish the crew behind this could have made a billion dollars from it, so they could produce more epics like this!  I've played hundreds of games, and few can actually get it right.  This one has story, game play, music, and art/graphics!
Oh man the attention to detail!  Things like limps, and recoiling because of being shot.  When they aren't dead yet but keep on living for a few more seconds, struggling.  The way the main characters evolve in front of you as the story continues.  The amount of war all over them, getting beaten and dirty and worn down.
The gameplay is great.  Being able to actually blind fire, hide behind objects, and blast through certain walls.  It's all very very well done.  The guns sound great, recoil differently based on type, and are different from each other.  There are lots to choose from too!  The AI is great.  The only downside I have in this game, is this.  If you ramp the AI, you'll be quicker and shooting head shots (adapt and overcome!), but your team mates are hitting WAY fewer targets and doing mostly cover fire.  They do help, but not as much as you, typical, but come on we are three Delta Operators.
The music!  You better like rock because it's all over the place.  I think there are 10+ tracks.  And it's not just played in the background to fill a void, it is part of the story, the ambience, the vibe of the situation.  Many times it's that perfect song to get you pumped up for what is about to go down!  No turning down the music track on this game, you crank it up!
The game starts out slow enough for you to get used to the controls, while bringing you up to speed on the story.  The game play is intense the whole way through.  The story is great and you keep wanting to know more.  But the reality of the story, is war, and it can be tragic and depressing and eye opening and many things.  This story will make you feel those things, live through the main character like few games ever can do.  I won't get into the story as other reviewers have, I don't want to spoil anything.  Don't read anymore anywhere, no spoilers, just play, don't question yourself as you go through it.  Just see it out!  At the end you will feel like you you were there with them.  Reality will set in.
Now enough reading soldier.  Grab your cash and buy this thing, thank me later!

I'll go ahead and get the bad out of the way first: The bad parts of this game is that it gets repeptitive and clearing areas can be a grind, especially clearing minefields. This is the biggest critisim I can give this game. I also think the game could have been helped if it didn't let the story be such a background thing, because the story (especially near the end) is actually quite good. A small gripe I have is that there are very few Australian accents for a game set in Australia. None of the major stronghold leaders have Australian accents.
Now, the good stuff. FIrst off, this game looks beautiful. The rolling sand dunes, impeccable lighting, and varied enviorments are all really great. The game is wonderfully optimized as well. On my PC I can run Fallout 4 on medium settings and I get 30 MOST of the time, on the same machine I can run this game on high settings at 50-70 FPS. The screenshot mode is great as well.
Gameplay wise, it gets repetitive and clearing out areas becomes a chore. Everything else in the gameplay is good: car battles are cool, and the upgrade system works well.
The 'camps' that you have to take out in order to clear an area are all varied as well. Despite the fact that clearing them can become a chore, it's nice to see a lot of variation and interesting, jury-rigged structures. Each camp is entirely unique as well. In all of my playthrough, I never saw the same design twice.
Lastly, what I believe to be the most important good thing about this game. It completely nails its atmosphere. The world is wonderful, Max's character and character development is wonderful, and the general feel of the wasteland is amazing. It's superbly well done.
In short, I recommend this game for its above-average gameplay and story, as well as it's great atmosphere.

Games based on movies usually suck. I didn‘t expect much when i first saw the trailer. But the game came out and it‘s pretty good. I love the postapocalyptic setting, i love Mad Max movies, especially the old ones.
This is not a Fallout and it‘s nowhere near it. It‘s a simple, quickly made game. No one expected a good game so maybe that‘s why almost nobody got disappointed by it.
The game begins when you lose your car and you need to get your car back. That‘s the story. Yeah it‘s crap, same as the latest movie. But this game is not about story. It‘s about doing repetitive tasks and it‘s kinda fun no matter how ridiculous it sounds. You drive around gathering scrap which then can be used to upgrade your skills and car. The combat mechanics are simple but fun. It‘s very similar to Batman games, you mash one button and press another one to counter attack. There are guns in the game but you rarely use them. Shotgun can be used to shoot the gas tanks to blow up the cars and also shoot bad people in the face then eat some maggots from a dead person‘s rotten stomach to replenish your lost health.
There‘s also some racing which is quite fun but sometimes can be really frustrating.
Resource gathering is simplified to the maximum. The gas will never end, you rarely will be out of bullets or with no health. You can replenish everything just by going to the base. Or you just find every resource on every step.
Graphics are beautiful in this game. The scenery is amazing. I have never thought that desert could look so beautiful. There‘s a screenshot feature similar to Shadow of Mordor, where you can stop the game and take the screenshot. This should be available in all the games. Some people love to take screenshots and it really helps and makes screenshots look so much better.
If you want a simple, maybe a bit relaxing game and you‘re not afraid of repetitiveness buy this game you will not be disappointed.

Bear with me as this is my first game review on Steam:
Pros:
- Great customization (Skills, Freestyle variability, Clothing, Stat allocation)
- Requires teamwork (Heavy)
- Crew matches (Like GvG in MMORPGs)
- Easy to pick up, Hard to master
Cons:
- Community can be toxic (Will explain more later)
- You can pay for stats
- Fluid gameplay relies heavily on latency (ping)
Freestyle2 is a great Multiplayer Online 3v3 Streetball game that pleases my thirst for basketball games.
It is very easy to pick up (You only use direction keys + 4 basic keys + 2 or 3 more for specific skills),
but hard to master.
It relies moderately on basketball knowledge, such as actual basketball tactics like Pick and Roll, which can be executed in the right situation. To win, you will have to try your best to fulfill your one of five (C, PF, SF, SG, PG) position's purpose.
Positions and their roles are generalized in FreeStyle2, although adventurous stat allocation may lead to fun and creative plays (like improving 3 pointers success rate on C or PFs).
C: Rebounding and blocking, setting up plays under the paint
PF: Similar to C, but takes an offensive role
SF: All-rounder (Dunk, rebound, middle jumper, 3s)
SG: Also an all-rounder with heavier emphasis on 3s
PG: Playmaker (Passing and loose ball grabbing)
Playing the position that fits you and doing it right comes with a great rewarding feeling.
Also, there are many team compositions which are strong, but you will run into hell lot of weird ones online (Triple Cs)
If you aren't good at what your position is supposed to be doing by Major (past level 11), you will most likely be dealt with offensive words, telling you that you suck and that you should quit.
The playerbase isn't large enough to have the greatest matchmaking system and tiers - and this is why sometimes you will face teams that will totally♥♥♥♥♥♥on your face. Knowing your position and having individual skills is very important in this game and when a single teammate is not pulling their own weight, it shows definitely.
I highly suggest trying each of the 5 positions before moving onto Major (level 11+)
You can pay for extra stats (btw you can also do this for free, but not as much).
Does it help? Yeah, I guess.
Does it win games? Maybe - it makes minimal difference.
Why is that?
Let's say a player purchased items and also obtained cards to improve his 3 pointers.
If you are guarding him perfectly, he won't score any 3 pointers.
If you don't and give him open shots on 3s, you should really blame yourself.
Teamwork (Strategy, Individual talent, knowing how each other reacts in certain situations) is much much much much holy freaking so much more important and impactful than stats.
Gamekiss will be adding controller support very soon, and I am so excited for that!
Give this game a try. If you like working as a team and enjoy basketball in general, you will love it!

Excellent game for those looking to scratch that hunting itch. Not so excellent, however, for those looking for a game to digitally explore various types of wilderness and wildlife without the occasional glitch or bug. Call of the Wild is a very enjoyable, very beautiful game that I personally see a great deal of potential in. However, there just isn't much in the way of variety. High graphic fidelity
Realistic hunting/stalking systems (or as realistic as possible while still being fun)
Expansive reserves
Great animal AI (aside from minor animation glitches)
Cons:
Very limited equipment, animals, methods of hunting, etc.
Maps are large, but quite monotonous
Minor glitching that can break immersion
Outpost/structure system isn't great and saps a lot of time

I'll be honest, I don't like unforgiving platformers that often throw you in what seem to be impossible situations. I've moved on from the 90's and i suck at 'em. Yet I don't seem to be able to get enough of Rogue Legacy. I've had numerous "alright, one more go" moments after dying.
So why is it that something that i usually steer clear off mainly because i'm not all that good at it and has me dying 14 times in 30 minutes,  doesn't frustrate me as much as it should and  instead makes me come back for more?
And then , while upgrading my health and bying a new piece of armor after dying for the 8th or so time, it suddenly hit me, it's because the game gives a positive spin to dying imposed to it being the negative experience it usually is by rewarding you .
But while rewarding you with upgrades after death that make you stronger in the process (which you do have to buy with the money you gathered in your pre-death run) and give you a sense of progression , there are also the rogue-like elements this platformer implements that help a replay from becoming  repetative, unlike your typical (classic) platformer. I remember playing the original Super Mario Bros. and making it to world 7 or 8 or so where i had to clear this massive chasm in the ground by jumping over it and using this tiny piece of ground sticking out in the middle of it as a stepping stone of sorts. You had to do a speed run, jump, then land on this little bit of ground and straight away do another jump to reach the other side, and i just couldn't clear it, up til the point i was game-over and i would have to start the whole game over again. This was so utterly frustrating. Not so much because i wasn't able to make the jump, though it didn't help, but more because i now had to go through all those levels again just to reach that one bit where i would probably die again like i already did so many times before and start the whole thing over yet again. It's a vicious cycle i tell ya, and i hate it.
Rogue Legacy doesn't have that. Well it does, but not in the classic 'game-over, start-over' kind of way. By randomly placing and re-using different rooms in the castle your adventure takes place in each playthrough,  it will take away a bit of the frustration that comes with character death and at the same time creates a new and different playthrough for your next try. You will come across rooms you've been in before eventually but by that time you will most likely be ready to try it again, or not and you'll just head the other way as soon as you can.
This together with the upgrading system that will make you stronger and give you better abilities each time you  die creates a game that makes parts of it progressively easier over time while still giving you a different experience every playthrough. Not to mention that with every playthrough you will play with a different character, a descendant of your former deceased character, who each have their own abilities combined with both good and bad qualities which on a side note often make for very clever and hilarious outcome that also affect the gameplay in either a positive or a negative way, or both.
Does that mean the levelling up system and becoming more powerfull in the process will make the game too easy for the veteran platformers umong us? Well no, because here's the beauty of the whole thing. While everyone will go through the same tough experience at the start of the game, the more experienced players will have less trouble progressing through the game while still on a lower level, where as someone like me who is not all that good at avoiding hits and has the reaction speed of a sleeping baby will have to grind longer and level up a bit more (a lot more) before he'll be able to defeat the first boss without too much of an issue. This works really well and is genius in my opinion. It just opens this type of genre up for a wider audience.
As for the presentation Rogue Legacy does it right as well. The visuals are simple, but it's no 8-bit retro look either. It's just enough to appeal to most modern gamers and pull of a convincing creepy castle atmosphere that with it's sense of humour creates a very enjoyable experience all together.
There are numerous treasure chests to be found scattered throughout the castle(grounds) of which some can only be reached by succesfully completing challenges. There are 4 dungeon bosses to be defeated before you can confront the final boss and as far as completion time, well, as mentioned before that will be entirely up to you and your playstyle. Will you grind up your stats until you're a double jumping ninja tank before you proceed any further in to the castle or will you aim to beat the game by relying entirely on your skills alone and level up as little as you can.
So yes, Rogue Legacy is a pretty solid rogue-like platformer with a well implemented upgrade system that give it a lot of replay value. Definitely worth a buy at it's current $15 price tag and a real steal if it's on Sale.

If you are a true fan of the Mad Max movie series, this game will astonish you, It has incredible visual effects and graphics, with that yellowish and redish style. It has good combat and driving mechanics, aswell as well designed and built guns and white weapons you will encounter in the wasteland. The AI is decent, they don't stand there waiting for you to punch them, but after you mastered the combat system (wich doesn't take long), they become really easy to kill. There are a looooot of scavenging points and camps for you to raid and restore you water, so even if you finished the game or if you just want to discover the wasteland by yourself, there is a lot to do. There is one more thing i will talk about, and that is the upgrade system, both for you and your car. You can modify and add almost everything in your car, like the tires, spikes, decals, exhaust etc. wich gives a lot of variety in the game. As i said, you can also upgrade Max itself, by improving his armor (with jackets, more improved jackets etc.), beard styles, guns, fists (put knuckle dusters, etc.) and overall make your own Mad Max. I would say it takes 35 hours for you to get tired of playing it.

Story
I had about 45 to 50 hours in the game when I finished the story-line. The story is actually quite short, compared to other games, but you won't notice it due to the imense map and huge number of side-quests and missions. You will surely start "farming" side-mission by the third of the five acts. The story, although short, is very well written and adds to the post-apocaliptyc setting. The characters are well written and drawn themselves; crazies, mad-men, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the most excentric survivors will surely give you the the feeling that you're the last sane man alive. There is absolutely nothing I disliked about the story. 10/10.
Gameplay
The gameplay in Mad Max is very simillar to the one in the Batman Arkham games. It's very responsive and atracting. The controls are very well mapped to the keyboard and feel natural; the driving is very good, but it's probably my least favourite aspect of the game. Don't get me wrong, I love it, but the camera usually positions itself where it thinks is the best angle, which is a crucial thing in tight situations, because it's hard to drive with the camera looking behind you. That's probably the only negative to this game. By the way, you can drive in first-person by pressing "v". 9.5/10
Graphics and sound
Mad Max isn't the prettiest game out there, but it does look good enough to pass as an early 2014 game. The animations are smooth and the character models are quite good. The sound on the other hand, is probably the best I'vve heard all year. The voices are amazing and so too are the car and gun sounds. 10/10
Verdict: 10/10

Picture this; you find a game that makes you cry, it rocks your world, and it has more meaning and power than you could have ever possibly imagined a game having. It's one of those games that you recommend to all your friends, so you can see them get just as emotional as you did, or judge them if they make the "wrong choices."
That's what Life is Strange was to me, and I can say it was that way for a large number of my pals as well. A conversation about that game that lasts more than 10 minutes among my friends... well, the phrase "ugly crying" might fit well here. So when I heard a prequel was being developed, and by somebody other than DONTNOD, I couldn't say I was keen on the idea.
I wasn't sure another game was on the table as a good thing in the first place, Life is Strange created a world so vivid and in-depth, I was wary there was even a possibility that could be recreated, let alone by a different group of people. I feared that a story told from Chloe's perspective might lose the gentle spark Max's personality gave the narrative. But loving the game as I did, I bought into the excitement as any fan would, and hoped dearly for Deck Nine to deliever a good game.
I'm pleased to say that my expectations have been far surpassed. They have done, a spectacular job creating their own game. Before the Storm is it's own brand new narrative, molding lifelike characters and storyline without stepping all over the previously lined up story that DONTNOD created.
While staying true to the original, Deck has enhanced some previously known character's personas, and brought out traits in our dear Arcadia Bay crew that were once glazed over and subtle. They've explored potential in characters that Life is Strange didn't have the time for, and turned it into a artistically faithful addition to the franchise.
The visuals they've chosen to use to convey emotions are evocative, astounding, and genuinely breathtaking, if I thought Life is Strange made me cry.. well... in just the first episode alone, I have cried more than all of said precursor's episodes combined. You've written a beautiful story Deck, I can't wait to play through more.
---------------------------------------
Additional thoughts
The system for inspecting has been changed from dragging the mouse to just pressing W, A, S, D. While this was weird at first, I had far less trouble, I think that was a great control change there.
Chloe's character has been perfectly portrayed in the time period the story is based, I cannot stress how well that has been done, and how much I appreciate the way it's been handled.
Daughter was a phenomenal music choice, and so far the music is stellar in general. I'm thankful that the music has stayed important to emotional aspects of the game the way it has.
------------------

Spec Ops: The Line is a fairly straight forward, third-person cover based shooter (like Gears of War). Set in the sand storm beset city of Dubai, you play as Captain Martin Walker of Delta Force, leading Lieutenant Adams and Sergeant Lugo in what begins as a simple recon mission but quickly becomes much more. Having been inspired by the book Heart of Darkness (which in turn inspired the film Apocalypse Now), probably the game's strongest suit is its story. We'll get to that in a bit. This review was written after one play through on the default campaign difficulty. GAMEPLAY The mechanics of the game are nothing revolutionary, but they work functionally. Controls are fairly responsive, and unlike Gears of War, I didn't run into the problem of sprinting into cover I didn't want or exiting it when I didn't want to. However, the sprint button and the enter cover button are on the same key, so if you are sprinting to cover you need to press the button once to enter a sprint (the button doesn't need to be held) and then press again to enter cover. Vaulting over cover is assigned to a separate button, which helps ease the pain of accidentally exiting cover when you don't want to. You carry two weapons at a time, and switching between them is bound to a key (by default, the mouse wheel toggles between your three different grenade types) while activating alternate fire/alternate functions is bound to a separate key. Aiming grenade throws is pretty easy as well, as all that is required is you hold the button to bring up a targeting arc that will show you where the grenade will land upon releasing the button. Lastly, you have a melee key, which will also trigger a brutalized execution animation for foes who have been temporarily incapacitated and are on the floor but not dead. The variety of guns is about what you would expect from a game of this sort. The major division of guns are rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, small arms, and heavy weapons. Most weapons have an alternative fire mode (such as burst mode for the FAMAS and the AK-47, which supposedly increases ranged accuracy) or an alternative function (such as the scope for the 417 or the suppressor for the M4A1). The game warns that ammo for weapons is scarce in Dubai, but there were only a few heavy firefights that left me strapped for ammo and most of the time enemies drop plenty (or there are ammo boxes scattered about the battlefield that refill a significant amount of rounds). The gameplay varies with the weapon you choose – shotguns and sub machine guns require you to get in closer and be more aggressive, whereas rifles and sniper rifles allow you stay at a longer range and take well placed shots to take out enemies. Generally, I found rifles to be the superior weapon type, as enemy AI played into rifle gunplay quite well. One thing this game is sorely lacking in is enemy variety and enemy AI. For the first half of the game, you'll be fighting the same type of enemy (sort of – without spoiling anything, enemies change models but are for all intents the same type) until you're introduced to a slightly more armored variant of the standard foe, who can take a couple headshots instead of just one before being downed. The last and most annoying enemy to face are called “heavies,” and they are heavily armored and armed foes that take several explosives or a lot of ammo to bring down (even if you're scoring direct hits to their unexposed face). As far as AI goes, most soldiers hide behind cover and pop out to take shots, advancing or retreating to gain a slightly better position, with shotgunners, SMG wielders or bayonet soldiers rushing you at melee range. From time to time, you can use the environment against enemies by shooting out ceilings and causing sand to fall on them, but opportunities for this are rare. The game also features a rudimentary squad based command system. Certain contextual situations will allow you to press a key (middle mouse button by default) to have your squad mates throw a stun grenade, or heal a downed squad mate. Holding the key and targeting an enemy then releasing the key orders your squad to attack that enemy, which usually results in Sergeant Lugo sniping them. In the rare cases where you're undiscovered by the enemy, ordering an attack will cause your squad to use silenced weapons so long as you remain unspotted from the enemy. I was unable to play any of the multiplayer modes the game has to offer. STORY The game's story is its strongest suit. The basic set up is as follows: Delta Force Captain Martin Walker is sent into Dubai along with Lieutenant Adams and Sergeant Lugo to assess the ongoing evacuation and report back to command. In the first level, insurgents have apparently attacked the 33rd Battalion, headed by Colonel Konrad, and so the mission changes to a rescue operation. Things become increasingly complicated as the game goes on, and it forces you into uncomfortable moral quandaries as only war can. But it appears that at the center of all the madness of war and the state of affairs of Dubai is Colonel Konrad, who Captain Walker pursues with a single minded earnestness. There are several factions at work in Dubai, including insurgent rebels, the local civilians, Colonel Konrad's 33rd Battalion, and even the CIA. The game features a twist ending as well that leaves final interpretation up to the player. GRAPHICS/SOUND Playing on max detail, I thought the game looked very good. It also performed well on my system, never losing frames even when there were dozens of enemies and explosions going off all over the place. However, the graphics options didn't seem very customizable compared to most PC games, giving you a scant handful of settings to tweak with. I could see how someone with a lower end system might have a problem configuring the game to look good and run well at the same time since the options are sparse. Sound was also fine. The music was entirely forgetable, but the voice acting was well done and sound effects were right for a game of this type. PLAY TIME/REPLAYABILITY According to Steam, I beat the game in six hours. Replayability is also low, unless you want to go achievement hunting or for whatever reason play on a harder difficulty. I played on the normal difficulty; if you pick the hardest one available from the start and beat the game on that, it unlocks an even harder difficulty, so if you're into that sort of thing there's some replayability there. FINAL RECOMMENDATION Spec Ops might not be worth the default asking price of $30 for such a limited experience, both in the time it takes to beat the campaign and the banal lack of variety that firefights provide. The experience amounts to an extended interactive movie, of a sort, and the story it has to tell is interesting and I believe well done. I personally purchased the game on sale for $15 and feel it was a worthy experience, and one I may return to at some point in the future.

The Prison Sandbox we have all been waiting for.
If your a big fan of tycoon and simulation games and have always wanted to build your own prison, then this is the game for you.
The graphics are simple and effective and the depth is sure to give you hours of enjoyment.
You start with a plot of land and limited funds to begin building the essentials to get some money coming in. Once your finished, you continue to expand your prison while aiming at completing specific tasks to earn lump sums of cash which will help with the larger expansions. Building a prison can be time consuming, so be sure to sell your old prison rather than just starting over so you can help reduce the funds required for your larger prison project. There is a great modding community and plenty of tools to let you tweak your prison building experience. If you are a fan of this genre, then you are sure to love this game.
You can look forward to things such as:
Prison fights
K9 units
Riot Police
Contraband
Escape Tunnels
Fires
Witness Protection
Gangs
Death Row
And so much more!

This game is one of the best Early Access successes.
I have been having so much fun with Prison Architect, trying to build the biggest, most efficient prison I can and the game itself encourages me to do so.
It's sandbox gameplay at it's best. You build the prison you want, from a small relaxed minmum security center, to a vast multi-cell block complex capable of holding hundreds of prisoners, the game doens't limit your creativity.
And if you don't like your prison, you can always sell it and start a new one with increased funds.
Also the accessibility of this game is one of the best there is, simple enough to get you hooked and complex enough to keep you playing for hours.
The developers update the game frequently but most importantly they ADD new content, not just bugfixing or redesigning like others tend to do with their Early Access games.
At it's current state it plays and feels like a complete product. Totally worth the money and your time.

pairs a not-so-memorable cover-based shoort with a much more memorable storyline. If you've played
, nothing in this game will surprise you. The story itself borrows a lot
(and is filled with deliberate nods to that movie, and/or the novel it was based on,
), but does a much better job avoiding the slavish commitment to genre conventions that characterize the gameplay. You lead a squad of three special operations troops through a Dubai that has been destroyed by massive sandstorms. The game sets out to deconstruct the genre trappings of other military shooters (the
series, and so forth), and does so in a way that's unrelentingly grim.
The mission, the protagonist and the antafonists--none of them are quite what they seem, and the surprises of the story are driven home with good voice acting, some great art direction depicting the swamped Dubai, and well-chosen popular music for the soundtrack. The voice acting in particular has an unusual twist to it, as the various things you and your squad mates call out in combat become more and more desperate as the game progresses and the squad finds itself more and more over its head.
If you don't mind gameplay that's nothing new, and a story that's so dark that it ultimately leads to a game that's compelling without actually being any
, I recommend picking SO:tL up. I'm not sure it's a great game, but it's a fascinating experiment.

What starts off an incredibly generic war game, with some less than tight controls, transforms into a look at the horrors of war.  This is not Call of Duty, this is not Battlefield, this is not a medal of honor.  This is not a "war is hell, but not this one!" type of game.  This is a game that tries to show the dark, depressing side of war.  It throws you in, and does not cover your eyes.  Spec Ops:  The line demands a mature audience to play it, for it deals with things that should not be approached by someone not mature enough to understand the messages it is trying to convey.
What makes Spec Ops: The line special is that it's not dark, just to be dark.  You get the feeling that the deveopers knew from the first day of development where they wanted the story to go, and they commited to telling a story of the evils of war, and the stresses it puts on the human body.  I literaly had to stop playing after one level, because I had committed an atrocity that I could not have forseen.  The aftermath was handled well, not heave handed or obvious.  It showed me what my decision had cost me, but did not outright tell me.  This game is wel worth any sale price, just for the experience.

Rogue Legacy is a hardcore, platform game with RPG elements and a wonderful concept.  Grind that procedurally generated dungeon to the best of your abilities, experience a state of permanent death for that character and leave an inherited legacy for your offspring.  Doing so will allow the next generation to benefit from upgrades that increase their chances of succeeding at this game.
Not only do you continue leaving a legacy for the next generation of dungeon crawlers, they may have interesting afflictions or character traits that can impact your play in negative (or challenging?), postive, aesthetic or pointlessl(asides from the humour factor) ways.    Dwarfism, giants, irritable bowels, OCD, ADHD, glaucoma, vertigo, nostalgia, eidetic memory...just to name a few traits amongst a heaping big spoonful of them.  Any of which can be potentially passed on to the next gen.
Rogue Legacy is certainly NOT for the faint hearted or those with short tempers.   This game is harder than Ron Jeremy on a metric poop-tonne of viagra.  I'm talking severely devious surprises that will wreck you when your game is going well, entering a room too fast and falling down a spike pit with a bunch of enemies smacking you on the way.  Walking into a room with an unexpectedly ludicrous amount of enemies firing volleys of projectiles in every which way...  And just when you think you've got the knack for handling this bout of baddies, you're confronted with severely upgraded and new versions of those enemies and less predictable behaviour.
There is little to no way of being able to conquer this game through trial and error muscle memory.  As mentioned above, the game is procedurally generated, meaning that you're never going to play the same game twice.
If/when you defeat a boss, however, that enemy will stay dead for future gens (thankfully).
As hardcore as this game actually is, there is definitely some measure of appeal to be had by the casual market.  The game plays in the same fashion as old-school 8 and 16 bit pixel platformers.  The concept and controls of the game are nice and accessible.  There's a great deal of nerdy humour, obscure pop-culture references and Easter eggs in the game (I think I might have seen a silhouette of Santa Clause and his reindeer outside of the castle).   I would recommend that casual gamers pick this one up at a good sale price, though  (like the 3 bucks at the time of this review).
