I first played Rogue Legacy at a friend's place, trading off the controller at each death. It wasn't much, but it got me instantly hooked on how fun it was. So hooked, that I downloaded Steam, bought the game for the full $15, and bought a $30 wired Xbox 360 controller... and I don't even have any Xboxes. All this for this one game... and it was worth it.
Rogue Legacy plays like Castlevania and Super Ghouls N Ghosts. You move, jump, attack, and use a secondary weapon. The uniqueness comes into play when you die, which you will... a lot. Once you die, you will be brought to a selection of three hiers to play as next. Each one has a random character class, secondary weapon, and set of traits. Classes determine certain stats and abilities. Secondary weapons, or spells as they are called, use up MP. That's all pretty basic stuff. But the traits are very interesting. Some traits are helpful, like a speed increase. Others are harmful, like giving your attacks no enemy knockback. And some are just... well... neutral things... like making everything black and white. Your heirs have a chance of having two, one, or none of the traits at random. With all the random factors, you have to really get lucky... or pick the lesser of three evils. Is getting your prefered class worth the traits? Are the spells to your liking? It also makes you think about the next area... skills.
After selecting your heir, you are then brought to a skill tree. You inhereit the gold of your dead relatives I guess, and you can spend it on upgrading all kinds of things, from stats, to passives, to new character classes. Do you want to build up a magic or melee character? Maybe focus on a specific class? Or do you want to play it safe and try to build up well rounded skills to work with the random factos? It's a lot to consider when purchasing points in the skill tree. And be careful. Every time you buy an upgrade in the skill tree, all of the others become more expensive. So plan accordingly. And try not to spend it all in one place because...
... there's another screen. Yes, another screen where you can do even more character customization. IF you buy them in the skill tree, you can open up three different shops outside the caslte: The blacksmith, the enchantress, and the architect. The blacksmith sells you armor and swords with different stats and perks, but you'll need to find the blueprints first so he knows how to make them first... some blacksmith, eh? The enchantress does roughly the same thing. She sells you enchantment of your armor and sword after you've found the appropriate runes. The big difference is that the blacksmith's wares have weight, meaning you can only carry certain pieces until your carrying capacity improves, while the runes are weightless. It give you lots of customization options between the two and the skill tree. The architect has only one purpose. He locks down the castle. The levels are randomly generated every time enter, but if you agree to give the architect a percentage of your gold on the current life, he will lock down the previous map so that you are not lost in a random new place. This can be helpful for retrying bosses, but be warned. Enemies will be back, chests will cannot be reopened, and as mentioned your gold gain is reduced for this entire life. So consider it for saving time and getting around.
Lastly, at the gates of the castle, you are faced with Charon, the gatekeeper. He will allow you to enter at the cost of all of your gold. This is where a lot of the motivation is built for the game. You'll want to spend as much gold as possible between the skill tree and the shops since you'll be losing it all anyway. You can't simply keep amassing gold over a number of lives. If you want a nice, expensive upgrade, you'd better not die and keep getting that gold. It's a nice way to give death some gravity, as getting upgrades and new characters already seems like REWARDING you for dying, and that needed to be checked and balanced somehow.
The basic goal is to become strong enough to survive the four areas, beat their bosses, and then defeat the final boss. There are lots of cool extra things to find along the way, like super bosses, passive items, challenge rooms, and even some cool secrets here and there. The game CAN become grindy, and if you don't enjoy grinding, then you might get a little upset at the difficulty. However, you always have the option to not buy anything and just try to beat the challenges old school style. Nothing bars you from doing so. So it's a nice duality. The game also goes from being a platformer in the earlier stages to being more akin to a bullet hell in the later ones. Master your movements, improve your aim, and pick your battles.
No game is perfect, so I had a few complaints. My main gripe with the game, though it's not a HUGE one, is that it doesn't really give you much incentive to stay alive. There's the thrill of getting more gold to get more upgrades, but eventually you'll want to keep dying so you can actually purchase and USE the upgrades. The only reason you'll want to NOT die, aside from adding to your gold count, is to beat a boss or, in the case of the final boss, beat the game. There are a good number of different room layouts and enemy combinations within, plus the challenge rooms the pop up now and then. However, after playing for so many hours, especially if you're like me and get really grindy with it, you'll start to recognize all the room types repeating. Even though the four areas are supposed to be different, they are all pretty similar. They have the same room types with different skins, more or less. And the enemies aren't really all that different between areas. They're mostly just more powerful versions of previous enemies in the harder areas, with maybe one or two new ones added. More variety would've helped, but there's already a lot of different things to deal with that it may be too complex to have more of everything, so I understand. Also, there weren't a lot of instances of this, but a handful of times I found weird floor glitches where gold fell through and I couldn't get it. That, and every once in a while my character would fall through and start randomly appearing in all the adjacent rooms for a few seconds. Nothing game breaking nor frequent, but a little spooky when they happened. Also... the music will wear away your sanity, but then again, so will anything when you play the game as much as I have.
There are lots of customization options, lots of random elements, lots of strategy involved, lots of skill required... and lots of hours of playtime and replayability in this game. I got 96 hours in my first playthrough. I love Rogue Legacy. The gameplay, the music, the sound, the graphics... everything comes together to make a game that feels like it was made for ME. It's the first time since Banjo-Kazooie that a game has felt like it was made just for me. It's an amazing feeling, and I can't recommend this game enough. Easily my favorite game on Steam and has instantly worked its way into being one of my favorite games of all time. I'd really say to just buy it now. Sure, you can wait for a sale if you're skeptical... or cheap. But it's definitely worth the $15 price tag. I mean, I ended up esentially putting down $45 to play this game, and it was well worth it.

Purchased for $30 during a sale.  Absolutely worth it.  This is essentially Shadow of Mordor: Wasteland Edition.  Whatever you think of Shadow of Mordor, I can almost guarantee you will feel the same way about this game.
Mad Max has a large open world, with tons of small objectives to complete all over.  Fully exploring and completing this game will take some time.
Ground combat is the system popularized by the recent Batman series, where you strike and counter to build combos.  It is a bit more difficult than in Batman/SoM though, as Max lacks the super-human moves like leaping over enemies, and weaponry is scarce.  There are a variety of enemies, anyone who has played Batman/SoM will recognize the types right away.
The game also features vehiclular combat.  You can do things like ram other vehicles, or use your weaponry to shoot vital parts of enemy vehicles such as fuel tanks, wheels, or even the drivers.  If you manage to disable the driver and leave their car undamaged, you can even 'disguise' yourself using enemy cars.
A robust but mostly linear upgrade system is included, both for your character and your vehicles.  'Scrap' is the currency used to purchase your upgrades, as well as tokens you earn by completing in-game challenges such as 'reach a combo of x20 or higher' or 'perform 5 finishers.'  Pretty much all of the vehicle upgrades are gated by story missions, while the character upgrades are gated by your level.
The story of the game involves Max trying to find the "Plains of Silence," which supposedly will help him find inner peace.  In order to get there, he needs a vehicle.  That vehicle is the Magnum Opus, which the main story centers around finding parts for and slowly making the car better and better.  The game features a few locations & mentions from Fury Road, like Gastown and the Bullet Farm, but chronologically it's never made clear if the game takes place before or after the Fury Road movie.
In summary:  this is a great action game.  There's nothing earth-shatteringly new here, but it's built upon a formula that is just plain enjoyable.  You can learn a bit more about the world of Mad Max while building yourself up to an♥♥♥♥♥kicking machine of death.

So I haven't played a lot of this game yet, but as it stands....I can't get into it.
So I'll just do a quick rundown.
Pros-
Game is pretty, the wasteland is neat looking.  It's fairly bright and flashy effects were very good.
Lots of customization, skill trees and car upgrades are pretty cool.
Audio was good overall, explosions sounded good and so did other sound effects.
Cons-
The control-This is what kills most games for me and it's literally crippling my Mad Max experience.  Whoever designed the control for this game...my god.  You can't jump.  You read that right, you literally cannot jump.  Who the **** designs a game in 2015 and is like "HMMM THEY DON'T NEED TO JUMP!"  Steering your car?  A joke, even when I plugged in my controller the car just does whatever it wants.
The control-Yes, there are two of these sub-bullets.  Want to climb a ladder?  Wouldn't you just walk up to it?  Nope.  Hold E to climb.  Want to pick of this scrap, ok, maybe press e?  Nope hold e for two seconds.  Want to perform a neat move in your car?  Do this strange button combination that does not flow at all.  Yes I know you can remap your keys, but that would NOT fix all that is wrong with this.  It's job mind boggling how people can't get it right after all these years.  I get the control was probably BUILT for a controller but since it's on PC, we should probably do some quick optimization for the keyboard/mouse yeah?  Nope.
The voice actor for Max.  Seriously, whoever they cast for Max talks A LOT more than he should and does a terrible job of portraying how insane he is.  Now I know that's not what wrong casting means but when this guy talks, it does not sound like Max in my mind.  I don't know who this is but he did a terrible job.
The combat reminds me of the new Batmans...a bit.  It's not nearly as fluent or fun though.  It feels lackluster by comparison.
Overall-This is not worth the purchase, there is probably a reason it went 50% off in the winter sale RIGHT after it was released.  It feels like a gimmicky movie hyped game that was rushed to production.  Do not purchase.

I've been having fun with this game for a little over two weeks. I like it a lot and would recommend it.
I'll just give you some pros and cons rather than some tl;dr in depth review.
PROS:
Beautiful enviroment with immersive weather and day night cycles
Accurate, and immersive sounds from the environment and surrounding animals
Decently Realistic animal behaviors and senses, including smell sight and sound awareness
.
Option to vary the degree of realism (offers the choice of toggling various visual assistance effects)
Landmarks and Lore points throughout the map add depth and interesting information.
Good weapon mechanics
Fairly indepth tutorial
Good choice of weapons
Awesome X-ray view breakdown of kills to show shot placement and anatomy effected
European and American Pacific Hunting worlds available
Maps are EXPANSIVE. Lots of places to go.
Multiplayer Capable
Active Dev team making corrections often
Cons:
Honestly, the only real con I can think of that isn't just a subjective opinion  would be the Bugs.
There are several bugs, the most of these occur in multiplayer. Nothing gamebreaking per se, but some that can be quite irritating.
(I would personally like there to be even more types of animals to hunt, ie, Rams, Caribou, Grizzlies, Turkeys, more species of deer)
Quick Bug list and frequency of occurrence as of 4/2/2017:
1) Animal AI not initiating properly leading to helpless game standing still. (Occasionally in both SP And MP) (in 2 weeks of playing, iv'e seen it 4 times)
2) Animal Entity State failing to update properly, leading to animals running in place after being shot, and then being non-harvestable after being killed.   (In MP, Occurs Frequently (~30% of kills)  *NEVER occurs in SP.* ---Possible Netcode issue)
3) Deer Bleat call can be heard loudly by the player when being used by any other players on the map, regardless of location or distance in world. (Always/100% bug rate. MP bug only)
4) Animals Struck by Player weapon leaving no tracks or blood trails whatsoever. (Rarely happens on both MP and SP) (Happened twice in 45 hrs of playtime once each on MP and SP modes)
5) Certain Animal call lures will glitch when you crouch while they are triggering their animation/sound file, causing the player to be unable to use the caller again until after switching between active items. (100% with certain callers both MP and SP) --minor irritation.
6) Tritium (glowdot) iron sights auto-unequiping from rifle when switching between items. (100% MP and SP)
7) Scope sights removed from backpack and left in storage still equipable. (100% SP & MP)

While there are many jokes about this game being an Austrailian outback simulator, the game itself isn't a joke. For something sort-of was under the radar and had a very silent launch (If memory serves me right, MAD MAX launched alongside Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.) and while people were preoccupied with MGSVTPP, those that did pre-order MAD MAX got a very pleasant surprise, The game ran well at launch, hell it was really well-optimized.
To have to be surprised every time a new game does that sure shows the state of the games industry nowadays.
MAD MAX (2015) The game follows Max Rockatansky in his quest to cross the plains of silence. You are in control of Max, and while there are no far-reaching consequences to your decisions in game, playing as Max is interesting to say the least.
The game offers open-world exploration, driving in said open-world, melee combat and car customization. Melee combat is reminiscent of the Arkham games where combat is basically "punch, punch, heavy attack, dodge, counter, dodge, counter, finishing move animation, rinse and repeat." What makes the combat fun is when Max is swarmed and his FURY™ counter gets filled up and he goes into a powered up state in which he is almost able to one-hit almost any enemy type. This does not make you overpowered at all, but it does help in moments where you're really in need of a pick-me-up.
Driving in the wasteland is interesting as you will encounter enemy drivers who will not hesitate to ram you off whatever is left of the road so they can chew on your innards. Customizing your car, the Magnum Opus, grants you various advantages and disadvantages that you can of course tweak to your taste. You can also customize Max, but you are limited to a few options in terms of hair, facial hair, whether or not you want some oil, dirt or face paint on you, as well as different iterations of the leather jacket (or rather progression as it gets armored up as you progress.)
As I played the game, I tried to avoid the main quest for as long as I could before I either get bored or can't hold the excitement of wanting to know what happens next. If you want to finish the main quests easily, doing all the side activities will help. But if you choose not to, the experience gets a bit harder.
Do I recommend this game? Do I think you should pick it up? Do I think you should spend money getting it?
Well, yes.

This is a review for alpha 26. I'll probably update it later on in the games life.
TL;DR: This game is fun, but it's hard and takes time to learn. It's not your Roller Coaster Tycoon game, or SimCity, it's like Banished wish RCT thrown in together. It's fun and addicting but only if you put in the time to learn.
On the outside this may look like a Roller Coaster Tycoon game with a Prison skin over it. You're wrong! I went into this game thinking that and boy was I taken aback. This is a lot more in depth and so much harder because the inmates will kill each other if their not happy.
This game is dense. You start with an empty lot and must build your prison starting with the foundation right up to what's in each cell. You've got to manage whether you get low, medium or high risk prisoners, and most inmates have a special reputation like violent or something like that.
This isn't a game you can just play and alt tab while doing something else like Roller Coaster Tycoon, you need to be always watching. There's never an equilibrium that I've found.
But the question is, is it good? At the time of writing this review I've played about 4 1/2 hours of sandbox mode with unlimited money to get used to the game... I'm so far in dept in the game that it's not even funny, I've had an entire prison of inmates overdose at once... I learned from that and put in an infirmary to which they rioted and stabbed eachother... This game is hard...
And I'm addicted. You can spend 4 hours in sandbox just to learn the basics than start the real game and loose striaght up... this game takes time and patience, but it's not a wiki game, it's a "pay attention or lose" game. And it's fun.

I saw that some of my friends were playing this and from the title alone, was minded to look into it. I wasn't immediately taken with the graphical style as it came over in the videos and it seemed bit expensive for an unfinished alpha, nonetheless, I added it to my wishlist to keep an eye on it and decided to buy it when it came on sale.
I was not disappointed, in fact, I am slightly addicted - I can't wait to see what the future holds for this game.
First of all, the graphics - the way that people in the prison are represented is somewhat unique, and as I mentioned, I thought it was odd - but in practice, it really works! They each have a their own unique look to suit their personalities and everyone seems to move around fairly smoothly (there are a few occasional pathing issues with it being alpha - very rarely, a character will stick on something, more often, characters will try to take a route to a room that you didn't intend - ie, prisoners will huddle around a staff door because it's closer than the 'proper' entrance, when plainly the intention is that they should not be allowed to pass through those).
The object of the game is to build and run a prison - the game could just as easily be called SimPrison, Prison Tycoon, or Theme Prison. It's exactly that kind of game. Were it 'Theme Park', it would be easy - you'd build big rides, and shops and then open your park to as many visitors as you can find, whilst keeping the place nice and tidy. The more people you have in your park, the more money you make - right?
In Prison Architect however, things are subtly different - your 'guests' (prisoners) represent your income by means of a daily grant for each one you're holding on behalf of the criminal justice system - but you can't just pack them in - they have needs, and when those needs aren't met, they riot, they fight, they destroy stuff, they attack each other and your staff (they'll even kill them if they're angry enough). So in PA, you have to carefully balance how much you're building with how much you can earn, whilst monitoring the activities of the incarcerated, and preferably not allowing them to escape or misbehave.
So far, the balance seems really good and there's a lot of depth to the game, you'll build walls, furnish your rooms, connect them up to electricity and water supples, add different types of door (including remote and timer activated later on), you'll specify the regime your prisoners live to, when they eat, when they work, you'll try to rehabilitate them, keep the ex-cops away from the cop killers, and so on, so forth.
Early on, there's good money to be made from expansion grants (kind of mini missions to help you understand what you need to do next) but as you expand, grants become fewer and costs become higher as more prisoners require more guards - get it wrong and you'll be mopping up blood and shifting the bodies of your guards to the hearses that visit your prison daily.
I anticipate a lot more content to come and I look forward to seeing what it is.
In the meantime, this is one to watch - enjoy the fact that there are some bugs, some unexplained objects/rooms, some well hidden UI stuff that's pretty important (for the first two prisons I couldn't figure out how to stop receiving a new intake every single day until the point where the entire prison would go on a murderous rampage due too too many people with too few facilities in too small of a space).

While there are many jokes about this game being an Austrailian outback simulator, the game itself isn't a joke. For something sort-of was under the radar and had a very silent launch (If memory serves me right, MAD MAX launched alongside Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.) and while people were preoccupied with MGSVTPP, those that did pre-order MAD MAX got a very pleasant surprise, The game ran well at launch, hell it was really well-optimized.
To have to be surprised every time a new game does that sure shows the state of the games industry nowadays.
MAD MAX (2015) The game follows Max Rockatansky in his quest to cross the plains of silence. You are in control of Max, and while there are no far-reaching consequences to your decisions in game, playing as Max is interesting to say the least.
The game offers open-world exploration, driving in said open-world, melee combat and car customization. Melee combat is reminiscent of the Arkham games where combat is basically "punch, punch, heavy attack, dodge, counter, dodge, counter, finishing move animation, rinse and repeat." What makes the combat fun is when Max is swarmed and his FURY™ counter gets filled up and he goes into a powered up state in which he is almost able to one-hit almost any enemy type. This does not make you overpowered at all, but it does help in moments where you're really in need of a pick-me-up.
Driving in the wasteland is interesting as you will encounter enemy drivers who will not hesitate to ram you off whatever is left of the road so they can chew on your innards. Customizing your car, the Magnum Opus, grants you various advantages and disadvantages that you can of course tweak to your taste. You can also customize Max, but you are limited to a few options in terms of hair, facial hair, whether or not you want some oil, dirt or face paint on you, as well as different iterations of the leather jacket (or rather progression as it gets armored up as you progress.)
As I played the game, I tried to avoid the main quest for as long as I could before I either get bored or can't hold the excitement of wanting to know what happens next. If you want to finish the main quests easily, doing all the side activities will help. But if you choose not to, the experience gets a bit harder.
Do I recommend this game? Do I think you should pick it up? Do I think you should spend money getting it?
Well, yes.

My experience with this game can be summed as thus: every update I found myself testing the changes, nodding in satisfaction, then quitting the game to await the next update.
Arkane knows how to make a good game. No question. But if you film an Oscar-worthy movie and the lens is smudged while filming, you can't judge what's underneath without acknowledging what's been marring your experience the entire time.
=============================
PERFORMANCE
Everyone is aware of the performance issues, and these still persist to this day. It runs much better than at launch, where it was literally unplayable, but that's because the game looks worse than before - the most noticeable change being the extremely aggressive LOD scaling. Out of the corner of your eye you notice the shapes of window frames and posters on distant buildings morphing in shape, or the furniture at the opposite end of a long hallway suddenly blinking into existence. FPS dropped to 15 when stabbing a gravehound, so they simply removed the inky visual effect that was causing the problem instead of optimizing it.
Also, Denuvo authentication is one of the longest "loading screens" of the game. Around half a minute to a full minute or more every startup.
=============================
GAMEPLAY
For the most part, gameplay is excellent and is Dishonored's strongest suit.
Dark Vision was changed to a blurry short range sonar so unlike Dishonored 1 you aren't constantly seeing blue and yellow because you had no reason not to
AI is much smarter
Nonlethal combat options are a blast
Bonecharm crafting system allows for player flexibility and "builds"
Each level feels lived-in while maintaining the duality of directive flow and open options that made the first game so good.
Emily and Corvo have distinct animations and final weapon upgrades. The animations are supremely cool.
Each level is fairly distinct, some with extremely interesting central "gimmicks." I do, however, wish the game relied less on them and had more "regular" areas.
However, under the hood lie other problems. Most of them are quality-of-life issues:
Gone are the hotkeys for journal, inventory, bonecharms, powers. Only one "journal" exists now, despite still having separate subsections.
It took months for the power wheel to be fixed. It took almost a full second after activating to pop up and be usable, breaking flow so badly I almost never used it in the first place. It's finally fixed now, but this issue was glaring and it took so long to be addressed most of us played through without it fixed.
Thrown objects don't always go exactly where your crosshair is. While this adds a layer of difficulty, it feels noticeably more clunky than in the first game.
Mana regen is pitifully slow. From using a power to fully regenerating, Dishonored 1's time is 4.7 seconds -> 3.1 seconds with Spiritual Pool. Dishonored 2's time with 4x Spiritual Pool is 6.3s -> 5.5s. The devs said they fixed this effect, but it was only made worse.
Bugs. Street speakers not playing. Dying after possessing gravehounds. An arc pylon never shutting down after pulling out its power, leaving it to either be dangerous to you to dangerous to your nonlethal playthrough. Some of these still aren't fixed.
=============================
STORY AND ATMOSPHERE
Reactivity
Great. My favorite part of Dishonored. You need to hide from a gang member to access a certain black market shop, and there are different scenarios and dialogue for if you hide, if you run into him outside, kill him outside, or kill him inside.
Emily and Corvo
Emily and Corvo are voiced. And... they don't talk enough. It's good that they're silent for most of the game, but there are times when you come across a portrait or photograph with an "Inspect" prompt. I'd love to hear Emily's thoughts on the High Overseer as see how that compares to Corvo's, or if it changes based on whether or not you accept the Outsider's Mark. Instead, all I get is the protagonist muttering the name of the person pictured. What's the point? Might as well keep them silent.
It made sense to me to play Emily first, but her story felt lackluster, like people at every turn were saying "check your royal privilege" despite my efforts to resolve everyone's problems without drawing blood. Corvo's is MUCH more interesting as a veteran of Dishonored 1.
The Outsider and The Void
I hate the new Outsider and his new voice. He felt threatening and malicious in the first game due to how calm and composed he was, and the Void felt like a strange and otherworldly place. The vignettes of Dunwall made it feel both unnatural and unnerving yet fundamentally woven into the universe. In Dishonored 2, it's just smoky blackness and sharp rocks. The Outsider is much jollier and moves around erratically, making grandiose hand gestures. They actually had a plot plot that could explain this change, but it was never addressed, so it just seems like a pointless retcon to me.
Main Plot
Dishonored's worldbuilding was always one of its appeals, and that remains true in Dishonored 2. However, the villains felt lackluster. Only the main villain has a real presence throughout the game, whereas everyone else feels introduced abruptly only to fall by your hand, all within the same mission. In Dishonored 1 everything felt personal and real. Perhaps it was because of the long intro where you interacted with most of them, or the Hound Pits's cast of characters all having different connections to your targets.
=============================
As you can see, I've played this game a LOT and have put a lot of thought into it. It was definitely worth all those hours and all that money, but the condition it was at launch and the sluggish drip-feed of support we barely get now is unacceptable. To set a precedent for future games, I can't recommend buying this unless they manage to fix all the performance issues and bugs, which doesn't seem to be happening anytime soon.

I absolutely love sandbox building games that aren't a cosmetic tea party.  This game has done nothing but amuse me as I've tried and failed to manage a prison properly probably a half dozen times now, but that's really the beauty of it. I could probably read a guide and get a lot of "I win" information, but games like these are just big ant farms slash chemisty sets where I like to be forced to evaluate my choices and try to balance a ton of factors into the plan. The best thing about this game is that everything is staged and nothing is instant. Your plan has to work from A to B and it's up to decide what you build or research next, but once you do you've sacrificed something and opened a hole somewhere. Eventually you have moments of stability where things seem to be going ok, but another wrench is thrown and the whole thing can spiral into chaos quickly.
If you glanced at this and thought it would be a cheap imitation of something that should be labeled "Tycoon" and thrown in a bargin bin, then you are sorely mistaken. This is an OCD stress test of micromanagement, choice making and logistics. It feels like everything matters and sometimes it feels like  everything you do is 5 steps behind the thing you should have already been doing 10 steps ago. Of course you can pace the game at your choices and even play in full "free" mode where you have lots of money, but even still...you aren't inviting kittens into your Barbie Dream House that you are filling up full of cheap furniture. You are inviting murderers and thieves into a house full of other murderers and thieves and it's up to get a TON of variables to play nice with each other.  They are not stupid. They will revolt. They will try to escape. They will steal from the kitchen and try to stab people, etc etc.
The scope to which this game has expanded is more than impressive and for a game that started off mentioning Dwarf Fortress as it's inspiration, it's created something even more unique that casts it's own shadow. Of course there have been other prison games, but this one has nailed so many concepts perfectly and given the track record for upgrades and patches, there will be more. I have found some bugs and the foundation system took me a
to really get my head around. I have to say the "Planning Mode" is something that every single builder type game needs to embrace right the eff now as well.
This is a solid recommendation from me even in Early Access state. If you don't like to support that kind of thing, completely understandable. The devs are active and the game has had over 20 patches full of content and fixes just since I've bought it. I actually turned it on just to see how it was progressing and I'm sucked into it and hopeless trying to figure out how last more than 30 minutes without someone dying.  (I know I could read a guide or something but who the heck plays games like that?)

Spec Ops: The Line could have been amazing, but is merely good overall. However, aspects of it truly shines.
The sense of progression in this game is simply amazing. Starting out as a typical military shooter, over time it becomes something more - and quite subtly at that. At first the killing seems inconsequential, you're following orders and being the archetypal soldier, mowing down the opposition for the greater good. As things progress though, it starts to challenge that notion, albeit vaguely at first. The loading screen text at the start of a level (or reloading a checkpoint in the case of death) even starts to change its tone, and it's these details that I admire so.
As the plot progresses, so do the characters and their tone of communication. Your character model and the environment follows suit, ever altering as you move forward. There's a ton of commentary in the background and it's up to the player to explore it and read between the lines.
Down to gameplay:
This is where it stays typical, moving from cover to cover, shooting people in the head and waiting for your health to regenerate. That's pretty much what combat comes down to.
One thing I loathed was my squad. The AI is so incompetent, I wanted to wrap my fist in an eisbein and punch them in the face. Forever. They're less trained combat operatives and more overconfident football players. They would've been more in place in a Serious Sam game. I got so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at having to revive these guys all the time.
You can order your squad to attack an enemy, but not to hold their position or to move to another. Game devs, what the♥♥♥♥♥♥ man? I hated those guys. And yes, they need to stay alive, as they're not just generic soldiers, but characters essential to the story.
Other than that, solid stuff. Get it on sale. Experience your own Apocalypse Now.

While there are many jokes about this game being an Austrailian outback simulator, the game itself isn't a joke. For something sort-of was under the radar and had a very silent launch (If memory serves me right, MAD MAX launched alongside Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain.) and while people were preoccupied with MGSVTPP, those that did pre-order MAD MAX got a very pleasant surprise, The game ran well at launch, hell it was really well-optimized.
To have to be surprised every time a new game does that sure shows the state of the games industry nowadays.
MAD MAX (2015) The game follows Max Rockatansky in his quest to cross the plains of silence. You are in control of Max, and while there are no far-reaching consequences to your decisions in game, playing as Max is interesting to say the least.
The game offers open-world exploration, driving in said open-world, melee combat and car customization. Melee combat is reminiscent of the Arkham games where combat is basically "punch, punch, heavy attack, dodge, counter, dodge, counter, finishing move animation, rinse and repeat." What makes the combat fun is when Max is swarmed and his FURY™ counter gets filled up and he goes into a powered up state in which he is almost able to one-hit almost any enemy type. This does not make you overpowered at all, but it does help in moments where you're really in need of a pick-me-up.
Driving in the wasteland is interesting as you will encounter enemy drivers who will not hesitate to ram you off whatever is left of the road so they can chew on your innards. Customizing your car, the Magnum Opus, grants you various advantages and disadvantages that you can of course tweak to your taste. You can also customize Max, but you are limited to a few options in terms of hair, facial hair, whether or not you want some oil, dirt or face paint on you, as well as different iterations of the leather jacket (or rather progression as it gets armored up as you progress.)
As I played the game, I tried to avoid the main quest for as long as I could before I either get bored or can't hold the excitement of wanting to know what happens next. If you want to finish the main quests easily, doing all the side activities will help. But if you choose not to, the experience gets a bit harder.
Do I recommend this game? Do I think you should pick it up? Do I think you should spend money getting it?
Well, yes.

I do recommend a prequel to the original Life is Strange. It's a solid game. However in my opinion the game is not as flashy, as the first game was.
Firstly, there is no time manipulation in LiS Before the Storm. At least not in Act1, which is all that was released as of September 21st. Maybe in the next chapters they will add some time twists, we will see. The ability to turn back time / the butterfly effect was a major element in the first game, a definition of it. That's what it was all about. Now without it, LiS Before the Storm seems flat, seems a little like a Soap Opera, just relationship, some adventures, a drama game...
Another thing is... for true LiS fans, they could release thousands of acts like Act1 of LiS Before the Storm and I will gladly play them all. No matter if there is time manipulation or not.
Chloe's voice actor is different. She tried her best (and I will hand it to her: in a way she did a good job), however the 'first' Chloe was a true rebel, this one is not that much. In other words, the voice of 'this' Chloe is inferior. It is and it is not a major issue. It just bugged me.
The producers used almost all the same assets as they created in the original game without making any new ones. You may say that with little effort (or with no effort at all) they tried to "pump out" more money out of the game concept, which occured to be very successful. They milked that cow, using the same assets.
Some people complained that the animations were not excellent and sometimes they seem too 'clunky'. True, if you look closly enough they were not perfect.
The atmosphere of LiS Before the Storm, the ambience, was the same as in the first LiS. Slow, paying attention to details, excellent screenshots, some momements when Chloe sat down and reflected upon things... that's good. That's what we want. That is Life is Strange game idea at its best.
The beginning of Act1 was alright, it was slow as it required an intoduction of the new setup. The end of Act1 was too melodramatic and too artificial as to my taste. I mean (*spoiler altert*) Rachel did make too much drama about her father cheating on her mother. It was such a big deal for her... She hurt Chloe and rejected her, who was disoriented and angry and confused. It was disgusting. And she made SUCH a big deal out of it. Drama drama drama... too much drama *yawn yawn*. We don't want drama. We don't care about drama.
Something new and very cool was the RPG session, where (*spoiler*) Chloe joint a tabletop game and had a character and they fought monsters and roleplayed it. Very cool indeed and very interesting.
The achievements, they changed photgraphs to graphitti. OK. Fine with me. *shrug*
Overall despite all the drawbacks LiS Before the Storm is to be recommended. You can't go wrong playing this game and it's a guaranteed level of enjoyment, compared -partially and only partially- to the level of enjoyment from playing the original LiS.
Again... last, but not least: bring back the butterfly effect. That's what LiS was all about.

This is a great game and it's well worth the money.  It gets a lot of inspiration from another game that rhymes with ShmastleVania but I think it throws in enough unique twists that it's not TOO similar.  Choosing a character with unique attributes and running through a randomly generated castle each time is fun.  The remix bosses were amazing, the game wouldn't be near as good without them.  They're frustratingly difficult, but I did manage to beat them after fighting them about a hundred times each.
There are some things that in my opinion would turn this good game into a great game:
- Don't make me collect every single rune 5 different times.  It's only exciting the first time I discover a new rune.
- Don't make me upgrade the same trait 75 times.  Upgrading one of these traits has almost no noticeable effect, so it's not very satisfying to drop all your gold on them seventy...five...times...  (x4 traits)
- Don't make treasure chests that only dwarfs can get to.  It creates an impossible goal which is just frustrating.  Dwarf shortcuts are great though.  Same with chests that require a specific magic ability.
- When getting a new rune or blueprint it only tells you the name. Showing the description and/or stats would be nice.
- Vertigo is funny the first time I picked it.  Every other time I accidentally picked it I just suicided.  Make an unlockable trait that disables vertigo? And do you really need to have a gay trait?
- The castle layout is randomly generated but the rooms that it uses are the same so the castles don't really differ that much. Especially since the areas are always in the same direction. I think having 2-3 more areas would've made a huge difference.  Also more enemies that were unique to each area (not just upgraded) would make them less repetitive.
- Maybe add a difficulty setting that affects the remix bosses so that younger people or people that aren't as skilled/patient can still unlock everything.
Seems like a lot of complaints but it's only because I enjoyed the game that I noticed these things. I would buy a Rogue Legacy 2 if they made it.

I picked this game up on the cheap one sale, and I played it for about an hour at that time.
I was getting slaughtered so badly that I stopped playing and put it in my "backlog" list.
I came back to it last month to give it another try and I'm glad I did.
This is not a forgiving game for those that just rush through platformers/bullet-hell games, or just jump at enemies to attack them without planning.  You will get crushed, hard and often, and that it will be very frustrating.
If you take the time to approach each level properly, it is a challenge worth conquering.  The randomly generated levels (except mini-boss and final boss levels) and maps and loot and extras means that it's an almost endless number of different play-throughs each time.  This time, when I approached it with a different mind-set, I got hooked on this game in a bad way.  I was playing it an hour or two every other night for a month, and finally starting making progress in the game, to the point where I just finished it last night.
(Of course, you can jump right back in and continue playing in "+" mode (same format, difficulty cranked up), but I needed a break.)
Outside actually playing the levels and defeating the monsters/bosses/traps, the framework around this game gives you LOTS of variations on how to play it.
Multiple classes, multiple stat/class upgrades, multiple genetic traits (both positive & negative), multiple armour/weapon slots, multiple upgrades for those items, multiple runes for those items...there are so many different ways to craft your character.
Finally, there is a lot of humourous touches in this game that show through in little places everywhere.
I would highly recommend this game, but only if you have patience and perseverance.

Spec Ops: The Line is a modern military shooter you play for the story.
The gameplay is, well, "modern military shooter."  I think there is more gameplay variety in Candy Crush levels then in different modern military shooters.  And Spec Ops: The Line proudly continues that tradition.  OK, it does have this excitting new future where you can shoot out glass windows holding sand at bay so it drops on top of your opponents.  Innovation!
Yet, its hard not to get the gameplay right with a hundred examples to pick from.  Enough of the combat is tense and challenging that the game recieves passing grades for fire fights, but nothing really elevates it.
However, the story is absolutely phenomenal, albeit unoriginal as it is inspired by the Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness.  Still, if you are going to copy, might as well copy from one of the best.  In a fictional near future, a massive sand storm hits the city of Dubai destroying much of its infrastructure.  However, a batalion of US soldiers, the 'damned' 33rd, attempted to evacuate and save civilians before and during the storm.  However, all contact is lost with the city and the batalion. They are officially left for dead in a no man's land.
Until the game's protagonist (your character) Mark Walker, a member of Delta Force, is sent to make contact with any survivors.  What begins as a recon mission quickly escaltes as the city is divided into factions at war with each other.  Along the way, Walker tries to aggressively to play hero, and, well, mistakes are made.  This is not a heroic fantasy where a world in peril can be saved from a villain by a good hero.  So, you don't know how it will end, or what the price will be for simply to continue playing.  Which paradoxically is a much stronger incentive to play than simply klling Nazis.

Wow, 80 hours already. I think this is also my first Steam review.
I enjoy theHunter COTW. At the core it is a hunting simulator, and in that regard it performs somewhat admirably. The landscapes in both playable maps are expansive and beautiful. The game engine really brings out the beauty of these hunting grounds whether it's a clear summer day or moonlit foggy night. Seeing the jagged antlers of the buck you've been intently tracking for what seems like hours shimmer in the sun while it trots within the tall foliage is quite the sight to see. The sun's rays sometimes glow through the trees, creating an ambience that causes you to stop and just take it all in.
Through numerous patches that have come after the game's release, the game is in, at least for me, a playable state. As mentioned in many other reviews perhaps these bugs should have been ironed out before release. I won't get into that debate as it seems to be the industry-wide norm. Bugs are minimal now, animal pathing and AI seems to be working more reliabely (though with some major faults, such as herd behavior). I haven't spontaneously combusted by walking between two rocks or two saplings in a long time. Sure, there's still some issues with terrain and how the player/animals interact with it, buggy/misplaced things such as grass hanging in the air, etc. With a map this expansive there are bound to be some issues and animals will eventually get stuck. This is part of the process and is something I can live with. However, due to my aforementioned herd behavior mention, if an animal as part of a herd does manage to bug out on a rock and get stuck, the rest of the animals will circle voilently around it until it dies (or you get trampled). This can lead to some funny/fruitful opportunities but as a hunting simulator it greatly detracts from the immersion.
Multiplayer is bare bones minimal. The single-player questing system is absent in the multiplayer version, instead replaced with competitions you can start with other players. These include hitting an animal in the heart first, bagging 3 fallow deer trophies, etc. While it can be a worthy distraction it would have been nice to be able to quest with other players. Especially with those difficult missions (high level photos, gold star ratings, etc.). There remains the issue of connected players to a host server being unable to unlock new landmarks/outposts, etc. I personally never join a server if I play multiplayer as I always want the option, so I host. It explains why there are so many servers with just 1 player in them.
My issue is that this developer seems to be following the trend. A console release has been announced recently and with the lack of updates it will only get worse in my opinion. A guise of two separate console and PC development teams is their only defense - just take a look at the patch note comments. The sad truth is that development for the PC version will slow until they get their cash flow from the console release. The game takes a modestly beefy PC to render the graphics at their ultimate potential, and a lot of people don't have the pcmasterrace in them.  If they get a console version that runs at 30 FPS and has full game pad support, a lot of people might hop on that boat. Why wouldn't they release a console version? Lotta money potential. And that seems to be their game - hey, it's a business.
6.5/10

So... what I'm saying is I can't recommend this game if you are looking for a coop game, like I was.

Like WTF, I just met them, who are they, I DON'T GIVE A♥♥♥♥♥♥ I know they're suppose to be there to woke memory of your family and help you cross the "Plains of Silence".....but still...it's so....out of place.
The boss battles are repetative, they are all absolutely the SAME, just different colors. Like, come on WB, give us at least 2-3 mechanics when fighting them. The last boss of the game is no exception. Not that great in my opinion, but hey. Then, there is stuff like Max dies if he takes 3 or more punches to the face but survives the whole damn convoy driving over him, LOL!? Then, the game is filled with bugs, which some of them are HILAROUS like, car flying to the sky and exploding for no reason whatsoever, dying and flying to the air when talking to the NPC, etc....
But hey, come on, story is short, game is bugged, plot is stupid...What are you doing for 50 hours in it then? Well, there are stuff that this game has done right. Like god dayum right!
First of all, taking that this game is from WB, we all had our fears for the PC port, *coff*ARKHAM KNIGHT*coff*. FEAR NOT MY CHILD, the game looks and performes GREAT! I7, dual gtx970, 1440p with all settings on ultra, still well above 100fps. Didn't had a single crash in this 50 hours playtime, except the little hickups I encountered during territory transition, proly due to the loading and stuff. No biggy. Gob job.
Car combat is fantastic, and it just gets better later on through  upgrade system that will turn your eveyday family car into a mean lean killing maching on four wheels. Thunderpoons, flamethrowers, raming to death, grinding your enemies cars with rims, sticking jumping maniacs on car's spikes or blowing them off with your sawedoff shotgun? You name it, we got it. Can't have enough of that.
Melee combat is fun also. You feel the strenght and power of punches, and the sound of broken bones keeps the smile on your face. Oh, you get to uprade Max too, turning him into a rampaging fist of fury of unstoppable....whatever. It's fun, although the combat doesn't feel fast and responsive as it does in Arkham series. But then again, you're not Batman.
The main currency of the game is SCRAP. And you will need a loads of it. Both for Max and the Car. And the Strongholds that you use as a safe house. The map of the game is HUGE and filled with stuff to collect, find, explore, beat and burn. If you are one of those completionist guys that need to have that 100%, you will love the game. That's how I got those 50 hours anyways. And still more to go!! Though, I have to say finding minefields and disarming the damn thing is BORING and dumb...But gotta have that 100% right?
One more thing I want to mention is one of the games characters and easily the brightest point of the  game. Yep, it's the damn Chumbucket. Love that guy. That weird but cute abomination gets introduced into the story very early on and believes in the Angel of Combustion and IN YOU as a Holy Driver, THE SAINT, that is sent by the Angel of Combustion to drive his most sacred creation ever, THE MAGNUM OPUS. And that, my friend, is where your jurney begins. From a scrap on four wheels to the Angel of Death, The Great Magnum Opus shall rise.
My final score is a strong 8/10 with a recommendation.
Take care all :)

It's a real shame that Steam doesn't offer a "Neutral" recommendation.
[Positives]
The game looks great, it runs great thanks to great optimization (seriously hats off to Avalanche Studios) and the gameplay is solid. Fighting is fluid and once you learn how it works it's great, combos everywhere.
[Neutrals]
The driving is a bit... stiff, when I was turning right it would take a second or so for anything to happen and when I wanted to stop turning it took another second to straighten out. This is a pretty big thing too since the game features A LOT of driving around
[Negatives]
Repetition. I could play for about 10 hours before I was forcing myself to play. You drive around this huge wasteland, fighting the occasional bandit caravan or cars and then you hop off, fight more people with your fists. That's it.
Now there might be more content in the game, but honestly it should be unlocked much earlier to keep the player invested in the game (if there's any new content, besides driving and liberating areas).
[Verdict]
Overall Mad Max looks beautiful, is optimized wonderfully so it runs great even on lesser systems, gameplay (mainly the fighting) is fluid and feels powerful, like there's actually some weight behind the punches.
But the game suffers from repetition, the story couldn't get me invested enough to continue playing the game, all the missions feel lackluster as it's mainly "Liberate Area X of Scrotus' armies". The driving is a big part and feels really off, I didn't have that much fun driving around in the game.
I really wanted to like this game, but I couldn't. Still I'm recommending the game.
Buy the game when it is on sale, not for the full price.

For those new to the series, Mad Max revolves around the episodic adventures of Max Rockatansky - a former police officer who lost his wife and young daughter to a gang of murderous motorbike raiders not long after a cataclysm depleted the earth of most of its natural water. Civilisation has gone to hell and it's every man for himself on this new desert planet as Max, mad with grief and dead inside from the horrors he has seen and endured, wanders aimlessly in search of some intangible release. His only remaining instinct is to survive, although to what end, he does not seem to know. There is a flicker of humanity still left in him that we see manifested in his various exploits helping other wastelanders in their time of need, but in the end he is always alone, having lost everything he held dear to him. It’s not a tale of redemption as such, as Max never tempers his savagery in the face of opposition, but in his actions we see the way he does his best to make the terrible world he lives in a little better, and lightens the load on those who can’t defend themselves against the ruthless. The game’s narrative is flimsy, however deep these thematic suggestions might seem to go, and loses a lot of the urgency due to the fact that it’s an open-world game and filled with a solid amount of busy work, but its heart is in the right place.
Mad Max (the game) seemed to infuriate a few critics, who are understandably likely to be appalled by a lack of innovation, and MM isn’t going to reinvent the wheel when it comes to open-world games, but I do find it falls on the better side of the trough that the industry was making its way out of at the time (leaving a clutter of Ubisoft collect-a-thons laying at the bottom to decompose).
Functionally, MM plays like a Frankenstein’s monster of late-2000s open-world games featuring a simplistic version of Arkham’s fight mechanics, open-world driving, vehicular combat, upgrades, and (sigh) collecting, so there’s not a lot here gameplay-wise that’s going to stun you. It all works though, the only gripe I have with the gameplay is the brainless fighting. Hit Y when it tells you, and hit X at every other point and you’ll make your way through most battles easily enough. There’s a distinct lack of finesse and variation in the hand-to-hand combat – you can pick up weapons but these will break after a few strikes and you can use your shotgun but ammo is scarce – and when it’s all over you’re back to pummelling X again. This is exemplary of the game’s biggest failing and one could quite reasonably critique MM by ranking the various activities and features by how well the mitigate their repetitiveness.
Which is the primary point of contention for most people – the world tries its hardest to invest you, while the gameplay works to take you out of it. It’s a balancing act that so many open world games play, and one that MM just falls on the winning side of, in my opinion. You can run and punch and roll and drive, but you can’t jump, which is insane for an open world game, especially as some of the locations require you to traverse open gaps or inclines. Every time you collect water or eat food there are a few seconds of a cutscene or an action that you have to watch; it’s one of those things where the frustration adds up over time. The icon-littered map and the reliance on a minimap for navigation serves as a constant reminder that you’re the player, but these negatives are countered by some solid world building that a love for Fury Road and a nostalgia for the Mad Max series will foster.
Most of the icons on your map are going to be lootable locations, and you’re looting scrap which contributes to your upgrades. These upgrades make an appreciable mark on your quality of life in-game, so the compulsion to attend to these locations is quite strong, at least for the first little while. There will be a point later on in the game where you don’t have to worry about the small amount of scrap from these places, but for those that don’t mind taking the time, there are plenty of little things to be seen and found in each of these little areas. They’re not all mind-blowing treasure troves of detail and mystery, but there is enough variation and attention to detail to make it worth doing.
The upgrades themselves don’t feel too frivolous; almost all of Max’s personal and car upgrades come with a visual change and while you may think at first glance that you’re simply working towards having the biggest and best of everything, they’ve balanced the upgrades with positive and negative effects – bigger rams and stronger armour will weigh more and reduce your handling, top speed, and acceleration – and these changes will have real repercussions in-game, so if you simply want a bullish battering ram you can make one; if you want a light and manoeuvrable racer, so be it; if you want a balance, you can customise as you see fit.
Vehicular combat is enjoyable, and it’s quite fun to come across patrols of bandits on the road as the engagements are spaced out enough to make you hungry for the fight. Depending on your weapons, armour, and health you may prefer differing tactics, but if you’re tired of ramming them, you’re equipped with a shotgun and a harpoon that can disable vehicles, kill the occupants, and destroy wheels, doors, and fuel tanks sending the offending vehicle spinning through the air in a shower of flame and debris.
But as I was saying, this is standard fare for the most part. It’s the sandbox within which all these things sit that sets it apart from other games in the genre. Whilst Avalanche’s most well-known series, Just Cause, isn’t known for its nuanced and detailed world, MM excels at creating a believable and lived in landscape, with plenty of small details that activate your imagination. Rotting hulls of long-abandoned ships lay half-buried, and lighthouses and bridges erupt from the earth and soar into the sky; the day/night cycle is modelled accurately and the colour palette of the landscape changes as you venture to different areas; vehicles explode with an ear-popping bang, and dance through the air spewing orange and yellow flames; metal parts and debris fly from the wreckages and litter the area around them, and the destroyed hull of the cars grind to a halt, burning grimly by the roadside. The game performs exceptionally well, although I’ve noticed some occasional visual glitches particularly in the shadowing in some of the dust plumes, but there’s little lag, even when you’re tearing around the landscape. There’s a nice attention to detail, such as tire marks and footprints in the dust, the way sand spits up from your wheels, the way convoys are visible from afar by the dust clouds they stir, and the detail in the wrecked vehicles as they blast apart and then lay destroyed. It helps with immersion, which is something the game sorely needs to balance out the in-your-face-edness of its mechanics.
And that’s probably the core observation I have to make about the game – the quality of Mad Max (the game) in the eyes of the player is going to rely on how weight you place on each of the variables on the scales. I can see the frustration and validity of all the criticisms, but I’m also wooed by the qualities and intensity of the game world, and by the little details that show that, for the things they got wrong, they got something quite right as well. If you want to play ‘Fury Road: The Video Game’, then you’re in the right place. If you want to brawl and blow up, if you want to run and drive, then you’re in the right place. If you want a beautiful post-apocalyptic world, then you’re in the right place. However, if want nuance and subtlety, if you want a complex narrative, if you want an innovative game that will relieve your Assassin’s Creed fatigue, then, like Max in his search for peace in the Plains of Silence, you’re not likely to find what you’re looking for here.

A lot of people on boards and forums have been talking about it.  The scrap collecting system is glitched for me and the historical relics stuff is messed too. It needs a patch asap!  This is probably because the game was not fully tested long term and rushed for release or some locations are mayby locked in DLC? Anyway here are some good points and bad points.
Good Points:
Fun, fisty, fighting and driving.
Custom car parts and engines.
Fun car weapons & upgrades.
Bad points:
Camera sometimes has a mind of it's own in camps when things get tight in tunnels and shipping crates.
Very repetative character designs and sub bosses.
Stupid game breaking glitches, like not being able to go back into the airport desert stage, scrap picked up and not registering problems and many more......
Short story with no branching choices, no freedom to be the Road Warrior you want to be. NPC interaction is weak, there are alot of useless intel and loot encounters which are a waste of time and the post story ones just feel tacked on and lame.

This game could have been really awesome, I mean they can still patch it and fix alot of the problems.  They could add in an a update to generate more NPC and random conveys and populate the world a bit more.  I know it's supposed to be a vast decaying desert post nucelar world, but if you have camps and strongholds there should be raids going on constantly and interveneble side missions like saving a travelling group from raiders and other fun stuff. Seeing lots of people just wander the land dying of thirst and making me feel guilty to stop and give them some water is fun the first few times, but then I just want to run them down and put them out of their misery. I hate having to grind around looking for cars and enemies to take out.
Chums the best character, love that guy! If I was really in that decaying world, he'd be my friend for sure and we'd fight back to back against the whole world.
I do recommend this game for some short fun, it's not that pricey, don't really bother trying to 100% percent it right now, it's bugged big time. I also have it on the PS4. The PS4 version is ok, but it taxed my PS4 1st gen and blew up my psu! lol. I fixed it and also bought it on the PC when it was on sale as a back up and it was obviously a much better experience, smoother gameplay, better gfx and smoother counter timing when fighting.
Just go into it, have fun and try to resist the completionist temptation. A big salute to the dev team for working hard to create something fun, a big slap to the back of the head of the publisher WB for rushing a game that could have been a masterpiece.
I give it a 7/10. All the best.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

It's a fun game, the fighting and driving is decent.  Becoming the Road Warrior is the best feeling, the game is a alternative universe tale of Mad Max that's not connected to the movies.  The story is a bit weak and the ending is lame, but kinda suits the morbid world I guess.  The biggest gripe I have is that the game hasn't been tested propely and is full of game breaking bugs.
A lot of people on boards and forums have been talking about it.  The scrap collecting system is glitched for me and the historical relics stuff is messed too. It needs a patch asap!  This is probably because the game was not fully tested long term and rushed for release or some locations are mayby locked in DLC? Anyway here are some good points and bad points.
Good Points:
Fun, fisty, fighting and driving.
Custom car parts and engines.
Fun car weapons & upgrades.
Bad points:
Camera sometimes has a mind of it's own in camps when things get tight in tunnels and shipping crates.
Very repetative character designs and sub bosses.
Stupid game breaking glitches, like not being able to go back into the airport desert stage, scrap picked up and not registering problems and many more......
Short story with no branching choices, no freedom to be the Road Warrior you want to be. NPC interaction is weak, there are alot of useless intel and loot encounters which are a waste of time and the post story ones just feel tacked on and lame.
A stupid need to grind car deaths from different factions to achieve Road Warrior ranks, what were they thinking? That we would keep doing the races again and again? No convey respawns make getting spike impales and grinding achievements a real hassle.
This game could have been really awesome, I mean they can still patch it and fix alot of the problems.  They could add in an a update to generate more NPC and random conveys and populate the world a bit more.  I know it's supposed to be a vast decaying desert post nucelar world, but if you have camps and strongholds there should be raids going on constantly and interveneble side missions like saving a travelling group from raiders and other fun stuff. Seeing lots of people just wander the land dying of thirst and making me feel guilty to stop and give them some water is fun the first few times, but then I just want to run them down and put them out of their misery. I hate having to grind around looking for cars and enemies to take out.
Chums the best character, love that guy! If I was really in that decaying world, he'd be my friend for sure and we'd fight back to back against the whole world.
I do recommend this game for some short fun, it's not that pricey, don't really bother trying to 100% percent it right now, it's bugged big time. I also have it on the PS4. The PS4 version is ok, but it taxed my PS4 1st gen and blew up my psu! lol. I fixed it and also bought it on the PC when it was on sale as a back up and it was obviously a much better experience, smoother gameplay, better gfx and smoother counter timing when fighting.
Just go into it, have fun and try to resist the completionist temptation. A big salute to the dev team for working hard to create something fun, a big slap to the back of the head of the publisher WB for rushing a game that could have been a masterpiece.
I give it a 7/10. All the best.

An all-around amazing game. Breathtaking setting with stunning visuals, and all optimized well enough to run at around 30 FPS on a non-gaming laptop with graphics maxed out.
The plot is what really sets this game apart from other shooters. The devs have managed to highlight elements that really get burned into your memory, and whose effects are visible on the game's characters. Speaking of those, the AIs assigned to you in this game are so much more than the generic drones you so often get in CoD games and the like - excellent writing and voice acting makes them an integral part of the mind-twisting, gut-wrenching story almost from the get-go.
The game has even managed to get the over-the-shoulder POV right (I generally dislike that in a shooter). In this game, it keeps you from thinking, even for a moment, that your character, Walker, is just another template for players to visualize themselves in.
This game isn't for everyone; there are some profoundly messed-up things that you're required to do in pretty much every chapter. If you're undcided, watch or read some more thorough gameplay reviews online.

Ok, so first of all, i want to state that it is very hard for me to post a review about this game.  The reason being that i have so much to say about it, making it hard to put it all together or organize it into one conclusive review on the game.  I may review this review multiple times and change or add things to it.
Moving on to the actual review i would like to say, being a hunter in reality, that this game is trying its best to meet my expectations for a realistic, interactive hunting game. The graphics are absolutely incredible, I can walk almost anywhere on the reserve and either admire the view of far off areas, or simply enjoy the placement of the brush and trees in my immediate vacinity.  I admire this game for its graphic attention to detail.
The graphics are not the only thing i admire, as they do not make or break a game.  The gameplay and game mechanics are impressive as well.  The pause menu in the game impresses me for several reasons. I enjoy the design of the map and how the waypoint placement works (although a problem with previous waypoints interfering with current ones until removed is slightly annoying), the map works well and i like the ability to fast travel between discovered cabins. I enjoy the fact that missions are implemented but not essential.  I enjoy that the devs focused on both main styles of hunting, ambushing and stalking, and the available skills for both styles. I enjoy that with certain skills you actually have to activate them to use them, and that some have a cool down time. Personally i think it makes it more challenging, and makes you think more.
Moving on to the animals in the game... I like the fact that different animals react differently than others.  Not all animals react the same to sight, smell, and sound as others.  Implimenting those differences is attention to detail that i appreciate as a gamer and a hunter.  The only constructive criticizm i can give, is that i hope they plan to add a massive about of different species including different game sizes. An example being multiple small game type animals having their own scoring.
Moving to maps... I truly enjoy the detail put into developing both of the maps.  They are both huge and there are so many different areas to explore and new sights to see.  I have no complaints about the maps that already exist.  The only thing i coult hope for is that they add several more, just as intricate maps, from all over the world with scores of different species for each area.
Overall i think this game is amazing.  It is the game i have been waitng for since Big Game Hunter.  The "Perfect" hunting game.  Although they are onto an amazing start, i think there is always so much more they can add to eventually make this the most amazing hunting experience available without actually going into the woods with a gun.  If i had to add one suggestion to the game... It would be this...
I think it would be an amazing idea to add a trophy room to the game.  It should be a building you have to find in each region.  When you locate this "trophy room", and claim it, it should display a spot on the wall for each species in the area.  Each space should contain a mount of the largest scoring animal you have harvested of that species.  Along with a list of every other animal you have harvested in that species. Every time you harvest a bigger scoring animal of that species, the wall mount should be replaced with that animal.
This game is amazing.  Overall i have no complaints.  I look forward to seeing where this game goes and i am sure that i will enjoy it regardless.

Ok not going to rehash all the other great reviews out there already but as of this time I have 82 hours in it and i havent even made it to the second reserve . I dont know how some of you justify bang for the buck but with that much game play in half the game its pretty hard to ♥♥♥♥♥ even with the glitches which are certainly better than when released and being worked on all the time. If you like hunting games bingo its a winner if you like walking simulators also spot on. The rare few who actually like both its about as good as it gets in that sense ,plus a level grind aspect that keeps me playing with a goal to achieve . The glitches mentioned before while annoying are not game breaking the disappearing tracks issue is the hardest to deal with but also getting better (my suggestion is to be dam sure before you let that arrow or bullet fly). I like many others have literaly spent hours tracking a less that stellar shot to make sure i keep my consecutive harvest bonus going and it just seems wrong even in the game world to just take pot shots at everything then let them die slowly out in the brush to rot.
I find if i just pick an undiscovered spot on the map and walk ( not run sometimes even in stealth which seems agonozingly slow) there I will several chances to track seomthing or even straight out walk up on a clean shot situation.
I dont find the hunting blinds all that helpful but they do work you just have to use the calls but it seems boring when there is plenty to hunt walking around. Running is only a means to get from point a to b not a method to travel and expect to hun. The wildlife will hear you before you even get a warning call from them and its like your on a deserted planet. If your a twitch pvp gotta shoot a hundered rounds an hour player keep walking this isnt your game. There is however plenty of beautiful scenery and simply walking to open up map areas is enjoyable if you have a 5.1 or better headset or surround system crank it up and head into the woods listen for warning and mating calls and stealth towards them its very cool. Keep in mind which way your scent is going as it will tip them off before anything else does many times.
I love the direction this game is going and cant wait to visit the other reserve looking forward to some new reserve dlcs maybe a few more things to hunt would rock but still pretty darn good now. I would like the option to start a second data or more so as i go to a new reserve i can start from scratch while still having the option to bring my developed character to look for bigger game as well . I love the level asect of it for me i like to have a goal to work towards there is a good mix of xp grind and  money grind here to keep you motiviated. They cant give it all to you for free at the start or you'd get bored quickly. I do feel like having to start over from scratch on the consecutive harvest thing is a bit of a pain but not horrible. I mostly find it makes it impossible to jump in and play for short bursts because so much of the game requires you to get gold kills and that is ony going to happen if you have 100% modifier on consecutive harvest as well as quick kill and it needs to be basically mythical grade animal.
Graphics are really nice sometimes i just climb a mountain to see the view from up there some of the waters edge shots you get as well looking out over a tranquil mountiain lake or river is beautiful. Dont judge it by all the negative reviews while the points are valid a lot of times, many have been addressed and i have found none game breaking aggravating at times yes but not gamebreaking. I have only had one or two animals that i got any sort of decent shot into that didnt result in a successful harvest with diligent tracking and patience.
Almost forgot dont forget to try the bow I started this game thinking good lord I'll never get close enough to anything to kill it with a bow but you will and its a real sense of accomplishment when you take down a mythical level red deer lets say with your bow very cool. I hunt almost exclusively with it now but still break out the 270 as well ,sometimes you just want to make sure especially if your on a mission and have 100% harvest bonus and dont want to risk it.
There it is all i can think of hope it helps i enjoyed this game enough that i didnt even mind buying it full price 30 bucks is not outrageous . I looked at the classic version and I would never enjoy it as much as this one even with the larger number of things to hunt micro transaction games just leave me with a bad vibe and the days of monthy subscription games are pretty much done.
