I recruited an inmate as a confidential informant. He proceeded to slink off to the security room, check out the cameras, and chat with the guards stationed there. With his assistance, I was able to quickly clear two cell blocks of contraband weapons and escape tools. A day later I saw a death notification pop up. "Snitches get stitches," I thought, assuming that the informant had been slain for ratting on his fellow inmates. Such an event is common in Prison Architect, and one human life was a small price to pay to prevent future violence.
But then another death popped up. And then another. I panicked, thinking that perhaps a riot was brewing, and hovered over the death notification box, which zooms in on the most recent death.
My confidential informant was blasting guards with a shotgun in an escape attempt! Apparently, unbeknownst to me, he took advantage of his newfound position in the prison to break into the armory, steal a shotgun, and attempt to break out of the prison (or go down in a blaze of glory).

Everything about this game screams bad design. Consider this a first impressions review since I'm only 47 minutes in, but something happened at the 45 minute mark that made me instantly stop playing and get a refund. I want you to remember that: all of this happened within 45 minutes of first clicking Play on Steam. There will also be a couple of minor spoilers but again, nothing that occurs further in than 45 minutes.
The bad stuff starts before even getting into the game. On the main menu I hopped into the graphics options to make sure everything was on maximum. They wern't. Pressing a button to autodetect my system set most of the options to max, but the game hadn't bothered to do this autodetect when booting up. Then I turned off motion blur and depth of field, then the game crashed so I restarted it and had to re-watch all the unskippable developer credits and pre-menu cutscene. I got back into the options menu and turned off depth of field again because it was still on. Then I realised that it was still on because you can't turn it off. No, really. I Googled it. So now I'm stuck with a blurry screen unless the game engine and I can agree on what object to focus on. Great.
Well, after shouting at the main menu and making some choice remarks about the developers' parents I started up the movie. Sorry, game. I get confused because there were three seperate cool fights that I didn't get to play. In one of them a man got a chainsaw embedded in his head and still kept fighting long enough to throw another man off a car. If I could have chosen one of those fights to play it would have been that one, but I guess the game was scared that I would have messed something up and not looked as cool as it did.
Anyway, the game finally dumped me in a box canyon and let me play, for some reason the sprint button was locked and I walked a bit. Well I tried to walk but there's no button for that either; only a sort of middling jog. I tried to climb on top of a small rock but there's no climbing animation, Max can only get on top of objects lower than roughly knee hieght because that's how high he can jump.
I decided to get out of my chair and jump to test something: by jumping up and bending my knees, pulling my feet towards my torso, I get my feet up around waist hieght. I felt marginally good at being more physically capable that an action game's protagonist.
I found a pool of water and stared at it for a while pressing buttons until I realised you had to hold E and not just press it in order to fill my canteen from the pool. Why do you have to hold it? Who knows. My canteen is a TARDIS though, because the large bowl of water only filled up about a tenth of it's capacity. So that was cool. I also found a can of dog food that I could hold E on and I got to watch another cutscene of Max eating it, then he threw the can on the ground and when the cutscene ended I looked down and the can was gone. So that was cool too. Maybe the depth of field just made the ground so blurry I couldn't see it.
After a bit of wandering I found two shotgun shells and some guys so I tried to shoot them, but it turns out you can't walk while in aiming mode. If I pressed spacebar Max would do a full combat roll, but walking is beyond his cababilities. I got out of my chair again and picked up a Nerf gun I've got lying around to test something: it turns out that humans can in fact walk while holding guns. (Full disclosure: I did not actually get out of my chair for this. But in the past I have walked while carrying both a Nerf gun so I feel justified.) I felt more superiour about being more physically capable that an action game character. Then I felt ill because of the depth of field.
After Max's spectacular inability to use both a gun and his feet at the same time, I puunched the guys for a bit until they went to sleep then I tried to convince Max to pick up a large spear they had been standing over. Nope, can't do that. I did notice that Max carries a huge machete strapped to his belt, but I can't seem to use that in combat either. Well, whatever. I'd given up expecting quality at this point.
There was a collectable doo-dad on top of a crate so I jumped at it to climb on top. Then I went back and spent five minutes running about and jumping until I got the position exactly right so that Max's knee-high jump would get him on top of the crate. The crate was about shoulder height (it was a shipping container, but partially burried into a hill) but remember: Max can't climb. At all.
I ran back from this area, which took 2 minutes 17 seconds of just running - I timed it because by this point I was running a stopwatch app on my phone to ensure I didn't go over Steam's two hour refund limit, and had to pick up a dog I didn't care about and walk very slowly over to a car somewhere. At this point I discovered that if I moved by tapping W rapidly instead of holding it, Max would only leave behind footprints from his right foot. Wierd. Don't worry, I took a screenshot:
I threw the dog in the back of the car and got through some awful driving mechanics - the car continues to steer for a split second after letting go of the A or D keys which meant I spent more time in a wall than on the road - then I watched YET ANOTHER cutscene where Max stole some binoculars off a guy who had only been kind to him so far. The guy had a hunch back and a burn on his face though so I guess it's OK to be mean to him because bullying is fine as long as the victim has some sort of physical deformity? There are actually even more of these bloody cutscenes than I've mentioned, by the way, but most are so dull they don't even merit a passing remark.
It turned out that my car, which had been stolen in a previous cutscene, was being held and possibly being scrapped in a compound just down the road. The kind guy with the hunchback offered to build me a new car (seriously, I stole his binoculars and his response is to offer to BUILD ME A NEW CAR) but I decided to ignore him and run off to the compound.
Then the thing occured which convinced to to quit and get a refund. I got to the compound's front gate (which was suspiciously quiet since the guards from the cutscene wern't in the actual game - I guess the devs couldn't be bothered to add them twice) and dicovered a huge hole in the gate that I could crawl through. Another screenshot:
Except... I couldn't. I couldn't make Max do it. The graphics had a huge hole in the gate, but as far as the mechanics were concerned the entire thing was made of twelve inch steel. I even rammed the gate with my car for a bit but it had no effect. Unfortunatly, near where I live there are no holes in fences that I can get out of my chair to test, but I think I can make a reasonable assumption about my ability to get through them.

Download the inspector, open up the overclocking tab and move "base clock offset"  to the -55 mark or close to. Then hit apply. I would leave this inspector program running in the background. it seems to reset the settings when you close it. But otherwise that fixed my issue. I have only crashed a few times since and it was like I said it resets itself when closed.

The central turn-based rpg gameplay is full of small twists and reworkings that change up the gameplay every hour or so. Every battle is a puzzle and every puzzle has a new set of rules and pieces, and somehow it never feels inconsistent or cheap. (Outside of ONE particular boss against a certain someone with a trident, where the game breaks one of the most basic rules it's taught you without explaining what's expected of you, but aside from that...)
The appeal is all in its plotline. It does that thing where it uses really strong comedy and fluff to make you love all the characters so when it takes a hard snap into drama or danger or darkness (or at a few points, profoundly, viscerally unsettling horror) it hits you that much harder. And it does both steps of that one-two process alarmingly well. Its aesthetic quickly elevates, then subverts, then completely transcends its "generic retro indie game" low-pixel look. And Toby Fox did the soundtrack himself and it's all his best work. So literally everything in the game is gorgeous and arresting on literally every level. It made me laugh out loud, cry literal adult tears, tremble and sweat in terror and unease, and leap out of my chair in elation. It's going to be considered a classic for the next 50 years and it deserves it.
And no it's not about misandry or gender politics or how video games are bad or whatever ♥♥♥♥♥ hallucinated and then told you about. Don't be a baby.

Undertale is a unique experience. From the story, to the characters, to the music, Undertale is a game to play in one sitting and explore every nook and cranny. It's filled with details that give the world so much life and veracity that you really can't play this game in a hurry. While I was playing it, I felt a whole bunch of nostalgia, even if I never even played the game before or if it doesn't really remind me of anything. It just gives me this feeling of "remember the good ol' times". The characters and the story are innocent and have a childlike wonder to them, make someone think like "I wish I could meet this character in person" or "I wish they made a cartoon out of this".
One of the negative points are the art, which albeit charming it is kind of crooked and it looks like it was made by someone who used the project as a way to learn pixel art. It's not painful to look at, but it can be deceiving or hard to adapt.
Another one is the puzzles. They are either too easy or they drag too much to the point of feeling like a chore. It is a somewhat good idea to give a game simple puzzles so that the story can progress fairly, but if the choice is to progress a story, why have puzzles at all?
And there's also the reasonable replayability. In order to get all possible endings, you'd need to play the game to completion 3 times. If you want to 100% it, you'd need to replay it many, many times because one of the endings has small differences in dialogue, but the game only really changes if you do one of the three main paths. My suggestion is play it the three times and then play around with the different possibilities if you so desire.
Those negative points are tolerable and they don't ruin any playthroughs, but they are legitimate flaws that, in my opinion, could've been sorted out.
I say give this game a try and stay away from the fandom.

This game certainly has some strong qualities.
Great graphics. Excellent lighting effects, weather effects etc.
Really large map.
Nice weapons and accessories.
Tracking system is not overcomplicated.
But it also has some weak qualities.
No vehicles on a ridiculously large map. You have to walk everywhere. All of the time. It's so boring sometimes when you just want to go from point A to point B.
The level progression is insanely slow, to the point where it can take days to get a new weapon.
No way to pause the game, literally, none.
You can't rest without paying the money you earned from hunting. That's the dumbest thing I've ever seen in a video game.
In the current state I do not recommend this game. It is good for just relaxing instead of going fast paced like in most games, but other than that it needs some serious improvements in those areas.
EDIT: Still giving it a go. I just went up a tower to survey the land, with the intent on finding the nearest hunting camp afterwards. Fell off the tower, now I have to walk nearly 2KM to get to the new camp. All because there are nowhere near enough fast travel points. This is the main problem with this game. Rogue Legacy is a truly magnificent Indie game released back in June 2013 by Cellar Door Games .
It follows a story of an old family of Nobles, exploring the castle of Death himself to unravel the mysterious death of the King. You go along the randomly generated dungeons, finding Journals containing the thoughts of a Prince, the son of the murdered king.
The game offers a great system in which you fight through rooms of monsters, collecting coins as you go along. The twist is that every time you die the next character you can pick will be a heir from the following generation of the family. They all have different names, powers and traits: some are afraid of monsters and get scaredyfarts, others are colorblind or imagine enemies where they shouldn't be.. and then there's just gay (yup, an actual trait..).
You use the coins, picked up along the way, to build up your kingdom or buy weapons, armour and buffs, but upon entering the Castle again, your left overs will be depleted. Expand your kingdom with new helpful characters like the Blacksmith and Enchantress to unlock new power-ups.
Face difficult enemies and 4 powerful different Bosses. Find bonus rooms filled with crazy challanges, tough baddies or golden treasures. You can additionally find Runes or blueprints that can be crafted into armour and abilities.
The only negative critisism I can point out is that the combat system seems a little buggy at times. When switching directions the character sometimes gets stuck swinging the sword at the wrong side.
Overall, seeing as the Steam User reviews are Overwhelmingly positive, I'd have to agree. This is one of the most fun and inventive games i've played in a while and fully deserves it's 96% recommendation rating.

Pros:
-Fresh, vibrant artstyle
-Arcade style gameplay
-Decent Customization options

-Bot support
-Clan support
Cons:
-Annoying community
-Sketchy connection issues (On my first FSBB2 session, I was dropped from a game loading screen no less than 7 times in a row)
-Puzzling sound direction (I don't necessarily mind the Korean rap, but the voice acting leaves a bit to be desired)
-Too many unnecessary features. Booster cards, gachapon-style power-ups, robots that shout nice things and return balls for you after each shot in practice, a post-game breakdown that pats you on the back and lets you pick a mystery card: basically, every smoke-and-mirrors parlor trick mobile game designers have tried to implement into one gaudy, bedazzled cardboard box.
In short: yes, I found it fun. I found it fun the last time I played the same game 5 years ago. There isn't enough improvement here for me to specifically recommend the game to any of my friends, especially not the ones who abandoned the game with me last time. I was expecting something different out of a sequel to a game that already had glaring flaws regarding netcode and connection issues, honestly. Daily Login bonuses and fake tickets for electronic roulette prizes won't cover up the few issues that still seem to exist.

If you can get past the server issues the game is pretty good and has a large following.  The interface is a bit confusing and I still have no clue what some of the stuff does or what I should do with it but it's basketball and it's street basketball and that makes it a 10/10 for me.

####################################################
#########################
# How to ruin gameplay in 3 steps #
#########################
1) Put no Vsync option
Never seen a game without Vsync option... Devs will never stop surprising me with the lack of basic common sense. I mean what the ♥♥♥♥, we're on PC, not on a goddamn console.
I can't notice tearing in this game, maybe because I got 200FPS+ and 144Hz monitor, or because it's forced ON... Anyways, some people might prefer Vsync ON, and others like me would prefer this off to lower the horrible lag caused by Vsync; which leads us to the next thing...
2) Provide horrible mice controls
- Mice movements are smoothed
- Mice latency is high (might be cause by the stupid smoothing)
- Mice has a dead zone!
- Mice acceleration is forced on (like on Apple computers, lol)
Impressive! I hadn't seen a that much of a poor mice response since Battlefiled 3 when it was just released.
I almost sh@t in my pants the first time I played the game. Didn't do two steps before I pressed escape and went trying to fix this bullcrap. But no... There is no "acceleration" or "smoothing" or "dead zone" option, at best, you can lower the sensitivity that is way too high by default, which doesn't solve these problems at all.
If you try to make very tiny movements with your mice, they are not registered; if you try to turn around, you make two turns.
It seems like they're trying to work with the mice as if it was a controller, but so badly that even with a controller it would be horrible as well.
(Note that I'm a competitive CSGO player and got 0 acceleration and near 0 input lag hardware, so I know how it's feels when it's responsive).
We are in 2017 for **** sake. Back in 90's, they already knew how to make flat, linear, with low input lag mice response. What the hell?! Wake up!!
3) Add horrible controller response on the view stick (to give you motion sickness)
After hating the mice responsiveness, you might, like me, want to try with an Xbox controller, because "Hopefully it will feel better with a controller". Lol, nope! Smoothing is so high, and latency is so high, that it's still horrible to control the view with a controller. I almost felt sick, both because I was disgusted by such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and because of the near motion sickness that resulted from such a distorded response...
At least, developers fixed the Xbox controllers issues for most people (I gladly didn't have this issue with a wired Xbox 360 controller).
4) Oh, and one more thing...
I'd like to be able to skip this damn intro. It's funny once, twice, not 50 times after trying to restart the game in order to fix stupid issues with the game's responsiveness.
###########
# Conclusion  #
###########
Gameplay is so bad that it ruins gaming experience on a game with an amazing story.
Developers, what are you thinking? Remove your fingers from your arses, wash them, then go back to code!

I think this is a great follow-up to the first game. There's a few different elements that weren't present in the first game, but that's also what makes it interesting.
Pros
- In this game you play as Chloe.
It's nice being able to see the story from Chloe's point of view, as you didn't get that much info about her in the first game. You also learn a lot about her past, and her relationship with the mysterious Rachel.
- Grafitti (Compensation for photography).
I like that they kept this in some shape. In the first game, sometimes you'd have the option to take pictures of random scenery, which would result in an achievement. You still have that in this game, but as Chloe isn't into photography, she does grafitti instead.
Cons
- Chloe got a new voice actor.
I personally have no problem with the change, I didn't actually notice that big of a difference while playing the game. This might bug some people though.
- No going back in time.
In the first game Max had the ability to go back in time. This isn't an option anymore, so if you regret any choices you make, you'll have to go back to an old save. It's not a big problem, but it gets kinda annoying when you're used to that option, or if you want to see a different outcome.
- Emotionless characters.
It took me a while to actually get bothered by this, but sometimes when the characters have a certain emotion, it wont show on their face. For example; The characters are yelling at each other, but they have a neutral face.

Great game even thoug I had a very rocky start. For the bad part first, this game would constantly crash on me every 5-90 minutes, I had changed from ultra to lowest possible graphics settings to no avail. After the latest patch I thought the developers would fix this problem. Well still constant crashes. So I decided to go another route, and look a bit more at my hardware. I installed a utility that came with my graphics card, and lowered the clock speed down and limited the temperature, LOW AND BEHOLD success!!, So I looked further and noticed the graphics card was getting a bit high, not really out of the norm for cards nowadays though. A little further testing and I ended up changing the speed of my GPU fan to aggressive. This game is now rock solid on ULTRA setting and getting over 30fps. . This game really bothers me, and it's a bit difficult for me to explain exactly why. Still, if I had to explain (and I kind of do, otherwise this isn't much of a review) then I would put it like this:
Like most people, I originally loved this game. The exploration-based platforming and combat were fun and simple. More, the "inheritance" system - wherein each time you die you take over one of your character's children with a new class, special attack, and collection of traits - was something completely new, which I had never seen any game attempt before.
But of course, you do eventually realize the game's problems. For me, this realization came near the end of my first day with the game I looked over and realized I was level 60 already... and I was barely into the game. I hadn't even beaten the first boss. I wasn't even close to ready to beat the first boss.
This is because you advance SO slowly in this game. At that point, and heck still where I am now a really good run through the dungeon might net me a rune I'll never use and enough gold to get +1 attack power.
But that's not what bothers me.
Then I realized, this game is basically built to reward luck over skill. Everything about this game is luck; the luck to get a nicer build for the procedurally generated castle, the luck to get better rewards in the chests and from enemies. Even combat rewards luck over skill, as the one truly skill-based class (the Hokage) is quickly overshadowed by the others and you're forced to rely on things that are by definition unreliable to win: things like critical hits, MP-using magic attacks, and tanking with high HP.
But that's not what bothers me.
I realized that the game is basically just a time sink. If you really look at it, there's really not a whole lot of content here. If you could go straight through on one try you'd have about four hours of content. It gets stretched out because you die constantly, you advance so slowly, and every time you re-enter the dungeon you've got to run through the same regions you've already been through again and again.
But that's not what bothers me.
No, what bothers me is the fact that this stuff DOESN'T bother me.
The game is just plain fun. The platforming works really well and, while it can be difficult, you always get the sense that you could totally do it if you were just a little bit better. Combat is simple and enjoyable, but also a fair challenge.
The presentation is great, as well. The enemies and environments are beautifully drawn, and the music is the perfect amount of atmospheric without becoming just dull and moody -
's music composers could stand to take a few lessons from these guys.
This is a game I can get into and just play again and again. It's just too bad that every time I load it up I feel like I'm giving in to something evil...

This is a good rogue like game that has an interesting progression system.
This progression system is really one of the key reason why I put so many hours into this game. Most rogue like games have perma death. Where if you lose thats it, its done you start from the beginning. Personally I did not like the idea of perma death in my games. I like to feel like I am working towards something and not losing everything just to try to do it again. With this said, many people who like rogue like games will disagree whole heartily with my decision and I understand that. Well with this game people get a little bit of both worlds.
This game has perma death and progression. Each character that goes into that death trap of a castle will eventually die but his or her's gold will be sent to their child where he or she can spend it on upgrades to their castle (that supplies skills, armory, stats etc) and to buy armor, accessories and even lock the previous dungeon so you can attempt it again. Then that child will die and send it's money to the next child and so on. So people get their perma death and progression all in one.
The gameplay is fun with platformer elements to it as well as rpg. Its a 2d side scroller where you go around in a randomly generated dungeon looting for gold, trying to survive and fighting bosses. Thanks to the option to lock the previous dungeon you can keep retrying the bosses again and again, without searching for the boss door. Which is nice because the bosses can be extremely hard if your not prepared. Also the dungeon itself is hard as well and you will find that it will take many attempts before finding the boss doors.
So overall, the progression system as well as the gameplay makes for an addicting game. With this said, their are a few issues I have with the game. When your character dies you get a selection of three (maybe four) randomly generated characters to choose from. All of these characters have different classes, special attacks and/or different qualities. Although the qualities like vertigo can really mess with you, most of the other qualities are forgettable after a while but it does add another element to the game at times. The random generated abilities on the other hand, were for the most part useless because most of the classes (except maybe mage and spell sword) had very little Mp to work with. I found that the normal attacks were sufficient in getting me through the dungeons.  It could have really helped if the characters had a bigger Mp pool to work with and maybe some different spells and abilities.
Overall, good game with a few issues with the characters abilities, still very fun to play and has a game plus mode so good replayability as well.

####################################################
################### Review ###########################
####################################################
#########################
# How to ruin gameplay in 3 steps #
#########################
1) Put no Vsync option
Never seen a game without Vsync option... Devs will never stop surprising me with the lack of basic common sense. I mean what the ♥♥♥♥, we're on PC, not on a goddamn console.
I can't notice tearing in this game, maybe because I got 200FPS+ and 144Hz monitor, or because it's forced ON... Anyways, some people might prefer Vsync ON, and others like me would prefer this off to lower the horrible lag caused by Vsync; which leads us to the next thing...
2) Provide horrible mice controls
- Mice movements are smoothed
- Mice latency is high (might be cause by the stupid smoothing)
- Mice has a dead zone!
- Mice acceleration is forced on (like on Apple computers, lol)
Impressive! I hadn't seen a that much of a poor mice response since Battlefiled 3 when it was just released.
I almost sh@t in my pants the first time I played the game. Didn't do two steps before I pressed escape and went trying to fix this bullcrap. But no... There is no "acceleration" or "smoothing" or "dead zone" option, at best, you can lower the sensitivity that is way too high by default, which doesn't solve these problems at all.
If you try to make very tiny movements with your mice, they are not registered; if you try to turn around, you make two turns.
It seems like they're trying to work with the mice as if it was a controller, but so badly that even with a controller it would be horrible as well.
(Note that I'm a competitive CSGO player and got 0 acceleration and near 0 input lag hardware, so I know how it's feels when it's responsive).
We are in 2017 for **** sake. Back in 90's, they already knew how to make flat, linear, with low input lag mice response. What the hell?! Wake up!!
3) Add horrible controller response on the view stick (to give you motion sickness)
After hating the mice responsiveness, you might, like me, want to try with an Xbox controller, because "Hopefully it will feel better with a controller". Lol, nope! Smoothing is so high, and latency is so high, that it's still horrible to control the view with a controller. I almost felt sick, both because I was disgusted by such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, and because of the near motion sickness that resulted from such a distorded response...
At least, developers fixed the Xbox controllers issues for most people (I gladly didn't have this issue with a wired Xbox 360 controller).
4) Oh, and one more thing...
I'd like to be able to skip this damn intro. It's funny once, twice, not 50 times after trying to restart the game in order to fix stupid issues with the game's responsiveness.
###########
# Conclusion  #
###########
Gameplay is so bad that it ruins gaming experience on a game with an amazing story.
Developers, what are you thinking? Remove your fingers from your arses, wash them, then go back to code!

I think this is a great follow-up to the first game. There's a few different elements that weren't present in the first game, but that's also what makes it interesting.
Pros
- In this game you play as Chloe.
It's nice being able to see the story from Chloe's point of view, as you didn't get that much info about her in the first game. You also learn a lot about her past, and her relationship with the mysterious Rachel.
- Grafitti (Compensation for photography).
I like that they kept this in some shape. In the first game, sometimes you'd have the option to take pictures of random scenery, which would result in an achievement. You still have that in this game, but as Chloe isn't into photography, she does grafitti instead.
Cons
- Chloe got a new voice actor.
I personally have no problem with the change, I didn't actually notice that big of a difference while playing the game. This might bug some people though.
- No going back in time.
In the first game Max had the ability to go back in time. This isn't an option anymore, so if you regret any choices you make, you'll have to go back to an old save. It's not a big problem, but it gets kinda annoying when you're used to that option, or if you want to see a different outcome.
- Emotionless characters.
It took me a while to actually get bothered by this, but sometimes when the characters have a certain emotion, it wont show on their face. For example; The characters are yelling at each other, but they have a neutral face.

I've been playing Rogue Legacy off and on for several weeks, now.  My estimation has gone up considerably since I first started playing.
Cons:
The game was frustratingly slow to get started.  As a level 1 weakling character, it was difficult to get enough coinage put together to buy upgrades or equipment.  Perma-death is tough in any game but made tougher by the fact your children are selected randomly from the available classes (no customization).  Having Death steal all of your gold before you can go back into the castle meant there's no way to build on past successes:  spend it all before you go in or it's lost.  Enemies are tough, traps are surprising, death inevitable.  You will die CONSTANTLY.  Don't get attached to any particular incarnation!  Oh, and Curse of the Hedgehog sucks big time.
Pros:
You get a different castle every time you play.  If you find one you just have to play again, you can sacrifice 40% of your gold-earning potential to keep it.  The combination of traits, skills, equipment, and runes means you can tailor just about any character to your play style.  Defeating the first boss resulted in a personal fist-bump moment, as it meant I could actually SURVIVE for some non-zero amount of time.  The game is highly addictive: it was nearly impossible to put down once I started earning an average of $10k coins per run.

Expecting a standard military TPS with some hamfisted morality message, I was instead treated to one of the greatest psychedelic war stories in recent memory.  The most I can say without spoiling anything is that Spec Ops: The Line calls to mind the 2nd half of Full Metal Jacket, Apocalypse Now, or the burning oil refinery scene in Jarhead.  It is a very well thought-out and self-aware commentary on the insanity of combat, culminating in an immensely satisfying and mindscrewing gauntlet.
Mechanically the game is solid, although snapping in and out of cover is occasionally more awkward than it should be.  Ammunition is scarce even on the default difficulty, and nearly every encounter is designed in such a way that the tools for victory are always available if you have the right strategy.  I never felt like I was dying for any reason other than my own lack of skill.  Checkpoints are infrequent, so the sense of tension and reward when you clear a particularly difficult segment is tangible.  Compared to most other recent shooters this was a huge breath of fresh air.  Spec Ops respects your intelligence enough to assume you can figure out a way to shoot everybody in the room if you just put some thought into it.
I bought and played this game on a whim (and because of a particular scene which you may have seen on Youtube involving incendiary weaponry).  If you've seen the same scene and felt the game was ruined/spoiled as a result, I assure you it's not.  That particular incident garnered a lot of publicity but only occurs about halfway into the game, with much more potent and interesting twists ahead of it.

For as many good things can be said about Call of the Wild, something seems to have gone awfully wrong throughout development for it to have this sort of inexcusable disregard for basic functionality. Keep in mind that this is a game that features fairly complex stealth systems, somewhat complex animal AI, and so on, yet needs months worth of patches to get an "Exit to menu" button, which still hasn't been implemented,
-in which debug menus show up for a split second when clicking on at least one of the buttons in the main menu,
-in which animal call markers sometimes appear and sometimes not for no apparent reason,
-in which there are no search filters, password protection or direct connecting in the server browser,
-in which most menus are a pain to navigate due to poor design choices,
-in which one ammunition stack always weighs the same regardless of its size,
-in which there are red dot sights for shotguns mentioned in one of the skill menus despite the fact that there are no available red dot sights for shotguns and other discrepancies in the information provided to the player,
-in which you can't buy more than 1 unit of ammunition at a time,
-in which you can buy a seemingly infinite supply of the one ammo type that's free,
-in which you can't interact with any of the unlockable hunting towers or land marks in a game you didn't host,
-in which there at least weren't any animations for simultaneously walking and using animal calls the last time I checked
and yeah, I just discovered that unlike its predecessor your character info isn't tied into your account or anything, but into the singleplayer match you need to start the first time playing. And since there are two areas to choose from, you'd better host a multiplayer match if you want to play the other map because you otherwise need to wipe your only save slot, because why not? Keep in mind that it probably takes weeks or months of playing in order to unlock the later skills, perks, and equipment, so why does the save system work in such an awful way?
Somehow, this is a recurring problem with Expansive World's games. There's always some insanely basic stuff that doesn't work or works in some astonishingly awkward ways that defies long-established conventions for no reason whatsoever. Having fun with this is task which currently demands a very high level of patience and tolerance for severely lacking functionality and polish, and I really, really don't understand how this trend can continue to persist within the games of a developer I'd think was experienced enough to make a keybinding menu that wouldn't completely break the control scheme if tampered with. This was fixed in an earlier patch, but yes, it was something that happened too. Call of the Wild is not a bad game if measured purely by its intended design, but this sort of garbage persisting is inexcusable and by now i feel pretty bad about supporting it in the first place.

Dont know what to write, so I will write a recipie for pancakes.
ingredients
100g plain flour
2 eggs
300ml semi-skimmed milk
1 tbsp sunflower oil or vegetable, plus extra for frying
pinch salt
Method
Blending in the flour: Put the flour and a pinch of salt into a large mixing bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the middle, then pour in about 50ml milk and 1 tbsp oil. Start whisking from the centre, gradually drawing the flour into the eggs, milk and oil. Once all the flour is incorporated, beat until you have a smooth, thick paste. Add a little more milk if it is too stiff to beat.
Finishing the batter: Add a good splash of milk and whisk to loosen the thick batter. While still whisking, pour in a steady stream of the remaining milk. Continue pouring and whisking until you have a batter that is the consistency of slightly thick single cream. Traditionally, people would say to now leave the batter for 30 mins, to allow the starch in the flour to swell, but there’s no need.
Getting the right thickness: Heat the pan over a moderate heat, then wipe it with oiled kitchen paper. Ladle some batter into the pan, tilting the pan to move the mixture around for a thin and even layer. Quickly pour any excess batter into a jug, return the pan to the heat, then leave to cook, undisturbed, for about 30 secs. Pour the excess batter from the jug back into the mixing bowl. If the pan is the right temperature, the pancake should turn golden underneath after about 30 secs and will be ready to turn.
Flipping pancakes: Hold the pan handle, ease a fish slice under the pancake, then quickly lift and flip it over. Make sure the pancake is lying flat against base of the pan with no folds, then cook for another 30 secs before turning out onto a warm plate. Continue with the rest of the batter, serving them as you cook or stack onto a plate. You can freeze the pancakes for 1 month, wrapped in cling film or make them up to a day ahead.

TL:DR - Its the most beautiful game you will ever see. The screenshots barely do it justice. Gameplay is pretty good, just what you'd expect from a hunting game. Multiplayer is very fun and easy to get into.
-------------------------------------------
Hands down, without question, THE MOST jaw-droppingly gorgeous game I have ever played. Turn your graphics up, your sound up, headphones on and just close your eyes. Its amazing. I moved out from the shadow of a tree into the sunlight and I would swear to you, I felt my arm get warm. THAT'S what kind of immersion this game delivers.
You are going to walk around, ALOT. But once you come across the huts, you can resupply and fast travel between any you've unlocked. Hunting feels rewarding and frustrating at the same time. You need to move slowly, keeping an eye on your sound levels, but its only natural to want to "hurry up" and catch your prey. I found that after hearing an animal call out, it was easier to take up a good position, use my caller and wait for it to come to me.
Multiplayer is very easy to get into and the fact that its up to 8 player co-op is pretty awesome. You can team up or go your own seperate ways and hunt "alone." You can even issue challenges and compete against one another.
The mechanics themselves can be a big grindy. You need to make sure you try your best to take down your target with one hit so that it goes down quick and clean. You're pay for the kill will change depending on those parameters. It definitely takes awhile to unlock the weapons but everything is available ingame, no micro transactions.
Shooting feels pretty good. Once you kill your animal and track it down (if you dont kill it outright) you can actually see where the bullet entered, what body parts it hit etc etc.
Overall, I recommend it. Its absolutely gorgeous, 9/10

TheHunter Call Of The Wild is such a supurb game, although i dont have stacks of hours yet since i have not long had the game, it gets me hooked for hours on end!
what i really love is how incredibly amazing the world looks, from the different times of the day, sun position with god rays beaming through tree lines, golden hour at the end of the day as you slowly make your way across an open cornfield to the dense forests with heavy downpour... It all looks so incredble and then as you are making you way through the land you have all the ambient sounds that sound so crisp and real, i found myself many times just walking, taking in the scenery and listening to all the ambient sounds, the wind gusts, birds chirping in the trees, the crunch as you trudge through the different types of ground. i get so lost in the atmosphere and kind of just zone out on what im actually meant to be doing...... and then you hear a warning call and some footsteps from one of the many animals in the game and you instantly get your game face on, trying to move slowly and silently towards the direction of the sounds you are hearing while trying not to spook the animal into running away. Binoculars out trying to get a tag and some information about what you are about to shoot, you crouch down and get your rifle out, line up your shoot through your scope waiting for the animal to turn broadside for that perfect shot on the lungs/heart and you squeeze the trigger to hear one of the best gunshot sounds you will ever hear in a game, honestly! the crack roars across the landscape echoing into the distance while you watch to see if you dropped the animal on the spot or if it still has some fight left in it and begins running off and then you start to track it to its final resting place to claim your trophy.
I honestly have hardly come across any flaws in this game except for when an animal is trying to run they will sometimes get stuck in between two tree's running on the spot, while it gives you an easy trophy you somewhat have to feel bad for taking such a cheap shot. other then that this is an amazing game and definitely worth investing the money into the game, it will satisfy you greatly.

There is a great range of weapons and items to choose, from rifles, handguns, compound bows, shotguns and then you have your different types of ammunition to many types of animal callers and scent sprays to lure animals to you when sitting up in a tower or ground hide.
You also have standard binoculars which you can upgrade to a range finder and then a set of binos with a range finder built into them.
There is plenty of content to work towards and unlock so you are insure many hours of gameplay, plus all the skill and perk tree's to unlock and help you track animals that bit easier.

567 hours played, please Bohemia Interactive and other readers  hear me out.
The reason people hate this game is because it is too punishing for a game in Alpha.
Before the .47 patch, getting military gear and getting into gun fights was a simple task.  Simply spawn near Elektro or Cherno and loot them, wait for a server restart, reloot (loot used to respawn upon restarts) and then exit with a great kit onwards to Balota Airfield and beyond.

Guns are pretty much non-existant, infact loot is really scarce altogether - leading to people to abuse the game just to get some enjoyment out of it [see apple glitch].

After hours upon hours committed to running around from house to house, town to town and eventually getting some worthwhile gear being suddently being taken away from you because you walked down a staircase and died it's not a tough question for why people stop playing.
So, I propose the devs massively increase loot spawns, make military gear abundant.  Make deaths from glitches and hackers something that can be recovered from.  Bring back the deathmatches at Elektro and Cherno to have action in the game.  This is what 90 percent of players want, please do it.
Bohemia Interactive, you have a choice continue on your crusade to make the game some running farming sim with a dwindling playerbase OR you can revert it back to what it was and see the numbers increase.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Holy crap. I didn't think it possible for there to be a game whose story made me feel these strong of emotions, yet here's Spec Ops: The Line. Corniness aside, this game's story really is absolutley fantastic. It begins like any other military shooter, seeming cliched and even a little unlikeable character-wise, but that soon fades quickly with the situations the characters find themselves in. What makes this game's story and themes so effective, is that in most shooters, war and killing are portrayed as being glorious and even fun. In this game, however, war and killing are portrayed being much more gritty and unpleasant. Many parts of this game made me full of disgust, terror, and some particular scenes made me feel physically sick. It questions why we so often use war as a form of entertainment, when in reality, it causes much suffering and pain. In several points throughout the game, you are given a moral dilemma, and are asked to make a choice. None of them are simple, and none of them are easy. It really makes you question your own morality in what is right and what is wrong, especially in a warzone.
The major problem with the game though, is the gameplay. It's just simply not very interesting or engaging. You do get to command around the two soldiers that tag along beside you throughout the game, but you don't have many options for them. You're pretty much only confined to telling them which one enemy you want them to kill. Usually, though, just taking the enemy out yourself is a lot easier and faster. The tactical element feels rather barebones, really. Also, at times the enemy AI just didn't seem that great. They sometimes stood right out into the open ready to be shot, or charged straight into oncoming fire. The gameplay isn't totally awful though, the actual shooting is satisfying, and there are variations on any given enemy's tactics based on what weapon they have, which is more than a lot of other shooters can say. Story-wise, there is not a lot that The Line gets wrong, only that it's not very subtle in it's message and theme, but that can be forgiven for how good it is presented.
Some people have pointed out, however, that you're not supposed to totally enjoy the combat, that killing other people isn't supposed to be fun or enjoyable. Whether you may think that was intentional or not, this game is still great for it's accomplishments in its story and themes. Those alone kept me hooked and those alone are far more than enough for my reccomendation.

Spec Ops: The Line surprised me. I got the game in one of steams many sale bundles, and put off playing it for a long time, as it sounded like a stupid Call of Duty rip off. I have to say, it does have a pretty silly name. However, after playing through the game I can say my opinion has changed.
Spec Ops has a very cool story. It is incredibly emotional and one of the few games to bring me to the edge of tears. Not only does it have an interesting story, it also has (while a bit repetivtive) some pretty solid third person cover based shooter gameplay. There is nothing very innovative about it, bt it is definitely a good way to spend 8 hours.

One of the best storylines of any shooter I've ever played - this has some very controversial and emotional moments. There were quite a few cutscenes, but they were definitely worth it.
Gameplay is pretty typical for a third-person shooter. You'll probably be slipping in and out of cover a lot. The weapons weren't anything too special, either, though I seemed to have more fun using grenades in this game than in others. It is possible to use the environment (bury enemies in sand, shoot out glass floors, etc.) to your benefit, however, and that made combat a little more unique.
There are AI companions throughout the game, and there's a "revive companion" feature that's pretty typical.
The game is very short, though, and doesn't have that much replay value. I'd say pick it up when it's on sale, or in the Desert To Sea bundle (Bioshock 1, Bioshock 2, and Spec Ops) which shows up pretty frequently on Amazon.

The graphics are spectacular; everytime I start up the game, I find myself continually in awe at the pretiness of the environments and beautiful graphical detail. Even better, this is an amazingly optimized game, so maintaining high-end settings won't be a problem for most people. The sounds, from the roar of car engines, the fiery explosions, and even the small echoes in the wind are appropriately mixed and sound excellent. The music however is not all that great and ends up being very forgettable, which is a shame given the epic score Junkie XL recently made for Fury Road. All these elements work together to create a world that really feels like a good blend between the feel of George Miller's original Mad Max films and the visual asthetics of Fury Road.
You are Max. Your world is fire and blood. Chances are if you've seen a Mad Max film, you know exactly what kind of post apocalyptic wasteland world Max lives in. But if you haven't, the game provides an intriguing look into the Mad Max world that's friendly to newcomers of the series. Lord Scrotus, son of Immortan Joe (the villain from Fury Road) has stolen Max's Interceptor, so now Max is on a quest to get it back. In doing so, he'll team up with the love child of Gollum and the Hutchback of Notre Dame, Chumbucket, a lowly mechanic who will help Max build the ultimate car,
.
The story, in spite of introducing characters and plot points that try to imitate the madness one would come to expect from a Mad Max story, just ends up being mostly forgettable. The story's greatest strength however is the fact that it is weak; it allows you to enjoy a much greater wasteland adventure outside the main quest line, and at no point attempts to pull you away from the fun you'll have exploring the world. So while it may be far from remarkable, the story in Mad Max is certainly passable, and does feels like the type of tale you'd expect to see in the films.
As simple as a desert wasteland open world may sound, it's actually treated with incredible care and attention to detail. Driving through the abandoned leftovers of civillization and exploring landmarks such as highways or submerged airports provide a unique-feeling open world that's never boring to explore. Unfortunately, its paired with a mixed bag of side acitivies that may provide for several hours of gameplay, but quickly boil down to an Ubisoft-style arrangement of side-content. Some activities are very fun and usually worthwhile, but begin to feel repetitive after some time playing. The thing that keeps you coming back to do more of these activities is the sheer fun of exploring the beautiful and dangerous open world.
The gameplay formula in Mad Max is probably best comparable to Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag in the sense that roughly half the game is spent on land while another is in boat/car. Your car is fully customizable and upgradeable-- engine, suspension, armor, exaust, etc. are ALL elements that can be upgraded. Not all of the upgrades progress linerally (ie some upgrades raise certain stats while lowering others), forcing you to create a car that best fits your needs. Max also has a variety of upgrades to improve health and damage, but they're no where near as useful or as necessary.
The driving is a big sluggish at first, but only takes a few hours of playing to master. Car combat is amazingly fun and the most well-done element of Mad Max. Every car combat encounter can be tackled with clever use of your harpoon, shotgun, thunderspoon, or just straight-up charged ramming into other vehicles. Factor in the wide variety of enemy types and levels, and you have a fairly deep car combat system. The harpoon and thunderspoon also double as a useful tool for destorying environmental obstacles or clearing pathways. Ultimately, this game really sets the bar for car combat/encounters in video games (*cough* Arkham Knight *cough).
The on-ground gameplay is not so stellar. Mad Max is yet another game that borrows its combat system from the Arkham games, though admittedly this is one of the better takes on it. Max is a dirty fighter and the combat emulates that pretty well, but it eventually becomes repetitive and a bit clunky due to an awkward camera that actually makes combat harder than it should be. There's also a fair bit of boss battles throughout, but most of them end up not being fun or all that challenging due to the combat's simplicity. On-ground combat may occupy a good bit of the game, but it's not enough to stop you from pushing on.
Max Max is a fun and action packed adventure that provides a faithful representation of George Miller's Mad Max world. The story, though weak and somewhat forgettable, sets up a grander adventure outside the main plot you're bound to enjoy. As beautiful and unqiuely designed as the open world may seem, it's paired with a lackluster variety of side content that's fun, but somewhat tedious. The car, including its combat and upgrades, is a huge truimph and the best element of Mad Max. On-ground however, Max's gameplay falls a bit short due to clunky combat. In the end, while Mad Max may be somewhat repetitive and uneven in its design, it has several moments of greatness and kept me coming back again and again to play more.

So another positive review, not played a PC hunting game in years, as I really hadn't seen anything particularly interesting on the scene. Then along game theHunter, looked amazing, but I was put off by Microtransactions, so when I saw theHunter: Call of the Wild, with no microtransactions I gave it a shot (pun intended).
A number of reviews have called the game buggy, but aside a minor quirk with the waypoint system, I've seen no bugs of any kind, and the game has run solidly and consistently for hours on my first load up, visually it is the most beautiful game world I've ever seen, the day/night cycle, and the quality of the lighting is truly a new standard in PC visuals for me, think "Vanishing Of Ethan Carter", turned up to eleven. Its absolutely stunning, day or night, rain or shine.
Weapon feel is fantastic, the range is more than sufficient, and the tracking and post-kill analysis is beautifully handled.
Audio, rather like the graphics, is absolutely first rate, beautiful ambient sounds, superb audio positioning makes it easy and accurate to place animal direction, and the foliage sounds and crunch and crackle under your feet are superb.
Really amazing job guys, such a beautiful environment. But, be aware any newcomers to this genre, it is NOT a fast paced game, it takes patience, it takes planning and it takes thought. If you want something to burn up your time, in a beautiful place, with fantastic environmental and weapon details of all kinds. Give this a shot! ;)

Spec Ops: The Line surprised me. I got the game in one of steams many sale bundles, and put off playing it for a long time, as it sounded like a stupid Call of Duty rip off. I have to say, it does have a pretty silly name. However, after playing through the game I can say my opinion has changed.
Spec Ops has a very cool story. It is incredibly emotional and one of the few games to bring me to the edge of tears. Not only does it have an interesting story, it also has (while a bit repetivtive) some pretty solid third person cover based shooter gameplay. There is nothing very innovative about it, bt it is definitely a good way to spend 8 hours.

One of the best storylines of any shooter I've ever played - this has some very controversial and emotional moments. There were quite a few cutscenes, but they were definitely worth it.
Gameplay is pretty typical for a third-person shooter. You'll probably be slipping in and out of cover a lot. The weapons weren't anything too special, either, though I seemed to have more fun using grenades in this game than in others. It is possible to use the environment (bury enemies in sand, shoot out glass floors, etc.) to your benefit, however, and that made combat a little more unique.
There are AI companions throughout the game, and there's a "revive companion" feature that's pretty typical.
The game is very short, though, and doesn't have that much replay value. I'd say pick it up when it's on sale, or in the Desert To Sea bundle (Bioshock 1, Bioshock 2, and Spec Ops) which shows up pretty frequently on Amazon.

Spec Ops: The Line is a very underrated game, maybe thats a good thing, since it surprises you in many ways.

This game has abysmal level design where you frequently die the first time in an area because you didn't know where the army of bad guys was going to spawn, so you need to load the checkpoint and be on the correct side of all the cover so you don't get perforated instantly.
Also the game tries to put you on a guilt trip for your actions without, unlike e.g. bioshock, crafting any illusion of choice whatsoever, so it just comes across as annoying, like the way a 2nd-grader thinks that an intentional-miscommunication trick question is funny.
Also there's a huge dramatic point where something awful and disturbing is supposed to happen; I managed to sidestep the thing that would cause it to happen completely without even knowing about it or trying to, which was possible because of a design/programming oversight; the awful thing spontaneously happened without me being involved, and there was no logical reason for it to happen. The whole dramatic turn of the game came off more hilariously stupid than disturbing.
The game also frequently reminds you about how you're bad for playing the game, as if it would rather  you stopped. There's no payoff at the end either; it just kind of peters out. Ultimately the game can't seem to decide what it's trying to say. The biggest message I got out of it was, "the armed forces should always follow the procedures and protocols established by superiors," which seems completely contrary to the edgy, anti-war themes laid over the whole thing.
Basically the whole thing is really slap-dash, and you can beat the entire thing in 7 hours or so (8 if you want to see all the endings). If you're aching for some cover-based shooting and there's a BIG discount on it, then this thing has decent weapon mechanics and a good soundtrack, but in general don't bother. If you do get it, then be absolutely sure NEVER to secure or search any new area upon entering it if the NPCs stop to talk. Wait next to the friendly NPCs or the scripted battle is liable to start when you're on the opposite side of the enclosure, and half a dozen enemies will jump on all sides of you at point blank.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of those games that everyone should play. The cover-based combat is smooth and better than any other cover system I have ever seen in the game. But the combat isn't what's good about this game. Technically, the combat is what's bad about this game and what's bad, is what makes it so good. I won't go into too much detail, but the choices in this game, they are hard. No the sort of, "Do I want bacon or ham on my sandwich?" kind of hard, the, "Do I use this weapon to clear my path through the enemies even though I know what this stuff does and I know that it kills you by eating away at your skin and there may be hundreds of innocent civilians nearby caught in the cross fire?" kind of hard.
This game is morally taxing. It questions everything you believe in, it questions everything you've learnt in other games. There is no easy way in Spec Ops. It's either bad or worse, but you don't know which is which until it's too late. This game will break you and leaving yourself just sitting there, staring blankly at the screen, crying and yelling at yourself, "Why did it have to happen like this?!".
Spec Ops: The Line. Is it a brilliant game? Absolutely. Is it one of my favourite games? Without a doubt. Is it a fun game? No way in hell.

Having played through the first episode (And more recently, the second), I now feel a more thorough review is in order.
(Note, this review is for Episode 1 of a 3 part game. When you purchase the game, keep in mind it is episodic in nature and they are not all available at launch. You can see the expected release dates on Wikipedia if you do a search for the game, though at the time of this writing episode 3 have not been announced)
This game is basically a love letter to the Life is Strange universe; it is clear that it was written by fans of the series. If you have not played the original Life is Strange game, do yourself a favor and pick that one up first. While BtS is totally coherent even if you have not played the original, you will be missing crucial context that is very important in a game focused on story and characters.
All that being said, this is an excellent start and I'm very much looking forward to the remaining episodes. Chloe and Rachel's relationship feels very organic, if a tad fast-paced at times (one could make an argument that when you consider how desperate each of them is for meaningful companionship, the fast pace makes complete sense. This is sometimes hard to understand if you have never been in similar situations as our two main characters, but I'd be willing to bet that anyone who has been in high school has seen these sorts of relationships played out on a regular basis).
As with the previous Life is Strange game, there are dozens of little tidbits in each scene that make the world a joy to explore. The inhabits of Arcadia Bay are interesting to interact with, especially when Chloe's sass is on full display (the "Backtalk" gameplay feature focused on picking the best responses for Chloe to argue with anyone and everyone is a fun feature, and what it lacks in the gravitas of Max's time-bending power, it more than makes up for in fun interactions.)
In short, if you are a fan of the original Life is Strange, you will find plenty to be happy about here. If you are not a fan, you might still be pleasantly surprised, but you will get a lot more out of it if you play the original game first.
Regarding the Deluxe version's particular features:: The extra outfit choices are great, as is the mixtape mode. However, if you plan on purchasing this version for the bonus episode (featuring both Chloe and Max, the main character of the original game) keep in mind that the bonus episode has also not been released as of the time of this writing. So don't expect too much right now, but based on the writing for this episode I believe it will be worth having for the future.

For a game of its scale, Undertale is a weird and endearing joy. It draws heavily from Earthbound, which shows at every turn with its offbeat humor and memorable characters. The main mechanical draw here is the nonviolent combat option, which allows you to defeat enemies with kindness rather than violence. This turns Undertale from a typical RPG about killing every enemy in sight to a sweet story about compassion and finding a way to live in harmony with your perceived enemies. To that end, it's a special little indie title that actually uses its mechanics to push its message.
However, I say "for a game of its scale" because Undertale kind of feels like a prototype for a more fleshed out experience. The nonviolent options are fun, but limited with each fight having one set of commands which can lead to victory. Everything here happens on a micro-scale, which works considering how short of a game it is, but definitely can leave you wanting more. If you're coming in expecting a full RPG experience, that's not really what you get here. It's more of an Earthbound-lite gameplay-wise.
But again, the focus is really on thematic elements here, so if storytelling is more what appeals to you in games, the mechanical shortcomings likely won't cloud its touching narrative.

Prison Architect is a very unique and addicting development game that takes both skill and time to complete. You start off with a plot of land to construct on and have the ability to either fall into the hands of bankruptcy, riots, and/or failure to control inmates; or evolve your prison into a sprawling supermax; it’s all about how you play it. This game takes hours and hours to play and I promise that you will not be getting bored anytime soon. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys development, strategic, and/or simulation genre games. The tutorial beautifully explains how the game works and how to begin, giving the player a head-start into the world of being a Prison Architect. Overall I very much enjoy this game and have spent countless hours messing around with it; I also enjoy playing with mods made by the games huge community, downloaded from the Steam Workshop, I recommend using them aswell, in order to customize your experience.
My Rating for Prison Architect is (10 / 10).

Every once in awhile, what I call a crime is committed in this industry, a game will be released and end up being one of the greatest games I've ever played. However for one reason or another, it ends up doing horribly. Spec Ops: The Line may be the biggest crime I've ever witnessed...
Spec Ops puts you in the shoes of Captain Walker, you and two squad mates are sent into a sandstorm destroyed Dubai to find survivors. At first glance the game may appear to be another Call Of Duty type of modern shooter. Disaster occurs and America comes in to save the day, but that is definitely not the case.
The first thing I noticed about this game is how beautiful it is, some may disagree, but Spec Ops on PC with max settings truly looks next gen to me, and this game was released a good while before next gen was a thing. The animation complements this point, for example since Dubai is a city destroyed by uncontrollable sandstorms, you will be traveling through a lot of buildings that are now buried deep below the sand. The moment when I first shot out a giant window I gleefully watched as the sand poured in and buried alive an entire squad of soldiers.
Everything that should be good in a 3rd person shooter gameplay wise is present in this game, but I do not want to waste any time so I'll just tell you about the one thing in Spec Ops that will make you love it, the story. This is hands down the greatest story I have ever had the pleasure of playing in a "Modern War" shooter. Within the first couple levels, Spec Ops shows you that unlike what other games will tell you, war nowadays isn't as clear as "America=good guys, Foreigners=bad guys". Without spoiling too much you quickly see other American soldiers killing innocent families. What choice do you have? Will you just stand by and let mothers and children get burned alive? No of course not, you are going to take action and start killing your fellow soldiers. While going through the campaign I couldn't believe the light Yager was casting on the American military...and I loved it. Just because you wear a uniform doesn't mean you are a good, or sane, person. Your squad has to witness the entire breakdown of a city, piles of bodies litter the streets, peoples are dying of everything you could imagine, soldiers killing the innocent for sport, but Walker keeps pressing on, because he believes he is doing the right thing.
The voice acting is also great and it isn't just because Nolan North plays the main character, it is because not only do you see, but you also hear the changes these characters are going through due to what they are forced to live through. Once again I do not want to spoil anything, but Walker starts off as a by the book, top tier soldier, and North does an incredible job showing just how much war can change a man.
Spec Ops: The Line is an incredible game that will blow you away. The graphics are beautiful though the images you will see are gut-wrenching. The voice acting is fantastic though what these characters go through is horrible. The story is perfect, you will feel like you have walked through hell with these soldiers. If you are not interested in the "Modern War" genre because of it's glorification and unrealistic approach on war, play this game. If you do like the "Modern War" genre because it is fun, action packed, and brutally violent, play this game. If you haven't figured it out yet what I'm trying to say is Spec Ops is a game you should play, easily an unforgettable experience. Play this game and lets give Yager the praise and recognition they deserve.

And I’ve enjoyed how the challenge of learning, leveling, and overcoming foes rewards my thrill-seeking self. But I don’t think it encourages me to think of what I might want to pass on to my kids. This wouldn’t be a problem if the premise was all about looting for my own satisfaction. But with a theme of pursuit of gain for the sake of others, it’s a shame that the feedback loop actually keeps me squarely centered on gaining things for myself.

Rogue Legacy is a game that I had a lot of trouble putting down. It's one of the few games I purposely got 100% of the achievements on because it was fun all the way through. It has everything a good old fashioned gamer will enjoy. Randomized maps, progressive leveling and difficulty, a choose-your-own-path to awesomeness, difficult platforming and puzzles, as well as fun boss fights.
This game is truly unique. The character you start with dies. You then choose from one of 3 heirs/decendants. Depending on what you often pick, the following heirs will have similar traits. The traits are important for many reasons that I won't go into - but Rogue Legacy is definitely worth your time.
There's pretty mimimal story-line but what story you do discover is rather well done. You'll find little tables with a book that progresses the 'lore' and I found myself always wanting to find the next one.
There are runes and equipment to unlock and choose from. You can be a life-stealing, life-to-mana converting caster if you want. You can be a brute force vampire. Maybe have extremely high defenses. Or maybe be a melee glass cannon. The best part is, all are viable and all may end up making certain bosses and combat easier. It's your job to find out how to adapt and evolve your lineage.

Pros:
+ Fantastic Sandbox Gameplay with loads of freedom
+ Beautiful if bleak world to travel around
+ Great atmosphere - really captures the feel of Mad Max
+ Loads of great customization with meaningful choices
+ Top notch combat both in car and on foot (uses a modified version of the Arkham melee combat)
+ Loads of value for money - will take dozens of hours to complete everything
+ Travelling is fun thanks to rewarding car combat
Cons:
- Mad Max style dialoge gets old fast
- Strange story that never quite finds its footing
- Slow to get going - too much hand-holding in the first couple of hours
Overall I really love this game. It shares many of the great features of Shadow of Mordor, but also brings enough of its own ideas to be a worthwile addition. It took me a little while (perhaps a few hours) to find my momentum, largely due to the strange hand-holding the game foisters on you to start with. However, once I was free to head off into the Great White and start having my own adventures I soon fell in love with it.
If you enjoy sandbox style adventure games then this is a great purchase and will give you hours of fun. It's not a story game in the way that GTA or Assassin's Creed is, so do be aware of that. But take it on its own merits and it's a wonderful game that is unique enough to warrant a place in almost anyone's library.

I used to be a big fan of management games such as Theme Park/Hospital, Startopia, Capitalism, Transport Tycoon, RollercoasterTycoon and so on. Back to those days i really wanted 2 types of those: a school management and a prison management game. Introversion Software realized some kind of childhood dream here, just thank you for daring to cover this harsh topic!
Prison Architect is a 2D prisoner management game. You'll be asked to give each wave of prisoners a place to sleep, to eat, to wash and eventually to learn as well as ensuring the atmosphere is safe enough for them to go out of there in 1 piece. There is always something to do in Prison Architect due to the pressure of the constant wave of prisoners coming. This brings good dynamics to the game.
Each prisoner has its own personnality, a good warden will quickly split those petty thieves and those murderers into different level of security within your prison. Treat any of them bad, and they'll soon riot. Give them a place to receive education and visits from their families, soon your prison will be famous for putting criminals back on the right track.
Most of the time in Prison Architect, you're buidling. New rooms, electricity, water, fences, the content is big concerning the building part. The gameplay diversifies when it comes to drug enforcement, establish a security strategy, tunnel digging counter measures... I really like the way  it densifies the game. You also need to research to get new features and get extra cash from grants when you achieve certain goals.
It's deep and well done. Graphics are unique, check the video above and you'll immediately understand. No technical problems are restraining you from playing the game except for the biggest prisons, but it's no big deal..
At the moment of this review (10/2014) the game is still early access. The team is working hard and keeps communicating with the community. I didnt want to play the early access not to waste the experience but at the moment the content is so important that you can really have fun with the game.
I strongly recommend you to play Prison Architect!

When I saw this, I was hoping for a competent street basketball game with some paid character customizations and some kinda gross paid stat boosts. What I found instead was a poorly translated storefront with a terrible basketball game attached.
Best I can tell, you are forced to control your character with the keyboard rather than a gamepad, which seems an odd choice for a basketball game. The rules of the game (both in terms of the rules in the rulebook and the way basketball works) are implemented very simplisticly. For example, if you want to block a shot, You'll need to be sure you're in front of the shooting player. It's literally impossible to block a short from the side or from behind.
It feels like a board game implementation of basketball, and, as much as I like board games, the beauty of video games is that the game can juggle as many rules and variables as you can throw at it. Board games have to be simplified because people have to manage all those rules themselves. For a game as dynamic as basketball, this implementation doesn't create a very satisfying experience.
The UI is ridiculous. Every screen has dozens of buttons labeled mostly with cryptic icons. As a new player, you'll be given several reward items after logging in, but you'll have no idea what they are or why you would want them. In this way, the game is extremely hostile to new players.
If there is any fun to be had in this game, it's well hidden behind a smokescreen of odd design decisions and mechanisms designed to get you to give them money.
