But real talk, as someone who loves the original, I am so pleased with this installment. Some people have expressed greivances with regards to Chloe's new VA, but to be honest, I didn't even notice the difference until I read about it. Honestly, I hear it as an ever-so-slightly less edgy Chloe. She's still figuring out how she fits in her world.
As far as game mechanics are concerned, everything remains pretty much the same. Now, instead of mousing around to issue Look or Speak (etc) commands, you simply press WASD accordingly. Minor change, but took about a half hour to get used to. I find that the scene layouts themselves are a lot more movement-friendly as well; the first game had a lot of thin corridors and uncomfortable rooms to walk around in, whereas here the environments are more open and non-invasive. Chloe also runs a tad faster. During dialogues, you might come to expect some verbally polarizing options... there are, just not verbally. Chloe is still rather savage and unpredictable regardless of your chosen dialogues, but I find that the results are far more rewarding than Max's predictable, introverted nature. It strikes a contrast to my own personal nature, which definitely increases the satisfaction for me in being able to somewhat experience it. Consequential choices have a much more defined impact on the story this time around. It's pretty clear to me what I've done to trigger what's currently going on. Whether or not you prefer transparency or enigmatic tendencies is up to you. Lastly, the rewind mechanic is replaced by what's called "backtalking". It's a neat little dialogue puzzle in which you attempt to outwit your opponent into achieving your intended result - there's a little bar to indicate whether you're fumbling or succeeding. I enjoyed it a lot especially as someone who isn't great at coming up with comebacks on the fly, so it was kind of a cathartic thing to be able to absolutely wreck some bullies.
Most of the original's core interface is back as well, you have the journal (this time written in Chloe's rebellious hand toward Max, who will never read it), collectibles (except now they're graffiti instead of photographs) and the text messages from other characters. I HIGHLY recommend you go back and read all the old texts Chloe has exchanged prior to the game. It gives you a load of insight as to what time period this is taking place in (and really pay attention to those dates/times!).
Now, onto writing and story. I loved playing as Chloe. She's much more expressive, and her inner monologues are less cringeworthy and more amusing. Her relationships with other characters seem fairly realistic within the context of the story and not a lot is left up to assumption, as you're keenly aware of her social inclinations. She doesn't take♥♥♥♥♥♥from people, she hates David, she makes her opinions known, e.t.c. By far my favorite (and apparently many others') interaction is playing D&D on the school grounds. That's the most I'll say on the subject... but yet again, this story is chock-full of nerdy nods and inside jokes I couldn't get enough of. Now the caveat to it all in my opinion, is Rachel Amber herself. Naturally, she takes the supporting role of the story, so you know you're gonna see a lot of her. I didn't dislike her by any means but I felt as though the tremendous buildup to what she could have possibly been for Chloe from the first game was a bit of a let-down. She's as I'd expected her to be. What I did like a lot however was the multiple ways her character challenged Chloe and really puts you in the actual position of trying to make a friend, along with all of its trials and tribulations.
Lastly, I want to address the technical side of things. The graphics are pretty much the same as the first game, very stylized and blurred. A lot of people expected a grandiose overhaul but I'm actually glad it's the same... it wouldn't feel right in my opinion. Facial recognition is still somewhat spotty, but I definitely notice an improvement in the way mouths form words... the first game had people moving their lips aimlessly whilst sound came out whereas here, all the mannerisms are accurate. As far as they could manage, anyway. Body movement is similar, but I notice a lot less 'forced' movements to mimic reality; people don't hold out their hands and move them while they explain something. Here it feels a lot more natural. The audio this time around is cleaner too. Voices carry appropriately with the environment so you have echoes or muted tones where they should be. The soundtrack itself is fantastic too, although it doesn't come close to the original's. There's a bit of punk rock as you'd expect mingled between the country tracks.
Overall, to me, this was a worthy purchase. If you loved the first, you'll probably love this. You get all three episodes when you purchase either the base version or the deluxe version, and they don't intend to release episodes separately either. The pricetag however does come across as rather high at the moment, and unless you really have an itch to jump back into Arcadia Bay, you might want to hold off until it takes a slight dip or goes on sale. As always, these games aren't a question of 'value for money' or hours per dollar, it's an experience akin to seeing an expensive movie in theaters - so don't judge the game by the amount of hours played by reviewers, judge it by your desire to undergo that experience. The deluxe edition is something I would highly warn against buying (FOR NOW) unless you're absolutely enamored with the Life is Strange scene. I don't regret it myself, but honestly what you get for it right now prior to the release of the "Farewell" bonus chapter is highly minimal compared to the cost. You get the "mixtape mode" which essentially plays a looped scene of Chloe chilling on her bed listening to a playlist of in-game tracks that you can play in whatever order you choose. Cute, but nothing more. You also get some bonus outfits that Chloe has the option of switching to at will during the second scene in her room. By default you have a few choices already, and of the three you get, I only think one of them is notable as it's a nod to her Life is Strange getup. Something worth mentioning:
. If you're only interested in the deluxe version for the bonus episode, I'd urge you to buy it separately when it comes out since the bundle's 8% discount is negligible.
Final verdict: see first line.

A surprisingly deep game with lot of secrets and possibilities. The soundtrack is great and the pixel art is well done. And the gameplay is innovative, constantly forcing you to break the rules. And that is a great point of this game which keeps you entertained. It's like playing a final fantasy from the snes but where the commands are changing and the monsters keep interfering where they shouldn't. Also part of the game is to figure all the ways to finish the game, and by extend all the ways to win a fight. And that's one of the strong points of this game : replayability. The game has a predefined story but it has so many variations that you can replay the same game in different ways 4 or 5 times at least.
But the really best point of Undertale is definitely the story. It seems childish but, oh boy, it is deep and emotional. If I was to describe this game it would be like playing Shadow of Mordor but it was in a wasteland demolition derby starring Mad Max! The reason I say its like playing Shadow of Mordor is because both games were made by Warner Bros. games. You can see the similarities between the two mostly just by the type of game it is.
What I mean by that is both games have a map divided into regions that you can conquer, the combat in both games are VERY similar and fluid (What I liked most from Shadow of Mordor), and its an open world to explore with alot of enemies. But that is where the similarities end. Mad Max is a COMPLETELY different game far and beyond.
+The Map is VERY large in Mad Max and you can expect to finish the main questline in probably about 30+ hours of playing but it depends whether you clear regions out or do alot of side missions too
+Combat on the ground is similar to Shadow of Mordor except instead of a sword you have FISTS! But you do also have other things like melee weapons you can pick up, your shotgun, Shivs, and the use of the enviornment which can be quite "explosive"
+Car Combat is extremely exciting and challenging especially when you haven't gotten all the high-end upgrades for the Magnum Opus yet
+The Upgrades for both Max and especially the Magnum Opus are very satisfying and cool to put on
+The story was very enjoyable and trilling as you moved deeper into the wastes
+Very well optimized for PC
+/-The amount of lootable areas in the game was a bit overwhelming to me especially since alot of places are minor and have 1 or 2 boxes in them which made it so it almost isn't worth the time to go and get them. However, no place is same so if achievement hunting or exploring is your thing it's not bad
+/-I wasn't fond of the many death races you can do all over the map, compared to doing the story, side missions, or getting map control it never appealed to me. But it is an extra and its there. I know some people who would enjoy doing them
I would highly recommend this game and I would gladly pay the asking price for this game. No regrets. I bought both fallout 4 and Mad Max at the same time and I beat Mad Max before I got very far in Fallout 4 so theres that.

But real talk, as someone who loves the original, I am so pleased with this installment. Some people have expressed greivances with regards to Chloe's new VA, but to be honest, I didn't even notice the difference until I read about it. Honestly, I hear it as an ever-so-slightly less edgy Chloe. She's still figuring out how she fits in her world.
As far as game mechanics are concerned, everything remains pretty much the same. Now, instead of mousing around to issue Look or Speak (etc) commands, you simply press WASD accordingly. Minor change, but took about a half hour to get used to. I find that the scene layouts themselves are a lot more movement-friendly as well; the first game had a lot of thin corridors and uncomfortable rooms to walk around in, whereas here the environments are more open and non-invasive. Chloe also runs a tad faster. During dialogues, you might come to expect some verbally polarizing options... there are, just not verbally. Chloe is still rather savage and unpredictable regardless of your chosen dialogues, but I find that the results are far more rewarding than Max's predictable, introverted nature. It strikes a contrast to my own personal nature, which definitely increases the satisfaction for me in being able to somewhat experience it. Consequential choices have a much more defined impact on the story this time around. It's pretty clear to me what I've done to trigger what's currently going on. Whether or not you prefer transparency or enigmatic tendencies is up to you. Lastly, the rewind mechanic is replaced by what's called "backtalking". It's a neat little dialogue puzzle in which you attempt to outwit your opponent into achieving your intended result - there's a little bar to indicate whether you're fumbling or succeeding. I enjoyed it a lot especially as someone who isn't great at coming up with comebacks on the fly, so it was kind of a cathartic thing to be able to absolutely wreck some bullies.
Most of the original's core interface is back as well, you have the journal (this time written in Chloe's rebellious hand toward Max, who will never read it), collectibles (except now they're graffiti instead of photographs) and the text messages from other characters. I HIGHLY recommend you go back and read all the old texts Chloe has exchanged prior to the game. It gives you a load of insight as to what time period this is taking place in (and really pay attention to those dates/times!).
Now, onto writing and story. I loved playing as Chloe. She's much more expressive, and her inner monologues are less cringeworthy and more amusing. Her relationships with other characters seem fairly realistic within the context of the story and not a lot is left up to assumption, as you're keenly aware of her social inclinations. She doesn't take♥♥♥♥♥♥from people, she hates David, she makes her opinions known, e.t.c. By far my favorite (and apparently many others') interaction is playing D&D on the school grounds. That's the most I'll say on the subject... but yet again, this story is chock-full of nerdy nods and inside jokes I couldn't get enough of. Now the caveat to it all in my opinion, is Rachel Amber herself. Naturally, she takes the supporting role of the story, so you know you're gonna see a lot of her. I didn't dislike her by any means but I felt as though the tremendous buildup to what she could have possibly been for Chloe from the first game was a bit of a let-down. She's as I'd expected her to be. What I did like a lot however was the multiple ways her character challenged Chloe and really puts you in the actual position of trying to make a friend, along with all of its trials and tribulations.
Lastly, I want to address the technical side of things. The graphics are pretty much the same as the first game, very stylized and blurred. A lot of people expected a grandiose overhaul but I'm actually glad it's the same... it wouldn't feel right in my opinion. Facial recognition is still somewhat spotty, but I definitely notice an improvement in the way mouths form words... the first game had people moving their lips aimlessly whilst sound came out whereas here, all the mannerisms are accurate. As far as they could manage, anyway. Body movement is similar, but I notice a lot less 'forced' movements to mimic reality; people don't hold out their hands and move them while they explain something. Here it feels a lot more natural. The audio this time around is cleaner too. Voices carry appropriately with the environment so you have echoes or muted tones where they should be. The soundtrack itself is fantastic too, although it doesn't come close to the original's. There's a bit of punk rock as you'd expect mingled between the country tracks.
Overall, to me, this was a worthy purchase. If you loved the first, you'll probably love this. You get all three episodes when you purchase either the base version or the deluxe version, and they don't intend to release episodes separately either. The pricetag however does come across as rather high at the moment, and unless you really have an itch to jump back into Arcadia Bay, you might want to hold off until it takes a slight dip or goes on sale. As always, these games aren't a question of 'value for money' or hours per dollar, it's an experience akin to seeing an expensive movie in theaters - so don't judge the game by the amount of hours played by reviewers, judge it by your desire to undergo that experience. The deluxe edition is something I would highly warn against buying (FOR NOW) unless you're absolutely enamored with the Life is Strange scene. I don't regret it myself, but honestly what you get for it right now prior to the release of the "Farewell" bonus chapter is highly minimal compared to the cost. You get the "mixtape mode" which essentially plays a looped scene of Chloe chilling on her bed listening to a playlist of in-game tracks that you can play in whatever order you choose. Cute, but nothing more. You also get some bonus outfits that Chloe has the option of switching to at will during the second scene in her room. By default you have a few choices already, and of the three you get, I only think one of them is notable as it's a nod to her Life is Strange getup. Something worth mentioning:
. If you're only interested in the deluxe version for the bonus episode, I'd urge you to buy it separately when it comes out since the bundle's 8% discount is negligible.
Final verdict: see first line.

With that said it is also the reason why this game is so good. It evokes real emotion through you, the player. The game at points directly addresses the player and make them consider what they have done. Here's a great analysis of this:
.

I could go on and on about the way this game worked psychologically to get inside the players head but it really is something you have to experience and it is very subtle at times.
Gamplay wise it is nothing special just a generic 3rd person shooter and can be very tedious. But hey the game should feel like a chore. You are SUPPOSED to question whether to continue as it critiques those who do.

"Excuse me for asking but how did you survive?" - US Soldier

Highly recommend this game if you want to sit back, listen to music and while away the hours driving around Europe.

Mad Max:
It's like a rollercoaster, a specific type. You get in line, see how "awesome" it's going to be and get pumped up! As soon as the ride starts you begin to climb the first hill, and then WOOSH! Down you go screaming in a blaze of glory! Now you hear the click of the track as you begin another climb up a hill. You think "Okay, this is gonna be cooler!" and WOOSH! Down the same blaze of glory. Then another click and climb... 300 hills later you're thinking to yourself "This isn't bad but geez, I'm getting nausous from these hills."
That's Mad Max: The Video Game. A bunch of awesome hills that get old after 31 hours.
I will recommend this game. It's good. It does the "Open world" thing right. I do agree with the critics though. It's Open World: The open world game.  It's the same/similar thing over and over.    Take out this scarecrow, ram this car off the road, sabotage this outpost, race this race. Repeat. Plus they decided to go with the Arkham Rhythm Combat. Albet an unpolished version.
So it's just that. A game. Not trying to push the boundries of what it can do.  But hey, neither is Max... he just wants to be Max.

You quickly figure out all the patterns and attacks of the opponents.  For attacking there is punching, melee weapons, a limited shotgun and a knife used to more quickly kill opponents.
As for missions and story not that very well thought out.  You are going around taking over camps so your allies can occupy them, which they do instantly.  To take over a camp you go in and destroy all the oil and gas stored there.  Why am I doing that?  I am sure my allies and myself could use that gas.  I could see if there was an option and limited allies then going in destroying the reserves and the defenses of the camp would be an option I have to decide if I am want proceed with but here it makes no sense.

This is one of the better third-person shooters I've played in years. While the mechanics are your standard third-person shooters with cover, the story is where this game really shines. Try the demo, add a decent story, and that's what this game is.

Spec Ops: The Line is possibly the most riveting, most intriguing, most powerful shooter I have ever played. Whilst the gameplay mechanics are pretty traditional and bring little to the table, the story is fantastic. The Line is a linear game through and through but does a very good job of making the player feel responsible for the actions they carry out. Part of this is due to the illusions of choice that occasionally pop up through the game, allowing you to feel as though your decisions will make a difference. Multiple endings add a bit of spice to it as well. Without a doubt, Specs Ops: The Line is the best third-person shooter I've ever played that had me on the edge of my seat and constantly thinking about it when I wasn't playing it.

A nearly flawless third person shooter.
Let's get the story out of the way. You play as Captain Walker who, along with the other two guys, is sent to the destroyed city of Dubai in order to investigate a distress signal by the missing Colonel Konrad. Pretty soon you discover that the city is not empty and is filled with some civilians as well as the AWOL U.S. 33rd Army battalion which was supposed to evacuate the city after being deployed in Kabul. You then quickly proceed to battling and killing your country-men. Neat. I'm surprised this German developer didn't get any heat from critics yet for giving you the ability to kill U.S. army men. Along the way, you unravel the mystery as to what exactly is happening.
The scenery is quite breathtaking. The Unreal 3.0 engine makes character models and distant vistas look crisp. The desert is so well made that it reminded me of the Uncharted 3 desert. You also get to leave foot prints in the sand. There are no texture pop ins and every texture is pre-rendered. However, the amount of video options is limited. The engine provides no DX10,11 or anti-aliasing for that matter.
The game itself plays like a solid A/B action flick. There are some grand action set pieces, there is plenty of dialogue, there are opportunities to sneak up on enemy and there are some grave choices to be made and alter game in the process.
One of the most essential components of the game is the A.I. and boy is it good, both friendly and A.I. The enemy soldiers will communicate with each other, they will give out orders, they will attempt to flank you and sometimes attack you from both sides at the same time, they WILL run away and jump away from your grenades, they will retreat, raise alarms, call for back ups, they will also throw grenades pretty accurately and they will do suppressing fire as well. However, some handpicked A.I. will just stand there without taking cover, just waiting to be shot. The reason is that if they are standing on the glass or next to a mountain of sand behind glass, they can be killed with the force of the surrounding environment.
This game forces you to think when dealing with the enemy. They aren't supermen and they aren't pushovers either.
As for the friendly A.I., well just about the only way that you can order your teammates around is by telling them to attack this guy or that guy or flash bang them. However, once you do give the order, your team mates will do their best to take out the indicated guy either with regular rifles, sniper fire or grenades. At times, I saw my team mates stand their own ground pretty effectively. This feature is unparalleled with many shooters, wherein even IF you are a part of the team, you are the one getting shot at most and you are the one having to kill every foe. (COD ahem)
You also get to collect intel and figure out what happened to the populace and Dubai in general after the biggest sand storms decimated the city.
Something about the gameplay feels right, I can't quite put my finger on it. You can only carry two weapons and a handful of grenades. The ammo is always scarce so the game forces you to not waste ammo. I also like how any assault rifle magazine will be out of ammo after just a few bursts - it's all pretty realistic. There is no evasion button and there is no prone button. The constant sand storm atmosphere creates a hostile and extreme environment and the sound of sand storms is quite deafening. Also, what's awesome is that once your frag grenade explodes, it also creates a collateral sand fog which stuns the surviving enemies which can be plucked one by one.
As far as the weapons are concerned, well, every other weapon has a secondary feature. The M-16 or whatever has a silencer, so does the pistol, the AK-47 has a three bullet burst feature, the sniper rifle has a 8x, 16x zoom feature, etc.
The thing that quite often DOES mess up the gameplay is the sprinting, that's right. When you go forward press "space" for sprinting (default) and then let go of "space", Walker will just keep sprinting for an indefinite amount of time. And if you want to stop immediately, you have to press "S", to back up. So I decided to switch to the good old "shift" for sprinting instead. It sorta helped but the running still feels consolish, especially when you try to make sharp turns and attempt to take cover while being shot at. What sucks again though is that the crappy consolized controls made "shift" stand for both sprinting AND melee. It's like, seriously devs? You could not allocate a separate action key for melee for us, PC gamers? we do have a keyboard, you know.
Oh about that, when you are running toward cover and getting shot at, your character will automatically slide towards cover for about 2-3 meters, which is pretty neat because the game does not force you to press the cover button again. That's what they should have done in Operation Raccoon City instead of just adding automatic cover that doesn't work half the time.
I've also noticed that the devs put a lot of effort into level design which look as if they were taken from real locations. The flamboyant hotel rooms, the flashy lobbies, the elegant living quarters, the vanity statutes, the artifacts displaying wealth of the city now gone - all bring an engaging dystopian feeling. At times, there are also numerous ways of advancing and flanking your enemies.
The wobbly cross-hair is quite neat. The only time your aim is remotely steady is when you come out of cover, however if you sprint and then attempt to shoot, your aim will be all over the place. Thus, every other kill feels like a small accomplishment. If there only was no regenerative health. The good thing is that your team mates cannot revive you when you get shot up. However, you can pick them up and they can pick each other up.
I should also add that voice acting in the game is quite exceptional.
As for the multiplayer, well, it delivers on many levels. The crappy sprinting is still there, so it's best to not run at all. You get to customize your character as you progress. You get to choose 15 perks as you progress. These range between being invisible on the minimap while sprinting, increasing your protection against explosives, reducing the cross-hair wobble, increasing your weapon damage, increasing your mini-map (radar) range, etc. As for the weapons, there are 5 SMGs, 9 Assault rifles, 4 shotguns, 4 sniper rifles, 6 handguns, 2 machine guns and RPG. The levels are pretty balanced too. Some levels feature active destruction and temporary sand storms that reduce your speed, visibility and accuracy. Sometimes these storms cause collapse of nearby structures so you better stay clear.
However, if you are playing a 30 minute match and then all of a sudden "lose connection to server" all your progress is going to reset. Now this sucks big time because after playing for some time, I "lost connection to server" and reverted back to level 1. Now this is a certainly good feature to discourage rage quitters and quitters in generals but it sucks big time when you lose your experience points and perks.
All in all, this is a pretty solid M-rated (there is torture, mutilated bodes, up-close violence and executions) third person shooter with some new gameplay elements and addictive multiplayer that will keep your interested. Here are the minuses:
1. Limited video options.
2. No Co-Op campaign. (This could have easily been a 2-3 player co-op game).
3. Medium-length campaign. 15 medium-length chapters.
4. The pistol cross-hair sucks. And you can't turn it off.
5. No way to turn off indicators when in cover. (Indicators that tell you if you can swap cover; it's cluttering the screen)
6. Crappy consolish sprinting.
7. Limited destruction.
8. Bad grenade explosion animation.
9. Having to press "space" for springing, taking cover and reviving team mates.

This game is unfair!!!
Unlike other "hardcore games" Super Meat Boy, Spelunky, Dark Souls etc. this game is brutally punishing and unless you've played the game for hundreds and hundreds of hours, chances are it wasn't your fault. I like a game to punish me for mistakes, provided the game has taught me how to deal with certain situations (you know like good games do, they reveal mechanics and teach you how to effectively use said mechanic) this game does not teach you. You have to be dedicated enough from the get go to forgive the game for firing 30 projectiles at the the instant you enter a room. Most of the mechanics (in terms of movement and abilities) are pretty well thought out and interesting if not massively underpowered for the first 20 hours of the game atleast, which brings me to my main and biggest problem with this game.
In order to stand any chance whatsoever of making out of the first area alone you will have needed to play for many, many hours so you can gain enough gold to level your characters up. Which requires you to remember a list of ever changing gold requirements, spread across two screens. If you choose to not spend any gold on the first screen (the castle perk tree thing) and proceed to the second, spend gold and realize you could have gotten some upgrades from the previous screen too you cannot go back, only forward and you lose all gold in your possession at the end of the second screen. So many times I did well and felt accomplished it simply was for nothing.
I have been playing games for a long time and I don't think I've ever played a game riddled with so many terrible design choices yet I still find the game somewhat enjoyable. Sure most of the mechanics are pretty skill based and can be satisfying to master but this game has had me walk into too many random situations which are either way too easy or way beyond the expected difficulty curve. Most projectiles go through walls, some don't, good luck learning the difference before you rip your hair out. This game angers me, it's not like Spelunky! don't listen to people if they tell you otherwise, Spelunky is a gem, a masterpiece. This is a mess, an amatuers attempt at making something "highly-replayable" and the only reason to play it is if you have already got your fill of Spelunky, Super Meat Boy, Binding of Isaac or a skill based/roguelike of your choice.
The hours it says I have do not accurately reflect the time I have played this, I have also played it for atleast 10 hours on a friends account.

This game is difficult, but rarely challenging.  It is addictive, but rarely fun.  Many of their "challenges" are trivially easy if you have randomly picked the right class/spells/attributes for it, and literally impossible if you haven't.  Very often you will come across a chest that you could simply walk over to and open if the character you picked had Dwarfism, but you didn't, so you can't.  Challenging!  The game starts out feeling hard but rewarding, like Super Meat Boy, but after a while it just becomes a matter of farming until you're good enough to beat the bosses.  Two of their super-uber-boss fights actually require strategy and learning, but two others are entirely based on luck: the boss has a kills-you move and a you-can-hit-him move, and winning is just a matter of him choosing the you-can-hit-him move more often.
The game is filled with ametuer-feeling design descisions.  The classes are tremendously unbalanced, to the point where a spellsword with fire shield can easily clear the entire map on 2+ difficulty, while most other classes die in a few rooms.  A hokage is simply better than an assassin in every way.  One class's special ability is that they stop sucking after clearing half the map.  Gold is your experience, but they have a silly little curse that causes you to spew all your gold out when you get hit.  If they took eight seconds to sit down and think: "does this make our game more or less fun?" they would have never kept it.  But it's because Sonic the Hedgehog, get it!?  LOLZ!  In fact all of their attempts at humor are based on either pre-existing memes or potty noises.  There's nothing wrong with immature humor, but they forgot to include the "humor" part.
For such a small team, the game feels surprisingly corporate.  It's filled with in-game advertisements; yes, for other games by the same company, but advertisements still.  They definitely have the "minimum viable product" down: the game has surprisingly little content.  Their four (count 'em, four!) different tilesets get old quick, and it doesn't take that long before you've bought all the upgrades and have nothing interesting to do.  All in all, this game shows that Cellar Door has been going downhill since Don't Sh*t Your Pants.

I can't recommend this game highly enough.  It is definitely one of the best games I've played in recent years.
The jokes are genuinely hilarious and the game has a way of alluding to design quirks in games of the past that is funny while still being reverent to them, all while not coming across heavy-handed as a lot of indie games do when they try to do this sort of thing, and even often times has a sentimental tone in the midst of it all.  So it's not really about cynical, 4th wall breaking commentary.
The battle mechanics, with all the unique ways to end combat without fighting, keep random encounters interesting for the entire game. Never had to grind. Even if you're not into traditional RPG-type games, you will still have fun with this game because it doesn't really go down the route of repetitive menu fighting.
The story is a remarkable, fairy-tale type story though in a modern-ish setting, and all of the characters are likable and memorable, even the lesser NPCs. And of course the soundtrack is also really awesome (if you haven't heard), giving everything just the right mood.
There is also a tremendous amount of polish in this game.  Many characters are interconnected to each other, enemies behave differently depending on what other enemies they appear with, little effects punctuate things characters say or do, musical motifs recur in related places or for related characters, there are many ending variants and in-game results that occur based on things you do or don't do, the game remembers things from previous playthroughs, etc.
So in short, wonderful game.  If you haven't played it, definitely bump it up in your queue!

I got this game maybe a few months after its release in early access, and it was really interesting in the beginning. It had taken a mod thousands of people enjoyed and had the aspirations of turning that mod into its own, full game, with new features and better mechanics. I get really depressed thinking about it now. For a while this game offered me hours upon hours of entertainment, and was amazing. After playing it consistently for almost a year, the game began to become stale. there was a lack of updates, and the community began to die. The game just wasn't fun anymore, and everyones hopes for the game began to deteriorate when people realized that every attempt to better the game by the devs just made the game worse. Then, something I thought was a savior at the time, called update .60, was released. It made the game so much better for a decent period of time, by increasing performance, making loot a bit less scarce, and fixing many bugs. The game was fun again, and I was finally able to enjoy a game I had thought was ruined. Then, the inevitable happened. The devs once again stopped updating the game and there was nothing new. This game is nearly dead and still continuing to die. I have had hours upon hours of fun and entertainment on this game. I sadly have to give it a thumbs down however. This game is definitely not worth its current price because of how repetitive it becomes. Buy Arma 3 or Arma 2, for the zombie mods on both of those (especially dayz mod on arma 2) are way more polished and have more content than this game. I understand this is early access, but it's been too long and too strenuous of a ride for me to continue to support this community. I really do hope I get to see this game be released. Maybe once there's another major update I can review it once more, and maybe my hopes of playing the best DayZ experience will be revived. Sadly however, until then, I must say don't buy this game, it is currently a waste of your time and money.

You may have played sandbox action games (Assassin's Creed, GTA V, Shadow of Mordor etc) before and just assume Mad Max is the same formulaic drudgery. Well think again: This is the refined pinnacle of the genre.
The map is huge and littered with scanvenging POIs, camps and races and every single one feels and looks different. There is a vast variation in terrain considering it's all desert, and Avalance have surpassed themselves with the world-building on offer here and they seem utterly at home in the world of Mad Max. It's not often I feel compelled to leave no stone unturned in a game like this, but this is something special.
The driving and car combat is sublime, and the on-foot combat is bone-crunchingly brutal. I have a fairly modest PC and I could still run this in x1050 with 60fps on my 560ti, with no visible loss of quality.
I ecountered one minor bug in game. ONE. It's sad, but that's a rareity these days with AAA. The bug was something that was solved by a fast travel and all was right once more.
The story is not too surprising in climax for a Mad Max tale, and takes its cue mostly from Fury Road and its prequel comic, but with plenty of original content as well. Those used to the usual adventure tropes will be surprised, and those expecting a happily ever after will be disapppointed. Don't be. Enjoy the fact we've got a game here that takes its source material seriously, and manages to wrap it in a great sandox action game with plenty to do.

Where does one start with Spec Ops: The Line?
This is possibly the most controversial shooter in the past few years, not a game noted for jaw dropping graphics, stellar game play, but for the way the story is told.
The most successful thing a modern game can do is make you fall in love with the universe it creates and become enthused about the story. Spec Ops doesn't really sit here. What on the outside looks like a generic third person shooter, celebrating war seems more like a trap for your modern 15year old xbox live screaming Call Of Duty Player. But this game soon becomes something else. It soon gets you questioning "am I doing the right thing?" almost to the point were you do not really want to keep playing.
Though I do recommend playing this through. From a replable aspect this game has several endings which are taken from choice parts in this game, though these choices are not always obvious until you have made them and thought "could I have saved them?"
In terms of mechanics the game is solid. You will not find any revolutionary gameplay mechanics, but what is established is very solid. If the game mechanics were any more fidly or made you think about choices more then it would distract you from the point the developers are trying to make.
Now the story. This is were things get interesting, there are various theories across the board about what happens in this game and that is truely a wonderful thing. It is nice to see an action game were the story is what drives you, wanting to know what happens to your characters? Do they save Dubai? Do they go home? Do they put the villian to justice? This is what modern gaming needs to go back to. We have become so lost in how good a game looks and how close to reality it is that we  may have forgetten why we game.
Spec Ops: The Line will change how you see modern games, and maybe how you see yourself as a gamer.

(tldr: starting out is much too difficult in consideration of time and effort needed to put in with a community as toxic as it is. However, you can easily go onto a subreddit for rust that looks for starting groups to make your experience a lot more enjoyable)
It takes a good 30~ish minutes to farm enough for your own starting base, and half a second for it to be taken away from whoever you have the misfortune of seeing.
As a solo player, much too difficult to start off since making a codelock* is significantly more difficult to make since you cannot keep your base without a roof as anyone can now just build up** at any moment they feel like.
*Codelocks are an item that makes it so that you can open the door by a four digit pin number. The reason why this is important is that the other form of locking your door is a key. To get out with a door that needs a key, you need to bring the key outside when youre going to farm which can make anybody able to just waltz in your base as long as they:
1) Kill you and take your key, and finding your home (Then you're stuck inside and need to break your home (very loudly and resource heavy for starters) with no materials since its been raided.
2) Find your key if its hidden in a poor location. Even if in a good location, someone can sneak up on you, see you interacting with your hidden stash, and just wait for you to walk away, thus leaving you trapped inside your home with nothing effectively making your home useless)
**You used to be able to leave your roof open safely. But now, with the infamous "twig update", people can now build on your property using the weakest structures in the game, thus extremely limiting you in how you build. This made many things nearly useless, such as most forms of walls and obsticles. This makes it even more difficult as a solo starter since you need to sit down and dedicate handfuls of hours to build your home, which can be raided ten times easier than it was to make.
Since this game heavily relies on interactions with people and PVP, your experience relies on those you bump into and those around you. That means your average joe dictates how much fun or agony you go through to play. I personally believe this would be a good thing if there was roleplay involved, but there isn't a shred of such a thing here.
Those who intend to have fun interactions with others are significantly more likely to have almost all of their progress made useless in the blink of an eye, since there are FAR too many people who just sit on their roof and take pot shots at people to collect any shred of resource from them as possible.
The game is significantly easier and more lenient if youre working with friends. Having one or two friends can easily make times where it'd take 2ish hours to get a starting house to a meager 30 minutes since you have more people gathering resources and fighting.
With friends, you can easily turn the tides of a fight and have a much more enjoyable time overall. The only real byproduct of an issue is that clans and zergs (groups that consists of disgustingly high numbers, sometimes double digets) basically control the server. If you aren't on their good side or directly useful to them, consider keeping very, VERY far away unless you feel confident you can contest them.
I'd love to give rust a positive review, I honestly would. But after the twig update mentioned above, it sucked the charm out of rust for me. There's no more zany base designs as you can just build into them easily now. It's all just the same basic cookie cutter layouts with very little differentiation. You can't boost into bases to loot unsuspecting players. There's fairly overpowered yet easy to make turrets added in the twig update which make it so if someone accidentally leaves their door opened, you cant loot them without getting your health shredded and slowed down considerably.
So, the review stays negative mostly due to the twig update as its just nearly completely put me off from playing.

Where do I start? Well, let me start by saying that this game is great! Lots of fun and humor!
Pros:
1) Distinctive cell-shaded art style. Environments and characters are outstanding.
2) Gameplay is top-notch. Boss fights are intense and challenging.
3) RPG elements are very well done. I love that you can choose your own character with his/her own skill tree. You level up your character according to your play style and each character has his/her own special skill move.
4) Good script. Very funny and humorous.
5) Story elements and progression might not be the best but they are good enough. The hunt to uncover the secrets of The Vault will keep you pushing forth.
6) Multiplayer is an absolute blast. Playing with friends and family is non-stop fun.
7) Sound, music, and voice acting are well done.
Cons:
1) Too much loot. The array of guns, grenades, shields, and other items will clutter your inventory. The amount of guns and stats pushed down my throat was just too much, I'd rather have fewer guns and items to choose from, much less of a head-ache. Switching guns every two fights is not my idea of fun.
2) Quests can get repetitive and boring.
Conclusion:
FPS games were never my cup-of-tea, but Borderlands is a whole different story. Great game.

UPDATED REVIEW (07/07/15) :
------------------------------------------------------
About the games flaws;
This game includes 2 different game :)
a) before level 40, easy enjoyable, you can be Kobe, Lebron (you think so :)
b) after level 40 when you face the real players including very high skill guys, very good teams, very heavy pay to win guys. You will be shocked after playing against these guys, you will think they are cheating, you will be frustrated, may be you will quit playing the game. Now you are the ultimate rookie by getting to this point.
*  before level 40 this game may seem easy, but it is not. So after becoming level 40 and even being  a level 50, with good piece of equipment, you are so weak. (Put aside the P2W equipment, cards which some of the cards you can aquire with in game currency and events, but the best clothes are time limited, so you need to pay real cash to make them permanent.) The real problem YOU STILL HAVE NO IDEA about this game. Passing at the right time, finding the free teammate, when to fake, when to drive, when to shoot, All of them requires deep knowledge about the game play and big experience. Average player needs thousands of games to be a competetive "level 50", and for each different position you still need additional experience.
* You need a good team, or a good crew. And the friendship mechanics, crew mechanics are awful in this game. So basic like designed for handheld basic nintendo.
* You find a good guy, he knows about this game, so you be friends. But only with that position, you have no idea about his other chars. At some point you have 5 chars and you time to time play with each other like all the other guys who are into the game. So there SHOULD be a main CHAR NAME, so by only interaction with that char will be enough to communicate with players all other chars.
* The Crew Function ( Basicly your TEAM, CLAN,...) , totally awful, as a crew master, you have so limited options. You can not classify, sort, you can do nothing usefull. You can only delegate managers, accept players, or kick players out of crew. You have to spend enormous time to have a good crew, you have to know each player well, that is not practicable. YOU MUST HAVE (as a crew master) ability to see player stats, I dont mean attribs, but total stats or monthly stats, as you can see yours. I think you can not even see the level of your crew members (LOL), you can see this during their application only. You can not see inactive players, as you can not sort anything. YOU CAN NOT assaign them titles like, ROOKIE, VETERAN, PRO or whatsoever to classify them, which is a must in a serious clan, crew based mmo.
* The games lottery system, prize system so rigged. Lots of times you will get very piece of junk items like 100 points or even blank. If the system briefly tell you there is high chance of getting ♥♥♥♥♥♥ items IT IS OKAY. But you see the WHEEL OF FORTUNE for example, there is lets say 24 pieces, 1 of them is 100 points (smallest prize), you turn it 10 times and 5 times you get 100 points, come on this is BS! than put more piece and increase number of 100 points. This is like  slot machines with cheating mechanisms, casino wins all the time :)
* Information given by the game, about almost everthing is SO SMALL. Like 3 point attribute, 3 point success rate, which one is what ??? Which one includes what, which is better ? NO INFO !
What about Tussle, who needs tussle , what is that, ??? So you will spend your valuable points on stats you will never need, because you have no idea.
* There should be some graphical improvements like antialias may be?
* There should be optimisation of network code. Still we have disconnects from match loading screens, match would not start for multiple tiries. Some lags which affects gameplay, a player 3 meters left of you can block you with the help of Mr.Spock with a teleportation.
So final state of the game :
Pros:
+ Still Great gameplay
+ Seems like devs are listening players after steam
+ Some of the problems are sorted out after steam release
+ Old the pros are valid from first review
Cons:
- Still P2W.
- Big gap after level 40 with high levels, gap with experienced or/and p2w players.
- Awful friendship interface, lacking of an appointed main char for general relations and comms.
- Awful Crew system.
- Flawed lottery system.
- Lack of information about the game (stats,...)
- Need improved graphics.
- Need better network code.

I've been playing Freestyle for 7 long years. Since I was 12 years old, Freestyle has been my favorite game.
It has been with me throughout all my teenage years, and I don't regret a thing.
Ever since it first came out in 2006 (published by Activision), the game has had issues maintaining a good population due to lack of advertising and support from the foreign developers (JCE).
That's all hopefully going to change now that it has been released on Steam. It's a shame how we had to wait so many years for this because this is one of the most competitive games in the world.
Everybody who plays this game strives to ultimately be the best, and it's a team game so you have to find 2 other players who share the same mindset as you and want to be the best just as bad as you are.
A lot of this game consists of managing egos of not only your rivals, but your teammates also.
There is only one ball in the game of basketball, and scoring is only one part of it.
You have to have a good overall team that can not only score, but rebound, defend, block, steal, and pass at the right times.
This game is all about customization and making your player unique. There is a big item shop in the game that allows you to buy headgear,tops,bottoms, shoes, and accesories to make your baller look unique.
There are also Freestyles that allow you to change basic animations like dunks and shots so you can turn your simple one handed dunk in to a crazy 360 between the legs dunk!
Then you have your skills. Skills are new animations and upgrades you unlock through leveling your character.
Skills are the most important part of the game since they give really useful animations like diving for the ball or fading away.
When you first start the game and you go in to Rookies, you will be playing versus new players such as yourself who are also learning the game and it will be a cake walk for those who learn faster than others.
Beware though, there is a huge learning curve when you reach the big leagues (PRO Channel).
People do NOT like losing in Pros because it will result in their win % going down and the person that beat you having proof of them beating you.
I was never a guy to make many friends on this game, in fact I made a lot more enemies than I did friends and I am very hated but my advice to you new players is, make some friends before you reach Pros.
Try your hardest to communicate and socialize, post on the forums. MAKE FRIENDS. You do not want to be that "random" "unknown" person in Pros because nobody knows you and you will be kicked out of teams that have good players when you try to join because they simply don't know you.
You will be stuck on the "Noob Treadmill". That means you will be stuck playing only with players who are really bad and don't care who they play with, and other unknown players like you are which means you will lose A LOT and people will never see you as good.
So make friends before you get to pros! Get your name out there.
If you pick up this game and decide you like it and you're either a PG,PF,or C then you can add my character in game, I will help you. My IGN is: Zarry
So yeah, that is it for my long review and although my time on this game is coming to an end, I am happy it is finally getting the exposure it deserves because I know theres a kid out there right now maybe even reading this whos 12 or 13 years old that will fall in love with this game and aspire to be the very best player just like I did.

Hello All! I am known as Sinth, Cyntherea, BuckTucker and Persephone♥♥♥♥♥♥♥in this community. I have played the FSSB Series since its inception in North America.
In late 2006 I started playing the Sierra Online Alpha version when it hit North America. I was instantly hooked. The pace of this game and the intricicies involved in "Pro" play are what keeps me engaged.
We cannot compare this version of Freestyle with the versions that came before it so I will review FSSB2 on it's own merits.
This is a F2P game. You don't have to pay anything to get started and you don't have to pay anything to be "pro".

Create your character: Power Forward, Center, Small Forward, Shooting Guard, Point Guard.  It helps to have a basic understanding of Basketball to understand what these positions mean. You get a few default characters, with different stats based on position. Their are "Special Characters" or SPC's that you can buy with real money that have enhanced stats. What some people fail to realize is that if you are a "Free Player", that means NOT SPENDING $$$, you get a FREE SPC at level 50. So, no. you don't have to pay to get a Special Character.
People that play this game are gonna say, &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Sinth/Buck what about having to pay for extra skill slots?" Yes, extra skill slots cost $$$. My answer is, that if you want/NEED those then you are already high enough level or dedicated enough to "need" them. You can absolutely play without spending money. I have several alts that don't spend a dime and do just fine.
Now the the F2P/P2P thing is out of the way, onto the game.
This is an arcadey Street Basketball game with cartoony graphics and has an urban flavor.  If you like fast paced sports action and have a need for twitch reflexology, then I can't recommend this game enough. If you hate childish, racist, ageist (I'm 40 years old) smacktalk... Uh... Fun Factor: 1-10

I can't say enough positive things about this game franchise.  If you like Telltale games but feel they lack real effects for the choices you make then this is the game for you.  The first one, "Life is Strange," was such a good game that I though a follow-up on it would be the worst idea ever... but I was wrong.  So far this game is just as good as the original.

This prequel to Life is Strange gives so much more insight on Chloe and her character. You get to see the relationship form between her and Rachel and finally can understand the bond they shared. This beautiful game paired with extraordinary music makes for an amazing gameplay experience.

Life is Strange became a huge hit in 2015 and now Deck Nine has brought this beloved story back with this stunning prequel for PC. The story starts three years before the original game and Max Caulfield is nowhere to be seen. Instead, we follow the character Chloe Price in hopes of learning more backstory about her character and her relationship with Rachel Amber.
If you enjoy story and character based games you should definitely give this one a look.  I can’t even compliment the writers enough on their amazing story and character development which is very obvious when looking at both games side by side. Like the original game, we control the character in the third person. We are presented with decisions with varying degrees of impact. Small factors like the outfit you have Chloe have minimal impacts to the story line but things such as whether to run or attack effects the storyline a little more drastically. Objects in the area give you a chance to interact with them or just look. Looking at the objects in each scene allows you to uncover deeper levels of the story and uncover dialogue options.
The animation is beautifully done and the developer’s attention to detail is beyond impressive.The music in this game is one of my favorite parts. It is very fitting with the style and time period of the game. It is very reflective of the characters and their personal taste. Personally, this game is a little slow paced and a lot of the establishing shots seem drawn out and unnecessary to the game play. There are many scenes where you are given the option to let the scene continue as long as you wish or to press SPACE to leave. I feel like this mechanic should be applied to the opening scenes. Especially for people who are replaying the Episodes to uncover more decisions and story development.
Something that is discussed in depth by players of the original game is the cringy dialogue. I personally find it to be one of the more charming aspects of the game. I relate to the slightly awkward word choices of the teens and the cringy inner dialogue. Being socially awkward is just an aspect of being a teenager and it adds a realistic layer to the game. No one talks like people write and many writer’s struggles with realistic dialogue. Making the characters awkward in their own thoughts and in conversation was the right way to go in my opinion.
*SPOILERS OF LIFE IS STRANGE* If you haven’t played the first game and plan to – turn back now!
In the original game, Max uncovers her power to rewind time. This game doesn’t have that aspect, instead, Chloe has the ability to “Back Talk.” You enter an almost battle like format showing a bar with the number of hits Chloe has to make and how many her opponent has to make. You need to listen to your opponent’s hits in order to pick the comeback good enough to win the argument. Though many wouldn’t say this was much of a power. However, as you conclude the first episode there are hints to something more going on with Rachel Amber.
8/10

My opinion of Deck Nine being the creator of Before The Storm is much the same as what I have read from others in the community, in that they have (so far) done the series and its fans a great service. It's clear that the new developers have a lot of respect for Dontnod and the artist craft, patience and dedication that was spent in building these characters and the bitter-sweet plot and individual side stories that links them all together.
On a side note, I believe bringing Ashly Burch back as a character consultant for Chloe was a terrific move by Deck Nine, as if you watch some of the many Making Of documentaries that exist for the original game you will see how much emotion was drawn out from her and Hannah Telle as they portrayed the voice of their characters, which will surely have helped the game's directors at the time to tune the story and dialogue, and I am confident that Ash's insight into the mind of the Chloe will help to make BTS everything it should be.

As with the other reviews you're reading at this point, this review covers only the first episode and will be updated as the second and third episodes are released.
I discovered the original Life Is Strange through a steam sale and played the first episode for free before purchasing the full game. That first episode drew me in so completely that I hardly blinked at the price for the rest of the game, and the feelings the game left me with at each decision stick with me to this day.
Many people complain about this first episode because it doesn't have as good a hook as the original, and they're right. This first episode of BtS is well produced and has an interesting plot, but it doesn't leave me with anything near the feeling I had at the end of LiS's first episode. The gameplay is rather simple, most choices feel minor, and the story is compelling but does have quite a few inconsistencies that I hope will be explained in further episodes.
That being said, this game is excellent. No, it isn't Life is Strange. It's not supposed to be. Many people complain about the removal of the time travel feature, but time travel was such a Max aspect of LiS that it would likely cause more complaints if it was present in this game, which centers on Chloe a few years BEFORE the events of LiS (plus it would cause so many inconsistencies story wise that it just wouldn't work).
Chloe is a different character than Max, and so the game has a very different feel. The art style is the same, and the voice acting is just as excellent as the previous game's, but the choices available have a different feel and the "backtalk" feature feels slightly out of place. However, the game is still a story based game where choices do matter, and the story is still good enough to make me want more. Just as in LiS, BtS features choices that will affect the outcome of the story in some way or another, and the first episode, as an introduction to the game, asks quite a few questions that I hope will be answered further on.
TL;DR
I currently recommend Before the Storm, not because it's an excellent Life is Strange game, but because it's an excellent story- and choice-based game. Hopefully Deck Nine continues their faithful recreation of the Life is Strange universe and delivers good story and choice options in the next two episodes.

I have to say that this is perhaps one of the most beautiful games I've ever played. The scenery and the level of detail from terrain to lighting effects is amazing. I am running it on maximum setting. Visuals are absolutely stunning.
There are couple of things I'd like to see addressed:
1. Addition of a vehicle would be welcome. The area is expansive and talking simply takes too long to get from one area to another. Of course, the point of the game is to walk the vast terrain, to observe the pray and scout locations. It's a simulator in the true sense of that word. But having a vehicle to quicly reach a hunting area would be great. Yes, there are check points with fast travel, but it's not enough.
2. Walking noise could be improved. You have to move very very slowly to avoid making noise. That's also a very realisting idea but taken a little too far in my opinion.
3. Tracking animals is unreliable. At times the track simply stops as if the animal was abducted by aliens. At other times it reaches a point where it goes in a circle. It's a little frustrating when you track game for a good while only to reach a dead end.
4. Some bugs. Although the developer seems to be very engaged. It's a minor problem at this point. No crashes or anything. Just weird visuals. Once I shot a fox that was standing next to another fox and the second animal didn't even move. Just stood there. I could walk up to it and shoot it point blank. Odd. Unless he "froze" on purpose which I doubt.
Overall, very unique experience. Visually stunning. First hunting game I bought. It really is great and I would recommend it.

TL;DR; Disappointing bugs and instability, but promising game.
Let me start off by saying I've played the original theHunter A LOT, before it became the pay-to-play/win disaster that it is now. I played the original right when the game was released and only had one reserve, so I'm very familiar with the basics of the game and the team behind it.
That being said, I saw this game being reviewed and was fairly excited as it looked good and seemed to have taken a more mature turn.
However, the game in its current state has quite a large amount of bugs that (in my opinion) prevent me from having a fun experience. My main issue is that a lot of these bugs are super simple things that are obvious right from the start, so I'm surprised this hasn't been caught by QA,
For example: map marker will never show up in the location you try to put them in. I'm fairly sure this is tied to the fact that the engine doesn't have proper widescreen support (like the original) and scales the UI improperly (circles are ovals for me). Also, if you do place a marker, 100% of the time the marker will not show up currectly in the game until you reset the marker and add it again. Something that's incredibly annoying and it's a mystery how such an obvious issue has not been addressed.
Furthermore, the "tutorial" part is... a little bugged? I didn't find any tracks at all, until I was a good mile into a random direction, even though the lady announced "there's a track nearby". I've seen the same happening in a YouTube review of the game, so I'm not alone.

Spec Ops comes very close to being one of the greatest games ever, but the wonky combat holds it back. The story though, lifts this game out of mediocrity and into greatness. You are given difficult moral choices, some of which you don't know the consequences until after you've taken action, the white phosphorous scene for example. These choices wear down on the protagonists rather than the usual fare of a friend or family member dying. We see the characters debate whether to carry on after committing atrocious crimes themselves, and they decide to go on purely because there would be more death if they didn't. Dole out death to prevent a larger body count, a sad and dark choice that faces soldiers in modern combat.
You wander through the ruins of Dubai. Sand is everywhere, closing in on you giving a surreal feel to the game. You feel like you are wandering through Hell with Dante at your side, witnessing the punishment of the people of this city as it is consumed by the desert. The Line is a beautiful game. There isn't a robust list of new graphical features at use in the game, but they take the core graphical elements and craft a beautfiul game. You even have the choice to alter the appearance of the game. All of the choices still convey the stark, desolate landscape dotted with scenery of obscene wealth, but you can make it look like the color palette of a Tim Burton CGI fest or the blandness of a modern shooter game.
Your buddies can be ordered around to throw flashbangs, put down covering fire, revive each other. Your team helps push the story to a deep, rich level. They offer logical answers to solutions as opposed to the popular "my teammate is crazy and stupid and I have all the right answers always" , some of your team's suggestions even sound more sane that the main character's. They question who the real enemy is, just as you are. However, when it comes to gameplay your team is the big letdown of the game. You are constantly trying to get them to stay in cover or throw a flashbang or just plain don't stand in front of people shooting guns. Most of the campaign I spent reviving them, furiously taking out the enemies in front of them so they wouldn't go down. Teammates have a timer on their revive too, so if a teammate runs out of cover into a bunch of guys. Might as well reload the checkpoint.
Despite that and the not quite polished gunplay, I'd highly recommend this game. The story shines here, and it shines so brightly that you can get past some of the downsides and play a game that will haunt your thoughts for quite a while. I think of this game every time I play a shooter.

Undertale is amazing. It's an RPG chock-full of self-awareness, and as an interpretation of the role-playing tradition in videogames, it blends that self-awareness with alterations to your standard japanese/Earthbound-lite RPG canon that make Undertale feel utterly new and fresh. For example, as with most RPGs, there are battles to be had - but in Undertale, you're given the choice of attempting to communicate peaceably with your enemies, and try, through a range of actions, to distill conflict. Progress, therefore, need not come at the cost of the lives of many of the world's inhabitants. But it could. That's your choice to make.
If you're at all a fan of role-playing, you owe it to yourself to try Undertale. Thoroughly recommended.

(tldr: starting out is much too difficult in consideration of time and effort needed to put in with a community as toxic as it is. However, you can easily go onto a subreddit for rust that looks for starting groups to make your experience a lot more enjoyable)
It takes a good 30~ish minutes to farm enough for your own starting base, and half a second for it to be taken away from whoever you have the misfortune of seeing.
As a solo player, much too difficult to start off since making a codelock* is significantly more difficult to make since you cannot keep your base without a roof as anyone can now just build up** at any moment they feel like.
*Codelocks are an item that makes it so that you can open the door by a four digit pin number. The reason why this is important is that the other form of locking your door is a key. To get out with a door that needs a key, you need to bring the key outside when youre going to farm which can make anybody able to just waltz in your base as long as they:
1) Kill you and take your key, and finding your home (Then you're stuck inside and need to break your home (very loudly and resource heavy for starters) with no materials since its been raided.
2) Find your key if its hidden in a poor location. Even if in a good location, someone can sneak up on you, see you interacting with your hidden stash, and just wait for you to walk away, thus leaving you trapped inside your home with nothing effectively making your home useless)
**You used to be able to leave your roof open safely. But now, with the infamous "twig update", people can now build on your property using the weakest structures in the game, thus extremely limiting you in how you build. This made many things nearly useless, such as most forms of walls and obsticles. This makes it even more difficult as a solo starter since you need to sit down and dedicate handfuls of hours to build your home, which can be raided ten times easier than it was to make.
Since this game heavily relies on interactions with people and PVP, your experience relies on those you bump into and those around you. That means your average joe dictates how much fun or agony you go through to play. I personally believe this would be a good thing if there was roleplay involved, but there isn't a shred of such a thing here.
Those who intend to have fun interactions with others are significantly more likely to have almost all of their progress made useless in the blink of an eye, since there are FAR too many people who just sit on their roof and take pot shots at people to collect any shred of resource from them as possible.
The game is significantly easier and more lenient if youre working with friends. Having one or two friends can easily make times where it'd take 2ish hours to get a starting house to a meager 30 minutes since you have more people gathering resources and fighting.
With friends, you can easily turn the tides of a fight and have a much more enjoyable time overall. The only real byproduct of an issue is that clans and zergs (groups that consists of disgustingly high numbers, sometimes double digets) basically control the server. If you aren't on their good side or directly useful to them, consider keeping very, VERY far away unless you feel confident you can contest them.
I'd love to give rust a positive review, I honestly would. But after the twig update mentioned above, it sucked the charm out of rust for me. There's no more zany base designs as you can just build into them easily now. It's all just the same basic cookie cutter layouts with very little differentiation. You can't boost into bases to loot unsuspecting players. There's fairly overpowered yet easy to make turrets added in the twig update which make it so if someone accidentally leaves their door opened, you cant loot them without getting your health shredded and slowed down considerably.
So, the review stays negative mostly due to the twig update as its just nearly completely put me off from playing.

I will admit upfront that I am not the target audience for this game, so take this review with a grain of salt.  I am terrible at platformers.  Atrocious even.  To the point where I am pretty sure my only superpower in life is having my platforming characters be magnetically attracted to any spikes, pits, or enemies in visual range.  That being said, I still really wanted to try Rogue Legacy because the premise looked hilarious.
Playing this on PC, I found the controls frustrating.  The in-game prompts are still labelled with the original console controller buttons, so you have absolutely no idea which keyboard shortcut you should be pressing for any given action.  Additionally, while you can remap many of the keys from the options menu (if you can figure out which key accesses the menu), some actions are still automatically linked together in a non-intuitive manner.  I eventually got so angry with the PC controls that I borrowed my husband's Logitech USB wireless controller (similar to a PS2 controller), so that I could stand a chance of making through the tutorial, let alone playing the game.
I fumbled around for about 20 minutes, going through several lives, before ultimately giving up.  I did really enjoy the various character traits I got, including near-sighted, colourblind, geriatric, smelly, and plagued by halitosis, but I just couldn't make it far enough in the game to unlock anything.  You can't carry gold over between dungeons because the villain at the entrance takes all your money, so if you don't earn enough cash in one go to purchase something in town, then you basically have to restart from scratch with the next heir.
I did let my hubby, who is significantly better at platformers than I am, play through the game, and in 30 minutes he had unlocked almost everything there was to buy in town aside from the blueprints for equipment.  Although he was also frustrated by the controls, and even with the amusement of the character gimmicks he still wasn't interested enough to keep playing.
I appreciate the novel concept of the game, and I like that the randomly generated levels keep it from feeling repetitious, but I probably will not go back and play this again myself.  However, I might sit and watch a friend play it, just to see what other character traits and level designs pop up.
If you like platformers, and you are not playing this on PC, then by all means give it a chance.  Otherwise, I would suggest saving your $14.99.

As with the other reviews you're reading at this point, this review covers only the first episode and will be updated as the second and third episodes are released.
I discovered the original Life Is Strange through a steam sale and played the first episode for free before purchasing the full game. That first episode drew me in so completely that I hardly blinked at the price for the rest of the game, and the feelings the game left me with at each decision stick with me to this day.
Many people complain about this first episode because it doesn't have as good a hook as the original, and they're right. This first episode of BtS is well produced and has an interesting plot, but it doesn't leave me with anything near the feeling I had at the end of LiS's first episode. The gameplay is rather simple, most choices feel minor, and the story is compelling but does have quite a few inconsistencies that I hope will be explained in further episodes.
That being said, this game is excellent. No, it isn't Life is Strange. It's not supposed to be. Many people complain about the removal of the time travel feature, but time travel was such a Max aspect of LiS that it would likely cause more complaints if it was present in this game, which centers on Chloe a few years BEFORE the events of LiS (plus it would cause so many inconsistencies story wise that it just wouldn't work).
Chloe is a different character than Max, and so the game has a very different feel. The art style is the same, and the voice acting is just as excellent as the previous game's, but the choices available have a different feel and the "backtalk" feature feels slightly out of place. However, the game is still a story based game where choices do matter, and the story is still good enough to make me want more. Just as in LiS, BtS features choices that will affect the outcome of the story in some way or another, and the first episode, as an introduction to the game, asks quite a few questions that I hope will be answered further on.
TL;DR
I currently recommend Before the Storm, not because it's an excellent Life is Strange game, but because it's an excellent story- and choice-based game. Hopefully Deck Nine continues their faithful recreation of the Life is Strange universe and delivers good story and choice options in the next two episodes.

Why is this game good?
1. Paced to you. How quickly you progress through the game (multiple times over) is purely dependent on how skilled you are. Every child you play as will keep the gold from their deceased parent, so you decide when to challenge the bosses. Theoretically, you could buy every single upgrade (would take a very long time on your first run) before defeating a single boss, making it childs-play to defeat.
2. Extreme replayability. After you beat the game, there is a New Game +, basically means you keep your upgrades, and you get to play the game again. Gold collection is spiked, but so are enemies. I'm currently on my third runthrough of it.
3. Good controls. Although there is no mouse support for the game, playing the game feels solid with a controller (not so much with a keyboard, but still playable).
4. Good soundtrack. 'Nuff said.
5. Linux, SteamOS, and as before mentioned, full controller support.
6. Graphics fit well, the developers knew when more pixels were appropriate.
All in all, would recommend, 9/10 (lack of mouse support in menus kinda sucks). Definitely give this one a go, even if not on sale.

Do not mistake this as an anti-war piece. This is a game about games. It holds up a mirror to the player and questions their motivations. Why do you play military shooters? Why do you want to kill people? Why are you looking for excuses to kill people in these games? Do you think you're a hero? To go into more detail would be to spoil an experience that should not be spoiled. I may have given away too much already.
On the more mechanical front the game is a solid third person cover based shooter with some light tactical squad order mechanics. It plays well but within that genre but never steps into the realm of truly great gameplay. If you like cover based shooters you'll probably enjoy the gameplay.
The design and detail of the game is exceptional though. It looks lovely and makes great use of its setting in the environment design. Everything is highly detailed, even the voice lines. When giving orders Walker will say exactly where enemies are. "Under the bridge", "beside the statue", "on the staircase" and even, in the one area of the game where there is a T-Rex statue "next to the T-Rex". The tone and content of these lines changes as the game progresses, as do a lot of the details. This is a well crafted game and a lot of love has gone into it. Give it a go.
