In many ways, Borderlands 2 is a sequel done right; a new journey across Borderlands' Pandora with fresh faces, refinements across the board, and all the perks of a bigger budget. Alongside STALKER and the Fallout games on the Gamebryo engine, it is easily one of my favorite RPGs of all time and a great cooperative shooter, to boot.
In most cases, what Borderlands did, Borderlands 2 does better. Character balance, story richness, skill creativity, and voice acting - all took a great leap ahead. From the incredibly versatile Sabre turret of the Commando class to the stupendous performance behind Handsome Jack, from the wealth of audio dialogue to the insanity of dual wielding two fully automatic rocket launchers, Borderlands 2 is crazier than its predecessor in all the right ways.
That bold-faced lunacy manifests itself best in the game's humor. The bandits and psychos return with even more Looney Tunes-crazy lines, reciting Shakespeare in combat and offering the player finger pizza just two of the many examples. Brick, Claptrap, Handsome Jack, and nearly every other character breathe the comedy Borderlands thrives on with enthusiasm worth a hearty number of laughs. Only the pop culture references that go hand-in-hand might serve to drag it down; some may be divisive or fly over a player's head, while others may have aged too much to be significant anymore.
In gameplay, Borderlands 2 is more varied in nearly every way. Every item manufacturer now has a particular gimmick it adheres rigidly to, such as Hyperion's inverted recoil mechanic and Torgue's incredibly slow, but powerful explosive rounds. Player classes can vary wildly depending on their build, where a Commando can be a nigh-unkillable tank with an airstrike-in-a-can or a robust on-kill skill berzerker with a teleporting, slagging missile turret. Nearly every problem in Borderlands 2 has more than one solution, even if only just.
What the game does wrong is less objective. Its art style with outlines across everything is not for everyone and its extreme levelling curve - where the player outlevels enemies and their own equipment at an unreasonable speed just doing side missions - may put some off. Its often obstructive UI, with untoggleable damage numbers and item displays covering up enemies in combat, can prove to be a substantial annoyance. Average audio that pales in comparison to its voice acting often sticks out in gameplay and gunplay.
Overall, Borderlands 2 is a crazy experience full of robots, bandits, murder, and meat puppets I would strongly recommend to anyone with even a vague interest in shooters or RPGs.

In the interest of actually putting this review up anywhere in the near future, I drew the line at beating the main quest (once) and foregoing running through the DLC. It took an enormous amount of self restraint, but I did it. I did it for all of you. Just kidding. Let’s go.
I – Story [10/10]
Borderlands 2 is a first-person shooter, action RPG from the sheer brilliance that is Gearbox Software. The story starts five years after the events of Borderlands, in which four Vault Hunters (Roland, Lilith, Mordecai, and Brick) were guided by the mysterious “Guardian Angel” to an alien vault on the planet Pandora which housed a horrendous alien monster. The opening cutscene of Borderlands 2 introduces us to four new Vault Hunters: Axton, Maya, Zero, and Salvador. They are fighting their way through a Hyperion train to confront Handsome Jack, the would-be dictator of Pandora. The train, however, is a trap and ends up exploding. At this point, the player assumes control of their chosen Vault Hunter and enters the dangerous and exotic world of Pandora.
Your journey begins in the frozen wastes where you are discovered by the last remaining Hyperion Claptrap robot. The player is contacted by the Guardian Angel and instructed to follow Claptrap to the city of Sanctuary where they should join the Crimson Raiders. The Raiders are a resistance movement fighting against Handsome Jack and headed up by one of the previous game’s Hunters, Roland. However, when you arrive at Sanctuary, you learn that Roland has been taken captive by the “Firehawk”, a bounty hunter living in exile who turns out to be Lilith (another former Hunter and Roland’s girlfriend.
Lilith tells you that Roland was actually captured by a group of bandits called the “Bloodshots” and sends you off to rescue him from their clutches. Although you succeed at rescuing Roland from the Bloodshots, he is temporarily taken hostage by a cadre of Hyperion robots who have come to bring him to Handsome Jack. Following the second, more impromptu rescue, Roland and Lilith learn that the key to a new Vault is being transported by train and send you off to intercept it with the help of Tiny Tina (a thirteen year old explosives expert).
Once the train has been derailed, there is no Vault Key to be found, but there is Wilhelm (Jack’s cyborg bodyguard). Upon Wilhelm’s defeat, that player takes his power core in order to continue powering the shield over Sanctuary. The power core that was taken from Wilhelm, however, allows Jack to hack into Sanctuary’s defense grid via the Guardian Angel, who as it turns out, was working for Jack all along. Jack begins to level the city using Hyperion siege weaponry, but Lilith uses her Siren powers to phase the entire city to a safer location.
The player gets back to Sanctuary and Angel establishes communications with the group. Despite hostile treatment from Roland, Angel divulges that the Vault Key is kept with her in a Hyperion facility. She also shares information about the defenses of the facility. The Hunters embark upon a series of missions in order to assemble what they will need to overcome these defenses including: obtaining an upgrade for Claptrap, visiting the Hyperion city of Opportunity, and enlisting the aid of Brick (another former Hunter and now leader of the Slab bandit clan). During the process, Mordecai’s (yet another previous Hunter) pet bird Bloodwing is captured and killed by Handsome Jack and a grief-stricken Mordecai vows revenge, joining the other three former Vault Hunters at Sanctuary.
Roland and the Vault Hunters assault the Hyperion compound and meet Angel, who is not only a real person, but also a Siren, and Handsome Jack’s daughter. She orders the Hunters to kill her in order to stop Jack from charging the Vault Key and gaining control of the Warrior locked inside the Vault. Jack sends in waves of security forces in order to protect Angel, but, ultimately, the Vault Hunters (with the help of Lilith after her late arrival), successfully kill Angel. An enraged Jack teleports into the chamber, kills Roland, and captures Lilith, whom he forces to resume charging the Vault Key in Angel’s stead. Lilith manages to phase the player out of the facility and back to Sanctuary.
Mordecai and Brick decide to learn the location of the second Vault and confront Handsome Jack, the Warrior, and rescue Lilith all at once. While the player travels to the Hyperion Information Annex and obtains the Vault’s location, Brick and Mordecai steal a Hyperion barge. The Hunters approach the Vault’s location on foot, battling Hyperion security forces. Brick and Mordecai are shot down, but are revealed later to have survived the crash. The player confronts, battles, and defeats Handsome Jack himself, but they are too late to prevent him from opening the Vault. Jack summons the Warrior, an immense dragon-like creature, and orders it to kill the player. After (what can be) a long battle, the player defeats the Warrior and executes Handsome Jack in the aftermath.
Brick and Mordecai arrive just as Lilith attempts to destroy the Vault Key. However, she accidentally activates a secret information bank containing a huge map of the galaxy with several additional Vault locations marked on it.
Just fantastic the whole time. Not to mention the stories you can play through in subsequent DLC packs.
II – UI [9/10]
The user interface in B2 is pretty damned good if I say so myself, and I do.  You can easily find your health, shields, minimap, ammo, etc. I’m never at a loss to see what my stats are doing in combat. Also, on the topic of the minimap, it’s pretty good, but, like the larger map in the menus, it can be a bit misleading sometimes.
The menus themselves are set up nicely. Comparing items is easy as can be, as is sorting your inventory as a whole. Quests can be sorted in a variety of ways, your skills trees are displayed nicely, and the overall feel of the menus is rather unique. It reminds me a little bit of Dead Space.
My one complaint when it comes to the user interface is that, on occasion, items are trapped in terrain and become unobtainable. I once had this happen to me on an incredibly rare drop I had been farming for for hours and I have been extremely bitter ever since. It doesn’t happen often but it does crop up every now and then.
III – Gameplay [10/10]
Gameplay is exactly you might expect from any good FPS. It’s smooth, fast, explosive, and always a helluva lot of fun. Your character’s Action Skill adds nicely to the carnage and can indeed become central to any strategy when it comes to dealing with your enemies whether you’re going it alone or raiding Pandora with friends. (Co-op, by the way, is most certainly recommended. Borderlands and Borderlands 2 may well be the greatest cooperative games of our time.)
Whether or not you enjoy shooting hordes of enemies in the face, melee combat is still made viable in a lot of situations. In my experience, the two best characters for melee damage output are Zero and Krieg (the psycho character available via DLC). As far as those two are concerned, don’t count them out when they get up close and personal.
While some quests feel recycled at their core, everything in the game has it’s own unique feel and, more often than not, is overflowing with hilarious references to pop culture both past and present. Easter Eggs abound in this one and you’d be lucky to find them all.
The absolute, best aspect of Borderlands 2, however, is the sheer amount of loot found in the game. Loot is everywhere. There are toilets full of loot for Cthulhu’s sake. Finding that next amazing weapon is really what keeps you going and what keeps you coming back again and again. It’s pretty rare that you see the same item twice, especially with how many items are actually in the game.

Rogue Legacy is a Metroidvania-style game with a twist. True to its name, Rogue Legacy is about family, and in that sense, death is your friend. You start out at level zero, but you don't get more levels through fighting, you get them through developing a rather comprehensive skill tree. Here's the kicker, though: you can't develop the skill tree (in other words, your manor) after you enter the castle that the game takes place in. So, to get stronger, you have to die.
This is why the game is so unique, upon death, you become of the the children of the character that you just died as, each with different classes and different traits. Some of those traits will help (or hurt) in battle, such as being athletic or being insane, and some are just for individuality, such as Irritable Bowel Syndrom and swearing whenever they're hit. When you make your new character, you have to start the game over again. However, now you have whatever gold your previous character is, and you can develop your manor to upgrade your skills and stats and make for a stronger warrior.
Fighting is a delight as well. I'd recommend either a gamepad or the keyboard, both of them work pretty well. To make each game over unique, the castle that the game takes place it randomizes on each death. The game feels closer to a mix of traditional Castlevania and one of the newer titles, with the character having the use of a subeapon that can be used should they have the mana. From magic, to subweapons, to the variety of main weapons and the attack options for it, as well as the amount of abilities and supplements that can be unlocked from the manor/skill tree, the game never feels like a straightforward "jump and slash", and the action seems more responsive because of it.
Also, don't worry about backtracking. Because of its story-lite nature, you won't have to worry about getting new abilities that allow you to go to new places and backtracking to get to them. Having said that, be prepared to die a lot, because this game can be brutal. Not that it should matter, it's the amount of death and challenge that this game presents that makes it open to all types of gamers, regardless of whether they consider themselves hardcore, casual, or non-gamers. It's only through death that one will experience the game for what it truly is.
Still, if you want Rogue Legacy or if you're interested, check it out. It's a great experience and is probably worth whatever you pay for it.

Let me get something very confusing out of the way first: You will not enjoy this game. You shouldn't enjoy this game, or there is something very wrong with you. It is not a good game, it is the most evil game I have ever played. But I still recommend this game to every person I know. Why? Let me explain.
Spec Ops: The Line has the best narritive in a game ever. No compitition. You play as Captian Walker, and you command a group of soldiers named Adams and Lugo. Togather you make up Delta Squad, a recon squad sent in to rescue citizens from Dubai, which has just recently been hit by a massive sandstorm. Inside Dubai, you will uncover hell like never before portrayed in a videogame.
The best part of Spec Ops: The Line is that it is disgusted with itself and the player. I'm not going to spoil anything, but everything turns when the player does something bad...one of the most jaw-dropping moments in gaming. The game then turns it's sights onto you, and ever so slowly you and your squad of soldiers begin to lose themselves in their own emotions, trying to redeem themselves, trying to make things right, when things only get worse, and worse, and worse.
Spec Ops: The Line will change you. It will change the way you think about shooters, and videogames in general. If you fancy that kind of expirence, buy this game immediately. If you don't, consider picking it up if it ever goes on sale. It's a game that will truly change you.

I figured Rogue Legacy would be a solid homage to the Metroidvania genre with a nice, difficult twist, but it goes so much further than that. With its compelling progression and customization systems and an excellent use of randomization, Rogue Legacy is a clear and definitive step forward for the genre.
Any action-platformer game hinges on the player developing a set of reproducible skills -- learning how to read a room, confront enemies and chart a path through treacherous territory. Later Metroidvania games like Aria of Sorrow and Other M shied away from this and instead emphasized character empowerment and customization to the point where base skills like dodging and timing became almost unnecessary. Rogue Legacy deftly solves this problem by randomizing every room on each playthrough while also forcing the player to accept a unique set of strengths and weaknesses on each play session thanks to the game's hereditary system. After a couple hours, the player starts to understand the logic of the game: how each region works, where the greatest challenges are, how to chart a path through the castle and how to compensate for unexpected adversity. It's a brilliant example of a game that teaches the player a difficult and complex system at a steady pace over dozens of hours of play.
If you're a fan of Metroidvania games or a fan of challenging action-platformer games, you're more than likely going to get your money's worth out of Rogue Legacy. But if you appreciate dissecting and understanding great game design, Rogue Legacy is absolutely essential.

After 50 hours of gameplay I can make a review not based on emotion.
TLDR: If you like hunting games, or want a different experience from the action games / FPS, buy it!
Graphics:
The game is beautiful. Landscapes are gorgeous. Lighting is awesome. Wind is awesome, leaves flying with the direction and strenght of the wind...animals are beautiful too...Everything about graphics are great in this game. I've been playing video games for 30 years and this is the first time I really enjoy not doing anything but looking around.
My PC is not high end (i5 4460, 8GB, GTX 970) and I can play with good FPS on high, average on ultra.
Gameplay:
The game is hard. At least until you understand what is a hunting game, you'll probably get frustated. You will have hard time finding anything to shoot. And if you find, you'll ending doing a poor shot, because of the physics (they re very good).
And the game is slow. Not the movements and stuff, but hunting is a slow down experience...You cant go running all around.
So if you want a different experience from high speed FPS like Overwatch, CoD, BF, etc, this is a good game for you.
I'm really enjoying it. A lot. I see me playing this for like 1000 hours at least (if the game receive updates for more content). With the actual content, I guess I'll have like 100-200 hours of fun, because is kinda hard to get exp and money.

This game could become great if not for the amount of bugs. One bug for example which makes the animals run on one spot......and the game is released like this????? Think this game would be great if they fix all the game breaking bugs, but for now, nope, this game still belongs in Alpha.

TL;DR
If you are patient, enjoy wonderful scenery, leveling up really slow but like to have a goal that takes forever- then this is your game. It's wonderful to look at, but graphics are better in the gameplay-trailers- Which I find a bit misleading.
Besides that, it's all about being patient and taking your time.
It's not worth it's full price, but DO buy this if it's on sale.
-----
PLEASE NOTE
I played this only on Hirchfelden Reserve and the review is based on Singleplayer
isn't important and it's no problem straying from your given tasks. Not only is it optional but you don't get pressured into doing anything at all. They mostly sound like friendly requests, and that's what it feels like as well.
They do get more challenging the further you go. In terms of challenge, this goes for aquiring equiment, shooting challenging pictures and game.
I didn't really concern myself with the quests, but they do maintain a certain aspect of interest of the game. Both visually and gameplay-wise.
You do unlock lore by discovering/visiting places in the game. As since the reserves are based on real places,- the lore you discover is just as real. It's easy/interesting reading and you'll have something to do while waiting for an animal to pop up.
It's just a whole-lot of wonderful scenery and beautiful landscape to take in. If you keep moving from place to place- you never really get tired of the visually striking environment. For some reason, I have experienced multiple FPS-drops on different places. I don't know why but it's barely noticeable.
Animals ranging from bears and hogs to deer and rabbits- they all look fairly good looking and behave accordingly. Animal reactions to your presents and actions are quite realistic. Both you and all animals leave a trail on the ground, pushing bushes and grass aside to leave a mark of where you've/they've been. Details like these make it look and feel just so good.
Besides the fantastic graphics that some would mistake for real life, it's a downer when you are at the corner of a big cornfield watching for a fox or a red deer- that the drawing distance falls off. Beyond 100m, objects like corn and rocks gradually disappear. There are windmills east of the reseve. If you watch them from far away - these do not have blades on them.
My guess is that this is a camouflaged option of optimizing the game's FPS and balancing it with draw-distance. This reminds you that it's a game and kill the realism of it.
As mentioned above, there is a draw distance in the game and this is actually a problem for a achievement that tell you to hit a animal from 400m. Because at approximately 400-405 meters, the animals disappear from your screen. If you move closer to it, it reappears (about 380-390m). Beyond 350 meters, animals no longer react to gunshot sound either, and both of these factors can kill the thrill of the hunt.
I've encountered a few other problems during my travels.
I'm just gonna list some examples:
* Track-highlighting and animal outlines gradually stop showing when transition from day to night. Reappear once transitioned to day again.
* Animals get stuck in trees, rocks and other obstacles while running. Easy but boring kills do occur.
* Fast traveling sometimes remove explored animal-need-spots, like drinking spots or places they sleep. Uncertain if this is intentional.
* Rain does not show through riflescopes.
* Sound indicator rarely correspond to the given sounds you make. Sounds that sound noisy actually isn't. When standing still on certain places- like in a bush or next to a tree but look around you, you generate alot of noise but it doesn't show on the indicator.
* Loud sounds like thunder or powerful wind does not decrease/cover the sound the player make.
let this scare you! It's the small things that bother the most picky persons that hunt for both game and details. The gameplay itself if wonderful and intense.
When you hunt for anything particular and stick to a spesific game, that's when it starts getting seriously fun! Find tracks, estimate where it is, move slowly so it doesn't see you, thinking of the wind direction to avoid it smelling you- and so on. Once you hear it calling out, closer and closer, your heart start pumping faster. If you are lucky, it's walking your direction and you can hear it rattle the leaves and bushes. Rain dripping on your clothes and dense vegetation that decreases your visibility in the foggy forest start to feel extremely real at this point. All you can do it sit and wait with your rifle aiming it's direction until it shows it's feet or antlers. It's noisy, but everything feels more quiet until you take your shot. Even I got scared of my own shots multiple times.
I shot it just where I hoped it would, but it's running away. I start picking up the trail while reloading the rifle. Blood splatters indicate a vital hit and it's bleeding alot. just 3-5 minutes later, I find that beautiful creature and harvest it.
It's a REALLY slow process to level up, gaining perks and skill points. I don't know how it works, but I think it's like that you get perk points from lvl X and skill point after next one. When exploring, you can find collectables like antlers as well. These increase your XP and is a good addon to modestly increase the fun-factor of exploring.
Trackhunting, discovering new places, spotting animals and hunting them is the way to earn XP. If you are bad at hunting, then you'll have a hard time leveling up.
Perks increase spesific weapon-usage like the rifle and skill points increase your overall skills as a character. Skills have alot of variation, but I feel the perks lack alot more options per weapon.
The map is big. Really big. It pinpoints locations and points of interest for you to discover and it's actually fun exploring it. Alone or with friends, you can place markers on the map for you to follow. Those markers will also tell you how much time it takes to walk there and the distance to it from your current position.
The map is sadly not as detailed as I would prefer. The problem with this is that small details of the terrain do not show on the map, and doing a precise marking of something is hard to do.
* No DLC's! Good job with that!
* Not too bad arsenal of weapons, lures and scopes. I guess you could have more but I don't care.
* Slow-paced.
* Extremely big map and LOT's of hunting grounds
* Beautiful-looking game
* Fantastic sound-effects/quality
* Intense moments happen alot when tracking down your game, making everything really exciting
* Perks to increase e.g. tracking skills. This system feels realistic in terms of knowledge and experience you gain from hunting and harvesting.
* Slow-paced. Sometimes feel like nothing ever happens (this can be a good thing!)
* Stressing to find games to hunt and KoS- kills the joy of the game and makes it boring.
* Leveling up is based on kills, harvesting, spotting new places and building places to hunt. It takes a LONG time to get a high level.
* You are stuck with limited equipment and won't be able to aquire more unless you level up.
* You can get stuck and hurt yourself on objects, rocks etc. When crouching, you can't climb as well as when you are standing- meaning hunting in close-quarters near steep ground end up like if it's a invisible maze around you.
* "Applying" changes to resolution sometimes does not work for some reason.
* Player-markers, track-highlightings and wildlife appearances needs work as since they glitch/get stuck/don't appear after long-time traveling or transition from day to night. The only way to fix this is by fast-traveling or restarting the game.
I highly recommend this game to everyone.
It's slow paced, rich on details, and have alot of joy for hunters. I dare say that it's close to the best hunting-simulators there is.

First off I would like to say that I am a huge fan of the Mad Max franchise, and when I first heard of this game I was thrilled. I expected a lot from the game after watching it's trailers, and I was not disappointed.
Pros:
Absolutely amazing vehicular combat, completely surpassing my expectations!
Really fun ground combat! As a lot of you probably know the combat is very similar to the Arkham series of games, and that's definitely not a bad thing. You feel like the badass wanderer that Max has always been.
Nice graphics! On max graphics the game looks beautiful, though my computer can't run it at max quality without a significant drop in framerate.
Good voice actors! While some of the characters feel pretty lackluster, the majority of the characters are really brought to life by the actors.
Powerful Story! I know some people might disagree with me here, as this game definitely isn't "The Last of Us". However, the game does a fantastic job of capturing the old story of Max regaining his humanity in the wasteland.
Big (and beautiful) World! The world is big with plenty to explore, as well as tons of enemies to take down.
Cons:
The game can become somewhat repetitive as you grind away at clearing minefields or carrying gas can around trying to blow up every last transfer tank. However the game keeps things interesting with plenty of combat during these events so this isn't that large of a complaint.
Overview:
Really this is just a great game, and I highly recommend buying it whether you're a fan of the series or are just looking for a good open-world game.

While the action of Spec Ops isn't anything spectacular, it's solid enough to keep you playing to see the story through. And it's the storyline where this game really shines. It's refreshing to have to deal with genuine moral dilemmas and few games will leave you feeling seriously uncomfortable with the decisions you've made as this one. It's definitely not one for the kids.
Whereas the game encourages you to play multiple times, there's little reason to do so beyond the multiple endings which a strategic save file can net you in one sitting. And the major decision you have to make isn't really a decision at all as you're forced to do it, shattering the illusion of freedom.
Despite the gripes, it's worth playing at least once to experience a war game actually dealing with adult themes rather than the one man army game or the hyper realistic extremes the genre seems to gravitate towards. It won't last you long past the 6 hours or se needed to finish it but it'll stick in your head for a long time after. In terms of narrative it's unmatched at the moment and should be experienced.

Spec Ops: The Line is one of the greatest games I have ever played. It is a brutal, unforgiving experience that will stay with you long after you reach the credits screen. Despite this bleak description, it provides tons of moral and ethical questions for the player to consider throughout its solid 8 hours.
Don't be fooled by its generic third-person shooter description, Spec Ops is actually a critique and total breakdown of the military shooter genre. In fact, its truthful depiction of the horrors of war will leave you not wanting to ever touch another shooter game again. If this scares you, and it should, then Spec Ops is not for you. Go back to playing endless hours or CoD or Halo, always assuming you are a hero. If you dare to challenge what a game can provide you and change your perspective, give Spec Ops a chance. Also take a look especially if you are a fan of Heart of Darkness/Apocalypse Now.
Overall, I can't recommend this game enough. It will make you think, it will make you question your beliefs, and in the end, it will break you. No matter what, you will come away from it with a refreshing emotional experience that no other game can provide. I sure did.

Borderlands 2 is a game filled with comical characters, unique gun-play, and a story that will give you joy. Borderlands 2 builds upon knowledge more than skill. Of course there is some skill that is required to play a shooter but Borderlands 2 takes that to a different level. Knowing what gun is better than another, or what item is in favour of another is a constant thing in this game. Next, the world is huge. There are MANY secrets and the amount of content inside is unmatched in my opinion. Many missions and quests are given to you and its up to you if you want to complete them or not (You may have a hard time if you don't complete them though). Multiplayer is a big part of this game. Sure you can play alone like a scrub but thats no fun... CO-OP is the best way to play this game. Graphically, its great. I always am amazed by the game graphically. Audio wise, its amazing. There are so many phrases every character says and it takes HOURS to listen to them all. All the playable characters themselves have at least 30 minutes of dialogue just from the random things they say when traversing the world. Next is the acceptance of peoples choices. There will constantly be sexual humour, and there are many characters that would be considered apart of the LGBTQ Community. There is no discrimination and in fact it is a big part of the game's setting. Replayability... Yes... A lot of it... The amount of replayability in this game is outstanding! There will be constant killing for special weapons and items along with mulitple characters to do that with. In total there are 6 playable characters (2 require DLC), each having their own special skills. Playing through the game with each character takes days, and most likely months. The game is no downer for replayability. In short, Borderlands 2 is funny, accepting of the world, has loads of content and replayability, and is great to play with friends. It'll suck up your time but that doesn't matter because its fun to play! Oh and piece of advice, buy the GOTY edition (Game of the year edition for the scrubs who don't know what GOTY means). The DLC is worth the price and its a hell of a lot cheaper than buying everything individually. All in all, Buy this game.

The game looks good and has some great ideas. However I'm not seeing how it is a rogue-lite.  Rather it is a rogue like with persistant upgrades. The platforming is floaty and inprecise with some rooms filled with so many traps that your eyes roll. The enemies often feel like they are cheating with the ability to shoot through walls. Oh and why does touching a monster in a robe do damage to the armored guy(me)? If anything smashing into him in platemail should damage him!
But wait you say you can upgrade your character each death and hopefully get farther in the dungeon! That's true except if you don't get enough gold in a run for the upgrade you want then you have to give it all up for your next character to enter the dungeon. Oh and if you spend it on a cheaper upgrade so you don't waste that gold all the other upgrades get a little more expensive. I guess that I'm just not 'skilled' enough because I often have to grind through many pointless deaths with no upgrades until I get a dungeon layout that doesn't screw me over before I get enough gold to buy an upgrade. The option to simply turn Charon(the guy who steals your gold to enter the castle) off would have allowed gamers that are not so great with platformers to play and enjoy the game. For those that want a roguelike experiance the option to leave Charon on would work.
If I could keep my gold between runs I would feel like I was building up towards something even when the deaths are sometimes cheap. As it is I simply feel like I'm slamming my head against a wall and this game simply isn't for me. If I hadn't purchased this on sale I would be pretty upset.
Bottom line unless you are both good at platformers and like grinding away for hours on useless deaths until you can create a character powerful enough to win stay away from this game.

I was a little nervous getting this game, as many reports problems with game crash, lag and freeze. Guess i am a lucky one, as i never encountered this at all. It really runs smoothly even on the highest settings. I run the game on an MSI Intel i7-4720HQ, 16GB RAM, NVIDIA GTX960.
This is the most beautiful game i ever played where you walk in an astonishing surroundings. You just cant help but stop frequently to enjoy the view. The animals also looks good with nice animation. If i should put my finger on anything, the lake / ponds could maybe have a better texture.
The sounds are good and with no problems to hear where they coming from. But at some random events, some of the sounds dissappear or turns in to noise. Not the best thing when using earplugs.
You have the option to start in two different maps, Central European and North-west American. Both maps are huge with so many places to explore, you could easily play for houndreds of hours before you been on all the places.
The animals however, seems to need more work. As it is now, there are some issues. An animal trying to run away from you, can end up being stuck if a tree or rock stands in their path. I also seen animals getting stuck in a loop, such as an animal chance direction when hitting tree A, and turns towards tree B, so it chance direction to tree A again and therefor chance direction again to tree B. In the tutorial, they tell us about hunting pressure and animals would avoid areas where you just killed. This isnt true at all. Animals doesnt seem to care about this for a second and would gladly walk in to an area and stand besides their fellow mates who just got shot. There are a dozen number of animals to hunt, and some of them is to be expected to attack you in defence. But if i stand only 6-7 meters away from a black bear or big moose and shoot but only get a flesh hit, i am still not attacked. The only time i got injured from an animal was when standing at its running-away path, and was runned over. And since animals are running away from you, not towards you, this is obviously not something you need to worry happen often.
I have also come across animals who just stands there frozen. This is at night, so i guess they are sleeping. But if i shoot them without getting instant kill, they just run 2-3 steps before they stop and freeze again. It looks very weird.
One thing i noticed first time i played this was how slow i walk. Its realistic, as you are hunting and wouldnt like to make noise. So crouching should be slow moving. But normal walking are just as well slow and walking up the stairs to a watch tower reminded me of walking with my grandmother. So it all ends up with me running around. Thats actually not so bad. Its extremly noisy and scares animals around you. In this way i can find out if there is any animals around me at all and if there is, where they are from their warning calls.
The game have a nice earn money and skill system making you work to improve and afford better equipment.
All in all, this is a game i enjoy and would keep playing. You need a little patient, just like in real life. But is nice and relaxing game to play when you have no time pressure upon you. The only downside for me is the animal behaviour and running path that needs an improvement. This is not an alpha game, so i am not shure it will ever be fixed.

Going into Before the Storm, there was plenty of reason to worry. New developer, new voice actors, new main character, no time travel mechanic to lean on. And prequels can be difficult to pull off (looking at you, Star Wars).
At the time of this review I only have episode 1 to go by, but it seems Deck Nine have managed to create a game that captures the spirit of the original. Like its predecessor, the story and the relationships between characters are emphasized, and we get to feel some of the pain that led Chloe to where she was in the original game. As with Life is Strange, there are definitely some moments where the characters' raw emotions will hit you in the feels. Also, there are some enjoyable nods back (forward?) to the original game. And as before, the soundtrack is once again a strength.
Is it better than Life is Strange? Not yet, but it's still a very enjoyable play and manages to both fit with the original and also create its own subtly different feel. I'm looking forward to the final two episodes.

I'm not really the sidescroller type. Not because I think the genre's bad, or anything, but just because I never really got into it in the first place. Couple of Mario games when I was younger, and that's it. So it came as a pleasant surprise when this Steam Summer Sale $1.70 game turned out to be massively enjoyable. The Roguelike variance of the game combined with the means of making steady progress create a deeply engaging experience, which I gladly sunk hours of play into. The gold and upgrade mechanics are especially brilliant, in my eyes. They allow the game to essentially modulate its own difficulty level, with skilled players clearing the game easily on low gold counts while the scrubs like me can grind until it gets easy enough to beat. It's a beautiful effect that widens the audience hugely. Even better, the New Game+ and (so I've heard) New Game++ effects allow the game to extend its life even further. There's certainly a point where it stops being fun, but I've not yet found it. And all this without even getting into the birthline and equipment mechanics!
If you're patient player with a taste for fighting, this is definitely the game for you.

"Modern Military Shooter" typical gameplay (hide and shoot from cover) - i.e. rather boring - and stupid ally AI but nice graphics, soundtrack and story. The game is short enough to keep you entertained until the end.  Definitely worth a buy during sales.
In details:
The bad:
The whole game mechanic of shooting from cover is not what I consider exciting when it's against brainless AI. You stand up, kill 2-3 guys, then go back to cover waiting for your life to automatically regen. Rinse and repeat.
The bots in your own squad usually perform ok but they will sometimes for no apparent reason run out of cover like suicide bombers and end up waiting under heavy fire for you to revive them. I died a few times trying to get them back on their feet. And I played on normal difficulty only...
The good:
Graphics are pretty good and the game has a really good soundtrack (especially but not only the metal tracks during action phases).
The evolution of your character through the game is unusual and pretty mature for this kind of game. It successfully manages to avoid the usual and really annoying American-soldier-hero cliche. This aspect of the game shines at the end with the available multiple endings (4 IIRC).

I was a little nervous getting this game, as many reports problems with game crash, lag and freeze. Guess i am a lucky one, as i never encountered this at all. It really runs smoothly even on the highest settings. I run the game on an MSI Intel i7-4720HQ, 16GB RAM, NVIDIA GTX960.
This is the most beautiful game i ever played where you walk in an astonishing surroundings. You just cant help but stop frequently to enjoy the view. The animals also looks good with nice animation. If i should put my finger on anything, the lake / ponds could maybe have a better texture.
The sounds are good and with no problems to hear where they coming from. But at some random events, some of the sounds dissappear or turns in to noise. Not the best thing when using earplugs.
You have the option to start in two different maps, Central European and North-west American. Both maps are huge with so many places to explore, you could easily play for houndreds of hours before you been on all the places.
The animals however, seems to need more work. As it is now, there are some issues. An animal trying to run away from you, can end up being stuck if a tree or rock stands in their path. I also seen animals getting stuck in a loop, such as an animal chance direction when hitting tree A, and turns towards tree B, so it chance direction to tree A again and therefor chance direction again to tree B. In the tutorial, they tell us about hunting pressure and animals would avoid areas where you just killed. This isnt true at all. Animals doesnt seem to care about this for a second and would gladly walk in to an area and stand besides their fellow mates who just got shot. There are a dozen number of animals to hunt, and some of them is to be expected to attack you in defence. But if i stand only 6-7 meters away from a black bear or big moose and shoot but only get a flesh hit, i am still not attacked. The only time i got injured from an animal was when standing at its running-away path, and was runned over. And since animals are running away from you, not towards you, this is obviously not something you need to worry happen often.
I have also come across animals who just stands there frozen. This is at night, so i guess they are sleeping. But if i shoot them without getting instant kill, they just run 2-3 steps before they stop and freeze again. It looks very weird.
One thing i noticed first time i played this was how slow i walk. Its realistic, as you are hunting and wouldnt like to make noise. So crouching should be slow moving. But normal walking are just as well slow and walking up the stairs to a watch tower reminded me of walking with my grandmother. So it all ends up with me running around. Thats actually not so bad. Its extremly noisy and scares animals around you. In this way i can find out if there is any animals around me at all and if there is, where they are from their warning calls.
The game have a nice earn money and skill system making you work to improve and afford better equipment.
All in all, this is a game i enjoy and would keep playing. You need a little patient, just like in real life. But is nice and relaxing game to play when you have no time pressure upon you. The only downside for me is the animal behaviour and running path that needs an improvement. This is not an alpha game, so i am not shure it will ever be fixed.

The Creators of Euro Truck Simulator 2 (SCS Software) did their research on this style, it not only captures the raw nature of truck driving, but also the feeling of coming out into the world of truck driving.  I talk not from personal expierence but one of second hand as family does drive trucks for a living, but in the United States.
[Fun Factor]
I may not be overly interested in driving a truck throughout Europe, but this game makes that so entertaining and fun.  After several hours I already am transfixed and addicted to driving, it's almost meditative to me.  But also, after a long day of people ticking me off, it is also lovely to make a save and simply demolish every person on the road.
[Polish]
Graphics high or low this game has an extraodinary amount of detail, when driving down a road it doesn't feel like the road is repeated over and over at all, it feels like I'm GOING somewhere, not many simulators capture that these days.  If you look closely you can also see so much detail in the skys, from clouds brewing before it rains to airplanes passing by every now and again.
[My Recommendation]
Buy this game, but I would highly recommend using either a gamepad/Xbox controller or an actual steering wheel but keyboard works just fine.
[Cons]
Once you get into the meat of the game and buying garages it can sometimes feel unrealistic with your drivers just bustling around on their own free will and you can't actual request they take a certain job. But that is my only complaint.

This game is pretty boring, if you think about it.
Basically, you're driving trucks across increasingly larger distances throughout Europe, going from point A to point B, while at the same time managing your trucking company which also increases in scale over time. That's what this game is at its core. That's not the main reason I love this game, though.
With Euro Truck Simulator 2, I can relax and play a game that does not really require reflexes/coordination, does not cause frustration, I do not have to interact with "online community," but yet I am still playing a game and accomplishing goals. I can turn on music on my computer (or, utilize the "radio" features of the game which can play local mp3s or use internet streaming radio) and just drive and enjoy the (actually very good looking) scenery. I can customize my truck how I like, hire new employees and slowly increase the value of my trucking company as I play.
It's not very difficult, and it's incredibly relaxing. It's a game that you can jump into for as long as you like, and you can stop at any time with no major issues. You can even turn off the more "simulator-y" parts like fuel consumption, tired-ness, change transmission types, etc - all to make it easier, if you so desire.
This game also offers gamepad and steering wheel support alongside standard KB+M - all of which work very well (I prefer the steering wheel, for realism).
If you dislike driving in real life, you probably won't like it. If your idea of a relaxing game is something like an FPS or MOBA, you probably won't like it. If you have an irrational fear of large trucks or asset managment, you definitely won't like it.
If like me, you enjoy things like: nice visuals and locations, driving, listening to music, relaxing/simplistic gameplay, then you will probably like this game, and I definitely recommend it to those people.

Mad Max is basically Just Cause and Rage and Batman mixed together. It's a third person action adventure game a post-apocalyptic Mad Max world, with flashy explosions, lots of cars and lots of things to do. It's not doing anything new, but what it does it does pretty well indeed.
GRAPHICS
Mad Max is gorgeous. The wastelands never looked so good. Where Rage's wastelands and driving where just to get from point A to point B the wasteland in Mad Max is more of the Fallout kind. You see something pretty in the distance and just drive there to see what was it. Most of the time you drive through a vast desert with some settlements here and there, with ocassional wreck of an airplane or some broken windmills. The environment is bleak, as it should, but also amazing. Cars look as you would expect, with prevalent spikes and bolts. Not pretty per se, but true to the world.
AUDIO
There is little to no music, but the sound effects are very nice. The engines sound meaty, the explosions kablooie and in melee you can hear the bones breaking. Voice actors are on the level and all the talking seems legit.
GAMEPLAY
If you played any third person action adventure game since the first Remedy's Batman then you know how this plays. The game reminded me of Fuel with all the driving through desolated environments, and you can drive for quite a while. Just Cause, as everything is rather hectic and explosions can be aplenty. Batman, cause of the fight system. Fallout, because of the let's see what's that on the horizon feeling. Assassin's Creed, due to all the gazillion of things to collect.
Yes, it's nothing new, but if you like driving through desolated wastelands there is nothing better, except maybe Fallout 4, but it's a little bit different. All in all I definetely don't regret the buy and the 60hrs I spent with the game was a time well spent. There is a chance I'll play some more and get it to 100%. If you're on the fence, just buy it. It's fun.

Going into Before the Storm, there was plenty of reason to worry. New developer, new voice actors, new main character, no time travel mechanic to lean on. And prequels can be difficult to pull off (looking at you, Star Wars).
At the time of this review I only have episode 1 to go by, but it seems Deck Nine have managed to create a game that captures the spirit of the original. Like its predecessor, the story and the relationships between characters are emphasized, and we get to feel some of the pain that led Chloe to where she was in the original game. As with Life is Strange, there are definitely some moments where the characters' raw emotions will hit you in the feels. Also, there are some enjoyable nods back (forward?) to the original game. And as before, the soundtrack is once again a strength.
Is it better than Life is Strange? Not yet, but it's still a very enjoyable play and manages to both fit with the original and also create its own subtly different feel. I'm looking forward to the final two episodes.

Undertale is a pixellated RPG with a wonderful story, amazingly thought out characters, and a unique and fun battling system that is not too easy but not too hard as well. Each boss has it's own unique power and fighting style which gives the game a refreshing feel of having something new each fight instead of the bland repetitive taste that a lot of games have today.
Not only is the style and system unique, as is the story. This game doesn't have just one ending which makes it a delight to play over and over again. In fact, this game has three endings: Genocide, Neutral, and True Pacifist.
The world that you play in, called the Underground, has a broad aray of different sceneries each much different than the last but each one very well thought out.
Now, this game is loaded with puzzles however they are fairly simply and easy to figure out so even a person who hates puzzle games (like I do) will find enjoyment out of it.
So should you play this game? Well, do you like RPGs, Pixel art, easy puzzles, fantastic characters, and a kick@ss story? Then yes. Yes you should. Like, right now.
Do you not like all the things I mentioned? Well, you should play it anyways.

Fantastic little indie game. It's basically a Castlevania style RPG but with more of a twist on it. Using characters with abilities (and disabilities!) that effect things like having the entire game play upside down, being able to avoid all floor traps, being massive, small, or just neutral random traits such as balding, being gay and flatulence.
The progression is somewhat grindy with randomized loot chests and expensive upgrades for your keep. Still, the classes are interesting and mostly allow for unique playstyles and can help with puzzles, specific bosses or just navigating the castle.
There's a somewhat interesting story to follow if you don't mind a bit of reading and exploring, I personally loved it and was disappointed when I ended up missing a few journals before completing the game. Though it definetly starts out slow.

To put it simply, if you enjoyed the original Life Is Strange then you'll enjoy this one, possibly even more. This prequel keeps the trend of the first game by having a rich and immersive story, interesting and relatable characters, and a great soundtrack to go along with it all.
If you haven't played the original, I highly suggest doing so first because it allows you to appreciate the prequel more, but it's not necessary because the prequel is just that good. It sets up the story and characters well enough that you wouldn't need the first game to enjoy it. I believe it has improved from the first game in terms of both the game engine (animations and lip-sync) and the dialogue (not cheesy or cliche).
I am eagerly awaiting the next episode, and if you need convincing to play the orginal, here's my review for it:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Life Is Strange
To start off, this is the best choice-driven narrative game that I've ever played, and it opened me up to a new selection of music that I would of never heard otherwise. The first episode is free so there's no reason as to why you shouldn't at least try it.
I tried out Episode 1 because I was bored, and then proceded to stay up all night finishing the entire game because I was so hooked on the story and characters. Also you may or may not shed a tear at the end of Episode 5.
PROS
1. The story is amazing, if you immerse yourself in the game you will get invested in it easily. It touches upon real world subjects like bullying, suicide, and all sorts of things that add depth. It even has some dark twists and turns that keep you guessing throughout the game.
2. The soundtrack is amazing, the music sets the mood for the situation, aids the story telling process, and never brings you out of the moment.
3. The characters are relatable, considering most of them are based off sterotypes or cliques in a high school. On the surface they seem sterotypical, but as you play you learn more about them that builds their character to make each of them unique.
4. The choices you make throughout the game will affect you, some are small while others are big and their consequences are equally so. There are big events in certain parts of the game that will play out differently depending on multiple choices you made before hand.
5. The "rewind" feature makes this game stand out from other choice-driven narrative games, due to you being able to easily experiment and try out multiple options. It's hard to explain unless you've played it so go ahead and play it.
CONS (Gotta have an honest review)
1. There are only two endings to the game (Episode 5), and they don't take into account the choices you made throughout the game. I personally didn't mind too much because the journey to get to these endings and the choices that did affect my gameplay made it worthwhile.
2. The dialogue may seem a bit cliche or weird at times but it grew on me and I attributed to those characters which just added to the experience. Considering it was wrriten by grown French males for mainly teenage American characters it ain't too bad.

Mad Max is basically Just Cause and Rage and Batman mixed together. It's a third person action adventure game a post-apocalyptic Mad Max world, with flashy explosions, lots of cars and lots of things to do. It's not doing anything new, but what it does it does pretty well indeed.
GRAPHICS
Mad Max is gorgeous. The wastelands never looked so good. Where Rage's wastelands and driving where just to get from point A to point B the wasteland in Mad Max is more of the Fallout kind. You see something pretty in the distance and just drive there to see what was it. Most of the time you drive through a vast desert with some settlements here and there, with ocassional wreck of an airplane or some broken windmills. The environment is bleak, as it should, but also amazing. Cars look as you would expect, with prevalent spikes and bolts. Not pretty per se, but true to the world.
AUDIO
There is little to no music, but the sound effects are very nice. The engines sound meaty, the explosions kablooie and in melee you can hear the bones breaking. Voice actors are on the level and all the talking seems legit.
GAMEPLAY
If you played any third person action adventure game since the first Remedy's Batman then you know how this plays. The game reminded me of Fuel with all the driving through desolated environments, and you can drive for quite a while. Just Cause, as everything is rather hectic and explosions can be aplenty. Batman, cause of the fight system. Fallout, because of the let's see what's that on the horizon feeling. Assassin's Creed, due to all the gazillion of things to collect.
Yes, it's nothing new, but if you like driving through desolated wastelands there is nothing better, except maybe Fallout 4, but it's a little bit different. All in all I definetely don't regret the buy and the 60hrs I spent with the game was a time well spent. There is a chance I'll play some more and get it to 100%. If you're on the fence, just buy it. It's fun.

Review:
This game is an awesome Roguelike hybrid. It is a bubbling cauldron of 2-D action platformer, Roguelike, and tower defense. AND IT'S STILL GREAT! When you die (WHEN you die), you upgrade various slots on your Mansion with the gold you earned going through Castle Hamson to better various skills and attain new abilities. Then (the most interesting, unexpected, and well-blended feature I've ever seen in a Roguelike video game) you choose one of three heirs to go through the castle again, with the new skills/abilities/equipment/runes you got with the previous character[s].
This game is a STEAL at $15. Get it now.

Starts out really addicting, but at a certain point it becomes a grind for money in which to level up your character. Unlike other roguelikes that introduces new powerups and abilities as you progress, your character traits and abilities are set before entering the dungeons, castles, and outdoor areas. New abilities and armor upgrades can be found littered throughout the areas in the form of challenges and chest drops. Abilities come in the form of Runes and armor upgrades drop from certain chests.
While it's a good encentive to replay the game over and over again to find all upgrades, it unfortunately requires money to equip them, which increases in cost after each purchase.
Along the way you'll pick up some passive powerups such as ones that gives you more money drops or another that lets the player walk on spikes, but they rarely change up the gameplay and is active only on the current playthrough until found again on other playthroughs. Majority of the time you're using your sword to attack with the addition of a side weapon that uses MP points, very much like Castlevania games.
Enemies often repeat thoughtout each of the form areas. Their size, color, and health are different, usually increasing for the difficulty. The boss enemies of each area are large and require a lot of damage. While they're fun and challenging to fight, you'll spend most of your time to grind even before attempting to take them on again. And after defeating them the first time, the next time you want to take them on, they are stronger, faster, and have different movements. The game also forces the player to  use a set character, but are given unlimited tries. In my opinion it's a poor choice to not allow the player to take on the original version of the boss. It makes most playthrough a money hunt and regular enemy whacking game.
Rogue Legacy is worthy of your time if you enjoy rogue-likes, but there are better ones out that reward the player better and have better incentives to keep playing.

Now in general I am not a big fan of "rogue" games, the idea that you need to start all over again, every time you die is annoying to me, but this game just looked really fun so I decided to buy it when it went on sale.  Each time you die in this game you get to keep all the loot and weapons you found in the previous run to upgrade your character in a number of different ways so you are not starting from sqaure one every time, and you always keep all your upgrades.
Each castle is randomnly generated, so every time you play the castle seems fresh, but there are certain things that are consistent in each generated castle.  The castle is divided into 4 sections, and they are in the same relative location each time you play(for example the forest is always located to the right, so if you keep going right you will eventually hit it) which makes exploring and reaching the areas you want to reach very seamless.
You also have the option of "locking down" the castle.  So you can replay the same castle if you think you missed some weapons/armor/runes, and more importantly you can lock down the castle so when you are ready to take on a boss you can just keep locking down the same castle and teleporting right to that boss(providing you find his location first) which makes multiple boss attempts very seamless and not frustrating at all.  usually the worst part of rogue games is replaying large boring sections just to replay the boss battle until you get it right, but you never have to do that in this game
Once you beat a boss, they are dead so you do not have to beat them all in one run.  Once you beat the game you unlock new game + and then new game ++, each substantially harder and more rewarding than the last.  I am not the kind of gamer who plays a game more than once, I usually beat a game and move right on to something else, but this is the first game since resident evil 4 which made me want to immedialtely replay it when it was over.
I cannot recomment this game enough, if you are into hack and slash metroidvania type games you will love this game, I usually do a pro/con section with my reviews but I can't think of anything about this game I did not like.  Just buy it, you will not regret it.

Rogue Legacy is one of those games that will help introduce you to the Roguelike genre. A typical Roguelike game will give you a single character starting out with basic weapons and armour (or neither in some cases), send you into a dungeon of sorts and expect you to make it to the end using whatever resources you can find. If you die, you start from scratch until you get it right.
Rogue Legacy takes the harshness of Roguelike games and gives players the opportunity to slowly adapt to the intensity of those in the genre, such as The Binding of Isaac, Spelunky and Legend of Dungeon. In Rogue Legacy, you initially start out with basic gear, but each time you die, the character that died leaves behind their weapons, armour and stats for the next one that comes along. Essentially you become stronger each time you die.
Additionally, each character you play as can have different traits, such as dwarfism, colourblindness, baldness and gigantism. Plus, each will have an individual magic skill (aside from the Archmage class that has three) that you can use, which gives character selection a lot more meaning.
As you play through the game you will also be able to unlock special classes and their upgraded variants which will make playing through dungeons easier (or possibly harder depending on your luck). These classes all have their own stat modifiers and special skills that you can use to make your way through every map.
The game also gives you access to weapons and armour that you can purchase at the blacksmith once you've obtained the blueprints for them (which you get inside chests). You also get access to enchantments for your weapons and armour that you can get from the Enchantress once you've obtained the relevant runes (which are found inside fairy chests). Thirdly, you have the ability to use the Architect to lock the dungeon to the last map you played through so that you can go back and try to beat certain rooms you failed at before. The only cost is you get less gold from your runs.
One last thing. Each time you go in the castle, you have to pay up all (or some) of your money to Charon. So spend your gold when you get it. No sense earning it all to get taken away.
If you haven't played any Roguelike games before and you want to get a feel for them, start with this one. It'll ease you into the genre perfectly and give you a lot of valuable experience you can use to overcome some of the newbie traps in more difficult Roguelike titles. If you have a bit of experience with them already, then Rogue Legacy will give you something different that other Roguelikes don't have, and variety is the spice of life.
Either way, it's a great game to play. Just expect to die a lot in the beginning. It'll take time for you to get ready to beat bosses.

To put it simply, if you enjoyed the original Life Is Strange then you'll enjoy this one, possibly even more. This prequel keeps the trend of the first game by having a rich and immersive story, interesting and relatable characters, and a great soundtrack to go along with it all.
If you haven't played the original, I highly suggest doing so first because it allows you to appreciate the prequel more, but it's not necessary because the prequel is just that good. It sets up the story and characters well enough that you wouldn't need the first game to enjoy it. I believe it has improved from the first game in terms of both the game engine (animations and lip-sync) and the dialogue (not cheesy or cliche).
I am eagerly awaiting the next episode, and if you need convincing to play the orginal, here's my review for it:
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Life Is Strange
To start off, this is the best choice-driven narrative game that I've ever played, and it opened me up to a new selection of music that I would of never heard otherwise. The first episode is free so there's no reason as to why you shouldn't at least try it.
I tried out Episode 1 because I was bored, and then proceded to stay up all night finishing the entire game because I was so hooked on the story and characters. Also you may or may not shed a tear at the end of Episode 5.
PROS
1. The story is amazing, if you immerse yourself in the game you will get invested in it easily. It touches upon real world subjects like bullying, suicide, and all sorts of things that add depth. It even has some dark twists and turns that keep you guessing throughout the game.
2. The soundtrack is amazing, the music sets the mood for the situation, aids the story telling process, and never brings you out of the moment.
3. The characters are relatable, considering most of them are based off sterotypes or cliques in a high school. On the surface they seem sterotypical, but as you play you learn more about them that builds their character to make each of them unique.
4. The choices you make throughout the game will affect you, some are small while others are big and their consequences are equally so. There are big events in certain parts of the game that will play out differently depending on multiple choices you made before hand.
5. The "rewind" feature makes this game stand out from other choice-driven narrative games, due to you being able to easily experiment and try out multiple options. It's hard to explain unless you've played it so go ahead and play it.
CONS (Gotta have an honest review)
1. There are only two endings to the game (Episode 5), and they don't take into account the choices you made throughout the game. I personally didn't mind too much because the journey to get to these endings and the choices that did affect my gameplay made it worthwhile.
2. The dialogue may seem a bit cliche or weird at times but it grew on me and I attributed to those characters which just added to the experience. Considering it was wrriten by grown French males for mainly teenage American characters it ain't too bad.

Let me get one thing clear straight away, I love this game! It hits all the right notes and I just hope so bad that the devs keep updating the game and adding new content. I played Classic but really didnt like how expensive everything was; as soon as I saw they were creating a one time payment game I couldnt wait.
The graphics and the audio for the most part are fantastic, while I would like to increase the draw distance its not as bad as the TheHunter Classic. There are a few sound bugs every now and then, epecially when you are close to water and its raining, the audio starts clipping and looping. Also I dont know how AA works in the game but I would like to be able to change it as I can still see jagged edges everywhere when in 1080.
Multiplayer is a lot of fun but this is where most of the work is needed; I have only played multiplayer for a few hours and there has been quite a few bugs. I have had a game where the other person couldnt hear or even see any of the animals that I could, another game where the other person couldnt get any of his items out even though they were in his inventory, and perhaps the worst thing for me with multiplayer is that only the host can unlock new camps, lookouts and anything else you can click on. Also we have to take it in turns to claim downed animals because only the person that harvests the animal gets a reward and there is no way to tell who hit it without clicking to harvest it.
Apart from the above problems I really have had a great time playing this game, I love the feeling of tracking an animal through forests and fields only to finally get that shot you wanted and hope that the animal doesnt run off for miles while spilling blood everywhere. You get a great feel of acomplishment with this game and it can be very rewarding. The items are quite expensive and take a long time to get and levelling is very very slow which is a pain when your waiting for those new skills and perks you so desperately need.
Things I would like to see added:
1. More animals - a lot more, especially birds as currently you cant harvest any flying animals.
2. More guns, scopes and other items like tents, portable hunting encloures, etc.
3. Missions for multiplayer, not everyone wants to go against each other, coop missions would be nice.
To me the game is still in early access but after some updates and new content I think this could be an amazing game. I know some of the new content will be DLC but I hope a good portion of it is free as the game does lack a bit of content at the moment especially in the flying department.
If and when things change I will update my review as necessary.

So I've decided ro review for this game as I see the previous hunter game didn't get much recommendations.
Firstly, this has to be the most beautiful game I've ever seen, it smashes any other game in terms of realistic colours and lighting, the sun bouncing off foliage is exactly replicated in this game and looks photorealistic when seen.
Secondly, the sounds are absolutely perfect, running through wetlands, rustling through bushes, all the sounds are perfectly recreated in this world, you can even hear the equipment your wearing rubbing against the objects around you.
Now I get onto the hunting, which is in it's early days and constantly being improved, the devs are hot on problems, and I no longer get crashes. There are few bugs, when playing for an extended amount of time, tracks and scents seem to stop being generated, making it almost impossible to hunt anything.
The actual hunting in itself is pretty decent, there's a nice flow to tracking to stalking to then finally killing the game, animals will nearly always hear you if you walk or run, so following a "fresh" track normally means crouching and taking it slow, running around everywhere wont get you any results, so if you're impatient, or don't like waiting 20-30 minutes + for a shot, then you obviously have never been hunting!
It's not all about stalking though, there are open areas where there may be drinking, feeding or resting areas, and near there, is most likely a chance to build a lookout stand, this is great fun if you dont want to be stalking, but requires patience as the area around you may only be visited at certain times of the day, so time management is key with sitting and waiting.
Once you actually find something to shoot, it's not a matter of shooting it "wherever" there is an art to knowing where and when to shoot, shoot them in the wrong place, and you're basically being cruel and irresponsible. shoot them through the heart, you'll most likely get a clean and instant death, and PETA goes home happy.
When you DO kill an animal, you'll get a reward based on the following, the animal you killed, whether it has a trophy rating, how long it took to die, the integrity of the shot (the right weapon choice) and obviously where the animal was shot. Getting a gold rating is always a big thing in this game, the ability to track, stalk and shoot an animal properly and cleanly, and this game graces the player when they complete this correctly.
Overall, some of the things I would like to see in the future include small game hunting, as an Englishman myself, I hunt rabbits with night vision, and do alot of pest control, night vision sights would be a great addition to the game, but also small game hunting. another great addition would be birds, pheasants for the english, ducks for the americans, would be incredibly entertaining and I look forward to what the game brings in the future.
I would recommend this game if you hunt in real life, if you don't this might be abit dull if you don't understand why this game is so good, but if your looking to buy something straight out rather than pay a subscription, this game is for you.

Rogue Legacy is one of those games that will help introduce you to the Roguelike genre. A typical Roguelike game will give you a single character starting out with basic weapons and armour (or neither in some cases), send you into a dungeon of sorts and expect you to make it to the end using whatever resources you can find. If you die, you start from scratch until you get it right.
Rogue Legacy takes the harshness of Roguelike games and gives players the opportunity to slowly adapt to the intensity of those in the genre, such as The Binding of Isaac, Spelunky and Legend of Dungeon. In Rogue Legacy, you initially start out with basic gear, but each time you die, the character that died leaves behind their weapons, armour and stats for the next one that comes along. Essentially you become stronger each time you die.
Additionally, each character you play as can have different traits, such as dwarfism, colourblindness, baldness and gigantism. Plus, each will have an individual magic skill (aside from the Archmage class that has three) that you can use, which gives character selection a lot more meaning.
As you play through the game you will also be able to unlock special classes and their upgraded variants which will make playing through dungeons easier (or possibly harder depending on your luck). These classes all have their own stat modifiers and special skills that you can use to make your way through every map.
The game also gives you access to weapons and armour that you can purchase at the blacksmith once you've obtained the blueprints for them (which you get inside chests). You also get access to enchantments for your weapons and armour that you can get from the Enchantress once you've obtained the relevant runes (which are found inside fairy chests). Thirdly, you have the ability to use the Architect to lock the dungeon to the last map you played through so that you can go back and try to beat certain rooms you failed at before. The only cost is you get less gold from your runs.
One last thing. Each time you go in the castle, you have to pay up all (or some) of your money to Charon. So spend your gold when you get it. No sense earning it all to get taken away.
If you haven't played any Roguelike games before and you want to get a feel for them, start with this one. It'll ease you into the genre perfectly and give you a lot of valuable experience you can use to overcome some of the newbie traps in more difficult Roguelike titles. If you have a bit of experience with them already, then Rogue Legacy will give you something different that other Roguelikes don't have, and variety is the spice of life.
Either way, it's a great game to play. Just expect to die a lot in the beginning. It'll take time for you to get ready to beat bosses.

A metroid-vania Rogue-like game with a randomly generated castle and and enemy placement but permanent stat progression and boss death.
Enemies have tricks to them and every room is it's own challenge, you'll be taking it slow and steady. While there's only four main areas the design of the setup phase adds depth instead of...
I'll call it "purposeless restarts with flavour", if that makes sense. More so than most Rogue-likes can claim.
This game singlehandedly made my change my mind about playing Rogue-likes in that fashion.
It's hard to get into at first, you might feel like you're making no progress, but you'll find traits in your character selection that will compliment your playstyle and it's smooth sailing from there.
Other upgrades are sprinkled in that make finding one, or completing the challenge for one, extremely rewarding. It's inspirations are plain to see, and it mashes them together very well.
The only bad thing I can think of off the top of my head is that the characters you can choose from when you die and restart could use more variety. You'll start to see everything about 10-20 times by time you beat it. And the story isn't the best, but it's certainly functional and thematic.
A recommendation goes to fans of the genre, and some people who are skeptical of the genre but still mildly interested.

An absurdly fun and addictive experience, Rogue Legacy achieves exactly what it sets out to achieve. This game is simple to start, but incredibly deep as you continue. For every life, you find yourself assessing the situation, and deciding whether or not actions are worth the risk. With a compelling mysteriousness brought by scattered snippets of story, you find a strange urge to press on that battles with a fear of death that is quite powerful despite each life being meaningless in the grander scheme. A hearty reccomend for anyone who enjoys metroidvenia style action platformers, or even people who enjoy the more tactical resource management that is brought by games like dark souls.
