(Mad Max was played according to the following PC SPECS:
GIGABYTE P55W
Intel i7 5700HQ
NVIDIA Geforce GTX 970m 3GB
8GB RAM
Windows 10 Home x64)
Mad Max, what a lovely game...
Mad Max is a post-apocolyptic action/adventure game in which you take control of Max Rockatansky, a road warrior searching for supposed "Plains of Slience" in order to escape madness. On his journey, he is attacked by Scabrous Scrotus and nearly killed. Max's car is stolen and he is now forced to build a new vehicle to replace it.
The goal of Mad Max is very simple: build the most powerful car you can inorder to easily progress through the story. To do this, you are to aquire scrap from the wasteland, do favours for stronghold leaders, and progress through the story. Almost all upgrades will have a benefit and a disadvantage to them, which encourages the player to make strategic decisions on how they want to build their car. The car is fully customizable, which truly makes the creation feel like your own.
OPTIMIZATION: 10/10
Mad Max is truly one of the best optimized games I have ever played. I am able to run the game on 1920x1080 with full details on everything. The game runs supposedly at 75fps but because of my monitors refresh rate being locked at 60hz, the game stayed at 60fps for the majority of the game. Frame drops to 55fps were seen in the Gastown area, most likely the cause of the higher density in the enviroment.
GRAPHICS: 9/10
Not a single Wasteland since the Fallout wastelands have made me say, "wow." Screenshots speak for themselves, this game is absolutely stunning. Vehicles have great emphasis on the scratches and dents with great depth. Characters look rugged and ruined by the trials of the Wasteland. Unfortunately, facing several characters in close proximity will reveal some low resolution textures. This is well covered by the game being in third-person.
STORY: 7/10
Mad Max's story did lock me in to play it for 30 hours before completing the story. The story is somewhat based off of the Fury Road Prequel Comic. I feel, however, that it would've been best for the story to be completely original, perhaps somehow picking up after the events of Fury Road.
GAMEPLAY: 8/10
Car combat was supposed to be the biggest focus of the game, but Max will also spend a lot of time on the ground, fighting. Driving a car in Mad Max feels like being behind the wheel of a war machine. Collision and impact have a real feel to them and general driving feels heavy or light, depending on what you are driving.
A big controversy over this game was the fact that it uses the same melee combat system that Batman games use. I do not know much about the Batman series as I have never played them. That said, I really did enjoy the fighting system in the game. The system made Max feel like a badass fist fighter. Crunches, blows, and swinging, looked, sounded, and felt painful as I delivered a 30 hit combo on a legion of War Boys in Fury mode. I did feel that the fighting system got repetative though. I wish that more time would've been spent in cars.
SOUND: 9/10
The Wasteland is windy and full of loud cars. Sounds deliver great ambience to the game and truly make you feel like you are in a new world. Cars sound heavy, strong, and intimidating, which is stronger once you begin to reach the end game. Voice acting is top-notch, with genuine feel to characters. The VAs captured each character's personality and you can personally know each character because of this.
VERDICT: 9/10
Mad Max is a lovely game that made for a fun experience of sitting at home for several days, trying to build a very spiky car.

As a long time fan of the Mad Max movies, I was looking forward to this game and I am not disappointed.  The combination of driving combat and hand to hand combat against a variety of foes is most enjoyable, and the vehicle customization gives you goals to work for. I have no problem with the controls, and the missions. The landscape of this world is right out of the movie Fury Road and very well done, and with no intrusive music soundtrack, which I appreciate .  Kudos!
Good combat, good driving mechanics, interesting characters, and fun stuff to do. Everything is really well implemented, and im very pleasantly surprised to find that the game is just really good.

This is a good game… but also not a good game. How do I explain? Quick thoughts below:
Just a line on the graphics and the performance of the game, both are excellent, it is a lovely ,looking game and it runs flawlessly (bodes well for Just Cause 3), now onto the game itself.
Mad Max about 3 things, Driving, Fighting and Upgrading your car, everything else in the game is merely a vehicle (no pun intended) to allow you to do one of those 3 things. Tasks in Mad Max are repetitive with copy and paste quests and objectives as you explore the map, which some people, including myself would describe as busy work, or padding, or even grinding if I were to be harsh.
Thing is though, they are all tasks which let you do three things;  Almost always you’ll first be driving around meaning you’ll be blowing up, ramming and dismantling other cars with your harpoon gun whilst hurtling through an apocalyptic Australian outback complete with dried up seabed’s and places to explore and scavenge.
You'll then get to where you're going and you'll be Fighting, usually against multiple opponents in an Arkham style fighting system with brutal animations and sound effects, Max isn't a well-trained ninja but a brawler, handy in a fight and able to look after himself and that really comes across.
After that you'll have earned some scrap to upgrade your car, as well as Max, buying new engines, tyres, armour, weapons, special moves etc etc.
And... rinse then repeat. It is this pattern over and over with some slight variance here and there for story missions. Whether you like this game or not comes down to how much you enjoy those 3 things, and for me, I really did. That's why I played it for 41 hours and finished a lot of the game before doing the story.
Of course it isn’t totally as simple as that, there are other things for you to do and even the above 3 activities are wrapped up in narrative driven reasoning or have a tagged on objective, but trust me when I say you’ll always be driving, fighting and upgrading. That is the meat and potatoes of Mad Max.
Those 3 mechanics might not work for some and therefore they would bounce right off it and think it is an average or even a poor game. Not in my eyes, one of the most enjoyable games in 2015 for me and I hope you think the same should you give it a go.

CONS!

A few months ago I made a review about The Hunter that got a several hundred "helpful" tags. The review basically read that the game was beautiful but severely broken due to bugs that made the game crash along with a multitude of smaller glitches that made it a less than pleasant experience.
Since then Expansive Worlds have been very busy fixing the worst of the bugs and they've been active in ironing out the glitches. I'd say that it's a very playable game now so dont let the "mixed" reviews scare you. Most of the negative reviews are about the DLC or the bugs from older builds of the game.
The DLC that was released not long ago is far from a must-have. You can ignore it and enjoy the core game just fine.
Old review below.
theHunter: Call of the wild is really a bittersweet experience. The landscapes and forests are some of the best that I’ve ever seen in a game. Nothing so far comes close to the beautiful scenery in Call of the wild. It’s very relaxing & the gameplay itself is what you can expect from a hunting game. The gameplay is slow and needs a lot of patience. The ambient sounds and weather effects are all excellent & really immersive. The animals look great and the animations look good.
Now the bitter part. theHunter: Call of the wild plays and feels as if it’s an early alpha. It’s riddled with bugs and quirks that really screws up the fun. The main thing that screw it up are the random crashes. There doesn’t seem to be a correlation between them and there’s no way to avoid it as far as I know. I even had my stats, inventory and cash all reset back to default after several hours of playtime.
In multiplayer, there are a lot of bugs as well. Simply by clicking “multiplayer” in the game menu it will randomly kick a player from my server. It does not save progress in terms of your current location & if you disconnect while you’ve  taken part in a multiplayer competition on the server it will count as if you’re back on square 1 once you reconnect.
It’s all very annoying little bugs that feel like something you could expect from an incomplete early access game. But a full release? Unacceptable.
The game is amazing while it actually works though. I hope that the developers will sort these bugs out soon.
If you’re looking to buy this game I suggest you head over to theHunters discussion forum & check the latest news for the game & see if they’ve recently patched it. If there’s a lot of complaints about crashes & whatnot then I suggest you wait.
Once they fix these bugs I will edit my review & give it a thumbs up.
As you can see by the developer response to this review they did sort out the worst of the bugs, namely the random crashes and they are working on fixing some QoL stuff related to the menu which is much appreciated. Multiplayer is still wonky in terms of progress not saving, joined players cant save outposts etc but at this point I feel like the game deserves to be recommended. As a single player experience it's a solid game & certainly the best hunting game that I have played.

I actually both recommend and do not recommend this game, because it's really about your tastes.
The game itself is straightfoward, you play a knight and try to beat the castle. You can level up to get a little better and spend gold to make a better caslte, and make better future knights.  There are bosses that remind me of old school games and plenty of abilities to earn by runes and armor.
This is where the path splits, because early on the game is hard enough to make you rip out your hair, and each character only has one life (technically), as well as the castle being randomized each time (technically), thus you can get a really, REALLY good knight and a really, REALLY hard castle and die within minutes, making the whole run a waste of time.  Being that gold is reset when you enter the castle (technically) as well it makes it hard to get any upgrades sometimes.
Some characters have a chance to defy death and come back to life and you can pay the architecht 10% of what you earn to keep the castle the same for another run, and there is an ability to give less gold to the reaper to enter the castle, so not all is completely lost.
But overall the game takes days upon days of playing before you can even go to some parts of the castle, and while this may not seem like a bad thing, (a game having some actual play time a bad thing?), it is more or less artifical play time, as you wont be able to go to more than 1/4th the castle for quite a while.
If you have some patience and aren't easily frustrated this game is good, but if you're looking for something to play to just relax from a hard day then I advise you to look elsewhere.

A lot of people call this "Open World Game: The Open World Game". A lot of people will hate on this because it does nothing especially new with the open world genre, or close combat fighting systems, given that the fighting is basically completley cribbed off Batman: Arkham Location's fighting system pretty much.
Personally I don't think these people are wrong, but they are focusing far too much on that. When it gets down to it, Mad Max is a very capable, very good open world game. There's lots of sidequests and things to do, taking out camps is a lot of fun, clearing out convoys, upgrading strongholds, upgrading the car and Max's equipment and max himself are great fun, the scavenger hunt for history relics is actually really interesting and really does enrich the world and setting...
There's a good deal of great characters used remarkably well too, though the scant female presence in the game is relegated to 'current necessary "move the plot forward" key', 'damsel in distress who could have been way more badass but in the end is merely a mcguffin for the story' and  'cute kid you see almost nothing of'. This is a little bit of a shame, but ultimately doesn't detract too much from the game's story.
Speaking of, I personally feel that the game's story is exceptionally well done. It's really well shot and acted, the graphics are fantastic and even when you aren't playing on full graphics with everything turned on it still looks great (apart from shadows feeling a little shonky at times). The cars drive well, the missions are great fun, and the story plays out wonderfully.
Hhhoooweeeverr... I do have one pressing issue. I am a big fan of all four Mad Max films. I actually have gained a new appreciation for even Beyond Thunderdome, despite how cheesy it is at times and how it devolves into Peter Pan: Wasteland Edition at the end. In all but the first one, Max isn't really the main character. He's not the character the story is really about. He is an observer to, a reluctant participant in, and essentially the mcguffin OF the storyline. The Road Warrior is more about a group of escaping survivors and their plan to be free of their pursuers. Thunderdome is about the rise and fall of Auntie Entity. Fury Road is about the rebellion of and eventual rise to power of Imperator Furiosa through brutal conquest. In all three of those, Max is simply (to steal a line from HL2), "the right man in the wrong place".
I suppose when it comes down to it, the game is more of a call back to the first film, where the story is rather squarely centralised around him, and that isn't necessarily a bad thing. It does feel a little like it's lacking somehow as a result, but honestly if you see it as a prequel to Fury Road, it does work rather surprisingly well, and the way it's all executed really grants a lot of depth to Max and his madness. There's lots of subtle details here and there, lots of tidbits of details that let you fill in the gaps on your own without you being left scratching your head in confusion.
Gameplay of course is pretty much rock solid, driving works great, fighting is visceral and brutal and very kinetic, and there's a lot to keep you busy. However I did find myself at certain points going through sidequests just so I could fully upgrade the car and wishing, wishing I didn't have to deal wth certain things. I imagine if you just went for the main plotline, the game would be over fairly quickly. I'd guess I spent the majority of my hours doing sidequests, exploring scavenging locations, building projects in strongholds and just bumming around doing stupid crap in the wastes, but I still had fun for the most part.
It does everything right for an Open World game, but it excels at very little. Nevertheless its story is definately worth experiencing and the game is really well done. Very, very, VERY few faults, and an exceptional port for PC.
Worth picking up, definately.

So what do I think of this game?
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;dr version:
Overall I give it an 8 / 10.
Should you get it? If you are worried about bugs/glitches then I would wait until they get some patches going to make the game more stable. Other than that, I say get it and enjoy it. It's amazing!
The new-release crashes/issues are dragging down the experience a bit (though this is of course temporary until they get it fixed) and the somewhat limited amount of animals and gear (compared to my experience in Classic) means it has some extra efforts needed to be put in to give a higher rating.
On the positive side it has amazing graphics, fun gameplay (easy to get into and find animals to shoot) and a progression and mission system which allows you to forget the time and stay in the game for hours. The developers have shown in the Classic that they always keep adding content to the game. I am confident they will do the same for this game.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
First off lets take a moment and realize that the game is fresh out the door at time of writing (currently patch 1.21), and some of things I will be mentioning in this review may be resolved in the near future.
(most of these are related to current issues and content, both which I am convinced will be improved upon in future).
So how what is missing compared to the Classic?
What I am hoping for in the future:
More animals (small game and birds especially)
More weapons
More equipment
Doggies!
Placeable equipment
All of these things I am sure will be coming in the future though. The Classic game has had many years of regularly adding content to the game to expand it to the huge hunting game it is now with such a rich and varied amount of content.
I have complete faith in this game as well and trust the developers to be adding more and more content to this game over the coming months and years ahead to make this new hunting game just as rich and amazing as it's older brother.
Stay with it and great things will happen!
Needs a few more animals and zones, but it has great potential. Loving it so far.

My TheHunter: COTW Review.
Graphics: The graphics are very pretty and really well done but it is sorta a wool cover over our eyes on whats hiddenly broken about this game.
Hunting: You have to either get a rare one hit shot on the game your hunting and take it down in that one shot but most of the time you will find yourself shooting an elk or bear or boar more than enough to take it down doesn't matter if you shot it in the spine or leg it well still be able to run. Also you can't hunt small game such as rabbits or other small critters same goes for birds you can't hunt those either. Also it would be interesting if they add fishing that is a form of hunting.
Shop-Locker: You spend hours gathering enough money for that one rifle you wanted for some reason it's more than 1k but you buy it anyways just to realise that you just spent $42,000 on a basic looking rifle no carved animals on it's stock no gold or silver enlays nothing just wood maybe some cheap camo bullet holder on the side nothing fancy isn't like you just spent aton of money. Then you notice for $680 you can get a signle pack of 10 rounds for your said rifle. "Side Note"
irl you can get a deer hunting rifle as cheap as $350 and for $20 you can get some hunting rounds for a scope it can be very cheap like the rifle or less or it can rack your price up to 6 times the price of the rifle.

Now of course in time there might be an update where they make the ui look way better but as of now it makes me think our hunters we are playing have a pair of google glasses on that's how bad it looks maybe have a more realistic looking map or have a campos that looks like something a hunter or hiking has. Maybe the ammo count is a pouch or something so it's more realistic looking either way it doesn't look that great.
Realisim: Now i know it's a video game but it's trying to be like a realistic hunting sim. I feel like just playing it these devs didn't do any research they were doing far more research in making the 2 maps look as realistic as they could or pretty as they could. Instead of going on irl hunting trips or just watching videos on it. Something that can give them a taste on what it is like. Then how it is now in the game where it almost feels like a pay to win but you can't pay with real money only in game.
Weapons: Where is all the 22's and air rifles. That's what id want to see people hunt with those type of weapons in Euro and Germany same with the west.
Gameplay: You well be able to spend lots of hours hunting unlocking new weapons exploring messing around in multiplayer. Finding all the relics or easter eggs. Climbing up high places taking pics of animals. Just enjoying the view

A few acoustic guitar notes, played right when the game is launched. That's all it took to get right back into the vibe of Life is Strange.
It's truly impressive how captivating the series has been thus far; the solid 10/10 rating on Steam is no coincidence by any means. Reason enough for this short prequel title to achieve an as impressive launch as Life is Strange Season One.
The story unfolds quickly, answering burning questions left by the first season about the life of Chloe Price, a non-apologetic social outcast with a 24/7 "♥♥♥♥ you"-morale, dealing with the difficulties of a teenager's life. Living the rebel phase, picking fights and headbanging to metal while trying to blur out reality and the past that formed her current situation.
Now this is basically all I can say without spoiling most it right away; with only the first of three episodes out, I already feel like this game delivered.
Sure, the game is not going to be as long and as in-depth in regards to explorability and secondary characters compared to episodes of Season One. The emphasis here is mainly on Chloe and understanding the madness and struggles of that character in the story before the time of Season One.
Safe to say is if you liked the first game you'll not be disappointed by this in the slightest, I cannot wait until the next episode is out. Also if you didn't play Season One you can check out the first episode of it for free.
Just be advised that playing this game is going to be an emotionally overwhelming experience, an outstanding showcase of video games as an art form and storytelling medium.

The feels... all the feels... are back straightaway. I love how this focuses more on Chloe, shows what is really going on inside of her, and gets the whole Life Is Strange look and feel again.
Also, I wonder how emotion wrecking it would be to make someone play this BEFORE Life is Strange...
The feels. Shut up and take my money!

I guess that's where the open minded would induce a prison riot or something for entertainment but I like games with more clear objectives. Even simcity games you were always trying to break million people or stockpile so much cash. I think it will be very worthwhile once it's released, but at current price for early access I can't recommend.

A few acoustic guitar notes, played right when the game is launched. That's all it took to get right back into the vibe of Life is Strange.
It's truly impressive how captivating the series has been thus far; the solid 10/10 rating on Steam is no coincidence by any means. Reason enough for this short prequel title to achieve an as impressive launch as Life is Strange Season One.
The story unfolds quickly, answering burning questions left by the first season about the life of Chloe Price, a non-apologetic social outcast with a 24/7 "♥♥♥♥ you"-morale, dealing with the difficulties of a teenager's life. Living the rebel phase, picking fights and headbanging to metal while trying to blur out reality and the past that formed her current situation.
Now this is basically all I can say without spoiling most it right away; with only the first of three episodes out, I already feel like this game delivered.
Sure, the game is not going to be as long and as in-depth in regards to explorability and secondary characters compared to episodes of Season One. The emphasis here is mainly on Chloe and understanding the madness and struggles of that character in the story before the time of Season One.
Safe to say is if you liked the first game you'll not be disappointed by this in the slightest, I cannot wait until the next episode is out. Also if you didn't play Season One you can check out the first episode of it for free.
Just be advised that playing this game is going to be an emotionally overwhelming experience, an outstanding showcase of video games as an art form and storytelling medium.

The feels... all the feels... are back straightaway. I love how this focuses more on Chloe, shows what is really going on inside of her, and gets the whole Life Is Strange look and feel again.
Also, I wonder how emotion wrecking it would be to make someone play this BEFORE Life is Strange...
The feels. Shut up and take my money!

Undertale is a GameMaker game combining RPG and bullet hell, in which combat is completely optional in every fight. It's very lightweight, able to be run on pretty much any system. The game focuses more on character interactions and its storyline, rather than on gameplay itself, and can be pretty boring if you're just playing for the combat. The game stresses pacifism, and you're able to get out of (nearly) any fight without actually attacking. An additional mechanic of Undertale is its ability to break the 4th wall, and do some pretty unexpected things.
The game features a cast of well-developed characters, great soundtrack, and creative combat mechanics. Keep in mind that in order to get the full experience of Undertale, you'll need to play each of the three routes: Neutral, Pacifist, and Genocide.

username: Mr JC Denton in Da Fresh
text:
It is quite ironic that the game which everyone was expecting to fail miserably, ends up being the "Surprise of the Year." Of all the WB games that were released on the PC this year, only Mad Max didn't crash and burn in terms of performance. The game's well-optimized state is a huge contrast to the Arkham Knight disaster.
As a game, Mad Max succeeds in doing what the devs (Avalanche) and distributor (WB) set out to do, which is to recreate the Mad Max experience in a video game. And boy they did. The car combat in Mad Max is fantastic and the foot combat, while it looks like a cheap copy of the combat you see in the Batman: Arkham series manages to hold it's own well enough. Every time you see Max break someone's arm or German Suplex him into the sand, you can almost feel it. While there isn't much variety in terms of enemies and the gameplay does get rather repetitive after a while, you're still guaranteed to have one hell of a time.
Surprisingly, Mad Max The Game does have a decent story. While it's pretty straightforward, you do find yourself caring for a few characters including the ever-spouting nonsense Chumbucket. Which makes the ending even worse. Most players aren't happy with Mad Max's ending and when you finally played till there, you'll know why. But I won't spoil it, it's something players have to experience for themselves but I can say it's very very typical of a Mad Max story.
If there's anything I dislike about the game, it's that the open-world is way too bland. You'd be expecting something like the Fallout series, considering the post-apocalyptic setting but the world design is just vast and empty. You'll find a few tiny camps here and there, then there's the bigger camps where you carry out objectives and get more scrap, upgrades and blueprints to upgrade the strongholds of the allies you'll meet on Max's story. But, that's all. There's nothing really exciting to find in this world.
Mad Max is a game to pick up if you're one for intense car combat and plenty of driving. If you're the type that complains about driving too much in a game like GTA for example, then this is not the game for you. If it's up your alley, try playing it in first-person mode. It's difficult but it makes for a very interesting experience as well. Mad Max is no GOTY contender but it's a solid game through and through.

Big Metroidvania fan, especially Castlevania, and after finishing the main quest of Rogue Legacy I have mixed feelings. I enjoyed the roguelike take on sidescrolling castle crawling, but it started to grate on me the further I played.
Rogue Legacy really is fun initially, with tight controls and plenty of challenge in the dungeons, but I got sick and tired of grinding after a while. After 15 or so hours, the random character element stopped adding anything - if you get something that you know isn't suited for bossfights (or whatever objective you've set for yourself), you can either grind the castle again or just kill yourself and hope for better luck.
After a few hours, the building blocks the level generator uses start becoming familiar and that fresh, random feeling goes away. There are just too few options for the game to alternate between.
I also felt that the gold requirements to buy runes and upgrade the keep got out of hand quickly, until you beat the game and NG+ starts paying out. I really think that a secondary currency for progression, beyond gold, would help the game out.
All in all, I'd recommend this for the great first dozen or so hours I had with it, until it turned into a chore.

So back when I was just in my teens I watched 3 random youtubers play this new game I had never heard of before. The game was called "Arma II" and they said it was a "mod" called "DayZ". I didnt know what a mod was, what Arma meant, or why this game was called DayZ. But having watched such shows as "Survivorman" and "Man Vs Wild" I instantly fell in love with the game. It was exactly what I was looking for, something for the hardcore survivor geeks. I quickly learned that not only was this a survivor type game but also a zombie game, I didnt really care for zombies but I saw that it added a certain flavor to the game, a certain mood. But most of all this was my first time being introduced to this type of "MMO PVP" style of game, the unease of knowing anyone could be watching at anytime was something I didn't know could be in a video game.
I came to watch many youtubers play this game and lived through them, sharing in their experiences. I eventually found Frankie's videos and those changed how I saw the game completely. Like many others I found out that DayZ is what you make it. Frankie made it into something worth watching and waiting on, something that had depth and an underelying story but that you could still be silly in.
I wanted this game so bad but at the time I didn't have a Pc that could run anything else besides Lego Island. So I just became content with watching. Until I found out that the man behind the mod had plans to make his own standalone game.
I was so excited, I saved up for almost a year in anticipation of the release. Some people don't undertand why we were so excited at that time, but y'all have to understand that this was the modern day equilivelent of PlayerUnknown releasing PUBG. We wanted to hop on this wagon because of the asured destination, a game that in time would succeed the mod.
I couldn't buy it right away but I purchased it sometime between initial release and when they had fixed the axe positioning (originally the axe was at a weird sideways angle, was playing before the movement update somewhere around there).
Here I was, first time ever playing DayZ, finally ready to make my story. I first spawned in as a black female, not the race or gender I had originally chosen, walked in the first building I found which was the construction layer cake building. Walked up the stairs, fell through the floor and broke my legs, zombie came and ate my face off.
Welcome to the Standalone.
I realized this was not the same game I once had a passion for, it was different. Still though I was determined to see this new experience through, I gave this game a solid chance. For as long as I played this game I've only had a handful of great experiences, but those experiences were absolutely amazing, something that could only happen in this game and the mod. The players were clever, atleast early on, which made for these mini stories to be had.
But after all that waiting and saving up and anticipation, it wasn't enough. I'm glad I had those times but in retrospect it wasn't worth it for the amount of time I invested in. It would be different if the game wasn't riddled with player killing glitches, the game only becomes enjoyable after the first 90 deaths because it takes that long to figure out where not to step, or to test the ground with a can of soda before dropping your weapon so that it doesn't get swallowed up.
To go through with this game you need to have alot of love for it, and some people have invested in much more time then I have and still have advised against getting this game. It would be different if the game had made any forward progress but unfortunately that is not the case. I'm still glad I was initially insterested in this game because it opened the door to learning about this great genre. I now have a love not just for survival games but also for more slowpaced games as well. Games like Arma III, Squad, Miscreated, The Long Dark, Escape from Tarkov etc. And it introduced me to the content creators of such games.
3 years ago I fell through the floor in my first time playing DayZ, 3 years later and it still happens to the most seasoned players.
This game isn't broken, something has to be whole to be broken.

Prison Architect Review
Topics covered:
- The game in a nutshell
- Worried about buying an Alpha?
The game in a nutshell.
Prison Architect is a Management Sim in which you build a prison from the ground - up. Some features include; construction, electricity and water supply, recruitment, patrols allocation, prison security, riot control and so forth. In essence, I guess the game is actually about securing those prisoners and prventing escapes but the game shows how much thought has to go into such a task, which on the face of it, may seem to be a rather basic task.
The monetary system works well, there is a modding system for the community to develop, prisoners AI works well... and most importantly, the game is fun. A recent update has given prisoners personalities which make the game more random, with some prisoners being more volatile than others, or extremely strong, amongst other random traits - all of which make the game all the more interesting. The recent introduction of snitches has also been a cool addition to the game as well as the 'Protective Custody' feature.
There is so much to say about Prison Architect. If management sims are your thing, Prison Architect is a great addition to your titles.
Worried about buying an Alpha?
I bought this indie on a whim. I like management sims and as so few good ones come out nowadays, I took the risk. Todays PC gamer is of course not unclimatised to risk in the purchase of indie games. I have a few heer on Steam which I purchased way too early and haven't been developed further in ages. This game is not one of those - not by a long shot. If you follow the development of this Alpha, you will find updates are frequent and detailed, often via a 1hr or so YouTube clip discuissing new game features. Plus; I trust these developers not because I am naive but because I can tell that these guys are developing this game for their own entertainment as much it is a profit venture. These guys are clearly passionate about the Prison Architect. In summary, as a game in development Prison Architect is well into its Alpha stage (in its current state it is certainly passable as a game in its own right) and thus, the purchase of the game in its current state is in fact a great buy. This game is the quintessential reason as to why I still purchase indie games during Alpha and Beta develpment.

text:
It is quite ironic that the game which everyone was expecting to fail miserably, ends up being the "Surprise of the Year." Of all the WB games that were released on the PC this year, only Mad Max didn't crash and burn in terms of performance. The game's well-optimized state is a huge contrast to the Arkham Knight disaster.
As a game, Mad Max succeeds in doing what the devs (Avalanche) and distributor (WB) set out to do, which is to recreate the Mad Max experience in a video game. And boy they did. The car combat in Mad Max is fantastic and the foot combat, while it looks like a cheap copy of the combat you see in the Batman: Arkham series manages to hold it's own well enough. Every time you see Max break someone's arm or German Suplex him into the sand, you can almost feel it. While there isn't much variety in terms of enemies and the gameplay does get rather repetitive after a while, you're still guaranteed to have one hell of a time.
Surprisingly, Mad Max The Game does have a decent story. While it's pretty straightforward, you do find yourself caring for a few characters including the ever-spouting nonsense Chumbucket. Which makes the ending even worse. Most players aren't happy with Mad Max's ending and when you finally played till there, you'll know why. But I won't spoil it, it's something players have to experience for themselves but I can say it's very very typical of a Mad Max story.
If there's anything I dislike about the game, it's that the open-world is way too bland. You'd be expecting something like the Fallout series, considering the post-apocalyptic setting but the world design is just vast and empty. You'll find a few tiny camps here and there, then there's the bigger camps where you carry out objectives and get more scrap, upgrades and blueprints to upgrade the strongholds of the allies you'll meet on Max's story. But, that's all. There's nothing really exciting to find in this world.
Mad Max is a game to pick up if you're one for intense car combat and plenty of driving. If you're the type that complains about driving too much in a game like GTA for example, then this is not the game for you. If it's up your alley, try playing it in first-person mode. It's difficult but it makes for a very interesting experience as well. Mad Max is no GOTY contender but it's a solid game through and through.

Big Metroidvania fan, especially Castlevania, and after finishing the main quest of Rogue Legacy I have mixed feelings. I enjoyed the roguelike take on sidescrolling castle crawling, but it started to grate on me the further I played.
Rogue Legacy really is fun initially, with tight controls and plenty of challenge in the dungeons, but I got sick and tired of grinding after a while. After 15 or so hours, the random character element stopped adding anything - if you get something that you know isn't suited for bossfights (or whatever objective you've set for yourself), you can either grind the castle again or just kill yourself and hope for better luck.
After a few hours, the building blocks the level generator uses start becoming familiar and that fresh, random feeling goes away. There are just too few options for the game to alternate between.
I also felt that the gold requirements to buy runes and upgrade the keep got out of hand quickly, until you beat the game and NG+ starts paying out. I really think that a secondary currency for progression, beyond gold, would help the game out.
All in all, I'd recommend this for the great first dozen or so hours I had with it, until it turned into a chore.

Life is Strange follows the TellTale release pattern (episodic releases every month or so, until the end of the season). The game is played in several acts, across several episodes. It is precariously on the edge of being a walking simulator if not for the BioWare-esque dialogue system, and dialogue-related puzzles. There is minimal basic adventure-game-standard puzzle solving. It is a game that has no action sequences, not even any quick-time events, all action is cinematic (yet still engaging).
Before the Storm is a prequel, but I must fully advise you to
(The previous game). I can't imagine this game being nearly as impactful if it is your first entry. If nothing else, if you're new to the series, playing the original first will give them time to get the remaining episodes out for Before The Storm. The first episode of that game is free, and will prepare you for no money, to experience the LiS formula (The interactive drama).
I wholeheartedly expected myself not to play it, or at least to wait until the season was completed. But I caved, and I'm glad I did. The writing is solid, despite being handled by a different development team than Season One. The original team is working on an actual sequel, which will not feature the same characters. This game is about Rachel and Chloe, who in one-way-or-another were present in the first game. I am going to avoid spoilers, and not elaborate.
I can tell you that those of you who enjoyed the first game will enjoy this. It's kind of killing me not to be playing Max, but the game succeeds fully with its own merit, while rewarding returning fans.
This is not a game for a lot of people, but if you're willing to try a game that focuses on EFFIN' INTENSE storytelling over almost any other metric, this is a game for you. If it seems they're rushing the story a little, they are. It's because fans already know where it's headed, and they had fewer episodes to get us from A-B. Also, the characters are younger -- everything is intense when you're younger. I could have lived with better pacing, but I'm hooked again.

It is quite ironic that the game which everyone was expecting to fail miserably, ends up being the "Surprise of the Year." Of all the WB games that were released on the PC this year, only Mad Max didn't crash and burn in terms of performance. The game's well-optimized state is a huge contrast to the Arkham Knight disaster.
As a game, Mad Max succeeds in doing what the devs (Avalanche) and distributor (WB) set out to do, which is to recreate the Mad Max experience in a video game. And boy they did. The car combat in Mad Max is fantastic and the foot combat, while it looks like a cheap copy of the combat you see in the Batman: Arkham series manages to hold it's own well enough. Every time you see Max break someone's arm or German Suplex him into the sand, you can almost feel it. While there isn't much variety in terms of enemies and the gameplay does get rather repetitive after a while, you're still guaranteed to have one hell of a time.
Surprisingly, Mad Max The Game does have a decent story. While it's pretty straightforward, you do find yourself caring for a few characters including the ever-spouting nonsense Chumbucket. Which makes the ending even worse. Most players aren't happy with Mad Max's ending and when you finally played till there, you'll know why. But I won't spoil it, it's something players have to experience for themselves but I can say it's very very typical of a Mad Max story.
If there's anything I dislike about the game, it's that the open-world is way too bland. You'd be expecting something like the Fallout series, considering the post-apocalyptic setting but the world design is just vast and empty. You'll find a few tiny camps here and there, then there's the bigger camps where you carry out objectives and get more scrap, upgrades and blueprints to upgrade the strongholds of the allies you'll meet on Max's story. But, that's all. There's nothing really exciting to find in this world.
Mad Max is a game to pick up if you're one for intense car combat and plenty of driving. If you're the type that complains about driving too much in a game like GTA for example, then this is not the game for you. If it's up your alley, try playing it in first-person mode. It's difficult but it makes for a very interesting experience as well. Mad Max is no GOTY contender but it's a solid game through and through.

It lays really solid groundwork for a possible sequel which could be very good, but for now rather use your 60$ to buy a game like the Witcher 3 or Metal Gear Solid V that really have amazing gameplay and story. I suggest you get this game when it costs something like 20$, because right now it really isnt worth 60$.

A clever experience, one wrapped in a familiar story and predictable rhythm:  A special operations team is dispatched to Dubai following a massive sandstorm and a communications blackout to determine what happened in the silent city.
The third-person gameplay feels immediately familiar with cover, headshots and team orders.  The colorful environments and dilapidated city create a wonderful background to close-quarters firefights and hallway progression.
Then...
Then something starts happening.  Your squad starts making decisions.  They aren't the cleanest kind.  The more you look at what you're doing (if you look at all between the gunfights) the more you question what's really happening.
By the time your tour in Dubai is over, you will have been witness to stunning human tragedy, a heavy-pitted feeling of betrayal and an aching need to determine just what the hell happened to make things go so bad.
And if for some reason you remain unfettered by moral quandary, at least it's a solid cover-based shooter.

In most shooters, you don't think twice about killing, who or why. In Spec Ops: The Line, the reason behind what you do gnaws at you constantly, making you ask questions you'd never expect to come from a military shooter. Many other games have tried this kind of introspection with ham-handed results, usually trying to tie it in with some sort of choice system that feels artificial and meaningless. Spec Ops manages to be extremely linear and yet make your actions feel extremely powerful and personal. Nothing you do feels forced - or does it? The gameplay, while generic, fits the story completely and actually makes it more effective. Even if it ends up not being your cup of tea, I reccomend everyone give this game a look.

It's certainly charming, with a clever premise, but I find Rogue Legacy to be ultimately unrewarding.
At its center, this game is a tight 2D combat-platformer, that makes sure to be fair while challenging; that's a stale genre on it's own however, which Rogue Legacy does not reinvent. I really want to like this game, I sent the devs an email and they reassured me that the game will get its patches. I can definetly see why people would be concerned about their commitment, the game is still in its extremely early stages and should be marked as so. This game has a ton of work that needs to be done. I will name off some of the things that bother me.

1st thing that makes me frustrated is how weak the weapons are, a Headshot with a 12 gauge shot is not enough for a deer apperantly. After still dumping another 4 slugs into it, the deer managed to survive with it only having a blood rate of low. Same thing goes for the bow. While I understand that their is a point to chase them down and finishing the job but having to do that everytime with any weapon but the rifle is a little excessive.

Next thing on my list is having to walk everywhere. you can only fast travel to the one campground so I try to avoid the missions because the map is so huge. While I understand that you should explore the map, it really bugs me having to fast travel to the one camp on the map after a mission to rest until sundown then have to do a 15 minute walk back to the same area from your last mission to hunt the same animals at night.

My final issue with the game is the prices of the items, while they lowered the cost of the actual firearms on the latest patch they raised the price of ammo making it ridiculous to actually get far. Once you purchase a weapon you barely are left with any money to buy ammo. It wouldnt be so bad but when animals only garnish ~$600 and you dump 5 out of 8 slugs into it you end not being able to afford it because you only get 8 slugs for $980.
The good things about the game are the graphics, the sounds, and the generally calming expirience of hunting. The AI is pretty decent when they dont run around in circles or get stuck between the rocks.  Tracking deer is an exciting experience with the help of the phone, when its not killing your fps it really helps out. Not a ton to hunt from yet, the deer seem to be more aggressive than a black bear when shot. Not sure if thats %100 accurate. Also something to note, this game requires patience. Unfortunately you cant run up to any deer and shoot them willy nilly. You actually have crouch and crawl to get close, if they dont pick up your scent from the gust of wind. Weapon selection is decent, they start you from a rifle and after a couple kills you can afford handguns, shotguns and, bows. From there you can customize them by adding a sight or getting better ammo. If you do get the bow I recommend restarting your game if want you use your rifle with a scope, bugs out and doesnt work right.
All in all its a great game but there is a ton and i mean a TON of work that needs to be done before this is even considered an actual game. At the moment as I write this review I do not reccomend this to anyone yet. Wait until a couple good solid patches are released. Until then my review will stay the same status unless they adjust it to an early access title. I believe that this game has a lot of potential and can easily be the greatest hunting game ever but the devs have a lot of work on their hands.
TL;DR Don't buy at all! gotta pay for DLC that should be free.

Where to begin with this one...
It's a slow starting game, I'll say that much. You are going to die - a lot - until you build up your stats, your equipment, and get used to the controls. Of course, if you're a fan of metroidvania-style games, the controls are going to come rather easily to you.
What puts this game into the "you should probably get this" circle is what it adds to the genre. Sure, you've got the whole "run around and kill things" aspect, the "explore the castle" aspect, and the "pallet and stat swapped enemies" aspect of the game that everyone knows and loves. The fact that you can choose a class (which gets extra abilities once you upgrade them) and traits that effect gameplay anywhere from cosmetically to significantly (play a character that has the trait "The One" at least once. Seriously) gives you a new character to do what you need to do each run. Amplify that with various stats you can upgrade, as well as different equipment you can use to alter how your character plays.
The randomized castles may seem like a hastle, but it allows you to collect all sorts of treasures that didn't appear in the previous castle. It boosts replayability significantly, especially once you hit New Game+ and go back to being a punching bag.
Eh, I seem to be going on a tangent. Bottom line's rather simple: BUY THIS.

In spite of the fact that I'm not a huge fan of the rogue-like genre, I do like this game.  However, I am recommending it with a caveat:  The likelihood that you, too, will enjoy this game depends heavily on your tolerance for slow progress.  The core concept of this game is repeated deaths and restarts.  And, particularly in the beginning, progress can feel painfully slow.
Even possessing this grindy aspect, the game does have its charms.  The gameplay and graphics are reminiscent of the old Super Mario Brothers games.  And there is an element of humor, as well.  The distinguishing traits given to your line of successors aren't always useful, but they are eclectic.
If you want to know whether you should purchse Rogue Legacy, ask yourself two questions:
1.  Do I enjoy rogue-likes?
2.  Is my attitude casual enough to withstand slow progress?
If you answer yes to both questions, give it a go, partcularly if you can get it on sale.
If you answer yes to one of the two, consider picking up the game if you see it on a deep discount.
If you answer no to both, odds are you should consider another game.

This game was one of the THE BEST games I ever played in 2012, second only to Mass Effect 3. I will not lie, I bought this 3 times, on PS3, Xbox and PC. This game is one of the best I ever played and is an unforgetable psychological ride.
The game play is nothing stellar if I compared it to anything, it'd be Gears of War 1. But the story is what is mindblowing. Easily one of the best, and most important stories ever told in video games.
Do not let Spec Ops lie to you. The cover looks like your typical Call of Duty game, the screenshots look like your typical Battlefield game, the demo looks like subpar military shooter... That's the point of Spec Ops. It supposed to feel like a typical current military shooter until a key event unravels the entire story and breaks down your characters psych and shows how tragic and shocking real war is.

The box art deceives you into thinking this is another Call of Duty or Battlefield, the first few hours do this as well, well it isn’t. Your expectations are turned in its head a few hours into the game. The game is highly engaging but is not that fun. It is based on the novella Heart of Darkness; following many of its story plots and tropes, but I’m not here to talk about literature. The game also tackles heaps of themes, from PTSD, the use of chemical warfare among others. . It does have a weak multiplayer but, this matter so little, we don’t need multiplayer in every game, the game is not worse of for the multiplayer existing. One thing that will strike you is the lack of a ‘normal’ enemy, it isn’t a Russian or Muslim, but American soldiers, the whole game you shoot and kill American soldiers, and it forces the player to second guess themselves. It creates a feeling of something not being right, it disconnects the player’s feelings from that the character is feeling, and you are discomfort able and numb.   The game is also an indictment of the mms (Modern Military Shooters eg cod)  genre. It uses all of the tropes of mms and turns them on its head and forces the player to evaluate them on a different scale. Gunplay is lacklustre, enemies spawn in obvious areas and its principle way of engagement isn’t through fun, but uses this and tropes to point at mms and laugh at them, showing the player the stupid nature of mms. However they the gameplay mechanics interact with the themes, not only this, but showing how far removed mms are from reality. Shooting is full of turrets, obvious spawn points, and suicidal enemies and of cause, exploding red barrels. However it works, as the game embraced it, to reinforce the narrative. The game also acknowledges the player, breaking the 4th wall constantly, to talk to you, to criticise you, laugh at you. An example is the load screens, when you progress they become more weird, one screen says “this is your fault”, there is more examples of this and it doesn’t speak to the character, it speaks to you, the cognitive dissonance you experience whilst playing the game.  The game questions you, why you play violent games? / Why do you kill? It tells you how pathetic you are for playing these games, that you’re a hero, I can’t go into it anymore because, spoilers, but serious it is a huge punch to the gut, right at the end, although there is 4 endings and I’m not sure if it is in every ending. Dubai becomes a psychological landscape that forces a dual nature in your character, blurring the lines of reality, and creating hallucinations, that confronts, not only the character, but you, the player. In the game, you are always descending, seriously, every level; even the earth itself drags you down, dragging you into your own hell, your own darkness. The moral choices, designed to make different choices, ones that are not explicit or even told to you, which is amazing, you can choose what you want, in a sense.  The game also has a good cover system and some destructible environments, which are always amazing. The game will constantly show the consequences of your actions, reminding you that these people are that, people. Moral absolution is critiqued, lines of good and bad is blurred. The game also has amazing voice acting. The game makes you do terrible things and then critics you for doing it, although you had no choice. The game lets you know that the people you kill are people; they have lives and families, the game critics you for killing them.  Collectable Intel gives you more context and further knowledge of who you are facing. The game is perfectly aware that it's incentivizing killing. It gives you achievements and constantly forces you to kill, and then critics you about it. It is a very unique game with an amazing narrative to be told, to those that can understand its meaning. However the game is very shot, 5-7 hours but the different endings and moral choices cater for some replay ability.

I will start of by saying that Life is Strange: Before the Storm is a good game, not better than the original game (yet). But a good game regardless. Whether or not this one will surpass the original depends entirely on the two episodes that will follow (there are only three episodes in this instalment, instead of five). To be clear, I don’t think this game has to surpass Life is Strange per se, I’m certain that it will end up being a great game in its own right. I will round up this introduction by saying that this game has premise.
Initially I thought it was rather strange that the developers wanted to make another Life is Strange. I didn’t see a point in making a second game for a franchise that seemed finished. So after hearing the announcement of Life is Strange: Before the Storm, I was surprised and sceptical. But after playing the first episode I will say that this follow up, which is a prequal, has left me satisfied.
The gameplay mechanics remain largely untouched. Life is Strange: Before the Storm is still heavily revolved around storytelling and most of the time you will find yourself listening to dialogue. Choices that impact the progression of the story are also still a thing. There are, however, some new mechanics that got replaced with the mechanics from Life is Strange. There is no time-rewind mechanic this time around. That mechanic got replaced with an ‘argue’ mechanic. No further explanation is needed, you just try to win arguments as Chloe [Main character]. I did feel like this mechanic could have been used better, and I hope it will in the following episodes.
The story of Life is Strange: Before the Storm sometimes feels like a supplement to the original game. I don’t see anyone who hasn’t played the Life is Strange appreciating this game.
Right now you might think that this game is much worse than the original game, or that it doesn’t have anything going for it. However, I don’t think that’s the case. For example, I found the progression of the story and characters in the beginning of this game a lot better than the story progression and characters in the beginning episode of the initial game. Moreover, Before the Storm felt calmer and a lot less chaotic than the original Life is Strange, a change that I welcomed. Yes, I think that you can only enjoy the story if you have played Life is Strange. But I found the beginning of this game way more engaging and enjoyable than the beginning of the original.
Right now we can’t say if this game is good, because we simply don’t know what is going to come next. To enjoy this game you need to have played and enjoyed Life is Strange. The people who liked Life is Strange will therefore like Before the Storm. And as I said, this game has premise. I think that this game will be a great addition to the ‘universe’ of Life is Strange. And maybe, just maybe, this game will life up to Life is Strange or might surpass it. We will have to wait and see…
(To clarify, if I am just referring to Life is Strange, I am referring to the original game)

Excellent sidescroller with tight controls and a great sense of humor that WILL kick your butt if you're not paying attention. Once you learn most of the enemy "tells" you'll have an easier time journeying through, but all in all the game never lets you get truly complacent. I do have a few minor gripes though:
-At first all of the homages and echoes to the Castlevania franchise were charming, but occasionally it feels more like a fan tribute than a full game with its own unique character.
-Could have benefitted from a greater variety of enemy designs. Most enemies are just recolors/palette swaps of the same 10 sprites (although they may or may not have different attack patterns). Furthermore, all of the bosses (except the final boss) are just giant versions of enemies you fight in the levels--most of which are floating enemies with some sort of projectile. I would have liked to see different types of boss fights with wildly different strategies.
All in all, this will be a game that will keep your attention if you're a fan of difficult sidescrollers like Mega Man, Castlevania, etc. Even if you're crap like I am, you'll still have a laugh or two. I was fortunate enough to pick this up for $1.50 during the Steam Sale, but I believe it's worth the full $15 normal price.

I'm kind of mixed on this one. Ultimately, I'll say it's worth checking out when it goes on sale. This is one of those games like Binding of Isaac and FTL where you'll be doing some form of dungeon crawling where the dungeon is randomly generated. There is a system that adds some interesting depth though. Gold collected during a run is used on upgrades/unlocks that'll make/unlock characters stronger on subsequent runs. Adding this RPG element is an interesting way of allowing players to customize the way they like the play. The only flaw with it is that you can't save any excess gold (you lose it starting the next run). While this is intended, and probably neccessary, it does kind of take away from that RPG element as you'll end up just upgrading whatever you can afford.
The real issue with the game lies in its uncreative creature design. While still fun to fight, stronger enemies end up just being larger versions of the previous enemies, with their attacks enhanced. I found this to be underwhelming, and helped to drive in the feeling of repetitiveness I started to feel after beating the game once (or even half way through the first playthrough for that matter).
The game is worth playing for the arcadey fast-paced action experience, so check it out. I just wouldn't recommend paying full price.

Mad Max is probably the single most, 'I'll just do one more mission - still playing many hours later' game ever. Time vanishes. What you thought was maybe forty-five minutes, was four hours. I think part of the reasoning behind this is because it's repetitive in every way. I am surprised it doesn't get more criticism for this. Everywhere just about looks the same. The camps which you clear are all similar. Scavenging destinations are all similar.
The really only parts that are not all similar are the main missions. However there are not many of those.
Mad Max has other issues too. The engine-exhaust noise of the car is diabolical. I wear headphones and it screams albeit mid pitched (not high pitched) almost all the way through. I play on speakers too and it's as bad. Only later when you get the V8 engine is car noise acceptable.
It is unfortunately nothing more than a long grind, and is possibly the grinder of all grinders. Salvage scrap, unlock upgrades, use scrap as currency to upgrade. From start to finish that is all you do.
It has plus points. It often looks good. Bosses are all the same technique: wait for charge, dodge, attack for a bit; repeat. In other words there is no googling every boss encounter because you can't work out what to do. Gameplay is straight-forward. In fact all the gameplay is relatively easy. It's filled out by there simply being masses of it.
Although I mark it 7/10 I could not in all honesty say to a friend, "You must buy Mad Max". Meaning no recommendation. However if you are fully aware of its format, you will have fun maybe half the time playing it.
Play if you want but they need to make it so we can do something to stop other people from attacking when you parry.

Although Pre-Sequel did not live up to it's expectations, this is the game to play and to be faithful to when it comes to Borderlands. A crazy, hilarious, fun role-playing first-person shooter that defines the series of Borderlands. Even if I don't have much time into this game, I feel it has hundreds more hours waiting for me, and I continue to find more to do. The best feature of this game, aside from all the DLC, weaponry, and side-quests, is the fact that you experience this game with friends. Four players control four Vault-Hunters in search of endless loot and the defeat of Handsome Jack, one of the most defining, most ruthless, and the funniest boss of any game in this genre. What makes me want to play it all the time, is the endless content I stumble upon in this game. Character customizations, new side-quests, massive playable areas, and hundreds of thousands of weapons you always seem to find to change up gameplay in any situation (the game does NOT exaggerate on how many guns you can find, there are a ton!). I enjoy playing as one of the playable characters, but there are three more, along with two DLC characters, that leave gunfights and exploration very different with each character. Borderlands 2 is one of those games you compare Skyrim to, a satisfying open-world with stunning graphics for it's time and bottomless content that leaves players wanting more. 10/10, expecting the third installment!

In a summation, you're basically looking at a GTA game with a Red Faction: Guerilla setting and Batman Arkham Asylum style fighting. That is to say, an open world game with missions in a post apocolyptic desert... with Batman fighting.
If you like cars, upgrading them to become death machines and then putting said death machines to use, then this is the game for you! I really got into cruising around and harpooning towers to bring them down and crashing into convoys. I was a little less thrilled with the on foot combat in the game (think Batman: Arkham Asylum) and not because it's bad but just that it gets a little old after 30 hours of gameplay. However, the car stuff was always fun and I can see myself returning to it just to take out buzzards and raiders!
There is some glitchy stuff going on in the game as well. Things like enemy cars disappearing and UI statusing disappearing (Like when the game tells you that you 100% looted an area, those messages went away). However, this was very few and far between.
The game also feels kind of janky at times. It's odd design decisions too, stuff that can be remedied. Like only being given the option to refuel your car or the air balloon on certain sides of it? Some times damage to your car and other cars doesn't register at all. Also, the controls are a bit wonky to get used to at first. But again, these are things that didn't bother me anymore after I played the game more and got absorbed into it.
So there are a few things to get used to in Mad Max but I feel the positives far outweigh the negatives. I Definitely recommended this for the open world/car game fans out there. I think you'll find a lot to like here!

The box art deceives you into thinking this is another Call of Duty or Battlefield, the first few hours do this as well, well it isn’t. Your expectations are turned in its head a few hours into the game. The game is highly engaging but is not that fun. It is based on the novella Heart of Darkness; following many of its story plots and tropes, but I’m not here to talk about literature. The game also tackles heaps of themes, from PTSD, the use of chemical warfare among others. . It does have a weak multiplayer but, this matter so little, we don’t need multiplayer in every game, the game is not worse of for the multiplayer existing. One thing that will strike you is the lack of a ‘normal’ enemy, it isn’t a Russian or Muslim, but American soldiers, the whole game you shoot and kill American soldiers, and it forces the player to second guess themselves. It creates a feeling of something not being right, it disconnects the player’s feelings from that the character is feeling, and you are discomfort able and numb.   The game is also an indictment of the mms (Modern Military Shooters eg cod)  genre. It uses all of the tropes of mms and turns them on its head and forces the player to evaluate them on a different scale. Gunplay is lacklustre, enemies spawn in obvious areas and its principle way of engagement isn’t through fun, but uses this and tropes to point at mms and laugh at them, showing the player the stupid nature of mms. However they the gameplay mechanics interact with the themes, not only this, but showing how far removed mms are from reality. Shooting is full of turrets, obvious spawn points, and suicidal enemies and of cause, exploding red barrels. However it works, as the game embraced it, to reinforce the narrative. The game also acknowledges the player, breaking the 4th wall constantly, to talk to you, to criticise you, laugh at you. An example is the load screens, when you progress they become more weird, one screen says “this is your fault”, there is more examples of this and it doesn’t speak to the character, it speaks to you, the cognitive dissonance you experience whilst playing the game.  The game questions you, why you play violent games? / Why do you kill? It tells you how pathetic you are for playing these games, that you’re a hero, I can’t go into it anymore because, spoilers, but serious it is a huge punch to the gut, right at the end, although there is 4 endings and I’m not sure if it is in every ending. Dubai becomes a psychological landscape that forces a dual nature in your character, blurring the lines of reality, and creating hallucinations, that confronts, not only the character, but you, the player. In the game, you are always descending, seriously, every level; even the earth itself drags you down, dragging you into your own hell, your own darkness. The moral choices, designed to make different choices, ones that are not explicit or even told to you, which is amazing, you can choose what you want, in a sense.  The game also has a good cover system and some destructible environments, which are always amazing. The game will constantly show the consequences of your actions, reminding you that these people are that, people. Moral absolution is critiqued, lines of good and bad is blurred. The game also has amazing voice acting. The game makes you do terrible things and then critics you for doing it, although you had no choice. The game lets you know that the people you kill are people; they have lives and families, the game critics you for killing them.  Collectable Intel gives you more context and further knowledge of who you are facing. The game is perfectly aware that it's incentivizing killing. It gives you achievements and constantly forces you to kill, and then critics you about it. It is a very unique game with an amazing narrative to be told, to those that can understand its meaning. However the game is very shot, 5-7 hours but the different endings and moral choices cater for some replay ability.

TL;DR: Fun, challenging roguelike platformer that'll take you a solid 20-30 hours of playtime to fully complete.
To anyone thinking of getting the game and just starting out, a few recommendations. First, a controller is almost mandatory for this game. There's no mouse support, and while you can use two hands on a keyboard, it feels pretty awkward (and this game involves a lot of twitch reflexes and precision jumping). Also, there's an option to just press down to perform down attacks in the air or fall off platforms (I forget the name, but it should be obvious in the options menu) that's very helpful. And finally, try not to spend an excessive amount of time on the grind - if it's getting repetitive, clear through the bosses and attempt the next game mode. The Steam achievements for this game are actually a good balance of "difficult but not impossible," and getting all of them should indicate that you're essentially "done" with the game. You'll likely get 20-30 hours out of this game before getting that feeling of "
" but if you enjoy a challenge and find it at a good price, it's definitely worth a look.
Rogue Legacy is an excellent roguelike platformer with a clever continuity mechanic. Gold and items collected during dungeon attempts can be used to provide static stat bonuses for future attempts, allowing the player to shore up their weak spots and fueling the game's progression system. The different classes and powers (via glyphs) provide enough variety to keep subsequent dungeon runs varied and interesting.
The game can be punishing at first, but this is intentional, as it allows the player to see the effects of their stat purchases and armor upgrades, as well as their improving play. Rogue Legacy is a game that encourages player mastery - better play will lead to greater completion of the dungeon and more gold to spend for the next round. And just when you've gotten good enough to clear the dungeon and defeat all the bosses, the game will ramp up the difficulty with a "New Game +" mode. The new mode allows you to keep all your progress, but is balanced well enough that the previously easy intro part of the dungeon is now challenging again. The game also includes five "hidden" bosses, which are far more challenging versions of the standard bosses. These can be taken on at any time (your purchased stat bonuses don't affect the stats of the avatar during these challenges), but they provide a sort of endgame for players who have found the rest of the dungeon too repetitive. That said, I'd recommend looking up the slightly gamey strategy for defeating Alexander IV, as the "normal" strategy will lead to an absurdly challenging and probably frustrating fight.
The game isn't without its downsides. The grind can feel a little repetitive at times, and there could be more indication that defeating the bosses on the first run through isn't the end of the game (as it is, it's confusing that by the time you're able to tackle the bosses in the first playthrough you've barely bought into the stats, and you won't have found all the armors). Not helping the repetitiveness is the music. It's not bad, at first, but after a few hours you'll want to turn on something else with more variety. But in the end, those are two relatively minor downsides in an otherwise great game.

As the Steam description for the game says, Rogue Legacy is a Rogue-”Lite” platformer-type thing where you travel through 2D rooms slaying the castle’s inhabitants either by sword or by spell. There is a large variety of traits you can get to either benefit or harm your Rogue Legacy run as the heir to a hero trying to save the king with a cure that can be found in the castle. There’s even a pretty interesting amount of different spells you can get, ranging from throwing a dagger, to a circle of fireballs around you, to a couple crows that will home in on enemies and kill them.
You might have heard that this game is extremely difficult, and in a way, it is. It’s hard to start out against the new monsters and the weird mechanics of the game, but once you get the hang of it, there really isn’t much else you can do to get better other than upgrade your castle. So rather than it being particularly challenging, it’s more just time consuming. I’m not saying this in a bad way though, I rather like it. It’s still never extremely easy, and as you complete the game more it still gets more difficult. It’s really fun to slowly upgrade your character, barely managing to pay for that upgrade and having to do another run to get some more.
The world generation in this game gives you a lot of different rooms that you will experience a lot and eventually get the hang of. There are spike traps, wall turrets and platforms that only come out when you hit them, all used to add to the challenge of moving around, which is a very important mechanic to get the hang of. Some rooms will be extremely challenging with valuable prizes when completed, and some rooms will be a simple stroll through a hall.
Spending your money properly is vital to performing well. You need to buy the things that will benefit you most and improve your runs. If you find yourself running out of mana quickly, maybe you should increase your mana capacity, or if you find yourself not doing enough damage, you should increase your health. If you find yourself playing as certain classes a lot, you should upgrade them to improve their abilities. And then there’s always the blacksmith and enchantress, who will get you very important items that may even benefit you more than a manor upgrade. You can buy swords and armour and capes from the blacksmith, along with runes from the enchantress to allow your character to do all sorts of different abilities like draining the health of your enemies and being able to fly, or making the difficulty a bit harder for better rewards. What do you think is more important? That will determine the success of a Rogue Legacy run.
Though the storyline isn’t one of the bigger aspects of the game, I find it kind of intriguing to learn things from the Prince’s Journal that you’ve experienced yourself. After completing the journal, I haven’t gone back to read them all in order but it was fun to find the journals scattered around the castles randomly and read a bit of the backstory of the game.
Although this game does last a lot of hours, and you will be able to play it for a while, it doesn’t have infinite replayability. Once you get through all the bosses enough times, all that makes the game harder is increased damage/health, and not new enemies to fight. It does get boring eventually, and once it gets to a certain point there’s just no reason to continue. Still, this game will last enough hours to be worth buying.
This game may not be worth $15, but any sale that happens for this game makes it probably worth looking into if you like Rogue-lite platformer type games. It’s extremely fun, a challenge worth looking into and plenty of gameplay to go through. I recommend Rogue Legacy to anyone who likes this sort of game.

This wasn't a game I was watching very closely at all, but once I saw a sale on it I grabbed it and haven't looked back.
In a summation, you're basically looking at a GTA game with a Red Faction: Guerilla setting and Batman Arkham Asylum style fighting. That is to say, an open world game with missions in a post apocolyptic desert... with Batman fighting.
If you like cars, upgrading them to become death machines and then putting said death machines to use, then this is the game for you! I really got into cruising around and harpooning towers to bring them down and crashing into convoys. I was a little less thrilled with the on foot combat in the game (think Batman: Arkham Asylum) and not because it's bad but just that it gets a little old after 30 hours of gameplay. However, the car stuff was always fun and I can see myself returning to it just to take out buzzards and raiders!
There is some glitchy stuff going on in the game as well. Things like enemy cars disappearing and UI statusing disappearing (Like when the game tells you that you 100% looted an area, those messages went away). However, this was very few and far between.
The game also feels kind of janky at times. It's odd design decisions too, stuff that can be remedied. Like only being given the option to refuel your car or the air balloon on certain sides of it? Some times damage to your car and other cars doesn't register at all. Also, the controls are a bit wonky to get used to at first. But again, these are things that didn't bother me anymore after I played the game more and got absorbed into it.
So there are a few things to get used to in Mad Max but I feel the positives far outweigh the negatives. I Definitely recommended this for the open world/car game fans out there. I think you'll find a lot to like here!
