The video game world is by no means short on post-apocalyptic wastelands to explore but unless a game comes out based on A Boy and His Dog comes out, none of them can claim to be based on one of the most influential pieces of Post-Apocalyptic media of the past 35 years. In this sense, Avalanche Studios’ Mad Max is an exciting licensed property in the game world and the prospect of playing another post-apocalyptic title, even amidst a market full of them, has only been sweetened by the most recent film in the Mad Max franchise: Fury Road. Given Avalanche’s mastery of creating exciting sandbox gameplay with ample opportunity for organic, play it your way hijinks, Mad Max seems poised to be this year’s Shadows of Mordor style sleeper hit.

Much like the films, Mad Max’s narrative is sparse but unlike the films, the supporting cast lacks the charisma to carry the events forward in a satisfying manner. Beginning with an overlong cutscene depicting Max’s clash with the game’s antagonist Scrotus. Their encounter ends with Scrotus suffering a major wound and Max stripped of his gear and left to wander in the desert. In typical video game fashion it’s up to Max to rebuild his car, re-acquire his gear and end Scrotus’ violent reign over the wasteland.
While its narrative is certainly in the spirit of the films upon which it is based, the weak supporting cast and unfocused objective make for an underwhelming narrative experienced, especially when paired with 40 hours of gameplay. Early on, Max encounters a mechanic named Chumbucket who helps him rebuild his car and suggests the next wasteland leader to ask for assistance. Upon encountering each leader not much interaction occurs between them and Max. Their trust and tolerance is easily gained and there is very little narrative surrounding them. Each leader has a handful of side missions, referred to as wasteland missions in the game, but these amount to petty errands rather than building a plot around each character. The NPCs stand around like props exuding zero personality and failing to reflect the kind of society that each wasteland leader has built. In this sense, Mad Max takes the scenic route to its conclusion, introducing you to various people of interest but doing little to make your encounters with them seem essential to your fight against Scrotus. Amidst the endless diversions in each of the game’s regions, you soon forget why you are there and what your objective is. Aside from Chum’s crazed banter, there is little reason to pay attention.

Upon receiving your bare bones vehicle and enlisting Chum’s assistance, Max’s journey begins proper and a routine is quickly established where players enter a territory, meet its leader, destroy Scrotus’ infrastructure in the area, obtain a vehicle upgrade that permits passage to a new territory and repeat. Mad Max relies on a series of mechanics familiar to those who have played open world games over the past five years. There are enemy strongholds to topple, weather balloons to utilize for reconnaissance and fast travel, loot caches to pillage for upgrade currency, races to partake in and convoys to smash. In addition to these activities there are special parts to be on the lookout for that allow max to upgrade the stronghold of each wasteland leader he encounters. Constructing these upgrades allow Max to replenish his supplies which would otherwise have to be scavenged. The problem is each stronghold requires the same upgrades and by the midway point, hunting down components for each stronghold feels like a chore. Likewise, once the allure of taking out the strongholds that dot each of the game’s regions grows tiresome after the novelty of their sometimes intricate designs ware off. These strongholds are in particular a point of frustration since in many ways they are some of the game’s most interesting set pieces but by being populated with the same handful of gimmicks and gameplay choices they grow dull long before the credits roll. Some of these strongholds are also home to bosses, none of which come close to living up to the eccentric antagonists of the films such as Toecutter, Humongus or Imortan Joe. Instead, expect to fight muscular men in gimp masks wielding polearms ad nauseam.
Further hampering the game’s mechanics is the mind numbingly dull combat lifted from the Arkham series which relies on counters and timed button presses. If you have better dexterity than a three toed sloth with rheumatoid arthritis, expect to yawn your way through the game’s uninspired enemies with barely a scratch. The combat system tries to spice things up with new abilities that Max can learn, melee weapons that break after a short period of time and finishing moves executed with shivs but due to the ubiquity of its design, combat simply doesn’t stand out.

While it may seem that Mad Max is another throw away game based on a licensed property it does manage to redeem itself with engaging vehicular gameplay. Your car, The Magnum Opus, starts as nothing more than an engine on a chassis, but as you explore the wasteland you can locate new car bodies, and lower Scrotus’ influence over each region to unlock more upgrades. At first, taking control of your car is an irritation; it’s slow, handles poorly and tends to spin out easily but after a few upgrades the Magnum Opus becomes a speedy death machine allowing you to terrorize your foes. What’s more interesting is that the upgrades in each category can have a negative impact on other performance categories so having the heaviest bumper may allow you to deal major damage but it’s weight also makes the car slower. You can shove a massive engine in your ride but it’s going to negatively impact the vehicle’s handling. This makes it worthwhile to have all of the upgrades and swap between them when the situation calls for it. The visual and performance enhancing upgrades prove to be the perfect carrot on the stick to motivate players to complete some of the game’s more tedious activities. You can also unlock additional vehicles by driving captured enemy cars back to friendly strongholds or by winning races.

Ultimately, Mad Max’s gameplay falls short by not featuring any gameplay mechanics that give the game a unique identity. Most of the gameplay elements featured in Mad Max can be traced back to half a dozen other games that share the same mechanics—two of which are also published by Warner Brothers. It’s easy to run headlong into a convoy of eight cars, turn them into a scrap heap in less than a minute and reflect back on both Just Cause 2 and Fury Road… Where are the massive war rigs? Why can’t you hop aboard other cars? Shouldn’t taking out a convoy be something more than blowing up a few cars? Your interest in playing mad max will likely only last as long as your enthusiasm for driving around the wasteland in a four wheel drive rat rod leaving a trail of destruction. Mad Max is a case of competency over excellence and it doesn’t help that the open world action adventure game has usurped the third person cover based shooter as the go to game design template. This isn’t the sleeper hit it could have been but it isn’t exactly a game to ignore if you are a fan of Mad Max or open world action games.

The question I asked myself prior to writing this was "What does Mad Max do that other games aren't doing?"  It feels like a game of missed opportunities.  There is this big, very well-crafted world set in a post-apocalypstic land with not all that much to offer an intrepid wanderer.  Yeah, you can drive around and see ruins of buildings and signs, but there is almost never a real point to doing so.  You can pick up tiny amounts of scrap (the game's currency), but after you've liberated some camps the scrap pickups become just another collectible.  Speaking of collectibles, the history relics started interesting enough - a photo, a postcard, a handwritten note of days gone by that Max wistfully comments on - but when I realized I'd collected dozens and wasn't even halfway through the list, I gave up.  They aren't THAT interesting.
The story is cliche at best, the anti-hero just looking out for himself until he meets someone who reminds him of better days and then has to systematically destroy the bad guys.  It's awkward.  At least when you fight, it has real impact.  Punching dudes never really gets old in this game, but the combat has its drawbacks as well.  There is "tap for light hit" and "hold for heavy hit", and a counter button.  You unlock various finishing moves throughout the game that can be useful in group fights, but sometimes the game doesn't respond quickly enough and allows Max to take a hit while setting up such a maneuver.  When in Fury mode, he hits real hard and does some incredibly satisfying suplexes, but there is no way to do it on purpose - you just get lucky.
Car combat starts off similarly, forcing you to think a little bit about your approach before you have upgraded your car.  By the time you can hurl thunderpoons at other cars, it's just not that fun anymore because everything explodes pretty easily.  As stated many times, the mini-bosses scattered around are a joke.  They all attack the same way (unblockable charge) and in most cases, you defeat them the same way - hit them with a real big wrench or something else lying around.  Occasionally there are environmental hazards that can aid you - say, but letting a boss charge into a flame burst - but it's nowhere near the extremes of something like Sleeping Dogs.
After a while, you realize that reducing threat across the various warlords' regions by tackling side actitivies (read: map vomit) has stopped being beneficial, as Max is decked out in crazy gear and the car is nigh invulnerable (car upgrades are often locked behind getting threat below a certain level).  It just stops being fun.  I mainlined the last several story missions to get it over with and wasn't left very satisified by the ending.
It's probably worth a play if you dig the universe and don't mind icons all over the place (complete with hot air balloons that let you identify all the actitives in an area!), but it's not really anything spectularly different.

This isn't yet another shovelware, mediocre "simulation" game. ETS2 is an accurate and advanced truck driving sim, with licenced trucks and cars and a beautiful (if very scaled down) version of European roads.
Start without your own truck, take quick jobs, buy your first truck and garage, then buy more trucks and hire drivers and grow little trucking enterprise. Unlock better upgrades and skills for you and your team.
All of these aspects are great, but for me - and it seems for a lot of people - the best part of the game is just the experience of driving. Discovering all the roads and locations, enjoying the views, navigating the long wide turns and tight corners, pulling off that perfect braking at the red light.
Driving at night in the game (and in the real world), listening to European radios online, or your own music collection, both accessible through the in-game music player.
There's something soothing and special about driving at night, in the rain, listening to oldies and talk shows on a Czech radio. To me, that's the real joy of ETS2.
Even with the next game in the series announces (American Truck Simulator), the developers are still upgrading ETS2 and releasing new content. I'm looking forward to the Scandinavian DLC. It's a good sign when you look forward to a game's DLC.
PS. Try with a controller / steering wheel and face tracking. (you can use FaceTrakNoIR, free)

NOTE: This is the only review i've written on steam since i've found no game really in need of it.
I started playing the old hunter game as an escape with one of my friends and it was all right but this one is one of the best games i've played. It's so relaxing so stroll around without any competition tracking down your prey and then taking a well prepared shot. The two maps that are available are huge and has by far the most beautiful scenery and environment that i've ever seen. Walking around the huge maps really takes your mind of everything in life, add some calm music and i'm in total bliss. The sounds made for this game are amazing and it's so much so that you might for a second actually believe that you're in whatever forest or field that you're currently tracking prey in.
The game is so calm, the only thing that disturbs the peace is your bullet leaving the muzzle.
I found this game awesome to play with a friends and ganging up on some resting bear that just happens to get shot 5-10 times it's just friggin' hilarious and also brings time to talk about other stuff that might not even be related to the game.
Now on to the bad parts, the game in single player for me is running flawlessly on my setup and i have no issues at all really except for some minor bugs that won't really affect the experience.
On the other hand, multi player is riddled with small bugs that actually stack up, one of my friends game crashes all the time whilst mine doesn't and i have almost the same setup as him. The mission system doesn't work in multi player, menu's will click without any warning and i have accidentally kicked friends from the multi player game by accident because of this. If you're the host you can still locate landmarks/cabins and get the experience and lore from interacting with them, BUT your friends that are clients on the server can't which hinders the experience on their part since they can't progress in the game world when they play on your servers. But this isn't really a problem if you switch between host/client from time to time. You're usually not even concerned by this since you always get sidetracked by prey.
I can wholeheartedly recommend this game for those with patience with some minor bugs. I would agree that this game should still be in a Beta stage. But it is so immersive that i'm glad that i can take part in it right now.
If you're constantly annoyed by bugs and can't let go. Then this game might not be for you right now.

I never thought I'd see myself falling in love with a hunting game, but theHunter: Call of the Wild has its claws in me and I'm not mad about it. The thrill of the hunt is visceral. You have to rely on sight and sound in a way that few games pull off. Hunting with friends is even better than hunting alone. One person can post up while the other wrangles or lures the prey. It's just dripping with fun if you give yourself the time to get lost in its world. The maps are huge, beautiful, and varied, with plenty of nice set pieces to stumble upon.
On the downside, the game is riddled with annoying bugs. Often they require a full restart, which is made worse by the fact that you can't simply back out to the main menu, you MUST quit to the desktop to exit the game. Ironsights will occasionally bug out, activating multiplayer quests will boot your friends from your game, animals will get stuck on geometry, netting you easy kills that cheapen the experience.
All of that said, the gameplay is worth dealing with the bugs and it seems the devs are working hard to fix the problems.
Pros:
Gorgeous Visuals
Excellent Sound Design
Damn Fun Gameplay!
Cons:
Bugs, bugs, bugs

Alright so, Life Is Strange Before The Storm was a game...
This review is probably going to be long, but if you want to know what an emo/scene/punk kid thinks about it, this is worth reading.
So first of all I've got to get the unpopular opinion out. I actually like Life Is Strange Before The Storm more than Life Is Strange season 1, and I think that getting rid of the time travel was a good thing. Even if there's only one episode out up till when I write this review.
Hear me out:
The lack of time travel makes the game a lot more realistic, it makes it more relatable. The way that Before The Storm accomlished to actually make an enjoyable intro episode without anything supernatural, is simply amazing!
There is a lot more atmosphere to this game. You get to know the inbetween of the different characters and who relates to who and the areas shows a bit more of Arcadia Bay. For example The Old Mill, it gets the feeling of the underground side to Arcadia bay that we got to know through Chloe and Frank in the first game.
The game also really captures the feeling of being an "Observer" (Someone who doesn't talk to many, doesn't have a lot of friends, keeps to themselves and just observes everyone around them). Again the game makes it more relatable to some people including myself.
The game has topped the first one with the music by some, with bands like: "Pretty Vicious", "Daughter", "Speedy Ortiz" and others. My personal favorite "Pisshead". The music is a mix of the old "Relaxing" music, and with a lot of new punk-rock music. Which again i personally love, and the music is very subjective if you like it or not. It does make the game a lot more enjoyable if you like the music, but doesn't ruin it.
The story, I will be honest has it flaws. There is some points that doesn't really capture you as much as others. Where the first Life Is Strange does this better. But in the end the story in Before The Storm, was so capturing for me that I cried 3 time throughout episode 1. Where 1 of those times was just simply from nostalgia from the first game. If me crying does not prove that the story is good, then I don't know what is.
The game is very punk, and if you didn't notice in the first game, Chloe is very punk. so it fits perfectly with her character and it makes the game very nostalgic or just simply better, if you have been or currently are punk.
The choices in the game are a lot more meaningful for the individual. Whether you choose to help people (even the worst people from the first game), talk back to people or a whole other choice is polished to the top.
Finally, the game has it flaws in some different things, the change of studio and engine is noticable but it's nothing major.

Straight to the point i was able to eat a plate of nachos while playing this game, thus making me feel like a real warden.
Now that i got that out of my system..Prison Architect is exactly what it sounds like. You're given funds to build and run a prison as you see fit. Want to make your prison a place of rehabilitation where these prisoners could potentially go back out in the world? Go for it because you can! Feel like making a prison so harsh and cold visiting Soviet Russia would seem like spring break? Do it!
Now your probably thinking 'Well that sounds a bit trivial and easy' You my friend could not be more wrong. As is standard fare with all building/managment simulators You've Got To Manage Your Money Wisely. However you can't just go throwing money at whatever you want, if your income isn't higher than your spending (such as wages for employees and so on) You're not going to be able to hire that one extra guard you need because you're getting in max security prisoners, or you won't be able to hire that doctor to lead your drug rehabilitation program because you want to actually help these people.
This also isn't a game you can just run and forget about. Oh No! This is a micromanager's wet dream i tell you! While you have some direct control over the people (being able to click on them and tell them where to go) The real control over them comes from handpicking their Regime. Want to set it where the prisoners are only allowed out for showers and food? Go for it, but let's be honest that's not much of a challenge. A real challenge is keeping tabs on all your prisoners while some are workin on laundry, the others a cleaning house, and a few are working in the carpentry shop. Because your prisoners can and will steal tools, which can cause all hell to break loose if your not pay attention.
All in all it's a great game, and you can expect great things to come from this game. i'd give it a 89/100 in it's current state. Plus there's Shawshank Redemption references in the game which is rather clever.

Rogue Legacy is one of the most maddeningly addictive games that I have ever played. Essentially, it's a metroidvania in an ever-changing dungeon. Each time you die, the dungeon is reset* and you have to start over from the beginning, except with all the purchases that you have made to improve your character. Each time you die, you choose between a handful of new characters from various classes (some are unlockable) and with various traits. These traits may help, hinder, or annoy you depending on which class they are affecting.
The controls are just plain perfect. So many times in this kind of a game you will find that the controls just don't respond exactly how you would like - a slight delay in a jump press or whatnot - but these are just flat out perfect to me. It's a true pick up and play game if you've ever played anything even remotely similar. The overall difficulty of the game is very high but you will find yourself getting better and better. As you improve your character, the enemies and hazards scale, BUT your overall skill will improve as well. The sound effects are good. The music is great, but repetitive because it uses zone-based music. Since each time you die, you have to restart in the first area and navigate through it again in its entirety, it can get old a little bit. Graphics are fun and quality.
Overall, I highly recommend the game. I would recommend using a controller for sure, even though with most PC games I'm a KB/mouse person.

So Castlevania: Symphony of the Night and Super Ghouls & Ghosts had a secret love child.  Seriously.  This game combines the difficulty of Ghouls & Ghosts with the candle breaking, castle exploration of modern 2D Castlevania games into one crazy rogue-like!
A nice twist involves your character.  Each time you die, you enter the castle as one of the previous character's heirs.  Each heir has traits, some good and some bad.  For instance, you die in the castle and are given three choices of your heir.  One of the choices may be a barbarian giant who is color blind.  This would make your character strong, your sprite larger and everything on screen grayscale.  That character dies and the next heir may be a hypochondriac dwarf who displays exaggerated damage numbers when hit and is half the size of the normal character.
Graphics:  The art of Rogue Legacy is on par with late 16-bit / early 32-bit 2D platformers.  Colorful palette with well animated pixel art is abundant here.
Sound:  Great sound track keeps the player engaged and fits the tone of the castle.  No complaints with the sound effects, though you will most likely hear the first castle music and the death screams quite a bit starting out!
Control:  Tight and well executed.  I played using an Xbox 360 wireless controller and found the controls precise and smooth.

The Good:
*Fun, action oriented gameplay
*An absolutely incredible weapon selection. Seriously, it's enormous.
*Great game to play with friends
*Creative art style + pretty decent music
*Long playtime, you really get your money's worth. Definitely buy this if it's on sale and you like western RPGs
*Large maps, with distinct geography
*Competent  voice acting
*No fall damage. You can jump off a mountain and live.
The Meh:
* The tech tree doesn't drastically alter the gameplay too much and the bonus stats don't make a noticeable difference either. Still, not a downside.
* Vehicles and fast travel are not present in the early areas, meaning that if you go back to do side quests, you'll sometimes find yourself walking large, tedious distances on foot. It also means you'll have to back track some. However this is limited to a few levels.
*It's a little bit lacking in the stealth department. I played as Assassin and was a tad disappointed that my special skills amounted to just a holographic distraction. There's no real sneaking in it, aside from staying out of your enemies' range of vision and sniping unsuspecting targets.
The Bad:
*For the most part, the writing in this game irritated me a lot. Almost every single line in the game is a joke--aside from key plot points--and sadly, most of them are not funny. Now, I feel that it won't bother most people, but it really started to get kind of grating after awhile. I'll admit there's a few good lines that I chuckled at, but it was more misses than hits. This hasn't ruined the game for me, but I honestly wish the developers had hired a better writer. The humor in this game is on par with something a highschooler could come up with. As for the story itself, it's completely acceptable. It feels a little drawn out in the middle, but for this kind of game, it's fine. The characters didn't really jump out to me, since almost every character is "zany" and "whacky". Thankfully several members of the main cast are grounded enough that the whole plot (and your involvement with it) isn't lost to the humor.
*While fun, the gameplay is really not that varied. You shoot everything you see, basically. It's good shooting, don't get me wrong, but that's all the game has to offer. As I started to play more and more quests, I began to assume any objective I got, no matter how mundane it sounded, was going to end with me shooting something. And aside from the driving oriented missions, that was exactly the case. In a nutshell the game is a huge, bullet-riddled fetch quest, and if that's something that bothers you, be aware of that.
Overall:
It's a straight up fun game that is only slightly marred by its annoying sense of humor and lack of variety. If you're a fan of FPS/RPGs, this is for you. You can think of it as a bit like the newer Fallout games, just more action oriented, without VATS, and significantly less serious (well, compared to 3 that is). If you like playing co-op games with your friends, this is a must-buy.

The video game world is by no means short on post-apocalyptic wastelands to explore but unless a game comes out based on A Boy and His Dog comes out, none of them can claim to be based on one of the most influential pieces of Post-Apocalyptic media of the past 35 years. In this sense, Avalanche Studios’ Mad Max is an exciting licensed property in the game world and the prospect of playing another post-apocalyptic title, even amidst a market full of them, has only been sweetened by the most recent film in the Mad Max franchise: Fury Road. Given Avalanche’s mastery of creating exciting sandbox gameplay with ample opportunity for organic, play it your way hijinks, Mad Max seems poised to be this year’s Shadows of Mordor style sleeper hit.

Much like the films, Mad Max’s narrative is sparse but unlike the films, the supporting cast lacks the charisma to carry the events forward in a satisfying manner. Beginning with an overlong cutscene depicting Max’s clash with the game’s antagonist Scrotus. Their encounter ends with Scrotus suffering a major wound and Max stripped of his gear and left to wander in the desert. In typical video game fashion it’s up to Max to rebuild his car, re-acquire his gear and end Scrotus’ violent reign over the wasteland.
While its narrative is certainly in the spirit of the films upon which it is based, the weak supporting cast and unfocused objective make for an underwhelming narrative experienced, especially when paired with 40 hours of gameplay. Early on, Max encounters a mechanic named Chumbucket who helps him rebuild his car and suggests the next wasteland leader to ask for assistance. Upon encountering each leader not much interaction occurs between them and Max. Their trust and tolerance is easily gained and there is very little narrative surrounding them. Each leader has a handful of side missions, referred to as wasteland missions in the game, but these amount to petty errands rather than building a plot around each character. The NPCs stand around like props exuding zero personality and failing to reflect the kind of society that each wasteland leader has built. In this sense, Mad Max takes the scenic route to its conclusion, introducing you to various people of interest but doing little to make your encounters with them seem essential to your fight against Scrotus. Amidst the endless diversions in each of the game’s regions, you soon forget why you are there and what your objective is. Aside from Chum’s crazed banter, there is little reason to pay attention.

Upon receiving your bare bones vehicle and enlisting Chum’s assistance, Max’s journey begins proper and a routine is quickly established where players enter a territory, meet its leader, destroy Scrotus’ infrastructure in the area, obtain a vehicle upgrade that permits passage to a new territory and repeat. Mad Max relies on a series of mechanics familiar to those who have played open world games over the past five years. There are enemy strongholds to topple, weather balloons to utilize for reconnaissance and fast travel, loot caches to pillage for upgrade currency, races to partake in and convoys to smash. In addition to these activities there are special parts to be on the lookout for that allow max to upgrade the stronghold of each wasteland leader he encounters. Constructing these upgrades allow Max to replenish his supplies which would otherwise have to be scavenged. The problem is each stronghold requires the same upgrades and by the midway point, hunting down components for each stronghold feels like a chore. Likewise, once the allure of taking out the strongholds that dot each of the game’s regions grows tiresome after the novelty of their sometimes intricate designs ware off. These strongholds are in particular a point of frustration since in many ways they are some of the game’s most interesting set pieces but by being populated with the same handful of gimmicks and gameplay choices they grow dull long before the credits roll. Some of these strongholds are also home to bosses, none of which come close to living up to the eccentric antagonists of the films such as Toecutter, Humongus or Imortan Joe. Instead, expect to fight muscular men in gimp masks wielding polearms ad nauseam.
Further hampering the game’s mechanics is the mind numbingly dull combat lifted from the Arkham series which relies on counters and timed button presses. If you have better dexterity than a three toed sloth with rheumatoid arthritis, expect to yawn your way through the game’s uninspired enemies with barely a scratch. The combat system tries to spice things up with new abilities that Max can learn, melee weapons that break after a short period of time and finishing moves executed with shivs but due to the ubiquity of its design, combat simply doesn’t stand out.

While it may seem that Mad Max is another throw away game based on a licensed property it does manage to redeem itself with engaging vehicular gameplay. Your car, The Magnum Opus, starts as nothing more than an engine on a chassis, but as you explore the wasteland you can locate new car bodies, and lower Scrotus’ influence over each region to unlock more upgrades. At first, taking control of your car is an irritation; it’s slow, handles poorly and tends to spin out easily but after a few upgrades the Magnum Opus becomes a speedy death machine allowing you to terrorize your foes. What’s more interesting is that the upgrades in each category can have a negative impact on other performance categories so having the heaviest bumper may allow you to deal major damage but it’s weight also makes the car slower. You can shove a massive engine in your ride but it’s going to negatively impact the vehicle’s handling. This makes it worthwhile to have all of the upgrades and swap between them when the situation calls for it. The visual and performance enhancing upgrades prove to be the perfect carrot on the stick to motivate players to complete some of the game’s more tedious activities. You can also unlock additional vehicles by driving captured enemy cars back to friendly strongholds or by winning races.

Ultimately, Mad Max’s gameplay falls short by not featuring any gameplay mechanics that give the game a unique identity. Most of the gameplay elements featured in Mad Max can be traced back to half a dozen other games that share the same mechanics—two of which are also published by Warner Brothers. It’s easy to run headlong into a convoy of eight cars, turn them into a scrap heap in less than a minute and reflect back on both Just Cause 2 and Fury Road… Where are the massive war rigs? Why can’t you hop aboard other cars? Shouldn’t taking out a convoy be something more than blowing up a few cars? Your interest in playing mad max will likely only last as long as your enthusiasm for driving around the wasteland in a four wheel drive rat rod leaving a trail of destruction. Mad Max is a case of competency over excellence and it doesn’t help that the open world action adventure game has usurped the third person cover based shooter as the go to game design template. This isn’t the sleeper hit it could have been but it isn’t exactly a game to ignore if you are a fan of Mad Max or open world action games.

The question I asked myself prior to writing this was "What does Mad Max do that other games aren't doing?"  It feels like a game of missed opportunities.  There is this big, very well-crafted world set in a post-apocalypstic land with not all that much to offer an intrepid wanderer.  Yeah, you can drive around and see ruins of buildings and signs, but there is almost never a real point to doing so.  You can pick up tiny amounts of scrap (the game's currency), but after you've liberated some camps the scrap pickups become just another collectible.  Speaking of collectibles, the history relics started interesting enough - a photo, a postcard, a handwritten note of days gone by that Max wistfully comments on - but when I realized I'd collected dozens and wasn't even halfway through the list, I gave up.  They aren't THAT interesting.
The story is cliche at best, the anti-hero just looking out for himself until he meets someone who reminds him of better days and then has to systematically destroy the bad guys.  It's awkward.  At least when you fight, it has real impact.  Punching dudes never really gets old in this game, but the combat has its drawbacks as well.  There is "tap for light hit" and "hold for heavy hit", and a counter button.  You unlock various finishing moves throughout the game that can be useful in group fights, but sometimes the game doesn't respond quickly enough and allows Max to take a hit while setting up such a maneuver.  When in Fury mode, he hits real hard and does some incredibly satisfying suplexes, but there is no way to do it on purpose - you just get lucky.
Car combat starts off similarly, forcing you to think a little bit about your approach before you have upgraded your car.  By the time you can hurl thunderpoons at other cars, it's just not that fun anymore because everything explodes pretty easily.  As stated many times, the mini-bosses scattered around are a joke.  They all attack the same way (unblockable charge) and in most cases, you defeat them the same way - hit them with a real big wrench or something else lying around.  Occasionally there are environmental hazards that can aid you - say, but letting a boss charge into a flame burst - but it's nowhere near the extremes of something like Sleeping Dogs.
After a while, you realize that reducing threat across the various warlords' regions by tackling side actitivies (read: map vomit) has stopped being beneficial, as Max is decked out in crazy gear and the car is nigh invulnerable (car upgrades are often locked behind getting threat below a certain level).  It just stops being fun.  I mainlined the last several story missions to get it over with and wasn't left very satisified by the ending.
It's probably worth a play if you dig the universe and don't mind icons all over the place (complete with hot air balloons that let you identify all the actitives in an area!), but it's not really anything spectularly different.

The game itself looked great, and it ran flawlessly on my PC. I read about some of the bugs but never experienced them myself while running the game with all graphics options maxed out.
The car battles and upgrading were a blast, the vehicles handling in a mechanical sense was just "ok" but it was easy to forget about because the actual battling between cars was pretty great.
The story was weak but ok and is mostly moments where you will say "wtf" to your self because you know your about to engage in another series of identical fetch quest which are the meat of this game. If the main audience for this game was  young teenagers the story may have cut it but im thinking there where a lot of adults playing this title for the nostalgia and it just doesn't cut it for us.
Go to this stronghold, complete the same objectives to control it then beat the main baddy of the building. rinse repeat. The worst part is even the mini-bosses are all the same they literally are identical right down to the models and attack patterns the only difference being the color their model is skinned with. Trying not to spoil but there is one battle set in a iconic road warrior setting (hint, it involves chanting) with a mini-boss where I essentially just spammed parry continually until I could attack over and over again. This should have been one of the highlights of the game but nope just another dull battle, TOTAL LET DOWN your doing it wrong WB.
It's to bad too because the voice acting dialog was pretty good and it was almost wasted on this title, it was great hearing the desert blasted heat stoke induced ramblings of the acolyte Chumbucket go on about the worship of the mighty v-8 or some of the mini-bosses talking about using your meat sack as a pleasure puppet after you died. I began to wonder if the games designers made a decision halfway through development whether the game was set in america or austrailia, because I found it hard to tell.
Repetitive sums up this game all to well, and that's a real shame, as a kid who grew up watching the road warrior on network tv and building up its mythos in my head when ever it was on I was sorely disappointing, after seeing Fury Road I was all aboard the hype train for this game. About halfway through the game I found myself just skipping through the dialog because I just wanted to finish the game and be done with it's repetitive grinding. I found myself saying "Just finish the game because you spent 40 dollars on it and you don't want to have it just sit in your library forever." and "Should have bought MGS:V.".
There is plenty more to complain about and not much to commend but this is the bulk of it, too bad the game has great potential but they just couldn't nail it down.
A note to other players who finished the game, we went though this entire game prying things open or kicking them open by mashing a button, but when you really wanted to use that mechanic to say pry something in or out of someones head or chest, nope, you got a cut scene for that......facepalm.

I like this game.  But let me start with the cons:
Slowest walking simulator ever made.  They need to increase run speed by about 30%,  as, when you're traveling at running speed, you generally don't care if there is prey nearby that will run.  You're just trying to get where you're going.  And as there are no real "save" points, you always spawn at the last outpost you were at.  It can take forever to get from one place to another and it just takes tooooo lonnnng.   Maybe make it so you don't need to jump to get over fist-sized rocks when climbing uphill, while you're at it.  I shot a moose, which glitched out- shot it again, then again, at point blank, then it rand at lightspeed away into the distance.  F that moose.  At one point I jumped near a small waist-height tree and immediately died.  Game is buggier than a termite mound.  I wish you could save at any point, and start where you left off, or maybe have it autosave every 10-15 minutes in case the game crahes, instead of at your last outpost.  They're miles apart, and take forever to get back to, so if you do die jumping near a tiny tree, you're going to cry when you respawn miles away.
Pros:
Apex engine is beautiful.  If you have the gpu/cpu to rock this at ultra, it's stunning.  Audio is gorgeous as well,  it puts you right into it's world with all of the ambience you'd expect from a living forest.  Tracking and hunting remind me of Witcher 3 without all the Noonwraiths.  I've only been playing the Pacific NW-ish map, and I really like the mission-giving walkie-talkie guy.  It reminds me of firewatch, but not as linear, with no plot.   This is a great game to play when you're tired of getting smashed in the face in For Honor or need a break from anything competitive or serious.  It's calming, slow, and patient.  I have an i5 4670 and an R9 290, and can play this at 1440p with most settings at ultra but a few turned down.  Apex engine is beautiful - but demanding.  Another thing I wish they'd fix is the cost of items.  The progression system needs skin unlocks or something to motivate you while you save 30000 for that one rifle.  Plus skins are cool!  People love skins!
Overall, there's a LOT to dislike, but TH:COTW still has somehow won me over.  There's a lot of heart in this game.  And a lot of shooting things in the heart, I suppose.  This will remain in my rotation as the game I play to chill after a stressful day.  Overall, recommended if you're looking for something different and don't mind early access (because that's what this really is, feels-wise).  If you have the cash, it's a fun diversion.  They've been steadily ironing out the bugs, and I look forward to future updates.

Before we begin, lets establish one thing: I like buggy games. I like the clunky, glitchy mechanics of DayZ and I enjoy the simplicity of watching a game slowly (oh, so very slowly) change.
I've been playing DayZ on and off for a couple of years, and so far I've still put less than 40 hours into it. From what I've heard from people who play similar games, it's way down the lowest end of the spectrum in it's own genre, but if you want simplicity and a small sense of achievement which comes with living more than a couple of hours, it's great.
However, I got this game as a gift, and there is no way I would pay the current asking price. The game is probably worth £5-10 if you're feeling generous, but I wouldn't pay more unless you literally have money to throw away.
Here's what I say you can expect from DayZ:
If you want a simplistic survival game, there are many,
better options. But, if you want to rage at the slow (practically halted) pace of development (because if you get it now, you have no excuse not to have done your research), feel real accomplishment when you come across a damaged tin of tuna, or savour a brief moment of friendship when you meet a friendly player in the wastes of Chernarus, get someone else to waste their money and buy you this game.
Can I get a refund?

Straight to the point i was able to eat a plate of nachos while playing this game, thus making me feel like a real warden.
Now that i got that out of my system..Prison Architect is exactly what it sounds like. You're given funds to build and run a prison as you see fit. Want to make your prison a place of rehabilitation where these prisoners could potentially go back out in the world? Go for it because you can! Feel like making a prison so harsh and cold visiting Soviet Russia would seem like spring break? Do it!
Now your probably thinking 'Well that sounds a bit trivial and easy' You my friend could not be more wrong. As is standard fare with all building/managment simulators You've Got To Manage Your Money Wisely. However you can't just go throwing money at whatever you want, if your income isn't higher than your spending (such as wages for employees and so on) You're not going to be able to hire that one extra guard you need because you're getting in max security prisoners, or you won't be able to hire that doctor to lead your drug rehabilitation program because you want to actually help these people.
This also isn't a game you can just run and forget about. Oh No! This is a micromanager's wet dream i tell you! While you have some direct control over the people (being able to click on them and tell them where to go) The real control over them comes from handpicking their Regime. Want to set it where the prisoners are only allowed out for showers and food? Go for it, but let's be honest that's not much of a challenge. A real challenge is keeping tabs on all your prisoners while some are workin on laundry, the others a cleaning house, and a few are working in the carpentry shop. Because your prisoners can and will steal tools, which can cause all hell to break loose if your not pay attention.
All in all it's a great game, and you can expect great things to come from this game. i'd give it a 89/100 in it's current state. Plus there's Shawshank Redemption references in the game which is rather clever.

Video Review:
A Rogue Like is generally a game defined by being randomized each run, and after every death, starting a unique run as to make every single run unique. Often it also randomizes the items you get, the power-ups, the layout, pretty much everything except the core mechanics. You work on mastering these mechanics to overcome all the obstacles, randomized, devilishly placed and configured as they might be so that the fact of getting a bad layout won’t necessarily make it a bad run.
Of these two main definitions, Rogue legacy completely follows the latter and sometimes follows the former. The enemy is this big castle, and the hero isn’t a single character, nor technically is it “you”. The hero is the entire family of Knights, Assassins, Shinobi, Barbarians and so on that configure your inheritors. You start each run with the upgrades and equipment that your father or mother wore before you, allowing you to make progress, but the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Charon makes you pay a toll of, initially, all the gold you have, in order to enter the castle again.
So in order to make progress, you  have to advance in the game, get enough gold for the upgrade you want, die, spend all the money you earned minimizing how much money Charon takes from you, and then rinse and repeat. FOR 15 HOURS. I may now have an addiction.
Stuffed to the brim with loot and branches up your metaphorical upgrade tree-family manor, there’s enough content here to keep you awake for days. But you have to add on one more element of randomization, and that’s each children’s traits. Aside from their class, they might be a dwarf. Or a giant. Or stereo blind. Or a hypochondriac. Each with it’s own quirks that punish you but CAN give some kind of advantage.
The main reason that the game clicks is the combination of addictive gameplay that comes from grinding to get better characters to explore more of the castle, and that comes from the upgrades in the manor, the new equipment, the new classes…essentially, the game eventually just throws out so many different things to work towards that you feel like you’re always progressing, which masks the real progression that sometimes is an impediment in games like Spelunky for example: the learning to play better.
When you combine this with the charm that comes from the randomized characters and sense of humor, Rogue Legacy easily excels to be one of the best games I’ve played in years, and it’s all held together by the fantastic gameplay.
Cellar Door Games has some easter eggs in the games showing development of previous titles they worked on. Band of Bears shows something similar to a co-op Binding of Isaac with puzzles being generated depending on the number of players,  and a rhythm based Shmup are both clear indicatives of some of the inspiration behind Rogue Legacy’s gameplay. It approaches Bullet Hell levels of dodging with hyper-precise inputs this side of Super Meat Boy and the randomization and procedural generation of games like The Binding of Isaac, and puts them to use within a gorgeous retro-yet-modern aesthetic that pays homage to the difficulty levels of classics like the Castlevania series. It combines a series of previously used mechanics and dashes their own style and creativity into it, and that’s a surefire way for success.
With this much charm, an amazing soundtrack, hours upon hours of well-crafted gameplay among the four zones in the game, 4 cool bosses and the ability to hit up NG+, it’s hard to NOT recommend the game.
It does have a couple of faults, including that depending on your luck and skill, the game can end up becoming a monotonous grind of dying over and over again inching your way towards success, but for the most part I felt the balancing was well done even if the game does slide a bit towards the extremely difficult at times.
Nontheless, faults like these are not even close to being enough to deter anyone remotely interested in having a good time from picking the game up.

BUY THIS INSTEAD OF FTL!
Top says it all. This game is pretty much everything FTL is not. Brutally challenging but...FUN. That's F U N, what's that spell? Fun!
RL is considered to be a Rogue Lite, as the game allows the player to gain experience/gold to spend on tech tree upgrades or armor upgrades. It uses an RNG to generate the castle map and enemy layouts and does create some creative ways to kill you. The upside? You can HIT the enemies 100% of the time! This simple idea, whose origins began BEFORE Super Mario Bros. and Castlevania... and somehow... escaped the two guys that made FTL is -I must say- pretty darn satisfying.
Who knew that an attack system based on simple spatial awareness could be so...intuitive and enjoyable.
Also when enemies attack you, you can...dodge.
"Dodge?" you say, "Sounds like some fool's flim-flamery to me!"
I assure you dear sir, or madam, that it is entirely genuine. When an enemy attacks the player's character you use the controller to move out of the way of the incoming projectile and thus, negate any damage.
"And what of these enemies? I suppose in the interim of this electronic experience I'm forced to grind these scallywags."
You may sir, you...may. You see, the point of Rogue Legacy is exploration, loot chests, and boss battles. You may kill them and receive a modest reward or avoid them entirely. Unlike FTL, the enemies are an obstacle not a resource.
"Well I say, this is starting to sound like a rummy good time."
I assure you it is. The graphics are pixel artwork and actual care has been taken to achieve a certain asthetic appeal. No longer do you shamble blobby vaguely human crew members about a static background (like FTL) but a valiant knight, mage, assassin and many more characters each with their own playstyle, pros and cons.
The story is a simple one, but it actually exists (unlike FTL). You play an adventurer searching a castle to find a lost prince and slay the monsters that dwell within. Everytime the character dies, decendants are generated to pick up the quest. Exploration reveals notes by the lost prince that shed light on the story, answering questions and eluding to new questions.
Death comes swiftly for any faint-hearted adventurer but the gold you have collected is used to help increase stats like health, mana, weapon and magic damage. Or, use it to buy better gear and weapons for the sons and daughters that come after. The game is filled with dead-pan humor and a lot of the messages and even some player traits will produce a gaffaw or two.
One minor criticism are the controls are a bit on the floaty side. Your character lacks weight and also the hit boxes can be a bit...vague. I don't believe the game has true analog. The player can only run at full speed which can and does get frustrating at times. Though these aren't enough to detract from the game, in this humble critic's opinion.
Pick it up in the steam shop. Full price and you'll still be satisfied, catch it on sale and it's a steal.

The question I asked myself prior to writing this was "What does Mad Max do that other games aren't doing?"  It feels like a game of missed opportunities.  There is this big, very well-crafted world set in a post-apocalypstic land with not all that much to offer an intrepid wanderer.  Yeah, you can drive around and see ruins of buildings and signs, but there is almost never a real point to doing so.  You can pick up tiny amounts of scrap (the game's currency), but after you've liberated some camps the scrap pickups become just another collectible.  Speaking of collectibles, the history relics started interesting enough - a photo, a postcard, a handwritten note of days gone by that Max wistfully comments on - but when I realized I'd collected dozens and wasn't even halfway through the list, I gave up.  They aren't THAT interesting.
The story is cliche at best, the anti-hero just looking out for himself until he meets someone who reminds him of better days and then has to systematically destroy the bad guys.  It's awkward.  At least when you fight, it has real impact.  Punching dudes never really gets old in this game, but the combat has its drawbacks as well.  There is "tap for light hit" and "hold for heavy hit", and a counter button.  You unlock various finishing moves throughout the game that can be useful in group fights, but sometimes the game doesn't respond quickly enough and allows Max to take a hit while setting up such a maneuver.  When in Fury mode, he hits real hard and does some incredibly satisfying suplexes, but there is no way to do it on purpose - you just get lucky.
Car combat starts off similarly, forcing you to think a little bit about your approach before you have upgraded your car.  By the time you can hurl thunderpoons at other cars, it's just not that fun anymore because everything explodes pretty easily.  As stated many times, the mini-bosses scattered around are a joke.  They all attack the same way (unblockable charge) and in most cases, you defeat them the same way - hit them with a real big wrench or something else lying around.  Occasionally there are environmental hazards that can aid you - say, but letting a boss charge into a flame burst - but it's nowhere near the extremes of something like Sleeping Dogs.
After a while, you realize that reducing threat across the various warlords' regions by tackling side actitivies (read: map vomit) has stopped being beneficial, as Max is decked out in crazy gear and the car is nigh invulnerable (car upgrades are often locked behind getting threat below a certain level).  It just stops being fun.  I mainlined the last several story missions to get it over with and wasn't left very satisified by the ending.
It's probably worth a play if you dig the universe and don't mind icons all over the place (complete with hot air balloons that let you identify all the actitives in an area!), but it's not really anything spectularly different.

I am conflicted leaving this game a negative review. For what it is, the game is very beautiful and is very well detailed. When you first start it up you will be impressed with the surroundings and weapon graphics. The phone UI is a little whacky. In fact the UI in general is kind of weird.
The AI is bad... really bad. When you first start, the game introduces you to tracking and killing an animal. This experience is pretty amazing. Then you go off doing "quests" and you realize that the open world AI is just flat out stupid. Animals walk into things. Deer literally keep coming back to the scene of the crime using the caller, until you murder their entire family. Getting into a hunting blind is cool... until literally everything becomes blind to you. I was calling for deer and a bear just walked up and stood there. Shot it in the neck for an instant kill and got a lot of XP.
Sounds are amazing, for a while. You hear wind, walking through brush, rain, and trees all over along with the wildlife. But it gets repetitive and it can get really loud when you are trying to listen to things. When you hear the fog horn sound of a warning call, you will wake up the entire house with a feminine scream.
All in all it's a cool game. But it is buggy and lacks real content. It's just a grind with a small variety of things to kill around you. I think this game could be amazing, and with some content and patches it probably will be, but for $30 I would just wait for a sale or some fixes. So my "negative" review is just one in waiting. I will pick this up again for sure when it goes on sale or a DLC comes out to fix and expand on things.

theHunter: Call of the Wild by Avalanche Studios, Expansive Worlds and astragon Entertainment might just be the “ground-breaking open world hunting simulator” you’ve been waiting for. The game implements realistic animal behavior, ballistics, and even weather cycles. There is not much of a tutorial and the player is dropped into the world with a gun and a map. Although there are initial voice overs and some tips, the player is pretty much left to their own devices.
In regards to gameplay, the tracking mechanic can prove to be both frustrating and exciting. This is perhaps what lends it so well to creating an immersive experience that feels pretty real. While deer don’t have glowing prints, it is difficult not to feel excited when you realize you are getting close to one of the many types of wildlife in the game. It is also important to be on edge because many of the animals can turn and attack at a moment’s notice. It is hard not to feel excited when you finally line up that shot and pull the trigger. This game’s ballistics really alter the success of each shot based off of distance and trajectory so accuracy matters.
However, I did find a few issues with the game. Due to the sheer size of the map and it being rendered all at once, the game is both beautiful and sometimes laggy. When prone I noticed that the grass does not connect to the ground, which caused clipping and obstruct the path at times. The most noteable glitch was a moose stuck in a hillside that would not die until it was shot five times. This is a big deal when ammo is limited and weapons are difficult to unlock in the beginning. There is also an auto walk feature, which is nice when walking great distances, but problematic when collecting trophies. This is because when doing so the game does not pause and you can walk off a cliff, be attacked by a bear, or both in my case.

I've been playing Rust since it's Legacy version and have to say this is one of the best games I've had the pleasure of playing and watching grow. I've been through the different directions and experiments they've tried, and they're nailing it!! The steady growth and expansion of how you can play, what you can create, how you interact is exciting and leaves me looking forward to the next steps in the evolution of this game. I see a lot of folks giving negative reviews since the "twig" update, and it boggles my mind that a step towards more realism is considered bad. Now people can use ladders to scale walls, build basic scaffolding next to a building to check it out and to be able to attack from different directions. The bases are no longer protected by the "magic" power of a Tool Cabinet, you have to be more creative and resourceful to defend your home. I recommend this game wholeheartedly to anyone who isn't afraid of a challenge and isn't afraid of change. I'd also recommend learning it on smaller private servers, which tend to be friendlier and more helpful than the larger public servers. When you're ready for the mayhem that is a large public server, jump in and see how it goes.

-Codex: Very bare bones for information. Doesn't quite explain the most important issues like how to use certain equipment and why the highest calibur rifle has an accuracy of 0. Looked for a wikia and didn't find much. But I shouldn't have to use google to have a base understanding of a game.
-Callers: Very very useful, almost to a fault. I've been hunting only a few times in the real world and callers have not worked so well for me. It seems like I just sprint through the forest, hear a warning call, use the correct caller and wait. Seems like the other methods of hunting in this game are much more difficult and I find myself using callers to farm money for hours just to buy a new rifle.
-Leveling up: Extremely slow leveling progression. I have 35 hours and about 150-200 animals hunted. I'm a total level of 15. Very few skills I can get and very few perks. I understand hunting is a time consuming activity and a simulation should be as realistic as possible, but it seems like grinding levels takes the fun out of it.
-Glitching: I've experienced many glitches. I press ESC and it sends me to another reserve, after taking a shot with the perk to stay scoped it shows me down the barrel of the gun instead of scope, serveral several animals are stuck on rocks and trees, [E] Inspect stays until restart of game, certain items requiring 0/0 skill remain locked through entire game, animals remaining upright after death, after coming out of aim it auto spins me 90-180 degrees instantly and animals shot over ~300m don't take off running.
It is a beautiful looking game and has a lot of good aspects to it. But the gameplay seems underdeveloped.

I'd like to say I love the idea of the game. However, I do not recommend it because it just isn't playable.
After 40 minutes (!!!) of moving around I finally got my first kill. I understand that a hunter needs patience, but this is just ridiculous. There should be many more animal spawns and they shouldn't be able to detect you so easily.. They run off and it's impossible to catch up to them. There's too much grass/brush/trees in the maps that scare them off when you walk. Either minimize the sound you make when walking through them or stop filling the maps with them... I hate the fact you have to walk 24/7 whilst playing the game because if you run they will run immediately. Sooooo boring.
I also hit a deer in the head and it still started running away? Wtf? I had to chase it for 5 minutes before I found it dead on the ground. In my opinion a headshot should be an instant kill, at least on a small deer.

Currently at 20 hours of gampelay in this and I can understand why the game is recieving mixed reviews.
First off: Bugs. Yes there are bugs. The game was JUST released and by a developer who is small compared to other developers. Give them time. They actively listing to the community and review what is said. Bugs will be fixed, have patience.
Some feel this game should be marked as early access. I personally disagree, for what it has it feels like a functional game, it just needs some patches/hotfixes. It is a full working game for the most part.
The graphics are absolutely stunning, even on the lowest setting.
If you've played The Hunter (Classic) you know what to expect, tracking, tracking, more tracking and finally the kill shot. This plays similar but the maps are MUCH larger. Hirschfelden is at least 6 times larger (IMO), the classic map itself is contained in the North East to give you an idea of size.
It has a decent amount of weapons, good selection of rifles, handguns, shotguns, and bows. All the necessary callers/scents for the current animals, and they will be adding more as they expand their reserves, why wouldn't they? Look at how many animals and reserves they have in Classic.
If you've never played The Hunter (Classic), this is not like other first person shooters, though I hope that would be obvious enough to not have to say.
Keeping in mind that the Dev's will be releasing more content, and If I remember correctly the price should stay at ~$30, compare the average cost for the Classic game: weapons, outfits, membership fees, all the reserves and animals possible to hunt. You'd be talking potentially upwards of $60 if not even more (I've sunk more than I care to admit into that game and I still love it). $30 is NOT a lot compared to that, and it's on a more modern engine with planned content being made.
For weapons each rifle and pistol comes with two different ammunition types that, I feel, are a little too similar right now. Shotguns still have three types of rounds.
Animals now have different classes that are used for them (0-4 currently). 0 being Coyotes and Foxs, 4 being bears and bison. Weapons have a specific class type that can be used for any animal of the same class or higher (not effeciently), if you use a higher class weapon against a lower class animal it will ruin the integrity, causing lower payout and score (potentially score).
Bows on the other hand have 3 ammo types, where each ammo type is a different class. I find that interesting because it makes it more versitile. Bows now take some getting used to due to the now random arrow off-set that can happen (The in-game dev's themselves state it is NOT the aim wobble but a different calculation) but is still a VERY powerfull weapon.
All in all, I'd say $30 is definitely a very fair price for the game, in it's current status and obviously as more content gets released.
EDIT: Forgot to add: NIGHTTIME HUNTING! I totally forgot about this. The game includes a FULL night/day cycle and you have a headlamp that is used to find tracks at night. This actually provides a bit more challenge because you can only see the tracks one of two ways: Stumbling over it or looking around with the headlamp on. I love the increased difficulty of this because it makes it more fun in my opinion. Couple that with the weather cycle that was heavily improved on compared to Classic (wind can affect your scent direction and distance, but also make you harder to hear), Fog makes you more difficult to see, and Rain can also affect how difficult you are to hear.
Overall a Great game! i give a 4 out of 5 starts because of the graphic content, gamplay, and  realism. if your looking for a realistic hunting game. this is it!

I had just spotted my first decent buck in Layton Lake and observed, attempting to get closer for a better shot. However, he quickly spooked and bolted off into the underbrush. I tracked him, but eventually gave up and decided to head for a nearby observation point and take in the scenery.
I'd like to say, this game has perfectly captured how it feels to be in the woods. I hike occasionally during the summer and this is the first game I've ever seen that had me convinced my character was actually in a forest instead of just a clump of trees. The underbrush is great and the topogrophy is excellent. The way the lighting interacts with the trees and brush is absolutely perfect.
Back to ingame, I continued along a path leading to the lookout tower. Then my attention was brought straight forward by the warning grunt of a black bear. I quickly dropped into a crouch and raised my rifle. Though some brush, I could see a bear with a cinnamon coat quartering towards me, coming along the path maybe 45 yards away. I lined up the reticle with the front of his shoulder, held my breath, pulled the trigger. He took a few more steps along the path, so I fired again, dropping him in his tracks.
This is what you get when you purchase this product. A convincing virtual world and a rewarding experience. At times it's a painfully slow burner, but when you finally get that perfect shot you know that the game didn't give it to you. You earned it.
P.S. to fans of turkey hunting, waterfowling and upland birds: They aren't currently included in the game but I have a strong suspicion they'll make their way in at some point.
EDIT: I should mention there did seem to be a large infestation of bugs when the game was first released but it has been patched multiple times since release and I have yet to experience any game breaking bugs, just a few very minor graphical glitches.

"That's right, ♥♥♥♥♥es - my big brudder's about to teach you some MANNERS. Nobody steals Mushy Snugglebites' badonkadonk and lives!" – Tiny Tina
Borderlands is a First Person Shooter, with a liner main story, set in open world areas that contain multiple side missions that unlock as you progress, with a random drop loot system, played as 1 of 4 [1 of 6 with DLC] uniquely skilled vault hunters, either solo or online with up to 3 others.
Borderlands is set on the planet Pandora. Once home to a very advanced alien civilization, that has left behind very little other than the ruins & legends of Vaults that are supposed to contain great wealth, technology and power.
Now though Pandora is a very different place. Following the quick withdrawal of DHAL who was faced with the more advanced forces of ATLAS, most of DHAL’s workforce was left behind including, scientists, workers, their families and the conscripted convict workforce. These have regressed into tribal groups of psycho’s, bandits, raiders and complete nut jobs [that make for great guilt free killing].
The main story will take you through many amazing environments and has some great twists and turns that help make this game so great. The side quest will have you exploring more of the areas, as well as giving you insight into parts of the main story, Pandoras history and its inhabitance. Whilst rewarding you with good and/or unieque loot.

There is as much humor in this game as there is loot, from the crazy to the bazar things the bandits shout at you to the monologs of the supporting cast and the outburst from your own character, I have found myself in stiches when I should be trying not to get shoot.
Once you complete the main story you can go back and explore or finish any mission you didn't before, or, advance to True Vault Hunter Mode[sort of a new game +] where you start the story again with all your skills, guns and other loot, but this time you will find different variations of pervious enemies, upping the challenge. If you take this play through to the end [with the DLC] you have the option to to start a Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode [UVHM], this is a little different, not only are all the enemies of equal level to the strongest player in your lobby, they have more health, do more damage and regen health, your best advantage is your skill s, loadout and slag damage multiplier now being 3x. This mode can be tricky and equally rewarding, as well as offering access to a new level cap & tier of loot.
The expansions/DLC:
Mechromancer pack - Adds Gaige the Mechromancer, new vault hunter – A must get.
Psycho Pack - Adds Krieg the Psycho, new vault hunter – A must get.
Ultimate vault hunter pack 1 – Up’ level cap by 10 to 61 and adds pearlescent weapons – A must get.
Ultimate vault hunter pack 2 – Up’s level cap by 10 to 71 and adds Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode, UVHM – A must get.
Mr. Torgue’s Campaign of Carnage – New story, sides, environments, loot, bad guys & so on – A must get.
Captain Scarlett and her Pirate's Booty – New story, sides, environments, loot, bad guys & so on – A must get.
Sir Hammerlock’s Big Game Hunt - New story, sides, environments, loot, bad guys & so on – A must get.
Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep - New story, sides, environments, loot, bad guys & so on – THIS IS POSSIBLY THE BEST EXPANSION TO ANY GAME I HAVE EVER PLAYED.
Sorry, I don’t normally type so loud but I cannot express how much I loved this expansion. I could go on for ages about it, but it would be best to just play it, I may even go as far as saying it’s better than the main game ... sod it, IT IS BETTER THAN THE MAIN GAME.  It’s not as big or contains as many locations, enemies, unique loot and so on.
BUT and it’s a big but. It is so well written, maybe because you are technically playing a FPS of a D&D style game hosted by Tiny Tina, allowing us to keep the madness & hilarity of Pandora whilst also escaping enough of the laws of physics to allow for some amazing moments and fun poking at all things geeky whilst being as big of one as possible, and at the same time allowing Tina to come to terms with the loss of good friends.
Damn, even writing this has brought a tear to my eye.
Tina is such a big character even though we see little of her, the background story of her dealing with the loss touches at the heart string. The loss of her friends through the game feels personal to me as well. I know there not real, I now I could start again and they would be there, but even so when they died I stopped, took a step back from my keyboard and even ended having a short soul searching walk to the local. That blow hurt. I hate the writers for it but at the same time realise that’s because they got me to care for them, to feel something more about a group of pixels than I have real people.   RIP my friends.
This expansion is one of the best I have ever played, the others are good don't get me wrong, but this is a step above.

After seeing Mad Max: Fury Road, which in my opinion is one of the best action movies I've seen in many years, I had serious high hopes for this game even though and let's be honest here, most movie licensed games suck. So I was pleasantly surprised to find out that Mad Max stays true to its roots and provides a very interesting open world game with a lot of freedom, excellent racing and solid combat mechanics. There's a ton of stuff to collect and although some people find the game repetitive after a while, I personally had no problems with it.
Graphically the game looks very impressive, probably the most beautiful depiction of a wasteland I've seen in a game so far. The game also runs buttery smooth with only a minor dip below 60 fps with absolute max settings running on a GTX 970. This is seriously one of the best optimized PC games I've played. Kudos to developer Avalanche for giving us such a solid PC port.
The story is surprisingly good and makes excellent use of the Mad Max universe we've come to love from the movies. Although the game doesn't directly tie into the last film Fury Road it does feature many of its plot elements such as the war boys, gas town and other things from the earlier Mad Max movies. Although the game misses the voice talent of Tom Hardy or Mel Gibson for Max, the voice cast does a fantastic job bringing the characters to life. Sound design and the music soundtrack are also top-notch and add a lot to the overall atmosphere of the game.
If you like open world action games then you should seriously consider picking this game up. Those who are expecting deep character customization or varied RPG like elements found in a lot of other open world games might be disappointed and the game does have a certain level of grinding to it. If that doesn't matter to you then Mad Max is definitely something you will enjoy.

Because the majority of this will be talking about the writing, let’s start with talking about the gameplay mechanics. The big change here over the original
is that instead of being able to rewind time as Max, you have a "Backtalk" mode that enables you to insult people to get what you want. It feels appropriately punk and adolescent, but it is also worth noting that it feels silly and forced, and is ultimately not very interesting. I can understand the need to put "something" in, and it does feel fitting for Chloe’s character, but it didn’t feel like it amounted to much. I hope the later episodes make better use of it, or scrap it. The writing itself is mostly excellent. There are cases where it feels over the top, and where dialogue choices flow very badly from previous statements, as if the conversational threads existed within a vacuum. But it also appropriately captures the feel, and it’s a very different one from
.
had a sense of how being a teenager is confusing. As Max, you were trying to learn who you are, and who you wanted to be. If you could rewind time, what would you do differently. Would you help people or exploit them? What would you do with that kind of power?
contrasts that wonderfully by being about having no power at all. It’s about being lost, and overwhelmed by a world that you don’t feel you fit into, where "life isn’t fair" and everything that happens is the end of the world. But don’t mistake it for "teen angst", it's genuine (and warranted) misery and frustration and loneliness.
Prior to spending the day with Rachel, the only time that you see Chloe happy or excited is during an extended sequence where you can play a sort of
game while waiting for class to start. It works because it shows how Chloe flourishes and gets into it when there’s a world where she knows who she is, what the rules are, and what her place is within it. As the game comes to a close, you’re left with the fear of committing to more, because caring is expressing vulnerability.
And that’s something present through this episode, with Rachel and Chloe both expressing that fear in different situations. At one point, Rachel expresses that she’s happy you opened up, and Chloe replies "It's not a big deal", but we know it is. It’s everything to have that trust in someone else. Your school is filled with people you don’t feel connections with, your mother is spending time with her new boyfriend, and the only people you want to be with, the only ones who would understand, are your deceased father, and former best friend Max.
The image that sticks out most in my mind after finishing the first episode is of Chloe crying in the fetal position, in a junkyard, after smashing things in a tear-filled rage of pure frustration. Is it melodramatic? Absolutely. But it’s honest, and it feels accurate to what it was to be a teenager and not know how to express what you were feeling.
With knowing, not necessarily how this game is going to end, but what happens to both Chloe and Rachel later, there’s some moments that felt like a punch in the gut. There’s a moment where Rachel says "I just want you to know that I’m lucky you were with me today, Chloe Price". And I know that there’s a day when she won’t be there. Just like how Max and her father weren’t there when she needed them most, no matter what I do, Chloe won’t be there when Rachel needs her.
The stakes work better here than
because we know what they are. We’re not embarking on some mystery and trying to save the city. Instead, the stakes are our happiness, and that of others. I got an in-game text that said Mikey’s been feeling down lately, but playing
with me really helped a lot. That’s what it’s about, these connections we form and what we experience together.
