Others have mentioned it before, but this game is far from being ready for release. For early access the level of bugs and issues would have been acceptable, but still better to call it an open beta.
The main problem I have with this, is that ExpansiveWorlds (Avalanche Studios) has a long-standing track record of releasing unfinished content and often never polishing it to perfection even way later. This is true for basically every update theHunter:classic received, but especially for theHunter:Primal - a game that was sold in some kind of beta-state (especially content-wise) and never made it any further.
The game looks awesome! The vegetation, the scenery, the lighting, the animal models, the animations (well, besides the players hands, what the frog am I doing? Running in the praying mantis karate base pose?) - all looks terrific and stunning. The way you leave a trail of flattened grass behind is just cool. Ok, it looks like you're a Mafiosi that just dragged a concrete-cuffed rival to his favourite dumpster lake, but hey, it's still a cool effect. A shame that the graphics are the only outstanding part of this game. I am more willing to overlook less-than-perfect graphics than flawed game design or mechanics.
So you got theHunter:classic, a massive open-world hunting game with plenty of content and great game mechanics. It just suffers from a meanwhile rather dated graphic engine  (fair enough being already 8 years old) and a microtransaction-based business model that has met plenty of criticism. Yet the cash-cow seems still lactating, as they are still keeping the game alive.
So what to do to lead theHunter into the future. Develop a successor and kill your cash flow of the old game? Much better to produce something slightly different that recruits new customers, fascinates your old clientèle and still doesn't stop them from spending on the old one. Much better idea indeed. If you're able to pull it off, that is.
So why not make an open world hunting game like the hunter that still has a story line. Red Dead Redemption hunting themed, basically. Nice idea.
But then why they got it all backwards? Why does the actual hunting feel like you're mowing down the imbecile cousins of some majestic animals you dreamt of hunting all your life? The actual hunting is no challenge at all, you just need to be in the right place, and the animals will be easy to harvest.
The "story line" (in brackets, as I am not sure yet, there's any red line through the story - it might just be random bits) on the other hand is slow as a sloth. A couple of hours in and I haven't even proceeded much in the tutorial story line (it is supposed to be a tutorial, right?). All I did is wander lengthily through a beautiful landscape getting sidetracked by some dull hunting while trying to get to a lodge or view point or camp.
I feel a good hunting game with a story line should be exactly the other way around: extensive, to some extend challenging hunting embedded in a faster paced, enthralling story line. That'd be an interesting cross-over game between an emersion-intense hunting game and a hunting-themed arcade/adventure game. This game is exactly the opposite. It got real dull real quick for me, and I am a sucker for a good hunting game.
I'll probably wait for a follow-up of theHunter:classic. Or maybe even a similar product by a competent competitor that might be released in a rather finished state - one should be allowed to dream big.

Yeah, all I do all day is (badly) drive around fake European roads and deliver fake goods. That doesn't sound very exciting.
If that's the case, why have I played it for more than 25 hours? Euro Truck Sim is weird in that way. It doesn't sound fun but yet it's hard to stop playing. It's almost like Microsoft Flight Simulator in that it's relaxing. Turn on the European (UK, Czech, French, etc.) radio, pick up a load and let's go crusing past the pretty terrain on my way to delivering that cargo for more money!. Delver that load, pick up another and head elsewhere. Maybe I feel like visiting the Danes today and those canals. Maybe I prefer the curvy roads of the Alps. Or maybe I'd like to visit Scotland.
Either way, it's addictive. After a while you get new trucks, hire drivers and expand your empire to become a shipping tycoon. It's not a particularly well done piece of the game but it does give the player a reason to keep hauling those loads. But overall it's just something you play to relax and enjoy. Now if you'd excuse me, I need to go tour the French countryside and get my hazardous materials bonus!

Others have mentioned it before, but this game is far from being ready for release. For early access the level of bugs and issues would have been acceptable, but still better to call it an open beta.
The main problem I have with this, is that ExpansiveWorlds (Avalanche Studios) has a long-standing track record of releasing unfinished content and often never polishing it to perfection even way later. This is true for basically every update theHunter:classic received, but especially for theHunter:Primal - a game that was sold in some kind of beta-state (especially content-wise) and never made it any further.
The game looks awesome! The vegetation, the scenery, the lighting, the animal models, the animations (well, besides the players hands, what the frog am I doing? Running in the praying mantis karate base pose?) - all looks terrific and stunning. The way you leave a trail of flattened grass behind is just cool. Ok, it looks like you're a Mafiosi that just dragged a concrete-cuffed rival to his favourite dumpster lake, but hey, it's still a cool effect. A shame that the graphics are the only outstanding part of this game. I am more willing to overlook less-than-perfect graphics than flawed game design or mechanics.
So you got theHunter:classic, a massive open-world hunting game with plenty of content and great game mechanics. It just suffers from a meanwhile rather dated graphic engine  (fair enough being already 8 years old) and a microtransaction-based business model that has met plenty of criticism. Yet the cash-cow seems still lactating, as they are still keeping the game alive.
So what to do to lead theHunter into the future. Develop a successor and kill your cash flow of the old game? Much better to produce something slightly different that recruits new customers, fascinates your old clientèle and still doesn't stop them from spending on the old one. Much better idea indeed. If you're able to pull it off, that is.
So why not make an open world hunting game like the hunter that still has a story line. Red Dead Redemption hunting themed, basically. Nice idea.
But then why they got it all backwards? Why does the actual hunting feel like you're mowing down the imbecile cousins of some majestic animals you dreamt of hunting all your life? The actual hunting is no challenge at all, you just need to be in the right place, and the animals will be easy to harvest.
The "story line" (in brackets, as I am not sure yet, there's any red line through the story - it might just be random bits) on the other hand is slow as a sloth. A couple of hours in and I haven't even proceeded much in the tutorial story line (it is supposed to be a tutorial, right?). All I did is wander lengthily through a beautiful landscape getting sidetracked by some dull hunting while trying to get to a lodge or view point or camp.
I feel a good hunting game with a story line should be exactly the other way around: extensive, to some extend challenging hunting embedded in a faster paced, enthralling story line. That'd be an interesting cross-over game between an emersion-intense hunting game and a hunting-themed arcade/adventure game. This game is exactly the opposite. It got real dull real quick for me, and I am a sucker for a good hunting game.
I'll probably wait for a follow-up of theHunter:classic. Or maybe even a similar product by a competent competitor that might be released in a rather finished state - one should be allowed to dream big.

Waited a long time for this game and fortunately it turned out to be everything I hoped it would be. There are some bugs and issues, but none have been in any way gamebreaking for me. The important stuff works.
So here's some of the things that are great:
- The visuals and sounds are gorgeous in every way and there's nice variety in locations.
- The chase gives you the same kind of thrills as when you go hunting for real.
- Tracking is done properly and is quite enjoyable.
- Player movement and gunplay is spot on.
- The statistics info on the harvested animal is done properly.
Some small things that still need some improvement:
- The menu and keybinds have some problems
- Gear needs a lot more variety, since now there's only a fraction of the items from the original. But I guess that's the DLC plan...
- Sneaking feels a bit dodgy and the vagueness of the movement sound UI doesn't help. Makes it a lot more difficult to track wounded animals.
- The animal AI sometimes does funny things like gets stuck on things.
- Freaked out wounded animals run around way too fast compared to the real thing.
- It feels like the bleeding mechanic also needs a bit of tweaking. If you miss all the critical target hitboxes, the animal always bleeds at the "Very low" bleed rate, even with clear head- or gut shots. Also, wounds bleed more if you run, so running speed should affect the bleed rate.
- I would prefer vehicles (or a horse) over fast travel any day.
Conclusion: A very enjoyable hunting game and I expect it only to get better.

Undertale is a fun and unique RPG game that allows the player to do something that most games do not.
Have you ever wondered, why in many RPG games, you have to kill everything, and you have to seek getting as much EXP as possible? Why do you have to kill everything? What if you could befriend them, and learn their story, instead?
In Undertale, you play as a human who has fallen into Mt. Ebott, somehow surviving their fall by falling into a bed of golden flowers. During this time, tensions are strong between humans and monsters, as the humans and monsters are involved in a war. The humans had sealed the monsters into the underground, trapping them with a barrier.
As you explore the Underground, and as you progress in the game, you will meet new friends, new enemies. you will meet many different kinds of monsters. Some hostile at first, and some friendly, each monster in Undertale seems to have a different and unique personality.
You can be either a pacifist or genocidal, but I prefer only taking the pacifist route, as the pacifist route of the game is heartwarming and uplifting, and it allows me to hear more about the Monsters and their perspectives and their story in Undertale, and also, well... if you're like me, you'll get quite attached to these charming characters. (I have played the Pacifist route four times, and the game is still super fun and charming!)
In Undertale, as you explore, you will also see all sorts of cool environments, and hear the game's acclaimed great soundtrack.
Every character in Undertale has their strengths and weaknesses, and their flaws and their good traits, too. With their unique and varied personalities, many of Undertale's characters have become relatable for quite a few fans of the game, and I admire games that put so much care and attention into its characters and its writing.
Although the game can be creepy and foreboding at times, the game also has many moments of humor, fun, and silliness!
Undertale, in its pacifist run, has been one of the funniest, most uplifting, emotional, and heartwarming games that I have ever played. I have no complaints about the game, and I would encourage anyone to play! Don't mind the fan-base, and give Undertale a try. In my eyes, it is essential that you go into this game blind, and not let yourself uncover spoilers, as the game has its share of surprises and events! ^.^

Mad Max is a very good open world game and deserves much more credit than some of the major crtitics gave it. Its a fairly standard layout of open world game, so I wont bother going into massive detail, but here's a summary
The Good Stuff:
-Massive, detailed and living open world map
-Loads to do in Free Roam
-Great customisation of Max and his car
-Driving is good fun (made better by how nice the world is to look at)
-On foot combat is good, ammo is realistically scarce
-Petrol and water add a nice but light dimension of survival
- Meaningful upgrade and perk system mean you feel yourself becoming more formidable
-Car Combat doesnt seem to get boring
-Good level of car combat difficulty
-Great all round graphics
The Not so Good:
-On foot combat/ enemy camp assaults are a tad too easy
-Very little strong narrative or story telling
- Survival elements could have been more developed (Petrol lasts way too long)
So to summarise, the game world is vast, varied , great to look at and a joy to drive through, and its this aspect of fully customizing/building your car from the ground up, and then racing across the canyons and desserts that forms the largest part of the games appeal. The on foot combat is fun and does a great job of giving you a break from driving, ensuring you dont get bored of the driving side of the game. The only things that stop the game being the best open world game I've ever played are the lack of exploration into max's interesting story and general difference in difficulty between car combat and on foot combat, i.e if you put the difficulty on hard, on foot combat would be pleasantly challenging but car combat would be frustratingly hard. That being said this is still the most fun I've had in an open world game since GTA 5 first game out. The beautiful world and fun of bouncing across it in your own personal magnum opus, stopping to beat the crap out of bandits on the way really makes for a great game.
As for its repetitiveness , its no more repetitive than any assassins creed game so if you like that kind of open world then you'll love this.

You play as Max, a former Road Warrior wandering the wastes in search of inner-peace and an escape from his past. Max, roaming across The Big White for a place known as "The Plains of Silence," is suddenly attacked by a horde of War Boys with Scaberous Scrotus, the tormenting tyrant of the wastes, at the helm. You're soon left in the desert with nothing but the shirt on your back until you stumble across Chumbucket - a paranoid hunchback who literally worships cars and sees Max as a figure sent from God, and with this enlightened vision he convinces Max to help him build the Magnum Opus - the Holy Grail of cars that will be used to finally bring justice to the wastes.
Now first of all I want to talk about the setting, and I have to admit it is one of the most gorgeous games I have played in a long time. Who knew that a bare backdrop of white sand and brown rock could be so beautiful. The map is divided up into regions - each with their own destinct personality and each feeling very different from the other. I do have to give the developers a lot of credit for how simply unique this sandbox really is. It's the little details that really set it off, with buried trains sticking out of dunes, crashed plains and jumbo jets which have been turned into scavenger camps, and huge volcanos which once sat under the ocean - all of it ready to explore, and not to mention the incredible weather effects from slight gusts of wind which blow away the fumes from your exhaust, to the gigantic sand storms which can be lethal. Easily one of the best looking games of 2015 thus far.
Though with all that said, when crunch-comes-crunch the majority of us care about the gameplay most and that's were I begin to struggle with what to really say about this game. The game plays best when you are behind the wheel of a car. Chasing down a convoy and taking on six enemy vehicles at once truly feels like something out of a Mad Max movie and is a real thrill. The sense of speed is great and at the same time it feels brutal. Smashing and ramming with huge explosions and impacts are what I was hoping for, and with this game I got it. There are also tons of upgrades to choose from, all which will effect your car in negative/positive ways so I'm sure everyone can find a formula to fit their own play-style. I just wish the same could be said about the ground combat.
Ground combat consists mainly of hitting 3 buttons. You use your attack button, the block button when prompt and the occasional roll to dodge attacks which can't be avoided. There are special attacks such as a 'shiv finisher' in which Max will fatally knife his opponent but these are optional. The combat is just very easy and not very exciting. The enemies do change and some are more difficult than others but they can all still be defeated with the same 3 buttons as long as you get your timing right. The closest thing to this type of combat is Batman: Arkham Asylum, though it never feels as responsive or as polished in Mad Max. The only positive side of combat is the use of Fury Mode which the player gains by chaining attacks and creating a combo. Eventually the screen will start to flash red and all of Max's attacks will deal a lot more damage. His fighting style also changes drastically. He suddenly has much more reach, swings his arms as if his fists turned into bricks and even performs wrestling moves. It's always fun to see Max suplex a skinny War Boy to his death, though this is the only redeeming feature here.
The general game-play consists of driving to markers on the map and initiating a mission, though around 80% of the missions seemed like fetch-quests to me. It was mostly "drive here - deliver that" or "drive here - kill some guys - drive back". Some missions were very fun, but those missions used the setting to their advantage. Driving into a buried airport and being chased by Buzzards is great, but the other missions hardly live up to the likes of those ones. Outside of missions there isn't much to do either apart from gathering scrap and clearing enemy camps. Clearing a camp consists of disabling the outer defences such as snipers and fire-traps and then running inside and killing everyone, and on top of that there may be an objective such as some oil barrels you have to destroy. At first it was fun, but when you are still doing that after the 30 hour mark it really starts to become tedious.
Scrap is the "Wasteland currency" which you use to upgrade your car and weaponry - but with the amount of upgrades to buy, gathering scrap becomes a complete chore. I found myself just grinding small campsites for tiny amounts of scrap and I had nothing else to do outside of story missions. It was at this point the game stopped getting fun and I knew this was as good as it gets. You can also use scrap to improve strongholds (bases belonging to allied characters), though this costs a lot of scrap to do. I was hoping that once a stronghold was fully upgraded that I would recieve some sort of benefit in return. Perhaps a large amount of scrap, or a scrap multiplier, or a new upgrade - but no, I didn't get anything. I grinded for ages just to improve the aesthetic of a place I will most likely never visit again, and it's this type of grinding and pointless options this game is full of once you get a few hours in.
Boss battles were the biggest let down of all. I fought my first boss after invading his camp and killing all his goons. The boss was a huge guy with a giant hammer/razor/mace hybrid and he wore a gimp mask covered in paint, and this all seemed very 'Mad Max' to me and I was happy to see the boss fights match the setting and I thought this was only going to get better (this was around the 6 hour mark). Then eventually I reached my second boss fight, and he was exactly the same with the same character model and weapon and everything, just with a different coloured paint on his face - and then I reached the third boss, and the fourth, all the way until the fifth boss and they were all exactly the same. Now this really annoyed me because it was so obviously lazy is was incredible. That's when I really got tired with this game - and to think it all started off so well. Grinding for scrap I can tolerate, and pointless side-missions I can also tolerate, but copy and pasting the same boss character 5 times in a row? C'mon...
It was then I realised that if I look past the immersive setting and the pretty graphics that Mad Max is as wide as an ocean, but about as deep as a puddle. Those enemy convoys which were so fun to chase down and destroy do nothing but drive around in circles forever following the same roads, and that the few set-piece missions were over within a few minutes of them just getting good. This can be extended to describe nearly all aspects of this game.
I feel after more than 30 hours of Mad Max I can come to a conclusion on it. Is it a bad game? No, it's not necessarily a bad game but it isn't good either. It had a lot of potential to be an incredible game and it's nice to see a developing team put so much effort into what is an amazing setting for a game - but with all that said, when clearly so much effort went into the graphics and setting, why did not an equal amount of effort be put into the actual game-play? The game starts of fantastically and then just seems to nose-dive after the 10th hour mark. It becomes a grind of banality and pointlessness and generally feels aimless when I look at the bigger picture -  and the lack of story in the later game doesn't do much to keep the player wanting to move forward either. It's hard to look past all of the problems which infest Mad Max.
I wish I could give this game a 'Neutral' rating, but as I can't I will give it a negative one instead, with which I will say to you that you should only buy the game when it's on special offer. Do not buy it for the full price as it simply isn't worth it.

Having been a fan of the Mad Max movies I was hoping to find the game to be a virtual playground that puts you in that world and after playing it for just over 90 hours I can see it succeeded. Mad Max takes place in post apocalyptic world where food and water are scarce and power is in gasoline and oil. The V8 engine is king and those that have it rule the wasteland. While Mad Max may not have a deep and moving storyline it does stay true to the films. You are Mad Max, you do what you can to survive and that revolves taking care of  you car.
Visually the game is beautiful with the wasteland depicted in all its bleak and colorless glory. There are several regions that are unique that can be differentiated upon so there is region specific looks but again the wasteland  is depicted true to the films and looks great. The cars look amazing and the explosions and fire are some of the best I've seen in a driving game. Everything looks fantastic and really adds to the immersion of the game.
Gameplay consist of a good mix of driving and combat in third person. The car battles are a lot of fun, especially the convoy take downs. While ammo is scarce in the wasteland the third person  combat offers many ways to fight enemies using melee weapons picked up along the way and explosions offering many creative ways to dispatch enemies.
Huge open world offers many things to do and see during your stay in the wasteland. While some of the car races can be challenging and some quest such as disarming mines can get repetative quick, there is plenty to do for achievement hunters.
This game seems to be on sale everywhere even before it came out. I got a great deal on this game and feel like I got my monies worth and then some. I feel Avalanche Studios did an excellent conversion of the Mad Max franchise to a gaming world and would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys open world games, driving, and lots of action all in a post apocalyptic settings.

Setting aside the main quests, this game heavily relies on exploration and side quests. It may seem that the developers spent more time in designing the entire world than focusing on its story that reminds me of some other post-apocalyptic themed games I played before ( Fallout ).
Bottom line is, this was an amazing hotseat video game that I could just turn my mind off to and relax.

It's between Borderlands 2 and Elite (C64) for my favorite game of all time.
The characters are well balanced compared to other games of the same age and all of the DLCs add real variety to the game.
It is quite easy to spend 100+ hours to play one character through from Normal, True and Ultimate modes playing all quests, add to that the Digistruct peak DLC and you have 80 levels and the ability to reset Ultimate Vault hunter mode on completion if you wish to.
All the DLCs are available for each playthrough and can range from about 20 hours to as little as 2 hrs for some of the Headhunter pack DLCs.
As you play a new character through each quest, the level of difficulty for each enemy type increases slowly, which is offset by list of challenges contributing to a Badass score feeding buffs.

The scaling is better than most games I've played once you get used to the combinations of weapons and elementals needed to do the most damage, and the location of critical hit points for the more powerful enemy types.
Loot is mostly from a random drop mechanism so the more side quests you do, the more enemy you kill, the more chance you have to get some of the more unusual and rare gear. Gear can be passed down to your next character if needed but only 4 pieces at a time which becomes tedious.
Multiplayer is great fun and the only way to defeat some of the DLC bosses at higher levels.
The only real annoyances are not having the ability to start a character in TVHM (True Vault Hunter Mode) or UVHM without having to play through Normal mode first, and a very small inventory compared to the variety of loot available or needed for specific quests as the difficulty increases.
Overall a great game, and if you are ever laid up for an extended period of time, a damn good time waster.

Rust is, in my opinion, the very best alpha survival game made to date, and the development team's dedication to providing a product that is as bug-free and optimized as possible in alpha stage is proof that an alpha game can indeed be worth the money. Let's not forget that for all the infinite possibility of fun, and nearly-infinite map generation possibilities that the game provides, it is only $20.00. A one-time payment for legitimately infinite potential.
Yes, of course, people are going to raid your♥♥♥♥♥♥ If you're new and build a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ base, you WILL indeed be raided. If you think that you're the best FPS player evz and don't know about how bullet drop, recoil, and supressing fire works, you will demolished. If you think that people are going to be nice to you because you scream friendly, you WILL be wiped.
Of course, these possibilities are obvious for those who enjoy the content of a survival game. The Devs constantly work and change things around that make the flow of the game different, as they warn you before you purchase. They cannot be more obvious or clear in stating that the game is in alpha - some things work, some things don't. They're making their vision of the best post-apocalyptic MMO survival game possible, and doing a great job at that - whether or not the plebs with 40 hours of Rust are whining that they allow ladders and twig foundations.
Having over 1,000 hours played I can say that any update made by the dev team affects the community as a whole and does not put anyone at a significant advantage or disadvantage. There is no buying skill, and there is no buying intelligence in terms of how to build your base, how to survive, how to conduct affairs between people on your server, and nobody is telling you how to play. You make your story, your world, and your base - and you defend it until your last breath.
Regardless if you like the normal, vanilla game, there is likely going to be a server to accomodate how you play - whether that may be with a higher rate of gathering, or mods to turn back updates that the devs made that you do not favor. One of the key factors in why Rust is so successful is its modability and the dynamic range of servers that the community hosts.
And one last note about the Dev team and why I believe this alpha game is the best one out there:
I played a few of the other Alpha games out there. The ones that I haven't played that are getting credit, I have watched and observed. To date I have not found a development team (Facepunch) that can promise their alpha game will be constantly improved. They will openly admit their mistakes when they make them, even if it is months later (such as what happened with the XP update) and correct it.
As a long-time player of Garry's Mod, having many deeply enjoyable experiences in my middle and highschool years with friends, I am capable and aware of how dedicated Facepunch, and especially Garry Newman, is to making a quality game. I played DayZ for a long time and could not be more disappointed by the failure of their development team in the long run to provide quality content and worthwhile efforts to expanding and improving their game.
Although the point of the alpha stage of videogame development is to add content and not neccessarily provide bug-free content nor fix bugs, an Early Access game was meant to be playable and enjoyable although not fully complete. Few alpha developers take your money, get bloated with cash, and actually care to sell more copies after their first few million. For instance, DayZ was supposed to have base building functionally implemented by the fourth quarter of 2015. It is now the end of the second quarter of 2017, and not an ounce of effort seems to have been put into these ambitious promises.
Rust, on the other hand, has made its intentions clear and left room for adding and removing ambitious goals by never promising anything - rather, they will make efforts to improve the game and add to it to create more working content until they feel content enough to focus solely on debugging and optimizing.
You get what you pay for, and the Garry Newman philosophy is and always has been cheap, good games. $20 got me over two years of a great time and a feeling of accomplishment on many weekends spent alone.
Kudos to Facepunch +1 11/10 Rust is my favorite PC game in over 18 years of gaming.

A wasteland game that is heavily influenced by the movie of the year (2015), Mad Max: Fury Road. Though the main story doesnt exceed even the least of my expectations before the game's release but it delivers a vast open world with so many unique places to discover and pillage. Which happens to be the best part of the game.
The main attraction of this game is the vehicular combat and the car customizing functionality. Learn to drive like a mad man to best your opponents in the desert wasteland and you will be visually rewarded with beautiful explosions and chaos. The combat style flows closely with the Batman: Arkham games ( made by the same developers ) but IMO: they made it much better and more violent like it should be. Experiment with all kinds of weapons you can find during a battle because they will never fail to amuse you. ( My favorite was the Thunderstick ). Setting aside the main quests, this game heavily relies on exploration and side quests. It may seem that the developers spent more time in designing the entire world than focusing on its story that reminds me of some other post-apocalyptic themed games I played before ( Fallout ).
Bottom line is, this was an amazing hotseat video game that I could just turn my mind off to and relax.
This game is AWESOME, I love it, and I strongly recommend that you buy and play it!

Undertale is a fun and unique RPG game that allows the player to do something that most games do not.
Have you ever wondered, why in many RPG games, you have to kill everything, and you have to seek getting as much EXP as possible? Why do you have to kill everything? What if you could befriend them, and learn their story, instead?
In Undertale, you play as a human who has fallen into Mt. Ebott, somehow surviving their fall by falling into a bed of golden flowers. During this time, tensions are strong between humans and monsters, as the humans and monsters are involved in a war. The humans had sealed the monsters into the underground, trapping them with a barrier.
As you explore the Underground, and as you progress in the game, you will meet new friends, new enemies. you will meet many different kinds of monsters. Some hostile at first, and some friendly, each monster in Undertale seems to have a different and unique personality.
You can be either a pacifist or genocidal, but I prefer only taking the pacifist route, as the pacifist route of the game is heartwarming and uplifting, and it allows me to hear more about the Monsters and their perspectives and their story in Undertale, and also, well... if you're like me, you'll get quite attached to these charming characters. (I have played the Pacifist route four times, and the game is still super fun and charming!)
In Undertale, as you explore, you will also see all sorts of cool environments, and hear the game's acclaimed great soundtrack.
Every character in Undertale has their strengths and weaknesses, and their flaws and their good traits, too. With their unique and varied personalities, many of Undertale's characters have become relatable for quite a few fans of the game, and I admire games that put so much care and attention into its characters and its writing.
Although the game can be creepy and foreboding at times, the game also has many moments of humor, fun, and silliness!
Undertale, in its pacifist run, has been one of the funniest, most uplifting, emotional, and heartwarming games that I have ever played. I have no complaints about the game, and I would encourage anyone to play! Don't mind the fan-base, and give Undertale a try. In my eyes, it is essential that you go into this game blind, and not let yourself uncover spoilers, as the game has its share of surprises and events! ^.^

If you've played and enjoyed the Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor, picking up Mad Max is pretty much a no brainer. It features the same close combat and upgrade system as the two other games.
The world and the visuals are extremely well crafted and provide the perfect Mad Max atmosphere. The game is mechanically very sound, which is no surprise considering the games it borrows elements from.
For actual criticism: the game gets very repetitive. If you're a completionist, you're going to spend dozens of hours looking for that last piece of scrap in a camp that bears an eerie similarity to another camp you visited ten minutes ago and beating basically the same 4-5 varieties of goons all over the place. There is SO MUCH to do in the game that I could easily see someone spending 100+ hours to loot every camp, finish all the races and so forth. Odds are though, unless you have superhuman persistence, you're gonna get burned out after completing half of the looting objectives and will just finish the story to be done with the game.
The close combat is not quite as satisfying or tight as in Arkham or Mordor, as the special moves are more generic and limited to things that counter a certain enemy type, such as Melee Reversal or Shield Shatter. If nothing else, it does make the game a touch more gritty and realistic. The countering mechanic is not quite as responsive and it is harder to read enemies. Getting hit doesn't reset your combo counter in Mad Max, so missing a counter is not a huge deal, but it takes away that certain satisfaction of getting a 'perfect combo'.
The story is great; however, it is sprinkled throughout the game rather unevenly. Of my 50+ hours of playtime, I'd estimate roughly 5 hours is actually advancing the story. It is mostly focused in the beginning and the end of the game, with only a few short missions placed here and there to keep you in the story and also gate your progress by tying up access to new zones and upgrades to beating the story mission. During the majority of the game the presence of the main villain is merely implied by the presence of his lackeys, and it was not until the last hour or so of the story that I felt reconnected to the events at the very beginning.
In short:
+It's as close to Mad Max as a video game can get
+Good Batman-style combat system
+Vehicle combat provides a nice change of pace
+Lots to do
+Excellent visuals that lend to a great atmosphere
-Optional objectives are repetitive
-Combat is not as responsive as in games it borrows from
-Story gets a bit thin during the middle part of the game

******** TL:DR
Just Cause + batman + lord of the rings

- wonderful wastelands
- good car combats
- good fight mechanics, satisfying hits
CONS:

- past a good start, easy to get bored.

Euro Truck Simulator 2... Great, another simulator game. This was probably made in a few weeks and is probably terrible.
Well, surprisingly this isn't the case. Euro Truck Simulator 2 is actually quite fun, what makes it fun is that there's a levelling system, so each time you complete a truck run which normally lasts on average 25-40 minutes, (depending what job you take) you gain XP and money for your own truck company. Aside from levelling up, you can accumulate money to purchase new trucks, and upgrades for them. Making your own business / trucking company more reliable and efficient.
That's pretty much all there is to it for the most part. The downsides to this game is that it can be dreadfully boring as there is no music playing whilst you're driving. You can put in .mp3 files into a folder in your documents (much like the GTA games did) and you can play your music whilst driving.
You can also use custom radio station links (e.g real ones) as well which is cool.
Putting your own music into your documents folder is pointless though as there is no special EQ or anything to make it sound as if its coming out of the speakers in your truck etc.
This game also allows a steering wheel, and foot pedals of course as it's a simulator.
ETS 2 is quite fun despite its simple concept of getting from point A to point B. I recommend getting this in a sale for £10, or less.

Undertale is a fun and unique RPG game that allows the player to do something that most games do not.
Have you ever wondered, why in many RPG games, you have to kill everything, and you have to seek getting as much EXP as possible? Why do you have to kill everything? What if you could befriend them, and learn their story, instead?
In Undertale, you play as a human who has fallen into Mt. Ebott, somehow surviving their fall by falling into a bed of golden flowers. During this time, tensions are strong between humans and monsters, as the humans and monsters are involved in a war. The humans had sealed the monsters into the underground, trapping them with a barrier.
As you explore the Underground, and as you progress in the game, you will meet new friends, new enemies. you will meet many different kinds of monsters. Some hostile at first, and some friendly, each monster in Undertale seems to have a different and unique personality.
You can be either a pacifist or genocidal, but I prefer only taking the pacifist route, as the pacifist route of the game is heartwarming and uplifting, and it allows me to hear more about the Monsters and their perspectives and their story in Undertale, and also, well... if you're like me, you'll get quite attached to these charming characters. (I have played the Pacifist route four times, and the game is still super fun and charming!)
In Undertale, as you explore, you will also see all sorts of cool environments, and hear the game's acclaimed great soundtrack.
Every character in Undertale has their strengths and weaknesses, and their flaws and their good traits, too. With their unique and varied personalities, many of Undertale's characters have become relatable for quite a few fans of the game, and I admire games that put so much care and attention into its characters and its writing.
Although the game can be creepy and foreboding at times, the game also has many moments of humor, fun, and silliness!
Undertale, in its pacifist run, has been one of the funniest, most uplifting, emotional, and heartwarming games that I have ever played. I have no complaints about the game, and I would encourage anyone to play! Don't mind the fan-base, and give Undertale a try. In my eyes, it is essential that you go into this game blind, and not let yourself uncover spoilers, as the game has its share of surprises and events! ^.^

Updated review after 52 hours in and 4 updates.
TL;DR: this game should be marked as an EARLY ACCESS GAME
While I can understand the dev's motivation to urge users to report bugs, I cannot fathom how they can release this game as a "finished product" but treat their customers as early access testers.
Bugs I've encountered:
- Animals get stuck and stand still. They cant run away. You can pet them.
- Sometimes you get stuck in a bush and then die of falling damage.
- Trashiest, clunkiest and buggiest UI ever. Even after the patch you have to (at least) click twice on stuff and pray for it to work.
- Apparently not only the wildlife, but also the UI buttons require a hunter's precision. If you don't click on a specific area within the option you want to navigate through, the game won't recognize your click (UI is absolutely buggy and has "hidden hitboxes").
- Map doesn't center around you when you open it. First few moments upon openning the map have to be spent on zooming in/out and finding where you are.
- There seems to be no consistency regarding the "loudness of the sounds" you create. Crawling through bush X in this area is silent. Crawling through bush the same bush in another area is suddenly loud. Also wind and rain seem to not have an effect on your (displayed) sound-level.
- After playing some time with your Phone (ingame item that helps you tracking) out, your fps start to drop from 50+ to 13. Only happens when the phone is out. Then the next bug kicks in...
- Suddenly all tracks vanish and don't ever appear again. Renders tracking impossible. You have to restart the game. Going into the menu and back ingame is not possible, since there is no button to return to the menu.
- The scope on the rifle bugs out as soon as you start using a bow. Use a bow and your rilfe's scope will be rendered useless (don't use a bow).
- Not receiving skill points all though I get notified I got one (?)
- Not receiving perk points all though I get notified I got one (?)
+ Many more bugs OTHERS discovered
Technically not a bug, but simply bad design:) You can't walk through some bushes (which is fine in itself), but in some areas they are placed en masse which turns said area into a maze. You have to navigate your way through hip-tall bushes that in RL you wouldn't even need to bend but here they are WALLS. Try to jump over them and you die of falling damage (that is a bug though).

At first glance, Spec Ops: The Line appears to be an incredibly generic game that we have all seen before. The name itself makes it sound like it is part of a series of cheap knock-off games you could find for $10. The boxart brings out the cliche black and white soldier with a automatic assault rifle (or brown and white in this case). But do not let all of that fool you though, because this is a really good game!
Gameplay: Spec Ops: The Line is a modern military cover-based third-person shooter. Though the combat is nothing revolutionary, as some might argue it's generic gameplay that we've all seen before, the game mechanics are very solid. All of the guns have kickback according to the size and weight of the gun you are using. The cover system is also very solid, though sometimes it can be a little clunky. Every shot has weight and you can feel on both yourself and on your enemy. The team commands are few in number, and sometimes you find yourself rarely using it. Since you are part of an elite delta squad, it would be nice to see really strong tactical orders that you can give to your squadmates, making the game more strategic and less run-n-gun. Not the most amazing combat for a third-person shooter, but does well for what it does. 7/10
Setting: The game takes place in Dubai, a Middle-Eastern city that is in ruins from the ravaging sandstorms that dramatically affected everyone who lived in the city. The sandstorms that occur during the game adds tension, as it blinds you, your squadmates, and your enemies while you are in the middle of a gunfight. The themes and images that you see in the city are horrifying, un-just, and will give you a sense of anger, grief, and suffering. The artwork for the game is truly magnificant, which is saying something for a modern military game. The ruined city truly does give you a sense of solitude, poverity, and fear, as the "antagonist" faction (depends on the player's perception), the Damned 33rd, "control a dictactorship". A city consumed by both nature's sandstorms and humanity's war gives a unique and interesting setting for the game. 9/10
Story: What happens when a violent video game makes you stop and question the actions that you are commiting? This is a mature story for a mature player. The story for this game is gripping, thrilling, horrific, haunting, surreal, and in an odd way, beautiful. You are Captain Walker, and you are sent to Dubai with your squadmates Lugo and Adams to confirm the statuses of Konrad and any survivors, then radio for extraction. What starts off as a simple rescue recon turns into a very wild ride fast. You find yourself fighting and killing fellow American Soldiers and you find out that the Damned 33rd went rogue. Further along the story, the story ACTUALLY gives you choices that you can make and those choices you make slightly affects what happens in the story (I haven't seen a single modern military game do this). The choices will question YOU as a person, as the choices are not black & white. You WILL experience what war truly is like. And unlike other games where you are always portrayed as the hero, you WILL ask yourself....are you truly a hero? How many fellow American soldiers will you kill to satisfy your goal? Will your vengeance blind you from the truth, and drive you to insanity? THIS is the reason why you should play Spec Ops: The Line, as it will incorporate very light psychological elements with the true horrors of war into the game. 9.5/10
As a person who never cared for modern military shooter games, I have to admit, I gave this game really low expectations. But once I started playing, I found myself continuously playing the game, curious to see what will happen next. This game truly impressed me, and I will give credit where credit is due.

I rarely do reviews, but I figured this game with it's current mitigated score could use a straight to the point review, I hope this helps you make a decision.
First off a little about me, I'm no real life hunter and this is my first hunting game. I had been interested by the different games that existed before this one, but the general consensus seemed to be that they were all rip-offs, trying to squeeze the players out of their RL money with endless micro transactions and DLC's, etc.
This game is gorgeous, they really nailed the outdoors feeling really well. I don't think I can name a game that has more beautiful trees/forests, it looks fantastic and the performance is also very good. I'm running it at high details (not ultra) and it's absolutely amazing and runs smooth on my mid-level gaming laptop (GTX970M, 16 gigs ram, i7 cpu).
There are bugs though... LOTS of bugs, but so far, none are game-breaking. Animals sometimes get stuck in trees and rocks... There are bunnies or whatever that do a stupid amount of noise that doesn't sound natural. You can't walk up a 30% incline (approx). Your walking and run speed is affected by your FPS (this is most noticeable in multiplayer, reducing image quality will make you run faster). I could go on, the game kind of feels like it should be a beta or early release, they definitely still had a lot of ironing out to do before calling it gold IMHO, but despite all this, it's still an amazing game.
So far, I'm getting my money's worth, there is no doubt, it's a unique experience, I really enjoy it.

Then I shot her and killed her
then I sold her fur in order to buy more ammo
then I used that ammo to finish of her baby.
Jokes aside, this game, while I've only played it for about two hours at this point and I have yet to try out multiplayer, feels great for what it promises to deliver.
With (extremely) beutiful scenery and graphics this game immerses you heavily into the mindset of a hunter, and while some of the hunting aspects are a bit clunky, like a deer being able to hear you crawling in the middle of a thunderstorm 60 meters away, the problems i've experienced are relatively minor and should be fixed very soon.
+No microtransactions, they have been replaced by gaining money from selling your kills; A quick and clean kill on a buck might yield you 1500 funbucks, and a new gun will cost you around 20-30k. The first gun is not bad, however, and its ammunition is free to refill.
+GRAPHICS
+Tracking, while simple, is a nice mechanic that I believe is unique for this game series.
+The new tracking system includes "need spots" where you can stalk out your prey, for example: One need spot might be a drinking area for a herd of deer, they'll come back here during the time that is stated, and you can simply wait for them to fall into your trap.
+A new trophy screen, where it will show you where your bullet hit aswell as a picture detailing the trajectory of it, and how much damage/how lethal it was on a % base, allowing you to learn where to aim next time. I, however, only aim for the neck, because there's nothing quite like paralyzing an animal and then simply walking up to it and finishing it off (thats ♥♥♥♥ed up).
+THE GRASS PARTS IF AN ANIMAL (OR YOU) WALK THROUGH IT
+The map is HUGE.
+The sounds are very nice, and immerses you into the feeling of being in a real forest...except for one of them...
-Theres this one sound that sounds exactly like something rubbing up against your jacket. This one sound has made me almost♥♥♥♥♥♥myself atleast 3 times in 2 hours played. I've narrowed it down and I believe it's the sound the rabbits make when they run through the underbrush.
-The weather system is out of whack. One minute you've got perfect sunny weather, the next you've got a thunderstorm on your hands which deafens and blindens you (and only you, by the looks of things).
-A glitch I've encountered after every 1 shot kill, the HUD of the scope will dissapear, leaving you staring through the plastic edges of a scope as if somebody removed the magnifying glass.
-The menu system is crap and needs a total rehaul. The buttons dont respond half the time and esc doesn't actually back you out of the current menu, leaving you struggling to get back in the game just in time to see a bear charging you because you dared exist in a 2km vicinity of her.
+-Relatively few animals, however this can be explained by the fact that they're trying to bring us a realistic biome, where every animal on earth doesn't actually live in the same park.
I'll try to remember to update this review after I've tried the multiplayer or after the next patch, whichever comes first.
However, as it is now, I would recommend this game for anybody who's not gonna get bored of walking through beutiful scenery where you get maybe 1 minute of action for every 10 minute walked.
EDIT:
Having put a few more hours into this game, it has become clear to me that it is an unfinished mess. While the scenery and all the positives I listed above still apply, the negatives turn this otherwise enjoyable game into a chore itself.
Not only do your graphical settings reset if you do ANYTHING other than walking (fire your gun? Your POV is going back to the default 60) but the menu you have to work through in order to change it is, as mentioned above, a pain.
I've also noticed a painful unfairness in how terrain affects you. The animal you are stalking can and WILL see or hear you through that mountain inbetween you, and you'll never see it again.
While the removal of microtransactions is a good thing, the fact that I have to level up my rifle skills in order to get anything other than the default rifle, sort of makes the same result.
They replaced the buying of guns with hours upon hours of grinding.
As of now, I cannot recommend this game in its current state. Wait a few months for patches.

Then I shot her and killed her
then I sold her fur in order to buy more ammo
then I used that ammo to finish of her baby.
Jokes aside, this game, while I've only played it for about two hours at this point and I have yet to try out multiplayer, feels great for what it promises to deliver.
With (extremely) beutiful scenery and graphics this game immerses you heavily into the mindset of a hunter, and while some of the hunting aspects are a bit clunky, like a deer being able to hear you crawling in the middle of a thunderstorm 60 meters away, the problems i've experienced are relatively minor and should be fixed very soon.
+No microtransactions, they have been replaced by gaining money from selling your kills; A quick and clean kill on a buck might yield you 1500 funbucks, and a new gun will cost you around 20-30k. The first gun is not bad, however, and its ammunition is free to refill.
+GRAPHICS
+Tracking, while simple, is a nice mechanic that I believe is unique for this game series.
+The new tracking system includes "need spots" where you can stalk out your prey, for example: One need spot might be a drinking area for a herd of deer, they'll come back here during the time that is stated, and you can simply wait for them to fall into your trap.
+A new trophy screen, where it will show you where your bullet hit aswell as a picture detailing the trajectory of it, and how much damage/how lethal it was on a % base, allowing you to learn where to aim next time. I, however, only aim for the neck, because there's nothing quite like paralyzing an animal and then simply walking up to it and finishing it off (thats ♥♥♥♥ed up).
+THE GRASS PARTS IF AN ANIMAL (OR YOU) WALK THROUGH IT
+The map is HUGE.
+The sounds are very nice, and immerses you into the feeling of being in a real forest...except for one of them...
-Theres this one sound that sounds exactly like something rubbing up against your jacket. This one sound has made me almost♥♥♥♥♥♥myself atleast 3 times in 2 hours played. I've narrowed it down and I believe it's the sound the rabbits make when they run through the underbrush.
-The weather system is out of whack. One minute you've got perfect sunny weather, the next you've got a thunderstorm on your hands which deafens and blindens you (and only you, by the looks of things).
-A glitch I've encountered after every 1 shot kill, the HUD of the scope will dissapear, leaving you staring through the plastic edges of a scope as if somebody removed the magnifying glass.
-The menu system is crap and needs a total rehaul. The buttons dont respond half the time and esc doesn't actually back you out of the current menu, leaving you struggling to get back in the game just in time to see a bear charging you because you dared exist in a 2km vicinity of her.
+-Relatively few animals, however this can be explained by the fact that they're trying to bring us a realistic biome, where every animal on earth doesn't actually live in the same park.
I'll try to remember to update this review after I've tried the multiplayer or after the next patch, whichever comes first.
However, as it is now, I would recommend this game for anybody who's not gonna get bored of walking through beutiful scenery where you get maybe 1 minute of action for every 10 minute walked.
EDIT:
Having put a few more hours into this game, it has become clear to me that it is an unfinished mess. While the scenery and all the positives I listed above still apply, the negatives turn this otherwise enjoyable game into a chore itself.
Not only do your graphical settings reset if you do ANYTHING other than walking (fire your gun? Your POV is going back to the default 60) but the menu you have to work through in order to change it is, as mentioned above, a pain.
I've also noticed a painful unfairness in how terrain affects you. The animal you are stalking can and WILL see or hear you through that mountain inbetween you, and you'll never see it again.
While the removal of microtransactions is a good thing, the fact that I have to level up my rifle skills in order to get anything other than the default rifle, sort of makes the same result.
They replaced the buying of guns with hours upon hours of grinding.
As of now, I cannot recommend this game in its current state. Wait a few months for patches.

TL;DR to start with - Lightning can be caught in a bottle twice. Chloe's new voice actor does a great job. If you are a Life is Strange fan, buy this goddamn game.
(Even if you aren't, this will probably make you a believer.)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
If still you're reading this, you probably already know what the game is about, so the next thing to address is: is it worth your money?
YES. /review
But in all honestly, the best praise I can lay on this game is just how I felt after firing up the game for the first time, and how I felt coming out at the end of chapter 1; invested more than I ever thought I would be.
The only expectations I had for Before the Storm was that I hoped it would be an extra part of the Life is Strange story that was worthy of telling. It didn't have to exceed the first game at all; if it was just more of a window in Chloe's life pre-Max - fleshing out her character more - I would have been happy with what I'd paid for.
I certainly didn't expect the impeccable level of polish applied to all aspects of this game. The characters are great, the "backchat" mechanic is fun, the writing is superb, and above all, it feels like coming back to Arcadia Bay.
As I hinted above, for anyone worried about the new voice for Chloe - Ashly Burch (the owner of Chloe's original voice) consulted and provided guidance for her replacement, Rhianna DeVries, and the result is another stellar performance. Ain't nothing to worry about here, she's in good hands :)
Deck Nine have absolutely smashed this out of the park. Not only is Before the Storm a brilliant game, it's a brilliant Life is Strange game, and it effortlessly meets the expectations set by its predecessor - even surpassing them, in my opinion, given just how STRONG the opening chapter is.
Honestly, I'm absolutely comfortable saying that I enjoyed chapter 1 of this more than the first chapter of the orginal game. If I had a friend ask which game to start with if they wanted to get in, I would probably tell them to check out Before the Storm first, as it definitely has a stronger hook, and I feel it can stand on its own two feet.
The only down side I can think of is that this may be the last time we see the characters in a game :( Savour it, people, you'll miss 'em when they're gone!
There's still two chapters to come, but if the first chapter is anything to go by, I think the faith I have in the things yet to come is well placed.

When I first saw this game, I got a little excited. I'm not a huge one for driving games, but a game where you can drive around a wasteland, scavenge scrap, and build up your own Magnum Opus? It sounded right up my alley.
I was right.
I began playing and I loved it. The controls were a little dicky, but I'd get used to them.
The more I played, the more I realised the physics was crap. Your car is a buoy. It's impossible to flip. Spinning around in the air and crashing spectacularly is half the fun of car games. Then they added in 'driving assist' toggle, where your car stopped being so buoyant. They still handle like boats. They honestly handle like they turn from the rear wheel. I drive a RWD car and I can say, without a doubt, no car handles like that, ever. That is how a forklift handles. The Magnum Opus is the world's most overpowered forklift.
Anyway, enough on that. Bascially, I never got used to the steering and physics. They were terrible, plain and simple. Warner Brothers certainly didn't go all out in that department.
Let's talk weapons. Harpoon, Thunderpoon (rockets), and flamethrowers. Badass. Having the game forcibly auto-aim the harpoon and rockets? Not so badass. More times than I can count, I've wanted to launch a poon right into the middle of a crowd, or I've wanted to hit the back enemy but the auto-aim system wouldn't let me fire at anything that wasn't the front enemy (even if I was aiming nowhere near him). The fact that aiming slows time way the hell down is its sole upside, since you can't just point and shoot. You have to point... adjust... adjust... finally, the target I want to hit is highlighted instead of that shmuck way over there.
A few times, I had to physically stop the car, run over to the enemies to make them charge at me, run back to the car, and /then/ attack them just so I could hit something that wasn't already a corpse.
Hand-to-hand combat was pretty bad at times, too. They knew it wasn't that interesting, so instead of adding more moves, they just spawned more enemies. Nothing quite like being in a melee where your primary focus is spamming right-click to block the near-constant stream of enemy punches and never throw one of your own.
Also, the Top Dog bosses were horribly executed. The first one I fought was a fun challenge! The others were not. They were literally all identical, except for that one who was vulnerable to bullets and I promptly shot 6 times and walked away. Every boss in the game, even Lord Scrotus himself, is a clone of the other bosses, and if I hadn't been interrupted by a cutscene, I would've killed Scrotus easily in Gastown. It's the mark of a bad game when the final boss poses no challenge, but you can't kill him yet so you have a cutscene come to his rescue instead.
I almost never review games I own, but the final straw for this one was the ending. I've just spent two days laboriously going around Pink Eye's territory and getting Scrotus' control level to 0 so I could buy the ultimate V8. Huge satisfaction when I got it. Like, wow. So, time to take on the big man, Scrotus the Immortal. The final rally fight was fun, except for occasionally hitting a rock and/or having to stop and let Chumbucket repair the Opus. Then I get to the end.
The final straw is that this game has the most bullcrap ending I've seen in a long goddamn time.
I've spent a month playing this game on and off. I've spent a month upgrading my Magnum Opus from a pile of nuts, bolts, and scrap on a Shovelface body with a little V6 engine into the most badass vehicle in the whole wasteland. I have 15 ultimate-sized Thunderpoon rockets. I have a tier 6 harpoon that can tear down anything it hooks into. I have side-burners that could char grill an adult bull in 10 seconds. I have a magnificent shotgun that will obliterate anything within 10 feet in front of it. And when Scrotus' truck is teetering over the edge of a cliff, what does the game suggest I do?
Trick question, the game doesn't 'suggest' anything, you simply have to drive your car off a cliff.
What. The ♥♥♥♥.
I can blast him off the edge of the cliff.
If I want to wait a moment, I can blast him directly when he climbs out of the truck.
I can harpoon him and take him for a ride around the wasteland via ground.
I can drive past and make some barbeque Scrotus.
Hell, I could even just get out and beat him to death.
But no. The 'only way to kill him' is to drive your car off a cliff. Totally.
I sat there for 5 minutes and listened to the audio loop because the only button that did anything was 'drive forward' and I refused. Eventually, I decided, screw it, let's be done with this progressively worse game.
Oh, and then? And then once your car is gone? SCROTUS DRIVES ON OUT IN THE INTERCEPTOR. WHICH YOU THEN BLOW UP. WITH CONVENIENTLY PLACED THUNDERPOONS.
It's like Warner Brothers created this whole game as a nice big dosage of lubricant so they could ♥♥♥♥ you over with the ending so much easier.
I'm mad. I'm honestly mad. Once I hit 'post' on this review, I probably won't play this game again. I really wish I'd never bought it. Better to imagine how good it /could/ be than to play and find out how bad it /is/.
Oh, and as a side-note, Max had a wife and ~3-year-old son, not a wife and teenage daughter. Way to change the story for sex appeal, Warner Brothers. Nothing quite like advertising a backstory with a photo of a 14-year-old in a bikini. Jesus Christ.
In short, no, I really don't recommend this game if you're a fan of anything Mad Max, if you're a fan of car games, if you're a fan of wasteland survival games, or if you have more than a third of a brain.

What a ride! I've had the pleasure of playing Prison Architect since around Alpha 12, and with every update I've had more fun. Hats off to Introversion!
In one of the update videos Chris Delay mentions a prison he came across in the workshop. It had a solitary confinement cell with a second door to freedom and an armed guard on patrol outside of that door. The obvious goal was to kill off undesirable prisoners. Another time he showed a prison with 2x1 cells and everyone was on 24/7 lockdown. They were great reminders that there are so many approaches to playing this game; it is a game of constant trial and error.
When things go wrong in your prison--I mean REALLY wrong--it can almost be a bit traumatizing. It has probably been a solid year since I've had a prisoner murder my warden, and I'm damn proud of that. In the early days it was almost riskier to be a warden in my prisons than a snitch.
ORIGINAL REVIEW (1 August, 2014):
Although Prison Architect is still in Alpha, it is beginning to feel very much like a complete game (which is exciting, because there are still more features to come). The game allows customization at every corner, and there are a variety of strategies players are able to use to confront a problem. Whether its cutting off the pipeline of contraband, suppressing a riot, or just trying to make money, Prison Architect offers a wide array of tools for players to inventively trouble-shoot their problems. The updated circuitry mechanism allows for much greater and finer tweaking of the workings of your prison. I think it is very likely this game will exceed your expectations.

I don't really like to buy early access games, even when they look like they have the type of gaming experiences I offer, but I picked up Prison Architect during a sale after considering the risk a number of times and don't regret it one bit.
Out of the Alpha/Beta/Early Access titles I have bought, this one offers the most consistent update frequency, bringing a new alpha build once a month on average. Each Alpha build offers something new, whether its a large number of bug fixes, or new room and object options that will change the way you can run your prison.
The current game offers quite a bit of depth and option when choosing how to play. You can be successful running a strict regime that punishes and supresses your prisoners, or you can go easy on your prisoners and try to reform them, or anywhere in between, and if you plan well it will still work out. Some imaginative players have even found ways to play the game in ways the developers have completely overlooked, such as running a forestry instead of a prison. The game provides a fun sandbox, that has come a long way since the buggy, and incompetant-ai of its early builds. Your staff seem to get a bit better with each patch, but AI is still something the devs are focused on improving further (at least based on their alpha videos.)
If you enjoy management, builder, sim stuff, you'll probably enjoy this title. To me, it seems like one of the easier ones to make a judgement call with. If it looks like something you'll enjoy, then you probably will. But if you don't like the core gameplay aspects the game offers, I doubt this title will change your mind.

First off, to explain why I recommend this game:
If you have been waiting for a hunting game to relive the old times like back in Deer Hunter 2005, this may just be it. However, if you are invested in theHunter Classic and have played that, you may want to stick with that for a while.
As many have said, this game feels like a Beta title. The bugs are there, and while I haven't had anything game-breaking, they are still there.
First, this game is beautiful. Just walking around, taking in the sights is a great experience that I find extremely relaxing.
But, I have a few small gripes with the game in my playtime so far. For one, I feel like the animal AI is strange. The deer move at such a rapid pace, and trot around way more often than I believe is realistic. Even in the Hunter classic the deer were more docile and seemed to behave more realistic than this. I feel like tracking a deer is extremely difficult if not impossible. Granted, it should not be easy, but I feel like they just move too fast for you to effectively keep up.
The noise mechanic is a nice feature of this game. However, I feel that the player character moves way too fast and makes too much noise. Sure, you must be careful and walk slowly, but I feel that crouch-walking the entire time is just not realistic/feasible. In real life, I can walk more carefully and tread lightly when needed. I know there are perks that can reduce walking noise, but it makes it hard to even kill anything and get to level up to get those skills. And then, since you have to crouch walk, you either cannot see the animals you are searching for, or you cannot keep up with a trail as the deer are moving away.
I'm not saying we need slow moving, deaf zombie deer, but I think it still needs a little work.
Now, I still recommend this game. I'm not a Hunter Classic player myself, but seeing how the devs have stuck with that game for so long gives me hope that they plan for this one to be around for a while too. I know tHuner Classic's subscription model might have been why they stuck with it for so long, so we will have to see. I do still have hope that they will fix this game and make it much better. The Hunter Classic 7 years ago would be laughable compared to what it is today. Let's hope they apply that work ethic to this title as well.

TL;DR to start with - Lightning can be caught in a bottle twice. Chloe's new voice actor does a great job. If you are a Life is Strange fan, buy this goddamn game.
(Even if you aren't, this will probably make you a believer.)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
If still you're reading this, you probably already know what the game is about, so the next thing to address is: is it worth your money?
YES. /review
But in all honestly, the best praise I can lay on this game is just how I felt after firing up the game for the first time, and how I felt coming out at the end of chapter 1; invested more than I ever thought I would be.
The only expectations I had for Before the Storm was that I hoped it would be an extra part of the Life is Strange story that was worthy of telling. It didn't have to exceed the first game at all; if it was just more of a window in Chloe's life pre-Max - fleshing out her character more - I would have been happy with what I'd paid for.
I certainly didn't expect the impeccable level of polish applied to all aspects of this game. The characters are great, the "backchat" mechanic is fun, the writing is superb, and above all, it feels like coming back to Arcadia Bay.
As I hinted above, for anyone worried about the new voice for Chloe - Ashly Burch (the owner of Chloe's original voice) consulted and provided guidance for her replacement, Rhianna DeVries, and the result is another stellar performance. Ain't nothing to worry about here, she's in good hands :)
Deck Nine have absolutely smashed this out of the park. Not only is Before the Storm a brilliant game, it's a brilliant Life is Strange game, and it effortlessly meets the expectations set by its predecessor - even surpassing them, in my opinion, given just how STRONG the opening chapter is.
Honestly, I'm absolutely comfortable saying that I enjoyed chapter 1 of this more than the first chapter of the orginal game. If I had a friend ask which game to start with if they wanted to get in, I would probably tell them to check out Before the Storm first, as it definitely has a stronger hook, and I feel it can stand on its own two feet.
The only down side I can think of is that this may be the last time we see the characters in a game :( Savour it, people, you'll miss 'em when they're gone!
There's still two chapters to come, but if the first chapter is anything to go by, I think the faith I have in the things yet to come is well placed.

Ok this is my first ever review on steam.
I see a lot of reviews saying “I really wanted to like this game” or “I have played the hunter classic for x amount of time”
This is a good game, is it great I don’t think so can it be great absolutely.
First things first. This game is nothing like the hunter classic. If you haven’t played the classic I would definitely recommend it download it and get the most basic bundle and some EM (in game currency) and get the .300 rifle you will be able to hunt all species and have a great time.
This game is much more arcade focused; there are a lot more animals that are easier to spot and make a lot more noise.
My biggest issue with this game is the “grind factor”  you start life with .243 great calibre for small game and small bodied deer (roe and fallow) but I would never expect to target bear, red deer with such a small bullet, “how do I get access to a more suitable fire arm” I hear you ask. Well play ALOT I have put 17 hrs in and am level 12 and I still can only access the 223 (which is smaller) I did purchase the premium .270 so that’s a help (although I thought it was a gift??)
The whole store system needs an overhaul which I think EW would admit they got wrong.
I have no idea what computer I am running (a friend built it for me but I am running everything on ultra and its looks and runs fantastic, the lighting fog and over all look of the environment (which is huge) is spot on. I haven’t encountered any major bugs but I am sure they exist hopefully not for long.
My biggest advice to someone thinking of getting Call of the wild don’t come into expecting the hunter classic (if you have played the hunter: classic), it’s not the same, this game is still a lot of fun, just be prepared to play ALOT. my tip if you want to level up fast and get some better gear just shoot every animal you see, don’t bother with heart/lung shot. Game is all about brain/neck shots. if you shoot an animal and it runs off check the blood sign anything less than vital hit just walk away, time is better spent looking for another animal and there is no real loss .243 ammo is free so stock up on as much as you want.

Alright the game has been out for just under a week and i already have >20 hours time played. Reading through some of the other reviews and discussions i think some people are definitely blowing the issues out of proportion.  I can recall a number of AAA titles with a $60 price tag in the last year that have had far far far worse bugs (i.e. AAA titles with actual game breaking bugs: falling through maps, blue screen of death, etc.) and i have not experienced anything even remotely close to that magnitude with theHunter.
